The state offers a Minimum Support Price (MSP) of ₹4,200/quintal, but only farmers receiving AI alerts qualify for a 5 % input subsidy. Monsoon variability (c12_geo_cbse_02_003) creates three agro‑climatic zones: high rainfall (40 % area), moderate (35 %), low (25 %). The AI model was trained primarily on images from high‑rainfall zones, leading to a 10 % lower detection accuracy in low‑rainfall zones.

(A) Calculate the expected average yield (quintal/ha) after AI‑based early detection, assuming the 15 % loss reduction applies uniformly across all farmers who receive alerts.

A 2023 study maps residential patterns in Bengaluru, showing that 68 % of Dalit households reside in the city’s peripheral wards, while upper‑caste groups occupy 82 % of the central business district’s housing. Activists invoke Ambedkar’s 1936 lecture to argue that the *setting* of entrenched caste‑based spatial segregation persists, and the lecture’s *atmosphere* of moral urgency should drive policy interventions like inclusive zoning. Critics contend that the study conflates economic class with caste, and that the lecture’s tone is overly academic for grassroots mobilisation. You must assess whether the lecture’s setting and atmosphere remain analytically useful for interpreting contemporary urban segregation.

(B) Explain how the lecture’s *atmosphere* of “reasoned urgency” can be leveraged to motivate grassroots action against urban caste segregation.
Determine the net annual profit per unit for District Y after applying the 10 % capital subsidy (depreciated over 5 years, zero salvage).

A consortium of private hospitals and tech start‑ups plans to establish a “Digital Health Service Hub” in Gurugram’s Cyber City zone. The hub will offer three tiers of services: (i) professional – tele‑medicine consultations by specialist doctors (requiring MD/DM degrees), (ii) business – health‑insurance claim processing platforms, AI‑based diagnostics SaaS, and third‑party administration (TPA) services, (iii) personal – home‑based nursing, physiotherapy at‑door, and wellness‑center memberships. The hub will be linked to a 5G‑enabled data centre and a dedicated EV shuttle fleet connecting it to nearby residential sectors. Sociological analysis predicts that 60 % of potential users are dual‑income nuclear families with children under 12, while 25 % are senior citizens living alone, and 15 % are migrant workers. Historical census data show that Gurugram’s service sector share rose from 22 % in 2001 to 48 % in 2011, coinciding with the arrival of multinational corporations. Students must (i) classify each service tier, (ii) evaluate the economic viability using break‑even analysis given fixed costs of ₹120 cr and variable cost per service encounter of ₹150, (iii) assess sociological barriers to adoption among the three user groups, (iv) analyze spatial suitability based on transport‑communication links, and (v) forecast employment if the hub targets 2 million annual encounters at an average of 4 encounters per worker per day.

(B) Perform a break‑even analysis: Fixed costs = ₹120 crore, variable cost per encounter = ₹150, price charged per encounter = ₹500. Compute the break‑even volume (in encounters) and the profit if annual encounters reach 2 million.

A metropolitan authority proposes to renovate a disused subway terminal into a “Heritage Transit Experience” that faithfully recreates the ambiance of Grand Central Station circa 1955, complete with period‑accurate signage, vintage trains, staff in 1950s uniforms, and a curated soundtrack of big‑band music. The goal is twofold: (i) alleviate commuter stress by offering a psychological escape from contemporary urban pressures (insecurity, digital overload, climate anxiety), and (ii) boost heritage tourism. A multidisciplinary committee must assess the proposal using (a) the textual evidence of Charley’s third‑level experience as a case of wish‑fulfillment escape, (b) the historical authenticity of the 1950s setting, (c) the psychological impact of escapist environments on commuter wellbeing, (d) the use of imagery and metaphor in both the story and the architectural design to evoke nostalgia, and (e) the legal and policy framework governing adaptive reuse of heritage structures under urban governance laws.

(B) Evaluate the historical authenticity of recreating a 1955 Grand Central Station for the heritage hub, citing two specific socio‑economic features of post‑war America that must be replicated to avoid anachronism.

A geological map shows a large, oval-shaped granitic body (batholith) intruding into metamorphic schists in the Dharwar Craton (Karnataka). The contact zone shows a 200m wide aureole of hornfels. Explain the formation of the batholith, the aureole, and why the granite is coarse-grained while a nearby dyke of similar composition is medium-grained.

Combine CRR/SLR analysis with credit creation (Credit Creation By Commercial Banks). A banking system has NDTL = ₹1000 crore, CRR = 4%, SLR = 20%, cdr = 0.15. Banks hold excess reserves of 1% of NDTL. (a) Calculate the actual money multiplier. (b) If RBI reduces SLR to 18.5% and banks reduce excess reserves to 0.5%, what is the new multiplier? (c) By how much does credit creation capacity increase for an initial high-powered money injection of ₹10 crore?

A biorefinery aims to isolate acetone and acetophenone from pre‑treated wheat straw using a ternary solvent mixture of water, ethanol, and ethyl lactate. The extraction efficiency depends on (i) the polarity/hydrogen‑bonding ability of the solvent blend (related to dielectric constant), (ii) the boiling points of the components (to enable solvent recovery by distillation), and (iii) the mutual solubility (miscibility gap) which can be predicted using Flory‑Huggins theory. The dielectric constants (ε) at 25 °C are: water = 78.5, ethanol = 24.5, ethyl lactate = 15.2. The mixture follows a linear mixing rule for ε: ε_mix = Σ φ_i ε_i, where φ_i are volume fractions. The target ketone (acetophenone) has a solubility parameter δ = 20.0 (MPa)½; the solvent blend’s δ_mix is approximated by δ_mix = Σ φ_i δ_i with δ_water = 47.8, δ_ethanol = 26.0, δ_ethyl lactate = 19.5 (MPa)½. The mixture must satisfy ε_mix ≥ 30 (to ensure sufficient polarity) and |δ_mix – δ_ketone| ≤ 2.0 (MPa)½ for good solubility. The boiling points (at 1 atm) are: water = 100 °C, ethanol = 78.4 °C, ethyl lactate = 154 °C.  
Using the above data, answer the following sub‑parts.

(A) Determine the minimum volume fraction of water (φ_w) required in the ternary mixture to achieve ε_mix ≥ 30, assuming the remaining volume is split equally between ethanol and ethyl lactate.

A 100 g arrow is shot vertically upward from a bow. The bowstring is pulled back 50 cm, and the average force exerted by the archer is 200 N. Assuming the bow behaves like an ideal spring and all elastic potential energy converts to gravitational potential energy at the maximum height, calculate the maximum height reached by the arrow above the launch point. (Take g = 10 m/s².)

In early 2024 a draft “Data Sovereignty Bill” proposed mandatory localisation of all personal data, broad exemptions for state surveillance, and heavy fines for non‑compliant tech firms. A coalition of women’s rights groups, digital civil society organisations, and student unions launched a nationwide online campaign (“#MyDataMyRights”) demanding withdrawal of surveillance clauses and stronger consent provisions. The campaign used encrypted messaging apps, organised virtual town‑halls reaching 1.2 million unique participants, and filed public‑interest litigations in three High Courts. The ruling party initially defended the bill as necessary for national security, while opposition parties criticised it for threatening privacy and women’s safety (citing risks of misuse of location data to stalk survivors of domestic violence). After sustained pressure, the government amended the bill to remove mandatory localisation and add a judicial oversight clause for surveillance requests. The amendment was passed in August 2024. Concurrently, reports showed a 22 % rise in online gender‑based harassment in states with weak data‑protection enforcement, and a gender‑disaggregated accounting of cyber‑crime victims indicated women constituted 58 % of cases. Using this scenario, examine the interaction between the women’s movement, digital activism, party politics, and constitutional safeguards.

(D) Compare the government’s response to the #MyDataMyRights campaign with Augustus’s consolidation of power via legal reforms (as studied in The Principate (27 Bce – 284 Ce)), highlighting one similarity in the use of law to manage dissent and one difference in accountability mechanisms.

Two identical cylinders A and B each contain 1 mole of an ideal gas at 300 K and volume 0.02 m³. Cylinder A is in contact with a thermal reservoir at 300 K; cylinder B is thermally insulated. Both gases are compressed to 0.01 m³ by placing identical weights on the pistons. The compression in A is done quasi-statically; in B, the weight is added suddenly. Compare the final temperatures, work done on the gas, and heat exchanged in the two cylinders.

"The boundary between Tropical Moist Deciduous and Tropical Dry Deciduous forests in Central India runs roughly parallel to the 100 cm isohyet but deviates significantly near the Mahanadi basin." Using your knowledge of rain-shadow effects, soil water-holding capacity, and temperature, explain this deviation and predict whether the deviation favors moist or dry deciduous type in the Mahanadi basin.

A university launches the “Digital Seniors Archive” project to record oral histories of citizens aged 60+ from urban Kerala. Teams of student volunteers visit homes, record video interviews, and upload clips to a public portal. The project aims to preserve cultural memory while addressing elderly loneliness. Preliminary data from 150 participants show: average age 68 years; 42% live in nuclear families, 38% in joint families, 20% alone; 68% expressed fear of being forgotten after death. The university’s legal team cites the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, requiring informed consent and protection from exploitation. Historians note that India’s elderly proportion rose from 5% (1951) to 8.6% (2011) due to declining fertility and rising life expectancy—a demographic transition documented in c11_hist_cbse_03_004. Sociologists argue that the shift from joint to nuclear families (c12_soc_cbse_04_007) intensifies separation anxiety, a feeling echoed in Kamala Das’s poem where the speaker observes her mother “wan, pale as a late winter’s moon” and feels “that old familiar ache, my childhood’s fear.” Students must analyze how the poem’s secondary themes (time’s passage, intergenerational bond, unspoken fear) intersect with the legal consent process, historical demographic trends, and sociological changes in family structure to suggest ethical guidelines for the archive.

(D) Using the demographic transition data in c11_hist_cbse_03_004 (elderly share rising from 5% to 8.6% 1951‑2011) and the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, evaluate whether the Act’s provisions are proportionate to the growing elderly population. Support your answer with a simple ratio‑based argument.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you're ______ at the Sanchi Stupa gate, reading Ashoka's edicts carved in Brahmi script—how did one emperor's orders reach village headmen 1,500 km away without phones or roads?
If the original square has side length 27 cm, what is the side length of each small square at Stage 3?

IndiCrafts Global, a Mumbai-based handicrafts exporter selling via Amazon.in and Etsy, processes 1,200 daily transactions across 18 product categories (e.g., Jaipur pottery, Kashmiri shawls) and 42 international destinations. Transactions involve multi-currency INR/USD/EUR conversions, destination-specific VAT/GST compliance (including reverse charge mechanism), and dynamic pricing based on real-time forex rates. Manual systems cause 3-day delays in GST return filing (incurring ₹1,500/day penalties), 18% forex reconciliation errors averaging ₹8,500/error, and inconsistent HS code classification leading to customs holds. Leadership proposes a CAS with ₹9,50,000 setup (Oracle NetSuite + Avalara tax engine) and ₹1,40,000 annual maintenance. Vendors promise 40% faster forex settlement, 90% HS code accuracy, auto-GST filing, and real-time currency hedging dashboard. The firm's forex volatility (USD/INR) follows a normal distribution (μ=0.5% daily drift, σ=1.2%). Using CAS advantages, evaluate the system's viability while integrating international trade law principles and statistical volatility modeling for emerging market forex.

(C) Explain how CAS-driven HS code classification accuracy (using machine learning) reduces customs duty underpayment risk for IndiCrafts' Kashmiri shawls (HS 6304.92), and identify two legal consequences if underpayment occurs due to manual errors.

A pharmaceutical lab plans to synthesize (S)-2‑aminobutanol, a key intermediate for an antiviral drug, by SN2 substitution of (R)-2‑bromobutane with aqueous ammonia. The reaction is carried out in acetone at 298 K. Initial concentrations are [ (R)-2‑bromobutane ] = 0.10 M and [ NH₃ ] = 0.20 M. The experimentally determined second‑order rate constant is k = 2.5 × 10⁻³ M⁻¹ s⁻¹. The cost of reagents is: (R)-2‑bromobutane = $120 mol⁻¹, NH₃ (aq, 30 % w/w) = $0.50 mol⁻¹, acetone = $10 L⁻¹. The reaction volume is 5.0 L. The isolated yield after work‑up is 80 %. The C–Br bond dipole moment is 1.5 D; the forming C–N bond dipole moment is estimated as 1.0 D. Assume a typical pre‑exponential factor A = 1.0 × 10¹² M⁻¹ s⁻¹ for bimolecular SN2 reactions.

(D) Perform a cost analysis for producing 0.50 mol of (S)-2‑aminobutanol (isolated yield 80 %). Calculate the total reagent cost, the cost of solvent, and the cost per gram of product (Molar mass = 75.13 g mol⁻¹).

Two metallic wires of lengths 360 cm and 540 cm are to be cut into equal-length pieces without any leftover wire, but an engineer also needs to determine the LCM of these two lengths to synchronize a manufacturing machine setting. Using prime factorisation, find the LCM of 360 and 540, and explain what this number signifies about their prime components.

In early 2025, the Government of India announces the abolition of the remaining **privy‑purse** payments to the erstwhile rulers of five large princely estates that had opted for a special financial settlement instead of full merger in 1949. The decision follows a Supreme Court directive that such payments violate Article 14 (equality) and constitute a fiscal burden on the consolidated fund. The total annual privy‑purse liability stands at **₹3,200 crore**, distributed as: Estate A – ₹800 crore, Estate B – ₹600 crore, Estate C – ₹500 crore, Estate D – ₹400 crore, Estate E – ₹900 crore.  
The Finance Ministry proposes to redirect these funds toward a **Universal Basic Infrastructure (UBI)** scheme in the erstwhile princely territories, allocating 50 % to road connectivity, 30 % to rural electrification, and 20 % to digital‑learning hubs.  
To assess the administrative capacity required, officials look to the **Neo‑Assyrian imperial tribute system** (c. 800 BCE), where vassal cities delivered quantified tribute in barley, silver, and labor—recorded on clay tablets using a sexagesimal (base‑60) numeral system. The tribute assessment for a typical vassal city was **12 ** **sar** of barley (1 sar = 3,600 liters) and **2 ** **mana** of silver (1 mana = 500 g).  
Using the data below, answer the sub‑questions.  
- Total privy‑purse outlay: **₹3,200 crore**  
- UBI sectoral split: Roads 50 %, Electrification 30 %, Digital 20 %  
- Neo‑Assyrian tribute per city: 12 sar barley, 2 mana silver  
- Conversion: 1 sar barley = 3,600 L; density of barley ≈ 0.6 kg/L → weight per sar = 2,160 kg  
- Silver price (modern): ₹65 per g  
- Barley price (modern): ₹30 per kg  
- Exchange rate (historical): 1 mana silver ≈ 10 sar barley (by value) – provided for consistency check.

(A) Compute the total annual privy‑purse amount (in ₹ crore) that would be redirected to the UBI scheme if the government decides to retain only 75 % of the original liability (i.e., abolish 25 %).

Case-based: You are a process development scientist optimizing recombinant human interferon-α2b (IFN-α2b, 19 kDa, non-glycosylated, 2 disulfide bonds) in E. coli. Current process: shake flask → 50 L → 500 L → 5,000 L. At 500 L, inclusion body purity drops from 90% to 70%, and refolding yield drops from 65% to 40%. Propose 3 root causes with experimental verification for each, and 2 corrective actions with expected impact.

A fintech startup “CrediSwift” uses an AI model that analyses alternative data (mobile recharge frequency, social‑media activity, utility‑payment timeliness) to approve personal loans. In a pilot of 100,000 applicants, the AI approved 68 % of urban applicants and 44 % of rural applicants. Traditional bank scoring approved 55 % of urban and 50 % of rural applicants. The AI model’s default rate is 4 % versus 6 % for traditional scoring. However, explainability audits reveal the model heavily weights “frequency of online shopping” – a variable strongly correlated with urban income and negatively with rural internet access. Sociological studies indicate rural users perceive the system as “elitist” (The Intellectual Context Of Indian Sociology). The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued a discussion paper on “Fair Lending in the Digital Era” requiring disparate impact analysis and mitigation plans.

(C) Identify the cognitive bias most likely influencing loan officers’ over‑reliance on the AI model’s “online shopping frequency” variable, and explain how it leads to systematic rural disadvantage.

A streaming platform announces a web‑series “विस्थापन” that dramatizes Firaq Gorakhpuri’s poem, depicting a fictional bureaucrat who orders forced evictions of river‑bank communities to build a dam, mirroring the poem’s imagery of “उजड़े गाँव” and “बेघर rodzin”. A civil‑society group files a defamation suit alleging the series vilifies a real‑life irrigation minister (named in the poem’s dedication) and incites communal hatred. The platform’s legal team, joined by historians, political scientists, and Hindi scholars, must defend the series under Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of expression) while addressing the claim that the adaptation misrepresents historical facts and harms reputation. The discussion requires students to (i) analyse the poem’s thematic core and its suitability for artistic adaptation, (ii) evaluate the extent to which the series’ portrayal constitutes historical distortion versus legitimate creative licence, (iii) apply constitutional reasoning on reasonable restrictions (defamation, public order) to the alleged harm, (iv) reference comparative historical cases where artistic works faced censorship (e.g., *Bandit Queen*, *Padmaavat*), and (v) rebut the argument that artistic freedom must yield to protecting individual reputation in the digital age. The panel will assess the students’ ability to sustain a 3‑4 minute evidence‑based discussion, cite stanza references, apply legal principles, and summarise peers—all in formal Hindi.

(B) Analyse how the metaphor “सर्कार की लाठी चलती है, खेत बर्बाद होते हैं” (the state’s baton strikes, fields are devastated) can be interpreted as a deliberate artistic licence rather than a factual claim about a specific minister’s actions.

Fill in the blank: Observe an electric geyser heating element: when cold, its resistance is low; as it heats up to 80–90°C, the resistance ______ noticeably, causing the current to settle to a steady value.

Smart‑City Y, a greenfield industrial corridor, employs 80 000 migrant construction workers (60 % inter‑state, 40 % intra‑state) sourced through labour contractors. Average daily wage is ₹500, with 10 % wage deductions for “contractor fees”. Workers live in makeshift camps lacking sanitation; 35 % report respiratory ailments from dust. The city’s master plan introduces AI‑driven brick‑laying robots that can replace 30 % of manual labour within two years. Contractors threaten to replace workers unless they accept a 15 % wage cut and forego overtime. A coalition of workers, local NGOs, and a regional trade union files a petition demanding (i) a living wage of ₹650/day, (ii) provision of portable sanitation units, (iii) a just‑transition clause guaranteeing retraining for displaced workers, and (iv) recognition of their right to collective bargaining under the upcoming Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code. Using concepts of workers’ movement evolution, new social movements, peasant‑movement linkages, and historical economic‑crisis analogies, analyse the situation.

(B) Using the economic‑crisis analogy from c11_hist_cbse_02_009, explain how the impending AI‑driven displacement could trigger a social movement similar to past crisis‑induced uprisings.

A board exam source-based question gives an excerpt from a ryot's petition to the Deccan Riots Commission (like Source 8, NCERT p. 252) describing how the sahukar takes harvest but doesn't credit the account, charges 25-50% higher prices for goods, and refuses receipts. The question asks: "Explain how this petition reflects the breakdown of customary norms and the imposition of colonial legal forms." Answer in 100-150 words.

After thawing a vial of cryopreserved HEK‑293 cells, a researcher mixes 100 µL of cell suspension with 100 µL of 0.4 % w/v trypan blue solution, incubates 3 min, and loads 10 µL onto a hemocytometer. In the four corner squares (each 1 mm², depth 0.1 mm) she counts 150 unstained (live) cells and 50 blue‑stained (dead) cells. Parallel flow cytometry on an aliquot shows 12 % Annexin V⁺/PI⁻ (early apoptotic) and 8 % PI⁺ (late apoptotic/necrotic). Determine the viable cell yield and the proportions of live, early apoptotic, and dead cells in the original thawed sample.

(A) What is the viability percentage (live / (total live + dead)) obtained from the trypan blue count?

An electric geyser is rated 2000 W, 220 V. It is used for 30 minutes daily. Calculate: (a) the current drawn by the geyser, (b) the resistance of its heating element, (c) the electrical energy consumed in one day in kWh, and (d) the cost for 30 days at ₹6.50 per kWh.

During the second wave of a global pandemic, 27‑year‑old Priya, a senior software engineer, shifted to permanent remote work. Her employer logs show she spends an average of 10 hours/day on official tasks, plus 2 hours/day in unscheduled video calls. Priya reports a persistent urge to check Instagram every 20 minutes while coding, which she admits provides brief pleasure but later makes her feel guilty for neglecting her 5‑year‑old son. She completes a daily mood log: on days she gives in to the urge, her self‑rated productivity drops from 8/10 to 5/10, and her salivary cortisol measured at 4 p.m. averages 18 µg/dL (baseline 10 µg/dL). Her partner notes that Priya frequently apologizes for “not being present” and feels she is failing both as an employee and a mother. A sociological role‑conflict inventory administered by her company’s HR yields a score of 38/50 (high conflict). Priya also scores moderately high on extraversion (E=15/20) in a Five‑Factor Model questionnaire. Using this information, answer the following.

(C) Name the ego defence mechanism Priya most likely employs when she justifies her Instagram use by telling herself, “I need a short break to recharge,” and describe its psychological function.

In late 2025, the ruling coalition proposes a universal basic income (UBI) of ₹12,000 per month for all citizens earning below the national median wage, financed by a temporary wealth tax on assets above ₹50 crore and a reallocation of subsidies. Proponents argue the scheme will eradicate poverty, echoing Indira Gandhi’s 1971 “Garibi Hatao” slogan, while opponents warn of fiscal inflation, market distortion, and a revival of populist economics that precipitated the 1969 Congress split and the subsequent centralisation of power. The proposal triggers nationwide debates, with economists citing data from pilot UBI schemes in Kenya and Finland, and political analysts drawing parallels to the 1971 election campaign that restored Congress dominance after a period of fragmentation. Students must analyse the economic, political, and ideological dimensions of the UBI proposal by invoking concepts from the Congress‑system crisis, populist leadership, and comparative historical experiences of welfare programmes.

(B) Assess the likelihood that the UBI proposal could revive a Congress‑style dominance akin to the 1971 election outcome, considering the fragmentation of opposition parties and the role of populist leadership.

The Ministry of Education, 2025, proposes a nationwide pilot to embed selected folk narratives of t;'kadj izlkn into the secondary‑school Hindi curriculum across 15 states, aiming to foster national integration while preserving regional diversity. The pilot allocates ₹120 crore for teacher training, digital lesson‑plans, and community‑led workshops. Baseline data from NCERT surveys (2023) show that only 41 % of Class 10 students can identify the central theme of “harmony between human labor and nature” in the bard’s works, whereas 58 % appreciate the use of vivid imagery. Post‑pilot interim results after six months reveal a rise to 63 % theme recognition and 71 % imagery appreciation in states with strong local‑language support (e.g., Punjab, West Bengal), but only 48 % theme and 55 % imagery gains in states where instruction is solely in Hindi‑medium (e.g., Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh). Critics argue that a one‑size‑fits‑all approach risks marginalizing dialects, while supporters claim it creates a shared cultural reference point. Using the chapter’s analysis of theme, imagery, and the bard’s role as a cultural mediator, evaluate the pilot’s effectiveness in achieving both national integration and regional preservation. Your answer must include at least two textual evidences with line/stanza references, explain the literary devices involved, and connect the findings to interdisciplinary concepts of history (curriculum as historical narrative), sociology (social cohesion and identity), and economics (cost‑benefit analysis of educational spending).

(B) Analyze the bard’s use of vivid imagery (e.g., “golden fields, flowing rivers”) and evaluate how the pilot’s varying imagery appreciation across states influences sociological notions of social cohesion through shared visual symbols.

In 2024, a fintech startup “AgriCredit” launches an instant‑loan app for cotton farmers in Vidarbha, Maharashtra. Loans are sanctioned within minutes using satellite‑based yield predictions and alternative credit scores. The nominal annual interest rate is 18 % compounded monthly, but the effective rate disclosed to farmers is 19.6 %. After a poor monsoon, cotton prices fall by 30 % and many farmers default. AgriCredit begins strict recovery, seizing farm equipment and initiating social boycotts of defaulters through WhatsApp groups. Farmers protest, burning loan agreements and demanding a waiver, echoing the 1875 Deccan Riots where ryots attacked sahukars, burnt bahi khatas, and socially ostracized moneylenders. The Maharashtra government sets up a “Farmer Distress Inquiry Committee” (FDIC) modelled on the colonial Deccan Riots Commission, while the central government debates a special credit‑regulatory bill under Article 246(2) of the Constitution.

(C) Using the colonial revenue demand (≈₹30/ha) and the estimated gross cotton produce value of ₹2,40,000/ha (from Seed 1B), calculate the percentage of gross produce appropriated as land revenue under the ryotwari system.

In mid‑2026, a resurgence of Virus X triggers a second wave in a metropolitan state with 12 million residents, 35 % of whom are migrant construction workers earning daily wages of ₹400. The government rolls out a mandatory contact‑tracing app that collects GPS location, Bluetooth proximity, and voluntary health symptoms data, storing it on centralized servers for 180 days. Non‑compliance attracts a fine of ₹5 000 or imprisonment up to six months under the amended Epidemic Diseases Act. Civil liberties groups argue the app enables mass surveillance, potentially targeting dissenters, while public health officials credit it with reducing the effective reproduction number (R₀) from 1.8 to 0.9 within three weeks. Economists estimate that lockdown‑adjacent restrictions cut informal sector wages by 45 %, pushing an additional 2.1 million workers below the poverty line. Food security surveys show a rise in household hunger scores from 2.1 to 3.7 on a 5‑point scale. Historical analogies are drawn to the 1975‑77 National Emergency, when preventive detention was justified on security grounds. Students must analyse how the intertwining of health surveillance, poverty aggravation, and food insecurity reshapes the traditional vs. non‑traditional security balance, evaluate the proportionality of the state’s response using principles of necessity and proportionality, and suggest safeguards that uphold both security and human rights.

(B) Apply the human security lens (Health Pandemics, Poverty, And Food Security) to calculate the percentage increase in the hunger score scale from pre‑outbreak (2.1) to peak (3.7), and interpret what this change signifies for food security as a security issue.

A teacher asks students to learn the word "photosynthesis". Group A counts the syllables; Group B writes a sentence using the word; Group C draws the chemical equation. Predict the recall order from best to worst after 24 hours and justify using levels of processing.

A renowned Bollywood actor, diagnosed with depression, grants a candid interview to *YouTube* channel “MindMatters”. In the interview, she describes her therapy journey, the role of familial support, and the societal stigma she faced. The video garners 12 million views in 48 hours, spikes Google searches for “depression help” by 180%, and leads to a 22% increase in appointments at urban mental‑health clinics. Simultaneously, some media outlets criticize the interview for invading her privacy and potentially triggering copycat behavior. Using concepts of interview ethics, psychological stigma theory, and sociological role theory, answer the following sub‑parts.

(A) Identify the sociological concept that explains how the actor’s interview may alter public expectations of the “celebrity” role regarding mental health.

In a physics lab, students measure the thickness of a single sheet of paper using two methods: (A) Measure a stack of 50 sheets with a screw gauge (LC = 0.01 mm, zero error = +0.02 mm). The stack thickness reading is 4.85 mm. (B) Measure the same stack with a vernier calipers (LC = 0.05 mm, zero error = -0.01 cm). The stack thickness reading is 4.8 cm. Calculate the thickness per sheet from both methods and comment on which is more precise. Also calculate the relative error in each method assuming the least count is the absolute error.

In 2025, the IMF’s World Economic Outlook flags that the Southeast Asian agrarian state of Mekongria faces rising rural indebtedness due to fluctuating rice prices and increasing climate‑related crop failures. Mekongria’s GDP is $110 bn, agricultural GDP share 22 %, fiscal deficit 5 % of GDP, and public debt‑to‑GDP 68 %. The government proposes a climate‑smart agriculture programme financed by a World Bank Results‑Based Financing (RBF) instrument: $500 mn disbursed upon verification of 2 mn hectares adopting alternate wetting and drying (AWD) irrigation, which reduces methane emissions and water use. The RBF carries a service fee of 0.3 % of disbursed amount and a maturity of 10 years, interest‑free. Simultaneously, the IMF’s Article IV consultation recommends: (i) a temporary targeted cash‑transfer scheme for smallholders (cost $120 mn/year) financed by reallocating fuel subsidies, (ii) adoption of a floating exchange rate to absorb external shocks, and (iii) compliance with WTO Agreement on Agriculture (AoA) “green box” criteria for subsidies. Historical precedents show that Mekongria’s ancient irrigation networks were managed by temple‑like institutions that allocated water based on ritual precedence (Cuneiform Script). The finance ministry must now account for the RBF as a contingent liability until performance milestones are met, and disclose the cash‑transfer scheme as a subsidy under WTO AoA.
Using the data above, answer the following.

(E) Record the initial recognition of the RBF in Mekongria’s government accounts, assuming the $500 mn is a contingent liability until performance milestones are met, and the government expects to receive $300 mn with 60 % probability. Show the expected value approach and the journal entry.

Meera, a Class 12 Home Science student, aspires to become a clinical nutritionist in a multispecialty hospital. She scored 88% in Biology (Class 11) and maintains a personal budget spreadsheet showing monthly savings of ₹2,500, indicating basic accounting competence. She has never undertaken a hospital internship but volunteers at a local health‑awareness camp. Recent WHO data show a 22% rise in lifestyle‑related disorders (diabetes, hypertension) in urban India, creating demand for nutrition consultants. Conversely, several AI‑driven diet‑planning apps now offer free personalized meal plans, threatening traditional consultancy. Meera must construct a personal SWOT matrix to decide whether to pursue a B.Sc. in Nutrition & Dietetics or a generic B.A. in Home Science.

(B) Identify two specific, evidence‑based weaknesses Meera should place in the Weaknesses quadrant of her SWOT.

In District X, the National Family Health Survey‑5 shows 38 % of children under five are stunted. The Zila Parishad has earmarked ₹2.4 crore from the State Nutrition Mission for a supplementary nutrition programme (SNP) targeting 0‑6 year children. The Gram Panchayats are to identify beneficiaries, coordinate with Anganwadi centres, and mobilise Women’s Self‑Help Groups (SHGs) for local production of fortified snack mixes. The Home Science extension worker assigned to the block must (a) ascertain which tier of PRI is legally responsible for SNP implementation, (b) work out per‑capita fund allocation, (c) select a suitable Participatory Rural Appraisal (PRA) tool to map seasonal food‑insecurity patterns, (d) gauge how existing social capital (trust, networks, SHG cohesion) influences uptake, and (e) design SMART indicators to monitor impact on stunting over two years. The worker has access to block‑level population data (4 blocks × 45,000 average), baseline anthropometry, and records of SHG savings‑credit activity.

(D) Explain how existing social capital (trust, norms, and SHG networks) in the block influences the uptake of the supplementary nutrition programme by women’s groups.

A phase‑II trial uses ex‑vivo CRISPR‑Cas9 editing of hematopoietic stem cells to reactivate fetal hemoglobin. The trial’s communication package must convey: (i) the molecular mechanism (DNA double‑strand break, HDR repair), (ii) off‑target risk estimated via GUIDE‑seq (average 0.8 off‑sites per genome, Poisson distributed), (iii) vector integration kinetics (lentiviral vector decay half‑life = 14 days), and (iv) socio‑economic impact (projected reduction in lifetime medical cost from US $1.2 M to US $0.3 M per patient). Stakeholders include: hematologists (need kinetic models), patient advocacy groups (need clear risk‑benefit narratives), insurance regulators (need cost‑effectiveness curves), and the general public (need analogies). Using the data, construct a communication strategy that selects appropriate media, quantifies uncertainty, and aligns feedback loops with trial milestones.

(C) Using the cost‑savings data, compute the incremental cost‑effectiveness ratio (ICER) in US $ per quality‑adjusted life year (QALY) gained, assuming the therapy yields 25 QALYs per patient and the comparator (standard care) yields 15 QALYs.

A spacecraft re‑enters Earth’s atmosphere at 7.8 km s⁻¹. The stagnation point temperature reaches 2500 K, causing the carbon‑phenolic ablative material to undergo the overall reaction:  
C₆H₅OH (phenol unit) + ½ O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O + C (solid char).  
The rate‑determining step is the collision between surface phenol radicals and O₂ molecules.  
Given:  
- Surface concentration of phenol radicals = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ mol cm⁻² (assumed constant).  
- Partial pressure of O₂ at the wall = 0.2 atm.  
- Temperature at the wall = 2500 K.  
- Pre‑exponential factor for the surface reaction (collision frequency × steric factor) = Z·P = 1.5 × 10¹² cm⁻² s⁻¹ atm⁻¹.  
- Activation energy Ea = 180 kJ mol⁻¹.  
Assume ideal gas behaviour for O₂ and that the reaction follows first‑order kinetics in O₂ pressure.  
(a) Calculate the rate constant k at 2500 K using the Arrhenius expression.  
(b) Determine the effective collision frequency Z_AB (in cm⁻² s⁻¹) for phenol–O₂ collisions at the wall.  
(c) If the spacecraft loses 0.5 mm of ablation layer per second, estimate the number of phenol sites consumed per cm² per second (use molar mass of phenol = 94 g mol⁻¹, density of ablative = 1.4 g cm⁻³).  
(d) Discuss how a 10 % increase in wall temperature would affect the ablation rate, quantifying the change in k.  
(e) Propose a short‑cut method to estimate the temperature at which the ablation rate doubles, without solving the full Arrhenius equation.

(C) Estimate the number of phenol sites consumed per cm² per second corresponding to an ablation loss of 0.5 mm s⁻¹.

Scenario: The Karta of a JHF business (textile trading) enters into a contract to purchase cotton worth ₹50 lakh on credit without consulting coparceners. The business fails, assets are ₹30 lakh, debts ₹50 lakh. The coparceners refuse to pay the ₹20 lakh shortfall from personal funds. Can the creditor recover the shortfall? From whom? Explain the legal basis.

An archaeological team discovers a parchment fragment. To estimate its age, they measure the remaining ^14C activity. Living wood has a specific activity of 13.56 decays min⁻¹ g⁻¹ of carbon. The fragment (mass = 2.00 g of carbon) shows an activity of 4.20 decays min⁻¹. The half‑life of ^14C is 5730 y. Assume the decay follows N = N₀e^{‑λt} and that the counting statistics follow Poisson distribution (standard deviation = √N counts). Using this information, answer the following. (Take 1 y = 3.156×10⁷ s.)

(D) Estimate the statistical uncertainty (standard deviation) in the age due to counting statistics, assuming the measurement was taken for 10 minutes.

A 2024 NGO report on internal displacement in India’s Bundelkhand region cites rising farmer suicides linked to groundwater depletion. The report draws a parallel between the plight of Bundelkhand farmers and the imagery in vkyksd èkUok’s poem “irax,” noting the ironic situation where land once fertile (the “irax” metaphor) now yields nothing despite state irrigation schemes. Simultaneously, Census 2021 data shows a 12% decadal decline in rural population density in Bundelkhand, while urban centers nearby have seen a 15% increase. The NGO seeks to use the poem in a advocacy brief that argues the state’s failure to ensure the right to livelihood (Article 19(1)(g)) constitutes a violation of the right to life (Article 21). Students must (i) detect irony in the poem, (ii) infer the poet’s implied critique of state irrigation policy, (iii) link that inference to population‑shift data, and (iv) evaluate the poem’s rhetorical strength for a rights‑based advocacy campaign.

(B) Infer the poet’s criticism of state irrigation projects using two textual evidences.

Fill in the blank: Water resources in the Indian economic context refer to the stock and flow of freshwater (surface water in rivers, lakes, reservoirs and groundwater in aquifers) that serve as productive inputs for agriculture, industry, and domestic use; water pollution is the degradation of water quality beyond permissible standards (BOD > 3 mg/L, DO < 4 mg/L for bathing) due to ______ discharge of organic, inorganic, and toxic pollutants, reducing the resource's assimilative capacity and imposing negative externalities on downstream users.

A contracts with B to supply a custom-built machine for ₹10 lakh by 30th June. The contract states: "Time is the essence of the contract." On 25th June, A informs B that a critical imported component is delayed due to a port strike (force majeure clause covers "strikes"). B terminates the contract on 28th June and buys a substitute machine for ₹14 lakh. B sues A for ₹4 lakh (difference) + ₹1 lakh (liquidated damages for delay). A claims force majeure. Decide, citing relevant provisions and case law.

**CircuiTech Ltd.**, an electronics exporter, plans to sell ₹800 crore worth of goods abroad in FY 2025‑26 (ex‑ante net exports, NX). It expects the domestic consumption function to be C = 200 + 0.65Y and investment to be autonomous at ₹120 crore. The firm finances exports by retaining earnings (no new debt or equity). Due to a sudden 15 % appreciation of the domestic currency, the realised export revenue falls to ₹620 crore (ex‑post NX). Assume no change in government spending, taxes, or investment. The economy initially operates at equilibrium with output Y₀. Using the open‑economy Keynesian model (X‑M = NX), answer the following.

(B) Derive the foreign‑trade multiplier (k_NX) for this economy, stating the condition under which it equals the simple spending multiplier.

In 2025 a coalition government (led by a national party, a regional Tamil Nadu outfit asserting fisheries’ rights, and an OBC‑focused party) launches a ₹18,000 crore green bond programme to fund mangrove restoration, seawall construction, and solar‑powered desalination plants along India’s 7,500 km coastline. The bonds carry a 5.5 % coupon, 10‑year maturity, and are rated AAA by domestic agencies. Projected annual cash inflows from carbon credits (₹900 cr) and water‑sale revenues (₹1,200 cr) total ₹2,100 cr, while operational maintenance costs are estimated at ₹600 cr/year. To ensure inclusive growth, 35 % of the construction jobs (estimated 25,000) are reserved for OBC workers, linking to the Mandal‑derived job‑quota policy. The Tamil Nadu partner demands that 50 % of the desalination output be allocated to local fishing communities at subsidised rates, citing historical precedents of state‑led famine relief (e.g., British‑era famine codes). Drawing an analogy from the Roman Empire’s 3rd‑century fiscal crisis (where debasement and over‑reliance on tribute weakened central authority), analysts warn that excessive dependence on volatile carbon‑credit revenues could undermine fiscal sustainability. Using the data, assess the bond’s debt‑service capacity, the political implications of OBC job reservations and regional resource allocation, and the historical warning from Roman fiscal management.

(E) Using the Roman Empire’s 3rd‑century fiscal crisis as a warning, argue whether over‑reliance on volatile carbon‑credit revenues jeopardises the long‑term sustainability of the green bond programme, and suggest a fiscal rule to mitigate this risk.

In May 2024, a severe cyclonic storm struck the Odisha‑Andhra coast, prompting the evacuation of 1.2 million people. The State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) relied on a hybrid communication setup: (i) satellite‑based VSAT terminals (providing 10 Mbps uplink) deployed at 150 relief camps, (ii) GSM‑based mobile towers (restored within 6 h using diesel generators), and (iii) a network of amateur radio (ham) operators coordinating ground‑to‑ground messages. Simultaneously, the Indian Railways ran 30 special freight trains carrying relief material from Vishakhapatnam to Bhubaneswar, utilizing the dedicated freight corridor (DFC) laid parallel to the NH‑16. Historical analysis shows that during the 1999 Odisha super‑cyclone, the lack of redundant communication delayed relief by 48 h, whereas the 2013 Phailin cyclone benefited from early GSM restoration. The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) now mandates that all district headquarters maintain a minimum of 30 % redundant communication capacity (satellite + ham) and that critical transport routes (rail and road) have optical fibre laid alongside for real‑time tracking.  
Given the following data: each VSAT terminal costs ₹2.5 lakh, each GSM tower restoration costs ₹8 lakh, each ham operator kit costs ₹12,000, the railway DFC length is 420 km with OFC laying cost of ₹1.8 lakhs/km, and the total budget allocated for communication redundancy in the affected districts is ₹180 crore, answer the sub‑questions below.

(E) Discuss how horizontal power‑sharing among States (c10_civ_cbse_01_004) and historical disaster experiences (e.g., 1999 vs 2013 cyclones) shape the NDMA’s guideline for 30 % redundant communication capacity.

A satellite startup produces two types of solar panels: **Panel A** (high‑efficiency gallium‑arsenide) and **Panel B** (low‑cost silicon). Each panel requires a certain amount of high‑purity silicon, silver paste for contacts, and undergoes electrical testing before integration. The factory has a daily supply of 800 kg silicon, 120 kg silver paste, and 1500 minutes of testing equipment time. Panel A consumes 0.8 kg silicon, 0.05 kg silver, and needs 12 minutes of test time; Panel B consumes 0.5 kg silicon, 0.02 kg silver, and needs 8 minutes of test time. The launch vehicle imposes a maximum total panel mass of 500 kg; Panel A has a mass of 4 kg per unit, Panel B 2.5 kg per unit. The mission requires a minimum total electrical power output of 200 W; Panel A yields 15 W per unit, Panel B yields 8 W per unit. The company wishes to **minimise the total mass** of panels launched while meeting the power requirement and not exceeding material, testing and mass limits. Using the facts that silicon purity and silver‑paste adhesion follow linear relationships with usage (derived from chemical kinetics and material science), and that test time scales linearly with number of panels (physics of sequential testing), formulate and solve the LPP.

(E) If the testing equipment time is increased by 20 % (to 1800 minutes), determine the new minimum mass and the corresponding production plan.

Bank Z operates with NDTL = ₹800 crore. Initial ratios: CRR = 5 %, SLR = 25 %. The bank’s portfolio: govt securities (SLR‑eligible) = ₹180 crore, loans = ₹500 crore, other assets = ₹40 crore, cash reserves with RBI = ₹40 crore (exactly meeting CRR). The bank’s average loan yield = 12 %, govt‑sec yield = 7 %, operating expense ratio = 1.8 % of assets. The RBI simultaneously: (i) raises CRR by 0.75 % points, (ii) lowers SLR by 3 % points, and (iii) conducts an open‑market sale of ₹20 crore of govt securities (reducing banking system reserves). Assume Bank Z participates in the OMO by selling ₹5 crore of its govt securities to the RBI at face value, and uses the proceeds to meet the new CRR requirement. Any remaining shortfall in SLR is covered by purchasing additional govt securities from the market at face value. Ignore changes in loan yields and operating expenses due to the shock.

(E) Using the post‑shock balance sheet (loans ₹500 cr, other assets ₹40 cr, govt securities ₹175 cr, cash with RBI ₹46 cr, cash in hand ₹34 cr), compute the bank’s Return on Assets (ROA) assuming operating expenses remain at 1.8 % of total assets and interest income is earned only on loans (12 %) and govt securities (7 %).

Compare the accounting treatment impact on financial ratios for a firm choosing between: (A) Operating lease of ₹50L/year for 3 years, (B) Hire purchase of ₹1.5Cr asset with ₹30L down payment and ₹40L/year × 3 years. Initial equity ₹5Cr, debt ₹2Cr. Compute Debt-Equity, Interest Coverage, and Return on Assets for Year 1 under both. Assume EBIT ₹2Cr, tax 30%, lease rental fully deductible, hire purchase interest ₹18L Year 1, depreciation ₹50L/year straight-line.

A psychologist conditions a dog to salivate (CR) to a 1000 Hz tone (CS) by pairing it with meat powder (US) for 20 trials. She then conducts extinction by presenting the tone alone. The CR strength (drops of saliva) across extinction trials is: Trial 1: 10, Trial 2: 8, Trial 3: 6, Trial 4: 5, Trial 5: 4, Trial 6: 3, Trial 7: 2, Trial 8: 1, Trial 9: 0.5, Trial 10: 0. After a 24-hour rest, the tone is presented again and the dog salivates 4 drops. (a) Plot the extinction curve. (b) Calculate the percentage of spontaneous recovery relative to the initial CR strength (assume initial CR at end of acquisition was 10 drops). (c) Explain why the recovery is not 100%.

Amit (businessman) threatens to file a false criminal case against Vikram unless Vikram sells his ancestral land to Amit for ₹10 lakh (market value ₹1 crore). Vikram, fearing arrest, signs the sale deed. Two months later, Vikram wants to cancel the sale. Can he?

Rising sea levels and increased cyclonic intensity have rendered 12 % of the Sundarbans’ arable land saline‑intruded, forcing an estimated 45,000 households to migrate annually to the peri‑urban blocks of Rajarhat, New Town, and Bidhannagar on Kolkata’s outskirts. Migrants are predominantly from Scheduled Tribe (ST) communities (60 %) and Scheduled Caste (SC) communities (30 %), with the remaining 10 % being OBC. Upon arrival, 70 % find informal employment in construction or domestic work, 20 % engage in street vending, and 10 % remain unemployed. The average monthly household income in the Sundarbans (pre‑migration) was ₹9,500; in the peri‑urban destination it rises to ₹13,200, but expenditures on housing, transport, and food increase to ₹11,800, leaving a net surplus of ₹1,400. The West Bengal Government’s “Climate Resilient Housing” scheme offers subsidized pucca units at ₹2,500/month rent, but eligibility requires proof of continuous residence for 3 years and a minimum monthly income of ₹15,000. Local NGOs report that 40 % of migrant children aged 6‑14 are out of school, citing language barriers (Bengali vs. tribal dialects) and the need for child labor to supplement family income.
Using sociology’s concepts of plurality, diversity, and stratification, together with geographical concepts of push‑pull factors (: Migration) and historical land‑revenue policies (: Trade, Commerce and Long‑Distance Exchange) that altered agrarian structures, answer the following.

(D) Using the concept of push‑pull factors, identify two push factors and two pull factors inherent in the scenario. Then, evaluate how the interaction of these factors contributes to the reproduction of caste‑tribe‑based occupational stratification in the destination, citing the historical land‑revenue legacy that commoditized labor and altered agrarian relations.

In 2024 the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) launched the Vikramaditya satellite, named after the legendary emperor Vikramaditya to symbolize India’s resurgence as a global knowledge power. The satellite carried a multi‑spectral imager shaped like a lotus, intended to represent purity of scientific pursuit. Official brochures highlighted the mission’s budget of ₹1,850 crore, framed as a “wise investment” in future GDP growth. Six weeks after launch, a micrometeoroid strike damaged the lotus‑shaped imager, reducing imaging resolution by 70 %. Simultaneously, the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) reported that ₹420 crore of the allocated funds had been diverted to cover cost overruns in a unrelated highway project, violating Article 282 of the Constitution which requires legislative approval for re‑appropriation. The launch site, Sriharikota, lies on the 13.5°N latitude, where the prevailing easterly trade winds increase payload drift risk by 12 % compared to equatorial sites. Opposition parties cited the mission as a classic case of “naming‑hope‑outcome‑mismatch,” while ISRO defended the name as aspirational, arguing that setbacks are part of scientific progress.

(B) Explain how the lotus‑shaped imager functions as a **symbol** of scientific purity and discuss why its damage intensifies the thematic tension between aspiration and reality.

An auto-component SME in Pune had revenue of ₹25 crore in 2000, selling only to Indian car makers. After globalisation, it secured a contract to supply brake systems to a German automaker's Indian plant and later to their European plants. Revenue grew to ₹180 crore by 2010. The firm invested ₹40 crore in CNC machines from Japan and trained 200 workers in statistical process control. Identify and quantify the positive producer effects.

In 2024, a major streaming platform releases a feature‑film adaptation of निर्मल वर्मा’s “नवल निरंकुश”, relocating the story from 1970s Delhi to a futuristic Neo‑Noida metropolis. The author’s legal heirs sue the platform for (a) infringement of moral rights under Section 57 of the Copyright Act, 1957, alleging that the adaptation distorts the protagonist’s internal monologue and replaces the story’s subtle imagery with overt product placements; (b) violation of the right to integrity under the Berne Convention; and (c) unfair enrichment, claiming the film’s ₹120 crore box‑office collection exploits the story’s reputation without adequate compensation. The plaintiff’s counsel submits: (i) a comparative textual analysis showing 68% deviation in key dialogues; (ii) econometric data indicating that films preserving ≥80% narrative fidelity enjoy 1.3× higher critical scores; (iii) a sociological survey revealing that 54% of urban youth perceive the adaptation as “cultural erosion”; and (iv) a geographic information system (GIS) map showing that 70% of the film’s shooting locations lie in SEZ‑designated zones, raising concerns about spatial gentrification. The defense argues that the transformation constitutes a legitimate creative reinterpretation protected under freedom of expression (Article 19(1)(a)). As a law‑literature expert, you must craft a PEEL paragraph that (a) states the legal issue (moral rights infringement), (b) provides two textual evidences (one paraphrase, one quote) demonstrating deviation, (c) explains how the deviation violates Section 57 and Berne Article 9, (d) links the explanation to the econometric fidelity‑criticism correlation and the sociological perception data, and (e) concludes with a recommended remedy (e.g., compensation, disclaimer, or injunction).

(C) Explain how the identified deviation infringes the author’s right to claim authorship (Section 57(a)) and the right to integrity (Berne Article 9), linking it to the econometric fidelity‑criticism correlation and the sociological perception data.

Using NCERT data (Ganga-Brahmaputra-Barak: 60% of 1869 km³ = 1121 km³ from ~33% of India's 3.28 million km²), calculate the specific yield of the combined Himalayan basin system and compare it with the Peninsular basin system (40% of 1869 km³ = 748 km³ from ~67% of area). Interpret the difference.

An automotive engineer seeks to replace Pt‑based catalysts with a Co₃O₄ spinel doped with Mn²⁺ to achieve CO oxidation at 150 °C. The catalyst operates via Mars‑van Krevelen mechanism: lattice oxygen oxidizes CO to CO₂, creating an oxygen vacancy that is refilled by O₂. Relevant data: Co³⁺ (low spin, t₂g⁶ e_g⁰) is diamagnetic; Mn²⁺ (high spin, d⁵) has five unpaired electrons. The standard Gibbs free energy change for CO + ½ O₂ → CO₂ at 298 K is ΔG° = –257 kJ mol⁻¹. The activation energy Eₐ for the undoped Co₃O₄ catalyst is 120 kJ mol⁻¹; Mn doping reduces Eₐ by 20 kJ mol⁻¹. The pre‑exponential factor A in the Arrhenius equation k = A e^(–Eₐ/RT) is 5.0×10¹² s⁻¹. Use R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. The engineer must calculate the rate constant at 150 °C, assess the magnetic moment of the dopant, and evaluate the thermodynamic feasibility. Additionally, the engineer needs to determine how many distinct ways the five unpaired electrons of Mn²⁺ can be arranged in the five d‑orbitals (considering only spin, not orbital occupancy) to understand possible magnetic microstates.

(B) Calculate the spin‑only magnetic moment (in Bohr magnetons) of Mn²⁺ from Part A.

The Government of India plans to extend the Dedicated Freight Corridor (DFC) from Delhi to Mumbai via a new alignment passing through Vadodara (GJ), Ahmedabad (GJ), and Surat (GJ) before reaching the JNPT port. The extension is expected to cut average rail transit time for automobile components from the Delhi‑NCR supplier belt to Gujarat’s ports by 40 %. Current rail transit time is 48 hours; the proposed DFC will reduce it to 28.8 hours.  

Automobile firms in the Gurugram‑Manesar (Haryana) cluster rely on just‑in‑time (JIT) delivery of steel stampings and electronic control units (ECUs). Their current inventory holding cost is ₹150 per unit per day. The proposed DFC would lower inventory holding cost proportionally to transit‑time reduction.  

Simultaneously, a rival cluster in Chennai (Tamil Nadu) is considering a shift to inland waterways via the newly operational Buckingham Canal link to the Ennore port, promising a 25 % reduction in transit time but requiring an initial infrastructure investment of ₹1,200 crore shared equally by the state and private players.  

Assume a mid‑sized automobile manufacturer produces 200,000 vehicles per year, each requiring 0.8 tonnes of steel stampings and 0.15 tonnes of ECUs. The weight‑based freight rate is ₹2,500 per tonne per 1,000 km via rail. The average rail distance from Gurugram to JNPT is 1,400 km; via the Buckingham Canal route the effective distance (including last‑mile road) is 1,600 km.  

Using this information, answer the following sub‑parts.

(E) Propose a multimodal logistics solution that could further reduce inventory holding cost for automobile clusters, and evaluate its feasibility using the concepts of agglomeration economies and transport cost geography.

A biotech startup plans to manufacture a chimeric anti‑PD‑1 monoclonal antibody (mAb) using a mammalian cell line (CHO) cultured in a perfusion bioreactor aboard the International Space Station (ISS). Microgravity alters shear stress, affecting cell viability and product titer. The bioreactor operates at a constant volumetric flow rate Q = 0.5 L h⁻¹, with a cell density X = 1.2 × 10⁷ cells mL⁻¹. Each cell secretes mAb at a rate q_p = 15 pg cell⁻¹ day⁻¹. The mAb undergoes first‑order degradation with rate constant k_d = 0.001 min⁻¹. The perfusion membrane has a molecular weight cut‑off that retains cells but allows mAb to exit at a clearance rate equal to the dilution rate D = Q/V, where V = 10 L is the reactor volume. Microgravity reduces the effective shear‑stress‑dependent death rate constant k_s from 0.02 h⁻¹ (Earth) to 0.005 h⁻¹ (ISS).

(D) If the bioreactor runs for 168 h (one week), calculate the total mass of mAb harvested (in grams), assuming the effluent concentration remains at the steady‑state value found in Part B and the flow rate Q is constant.

The Lok Sabha Secretariat maintains a BILLS table to monitor legislative proposals. Schema: BILL_ID (NUMBER, PK), TITLE (VARCHAR2(200)), INTRODUCED_BY (VARCHAR2(100)), INTRO_DATE (DATE), STATUS (VARCHAR2(20) DEFAULT 'Pending'), LAST_ACTION_DATE (DATE), COMMITTEE_REF (VARCHAR2(50)), FISCAL_IMPACT (NUMBER).  
Three new bills are ready for entry: (1) ‘Data Protection Bill’ introduced by Shri Priya Mehta on 2024‑04‑10, status default, fiscal impact 120 crore; (2) ‘Renewable Energy Incentive Act’ introduced by Dr. Arun Kapoor on 2024‑04‑12, status 'Under Review', fiscal impact 85 crore; (3) ‘Digital Education Access Bill’ introduced by Smt. Lakshmi Rao on 2024‑04‑15, status default, fiscal impact 0.  
A staging table NEW_BILLS_STG holds these rows with identical columns.  
Tasks: (a) Insert the three bills using INSERT … SELECT, but only those with fiscal impact > 0; (b) Update the STATUS of the ‘Renewable Energy Incentive Act’ to 'Approved' after committee clearance; (c) Delete any bills whose TITLE contains the word ‘Digital’ and whose INTRO_DATE is before 2024‑01‑01 (to remove stale drafts).  
Students must craft DML statements, anticipate row changes, and explain how DEFAULT, WHERE, and string pattern matching affect outcomes.

(B) Update the STATUS of the bill titled ‘Renewable Energy Incentive Act’ to 'Approved'. Use the exact title match.

A fintech startup has a fixed monthly operating budget of **₹5,00,000**. It can allocate this budget between two activities:  

* **Good X – AI‑development person‑months** (each person‑month costs ₹20,000).  
* **Good Y – Digital‑marketing impressions** (each thousand impressions costs ₹500).  

The founders’ satisfaction (utility) from the bundle (X, Y) is given by the Cobb‑Douglas function  

\[
U(X,Y)=X^{0.5}\,Y^{0.5}
\]

Assume the startup follows accrual accounting, capitalises AI‑development expenditure that meets the criteria of an intangible asset (useful life 3 years, straight‑line depreciation), and expenses all marketing costs immediately.  

Using the data above, answer the following sub‑parts.

(A) Derive the expression for the Marginal Rate of Substitution of X for Y (MRSₓᵧ) from the given utility function and show that MRSₓᵧ = Y/X.

In 2024, a Swedish NGO “Återvinning” launches a pilot program in the Bergslagen region, where historic iron ore mines have declined since the 1970s. The program recruits 30 former vagabonds (aged 20‑45) who previously survived by petty thievery and begging. Participants are taught to craft eco‑friendly rattraps from recycled copper wire sourced from decommissioned mining equipment. Over six months, the NGO tracks: (i) weekly income from rattrap sales (average SEK 150/person), (ii) attendance at mandatory civic‑education workshops on Swedish welfare rights, (iii) incidents of relapse into theft (recorded as 4 events total), and (iv) participant self‑reported sense of “unwonted joy” measured on a 1‑10 scale (rise from 3.2 to 7.8). The NGO’s director frames the initiative as a modern rattrap: society’s welfare system and vocational training act as bait that lures individuals out of the “impenetrable prison” of poverty. Using the textual description of the protagonist’s journey in “The Rattrap” (exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution), analyze how the program’s narrative mirrors the story’s plot structure.

(B) Determine the rising action in the scenario and justify which two plot‑progression techniques (from the text) are employed.

From 1951 to 2021, India’s proportion of households with three or more generations living together fell from 68% to 22% (census data). Concurrently, age‑adjusted incidence of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) among 60+ rose from 9% to 16% in urban centers. The decline is attributed to reduced daily intergenerational interaction, which traditionally stimulated memory through storytelling and shared problem‑solving. Politically, the National Policy for Older Persons (1999) emphasizes “active ageing” but lacks enforceable provisions for cognitive engagement programs. Geographically, states with higher literacy and stronger Panchayati Raj institutions (e.g., Tamil Nadu, 30% multigenerational) show lower MCI growth (8% rise) compared to low‑literacy states (e.g., Jharkhand, 25% rise). Psychologically, each 10% drop in multigenerational living correlates with a 0.3‑point decline in MMSE score over 5 years, mediated by decreased cognitive reserve. Sociologically, migration of youth for service‑sector jobs has weakened the “knowledge transfer” axis of the family life cycle. Using this landscape, answer the following.

(E) Design a cost‑effective scaling strategy that leverages existing Anganwadi infrastructure to deliver weekly cognitive‑stimulation kits to 80% of urban elderly within 5 years, estimating the per‑beneficiary annual cost.

A household consumes two goods: organic rice (X) and biodegradable packaging material (Y). Initial prices are Pₓ = ₹40/kg and Pᵧ = ₹20/unit. Monthly income is ₹12,000. Preferences follow the quasi‑linear utility function U = √X + 0.5·Y. The household currently purchases 15 kg of rice and 300 units of packaging. Each kilogram of organic rice is cultivated using a bio‑fertilizer that fixes 0.8 kg of atmospheric nitrogen per kg, contributing to ecosystem health; each unit of packaging sequesters 0.02 kg of CO₂. The household assigns an environmental benefit score EBS = 0.5·(nitrogen fixed) + 0.3·(CO₂ sequestered) per unit consumed, and believes overall satisfaction is U_total = U × (1 + 0.01·EBS).  
Suddenly, the price of organic rice rises to Pₓ' = ₹60/kg due to a supply shock, while Pᵧ and income remain unchanged.  
Using the data above, answer the following sub‑parts.

(E) Compute the environmental benefit score (EBS) for the initial bundle (15 kg X, 300 Y) and for the new optimal bundle after the price change (X'*, Y'*). Then calculate the total adjusted utility U_total = U × (1 + 0.01·EBS) for both bundles. Which bundle yields higher adjusted utility?

In the kharif season of 2023, Vidarbha region received 40% below‑average rainfall, causing a sharp decline in soybean and tur (pigeon pea) yields. The state government announced a Minimum Support Price (MSP) for tur at ₹6,600 per quintal, but procurement agencies reported that only 30% of the harvest was purchased at MSP due to logistical bottlenecks. Farmers, especially those from Other Backward Castes (OBC) and Dalit communities, turned to informal moneylenders for immediate cash to buy seeds and fertilizers for the next rabi season. These lenders, often operating through weekly *haat* traders, charged interest rates of 24% per annum and accepted future crop produce as collateral. Simultaneously, a digital agri‑fintech platform launched a “Crop‑Insurance‑Linked Loan” product that used satellite‑derived vegetation indices to assess risk and offered loans at 12% interest, but required farmers to have a formal land title and a bank account—criteria many smallholder Dalit farmers lacked. By mid‑season, Dalit farmers reported higher loan defaults and loss of land tenure, while OBC farmers with partial land documentation accessed the fintech loans and reported better input access. A parliamentary committee is debating whether the state’s agricultural credit policy is sufficiently embedded in local social realities.

(D) Using the historical crisis node (c11_hist_cbse_02_009), draw a parallel between the 17th‑century European credit crunch and the contemporary Dalit farmer credit squeeze in Vidarbha.

By 2032, rising sea levels and salinity intrusion displace approximately 4.2 million people from the coastal districts of Bangladesh, prompting a surge of undocumented migrants into India’s eastern states (West Bengal, Assam, Odisha). The migrants are predominantly young adults (average age 24) with a fertility rate of 2.8 children per woman and a mortality rate of 5 per 1000. Host states currently exhibit: West Bengal – CBR 16, CDR 7, working‑age share 60%; Assam – CBR 22, CDR 9, working‑age share 55%; Odisha – CBR 18, CDR 8, working‑age share 58%. The Indian government invokes Article 355 (duty to protect states) and the Disaster Management Act 2005 to set up temporary shelters, while the Inter‑State Council (reflecting power‑sharing principles) debates a uniform national rehabilitation policy versus state‑specific packages. Using Malthusian checks, demographic transition stages, age‑structure dynamics, and federal power‑sharing norms, evaluate the likely demographic and socio‑political outcomes.

(A) Estimate the annual natural increase rate (per 1000) contributed by the migrant population alone, assuming its CBR and CDR are as given.

GlobalEd Partners (India-US) dissolves 31-Dec-2023. Partners: Priya (India, 60%), Quinn (US, 40%). Balance Sheet (₹L): Fixed Assets 120, Unrecorded Patents (3, book value 0), Debtors 80, Bank 25, Creditors 50, Priya Capital 120, Quinn Capital 55, Quinn Loan 20. Realization: (i) Patents sold to US subsidiary at transfer price ₹200L (arm's length ₹250L); (ii) Unrecorded liability: US tax penalty ₹30L on transfer pricing adjustment; (iii) Priya takes over 1 patent at ₹60L; (iv) Debtors realize ₹72L (bad debts ₹8L); (v) Fixed assets sold ₹100L; (vi) Creditors paid ₹48L; (vii) Realization expenses ₹5L. Exchange rate: 1 USD = ₹83. Quinn's loan in USD ($240k). Indian tax: 30% on patent gain. US tax: 21% + state 5%. DTAA applies. Priya's capital includes ₹40L revaluation reserve (non-distributable).

(E) Evaluate dissolution from public economics perspective: social return on edtech IP vs private partner payout.

In early 2025 a state education department launched an AI‑based portal to shortlist candidates for government school teaching posts. The portal screened 2400 applications using a machine‑learning model trained on historical hiring data. Of the applicants, 960 were women (40%) and 1440 were men (60%). The model shortlisted 480 candidates (20% of applicants). Among the shortlisted, 120 were women (25% of shortlisted) and 360 were men (75%). The model’s internal fairness audit reported a false‑negative rate (qualified applicants incorrectly rejected) of 18% for women and 12% for men, while the false‑positive rate (unqualified applicants incorrectly shortlisted) was 6% for women and 4% for men. The department also recorded that 70% of shortlisted women accepted the offer, compared to 85% of shortlisted men. The average monthly salary offered was ₹28 000, with no gender difference in the offer amount.

(C) Using accounting qualitative characteristics, assess the reliability of the fairness‑audit claim that “the false‑negative rate for women is 18%.”

A 35‑year‑old woman fleeing conflict in Region X presents with intrusive flashbacks, avoidance of camp social gatherings, and emotional numbness after witnessing violence. A mobile health team offers three interventions: (a) trauma‑focused CBT (a form of behaviour therapy with cognitive elements), (b) psychodynamic psychotherapy focusing on wartime loss and disrupted attachment, and (c) logotherapy (existential approach) helping her find purpose in surviving to aid others. Salivary cortisol samples show elevated baseline levels, indicating HPA‑axis dysregulation. The NGO must allocate limited funds: trauma‑focused CBT costs ₹60,000 for 10 sessions, psychodynamic therapy ₹1,30,000 for 18 sessions, logotherapy ₹90,000 for 12 sessions. Projected improvement in community participation (measured by attendance at vocational training) is estimated as 30% for CBT, 45% for psychodynamic, and 35% for logotherapy. Using the six‑parameter classification, the team must decide which approach best fits the etiology, method, relationship, benefit, and duration while staying within a budget of ₹1,00,000.

(A) Which parameter most strongly indicates an *existential* origin for the woman’s distress?

An NGO based in Kochi conducts a rapid appraisal of households in Alappuzha district where at least one member works in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries. The team notices that many elderly parents live alone, receiving monthly remittances but reporting feelings of “abandonment” despite financial security. The NGO wishes to produce a policy brief that uses Kamala Das’s poem as a literary anchor to argue that remittance‑driven affluence does not alleviate the emotional void captured in lines such as *“soon put that thought away, and looked out at Young Trees sprinting, the merry children spilling out of their homes”*. The brief must (i) decode the poem’s imagery of youthful vigor contrasting with parental stillness, (ii) apply geographical data on Kerala‑GCC migration flows and remittance volumes, (iii) evaluate the effectiveness of the Pravasi Bharatiya Bima Yojana (PBBY) and state‑level NRI welfare schemes in addressing psychosocial needs, and (iv) recommend a community‑based “Virtual Visitation” programme using low‑bandwidth video kiosks, justified by interdisciplinary evidence.

(B) Using the data point “Kerala’s GCC remittances rose to ₹1.1 lakh crore in FY23”, assess whether financial inflows alone can mitigate the emotional distress depicted in the poem.

A central Indian river basin receives 1,200 mm annual rainfall, 85% concentrated in June-September. The basin area is 25,000 km². Runoff coefficient is 0.35. A multipurpose dam is proposed with live storage of 3.5 BCM. Calculate the annual runoff volume and determine what percentage of annual runoff the reservoir can store. Explain the implication for flood control and dry-season water supply.

In Ladakh, farmers traditionally cultivated barley and wheat at elevations up to 3,500 m, relying on glacial meltwater. Recent climate warming has reduced snowpack, shortening the growing season by 20 days. A government pilot introduces polyhouse greenhouse technology powered by solar panels, extending the season to 220 days and enabling vegetable cultivation (tomatoes, capsicum). The initiative is framed under the National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture (NMSA) and aligns with Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council’s water‑user association rules, which allocate irrigation based on historical use. A cost‑benefit analysis shows an initial investment of ₹1.2 million per hectare, annual operational cost ₹150,000, and projected net revenue increase of ₹800,000 per year from higher‑value crops. Farmers must decide whether to adopt the technology, considering environmental limits (low oxygen, high UV) and human agency (technological choice, cultural preference for traditional crops).

(C) Apply the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council’s water‑user association rule (historical‑use allocation) to the greenhouse project. Determine whether the rule supports or hinders adopters under possibilist thinking, and justify using principles of equity and efficiency.

Indian Oil Corporation Ltd. (IOCL) aims to achieve net‑zero operational emissions by 2046. As part of its waste‑management strategy, IOCL plans to recycle plastic waste generated at its three major refineries (Paradip, Panipat, and Mathura). The collected waste averages **1,200 tonnes/month**. IOCL issues a directive: *“All plastic waste collected at refineries shall be segregated into PET, HDPE, and other plastics before being sent to the recycling unit.”*  
The company must (i) classify this directive as a procedure, method, or rule; (ii) design an efficient **method** for the segregation step; (iii) estimate the **monthly cost** of implementing the segregation method if the labor cost is ₹150 per man‑hour, the process requires 0.5 man‑hour per tonne, and overhead is 20 % of labor cost; (iv) conduct a **cost‑benefit analysis** assuming recycling reduces CO₂ emissions by 1.8 tonnes CO₂‑eq per tonne of plastic recycled, the social cost of carbon is ₹800 per tonne CO₂‑eq, and the monthly segregation cost (from iii) is the only cost; (v) discuss one **limitation of planning** that could affect the effectiveness of the rule in the long run.

(E) Identify one **limitation of planning** that could render the segregation rule ineffective over time, and suggest how IOCL might mitigate it.

Country P has Life Expectancy Index = 0.82, Education Index = 0.76, GNI Index = 0.68. Compute its HDI, assign the correct tier, and explain whether a 10% increase in GNI Index alone could push it to the next tier.

A multinational research consortium (MRC) models the impact of rising CO₂ on the Pacific Northwest’s kelp forests, projecting a 30 % loss of habitat by 2040 if emissions continue unchecked. The consortium’s policy brief proposes a “Kelp Silence Initiative”: a yearly, globally coordinated 10‑minute halt of all offshore drilling, shipping, and sonar activity during the kelp spawning window, inspired by Neruda’s lines “fishermen not going to sea” and “whales not harmed.” The brief cites three bodies of evidence: (1) marine biology studies showing a 12 % increase in kelp spawning success when acoustic noise drops below 40 dB; (2) behavioral economics experiments indicating that groups exposed to a brief shared silence exhibit 20 % less conformity bias; (3) historical precedent: the 1994 moratorium on high‑seas drift‑net fishing, which followed a UN‑declared “quiet ocean” day and led to a 40 % rebound in certain fish stocks. Delegates from ten coastal nations must decide whether to adopt the Kelp Silence Initiative, weighing Neruda’s imagery of restraint against UNCLOS Article 194 (marine pollution mitigation) and the psychological concept of groupthink.

(B) Using the theme of collective introspection (The primary theme of 'Keeping Quiet'), assess how the 10‑minute silence could mitigate groupthink in the consortium’s decision‑making process.

In 2030, rising sea levels have submerged parts of the Sundarbans, displacing 1.2 million residents. A Bangladeshi‑Indian NGO organizes a symbolic wedding ceremony for a young Rohingya couple residing in a Kolkata relocation camp, blending Rohingya customs with Bengali traditions, and streams the event via a low‑bandwidth mesh network to diaspora communities worldwide. The ceremony incorporates digital twins of the couples’ ancestral villages (now underwater) rendered in VR, accessible only through donated solar‑powered headsets. Attendance logs show 850,000 unique viewers, with 40% from the displaced Sundarbans community, 30% from global Rohingya diaspora, 20% from Indian urban youth, and 10% from international NGOs. Critics argue the VR reconstruction romanticizes a lost ecology, potentially obscuring ongoing climate injustice, while supporters claim it fosters transnational empathy and preserves intangible heritage. Using Singer’s treatment of the wedding as a lens onto consciousness versus external reality, examine how this climate‑driven, technologically mediated ceremony functions as a site where personal memory, collective trauma, and environmental reality intersect, and assess implications for climate policy, digital heritage, and post‑disaster identity formation.

(B) Analyze the psychological impact on viewers of witnessing a climate‑displaced wedding, focusing on ecological grief and vicarious trauma, and connect this to Margolin’s internal conflict in the story.

In 2023, the government of a north‑Indian state launched “Swasthya‑Setu”, a mandatory health‑tracking app linked to Aadhaar for COVID‑19 vaccination and symptom reporting. The story’s 68‑year‑old protagonist, Lalaji, a retired schoolteacher living in a village of 2,400 inhabitants (≈18% aged ≥ 60), receives a government notice to install the app on his basic smartphone. Lalaji is skeptical: he recalls the 1950s‑60s rural health campaigns (e.g., malaria eradication) where trust was built through face‑to‑face interaction, not surveillance. His 22‑year‑old granddaughter, Meera, a college student in the city, urges him to comply, arguing that the app will secure quicker medical aid and that privacy concerns are exaggerated. The narrative describes Lalaji’s internal conflict, his observation of villagers queuing at the panchayat office to get the app installed, and a symbolic scene where he places his old spectacles on the village well—a metaphor for relinquishing his accustomed way of seeing the world. The text uses irony (the state’s promise of “health security” feels like an intrusion) and symbolism (the well, the spectacles, the app’s blinking notification). Data: village literacy rate 62%; smartphone penetration 34%; elderly app adoption 12%; youth (15‑29) app adoption 68%. The passage ends with Lalaji handing the phone to Meera, saying, “Let the young watch over the numbers; I will watch over the stories.”
