A community artist in Bengaluru’s Koramangala slum creates a large mural titled “Silent Streets”. The mural combines visual metaphors from Neruda’s *Keeping Quiet* – such as “fishermen who would not harm whales” and “hurt hands” – with concrete geographic markers: the location of the nearest water tank (300 m away), the density of households (8 houses per 10 m²), and the route taken by the 2020 farmers’ protest march that passed through the area. Local historians note that the mural invokes the spirit of the 1930 Salt March (peaceful, symbolic) and the 2021 Bengaluru anti‑eviction demonstrations (which used chalk‑drawn outlines of homes). A geography teacher uses the mural to discuss how metaphor can highlight infrastructural deficits, while a psychology student observes that viewers report a heightened sense of “collective efficacy” after spending two minutes observing the artwork. Using the poem’s imagery and metaphor, geographic data on slum layout, and historical examples of non‑violent protest, analyse how the mural constructs a narrative of resilience, what specific metaphors convey about the slum’s lived reality, and how the artwork bridges artistic expression with protest geography.

(C) Apply the historical concept of nonviolent protest to evaluate the mural as a form of symbolic protest, referencing both the 1930 Salt March and the 2021 Bengaluru anti‑eviction demonstrations.

BharatTech Ltd. (Indian listed) acquires 100% of SiliconValley AI Inc. (US) via share swap: 1 BharatTech share for every 3 SV-AI shares. SV-AI has 12 million shares outstanding. BharatTech issues 4 million new shares (face value ₹2, issue price ₹1,200) to SV-AI shareholders via private placement under FEMA automatic route. Simultaneously, BharatTech raises ₹800 crore via QIP (Qualified Institutional Placement) at ₹1,150/share (face value ₹2) to fund integration. QIP issue size: 6.96 million shares. SEBI ICDR requires QIP minimum subscription 90%. Applications received: 12 million shares. The board must allot pro-rata, adjust excess application money, and account for share swap. The merger creates goodwill of ₹2,500 crore. The CFO must also evaluate the impact on Book Value Per Share (BVPS) and P/E ratio pre/post merger, given pre-merger BharatTech PAT ₹600 crore, SV-AI PAT $50 million (₹415 crore at ₹83/$), and pre-merger market cap ₹12,000 crore.

(A) Calculate the minimum subscription amount for QIP (in ₹ crore). If applications worth ₹850 crore received, can allotment proceed? What is the pro-rata allotment ratio?

A consortium of Indologists plans to issue non‑fungible tokens (NFTs) representing high‑resolution images of rare Manu Smriti manuscripts held in private trusts. Each NFT confers the holder a license to display the image digitally but does **not** transfer copyright or physical ownership. The consortium must (i) decide whether the NFTs qualify as intangible assets under Ind‑AS 38, (ii) assess if the license terms violate Dharmashastra‑based restrictions on commodifying sacred texts (which prohibit sale of the Vedas but allow dissemination for education), (iii) compute the expected revenue from a subscription model where institutions pay ₹5 million per year for access to the NFT gallery, growing at 4 % p.a., discounted at 7 %, and (iv) determine the gotra‑based eligibility of a scholar‑trustee who wishes to serve on the consortium’s governance board (the trustee’s paternal gotra matches that of the trust’s founder, but maternal gotra differs).  
Relevant Dharmashastra excerpt: “The Vedas are not to be sold; they may be taught and shared for the welfare of all.” (Adhyaya 2, Verse 17).  
Using the data, answer the following.

(E) The consortium wishes to recognize the NFTs as intangible assets under Ind‑AS 38. State two criteria that must be satisfied and explain whether the NFTs meet each criterion given the scenario.

In 2025 the municipal government of Chengdu introduces a “One‑Centimetre Rule”: children under 120 cm travel free on buses; those 120 cm or taller pay full fare. Height is measured at the bus door by a conductor using a fixed ruler. The policy cites efficiency and fairness. Tao Ying, a factory‑canteen cook, regularly takes her 5‑year‑old son Xiao Ye (height 119 cm) on the bus. She notices that conductors sometimes let him pass without measuring when they appear “casual,” and she recalls a flashback to her own childhood when a similar rule was used during the 1960s “send‑down” movement to restrict rural youth’s urban access. Using the story’s linear plot (bus ride, jacket incident, measurement scene) and its flashbacks to her maternal resolve, analyse how the narrative structure reinforces the story’s critique of arbitrary authority, and compare this to the historical hukou‑based transport restrictions of the 1950s‑70s.

(A) Identify the three chronological plot points in the story that correspond to the linear timeline and explain how each point maps onto a stage of the “One‑Centimetre Rule” implementation (announcement, enforcement, resistance).

"The distinction between Private and Public Sector is blurring." Critically examine this statement in the context of post-1991 India using THREE specific developments: (1) Disinvestment below 51%, (2) Public-Private Partnerships (PPP), (3) Listing of PSUs on stock exchanges. For each, explain whether the legal classification changes or only the economic character changes.

A coalition of resident welfare associations (RWAs) in Delhi launches a mobile‑app‑based petition platform that collects geotagged signatures from citizens demanding the implementation of the Slum Rehabilitation Scheme (SRS) under the National Urban Housing & Habitat Policy, 2007. Within three months the platform records 1.8 million verified signatures, of which 62 % come from households earning below the poverty line. The coalition presents the data to the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, citing Article 38(2) (State to minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities) and Article 21 (right to life, including adequate shelter). Simultaneously, a real‑estate developers’ association lobbies the ministry to delay SRS implementation, arguing it would increase project costs and hinder economic growth (invoking Article 19(1)(g) – right to practice any profession). A newly formed political party, “Shelter Front,” promises to fast‑track SRS if elected in the upcoming municipal elections. Historical analogies are invoked: the coalition compares its digital petition to the British Chartists’ mass petitions of 1839‑1848 (c11_hist_cbse_01_005) and to the Mughal emperor Akbar’s farm‑land revenue records (c11_hist_cbse_02_001). The Election Commission notes that the Shelter Front has not yet filed its asset declaration under the Representation of the People Act, 1951, while the developers’ association’s funding sources remain opaque.

(A) Using the goal‑method‑accountability triad, classify the resident welfare association coalition in the scenario as a pressure group, interest group, or political party. Justify your answer.

A tech‑start‑up “HydroGenix” plans to set up a 10 MW electrolyzer‑based green hydrogen plant as a **single‑use** project. The project’s **Programme** includes: objective – produce 1 tonne/day of green hydrogen; policy – use only renewable electricity; procedure – EPC bidding, safety audits; resources – land, water, electrolyzer stacks. Capital expenditure (CAPEX) is ₹500 crore (electrolyzer, balance‑of‑plant, land). Annual OPEX is ₹30 crore (electricity, water, maintenance). Expected selling price of hydrogen is ₹350/kg. Variable cost per kg (electricity consumption) is ₹150/kg. The plant will operate at 90 % capacity. The start‑up expects to raise ₹200 crore equity and the rest as 8‑year term debt at 9 % interest, repayable evenly. The government offers a production‑linked incentive (PLI) of ₹50/kg for the first 3 years.  
Using the following:  
- Investment multiplier for green hydrogen = 3.0  
- Price elasticity of demand for hydrogen = –1.2  
- Corporate tax rate = 25 %  
- Discount rate for NPV = 10 %  
Assume straight‑line depreciation over 10 years, zero salvage.

(C) Construct a simplified milestone schedule (in months) for the HydroGenix project with five sequential activities: (1) Feasibility & permits (4 mo), (2) EPC contracting (6 mo), (3) Civil works (8 mo), (4) Electrolyzer installation & commissioning (10 mo), (5) Trial run & handover (3 mo). Compute the total project duration and the earliest start date for activity 4 if activity 1 begins on 1 January 2026.

In 2024, a coalition of 1.2 million Indian gig‑platform workers (ride‑hailing, food‑delivery, freelance micro‑tasks) launched a nationwide campaign after a series of algorithmic wage cuts reduced median earnings by 18 % over six months. The coalition split into four factions: (i) **Reformists** demand a statutory minimum wage for platform work and transparent algorithmic audits via a new labour‑code amendment; (ii) **Revolutionaries** call for the abolition of proprietary platforms, advocating worker‑owned cooperatives that replace the current capitalist model; (iii) **Resistance** groups seek to defend existing labour‑rights protections (e.g., the 2020 Social Security Code) against further erosion by platform‑unilateral policy changes; (iv) **Reactionaries** argue for a return to pre‑digital informal work arrangements, claiming that platformisation has destroyed traditional community‑based labour networks and advocating stricter immigration controls on migrant platform workers. The Ministry of Labour issued a draft notice permitting platforms to self‑regulate algorithmic pricing, citing “flexibility” and “innovation”. Workers’ unions filed a writ petition alleging violation of Article 19(1)(c) (right to form associations) and Article 21 (right to livelihood). Historical analogues are drawn from the 19th‑century Luddite resistance to mechanised textile mills and the early 20th‑century Bombay textile workers’ movement.

(D) Assess whether the Ministry’s draft notice permitting self‑regulation of algorithmic pricing constitutes a reasonable restriction on the right to form associations under Article 19(1)(c), using the power‑sharing model of Belgium (The Belgian Accommodation Model) as an analogy for accommodating divergent interests.

A satellite in low orbit observes a planet whose limb appears as a perfect circle of radius **R = 6371 km** (Earth). The day‑night terminator, due to the planet’s axial tilt and orbital geometry, projects onto the planet’s cross‑section as a straight line **y = (1/√3)x – 2000** (km). The satellite’s sensor can only use data from the **illuminated side**, i.e., points of the circle that satisfy **y > (1/√3)x – 2000**.  
**(a)** Find the x‑coordinates where the line intersects the circle.  
**(b)** Set up the integral (using vertical strips) for the area of the illuminated crescent (portion of the circle above the line).  
**(c)** Evaluate the integral to obtain the exact illuminated area (in km²).  
**(d)** Explain when it would be preferable to use horizontal strips (expressing the circle as x = …) and write the corresponding integral.  
**(e)** If the solar photon flux incident on the planet varies linearly with height as **F(y) = 1.5 – 0.0001y** (photons·cm⁻²·s⁻¹·km⁻¹), compute the total photon power intercepted by the illuminated crescent (in photons·s⁻¹) by integrating F(y) over the area.

(E) If the solar photon flux incident on the planet varies linearly with height as **F(y) = 1.5 – 0.0001y** (photons·cm⁻²·s⁻¹·km⁻¹), compute the total photon power intercepted by the illuminated crescent (in photons·s⁻¹) by integrating F(y) over the area.

NexGen Robotics Pvt. Ltd. (unlisted, Indian startup) has 2,00,000 equity shares (FV ₹10) outstanding. Capital structure: Equity Share Capital ₹20,00,000; Securities Premium ₹15,00,000; General Reserve ₹25,00,000; Retained Earnings ₹10,00,000; 10% Debentures ₹30,00,000; Bank Loan ₹20,00,000. The board proposes buyback of equity shares to settle vested ESOPs (8,000 shares) and return surplus cash to early angels. Buyback price: ₹250/share. Fresh issue: 20,000 8% Preference Shares (FV ₹100) at par for funding. Companies Act 2013 Sec 68 applies (debt-equity ≤ 2:1 post-buyback; buyback ≤ 25% of paid-up capital + free reserves; 25% of paid-up equity capital in a year). The CFO must maximize buyback quantity while minimizing WACC impact. Economic concept: Opportunity cost of using free reserves vs. fresh issue (c10_eco_cbse_01_002), and development trade-off between shareholder payout vs. reinvestment (c10_eco_cbse_01_003).

(E) The board considers buying back 8,000 shares (full ESOP) by increasing fresh preference issue to 30,000 shares. Check Sec 68 compliance. If non-compliant, suggest minimum fresh issue to make 8,000 buyback legal.

Imagine the Indian delegation at COP‑28 delivering a opening statement that mirrors Sen’s style. The speaker says:  

> “Our planet is a fevered patient, its temperature rising like a restless child’s sigh. We have walked the monsoon‑soaked plains of Rajasthan, felt the cracked earth of Vidarbha, and heard the lament of sinking Sundarbans. Like the ancient sages who debated under the banyan tree, we now sit in the glass‑walled halls of Sharm el‑Sheikh, arguing not for borders but for breaths. The Paris Agreement is a promise etched in sand; we must carve it in stone before the tide washes it away.”  

Supporting data (provided to students):  
- Average temperature increase over India (1901‑2020): +0.7 °C.  
- Share of renewable electricity in India (2023): 22 %.  
- CO₂ emissions per capita: India 1.9 t, USA 15.5 t, EU 6.4 t (2022).  
- Length of Sundarbans coastline: ≈ 350 km; projected loss by 2050 under RCP 8.5: ≈ 120 km.  

Students must identify imagery and metaphor, link them to Sen’s argumentative tradition, interpret environmental data, and assess rhetorical impact.

(A) Identify four distinct images in the speaker’s statement and specify the primary sense each evokes.

A farmer in Punjab mixes three types of fertilizers F1, F2, F3 (in kg) to get a blend. The nutrient content per kg is: Nitrogen (N): F1=2, F2=1, F3=3; Phosphorus (P): F1=1, F2=2, F3=1; Potassium (K): F1=3, F2=1, F3=2. He wants a blend with 10 kg N, 8 kg P, 9 kg K. Determine if such a blend is possible. If yes, find the amounts; if not, explain why.

The Cauvery basin (Karnataka-Tamil Nadu) has mean annual rainfall 950 mm, CV=25%. Karnataka (upper riparian) has expanded irrigation in the last 30 years, while Tamil Nadu (lower riparian) has established paddy cultivation. In a deficit year (rainfall = 700 mm), Karnataka withholds flow to fill its reservoirs. Analyze the conflict using: (a) rainfall variability data, (b) upstream-downstream asymmetry, (c) cropping pattern water demand, (d) institutional framework (Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal award). Propose a variability-adaptive sharing formula.
Fill in the blank: Observe a piece of bread left on the kitchen counter for 3-4 days in humid ______ monsoon weather — fuzzy greenish patches appear and spread rapidly.

In early 2022 a consortium of public and private firms received clearance from the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) to construct a 1,200 MW run‑of‑the‑river hydropower project on the Siang River in Arunachal Pradesh, threatening to submerge over 4,500 ha of forest and displace approximately 12,000 Adivasi (mainly Adi and Mishmi) households. Indigenous groups, supported by national NGOs (e.g., Narmada Bachao Andolan veterans) and student unions, launched the “Save Siang” movement. Protests combined traditional cultural rallies, sit‑ins at project sites, and a coordinated online campaign (#SaveSiang) that generated 1.8 M Twitter impressions and 650 k YouTube views of documentary clips within four months. The movement demanded: (i) immediate halt of construction, (ii) recognition of forest rights under the Forest Rights Act, 2006, (iii) an independent impact assessment by a tribal‑led committee, and (iv) compensation based on market value of lost livelihoods. The Union government responded by constituting a high‑level committee (including MoEFCC, Ministry of Tribal Affairs, and the State Government) that recommended a redesign reducing submerged area to 2,800 ha and offering a one‑time livelihood package of ₹4 lakh per affected family. The Arunachal Pradesh State Legislature passed a resolution supporting the project citing regional development needs, while the State Tribal Advisory Council objected, highlighting lack of free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC). By late 2023, construction resumed on a revised design; protest activity declined after the livelihood package was disbursed to 70 % of eligible families. Critics contend that the movement achieved partial environmental mitigation and monetary compensation but failed to secure FPIC, halt the project, or establish a permanent tribal oversight mechanism, and faced state tactics such as internet throttling in border districts and filing of cases under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act against activists. Using the concepts of popular movements, power‑sharing (Belgium and Sri Lanka models), and limits/achievements, evaluate the movement’s achievements and shortcomings.

(A) Classify the Save Siang protest according to the leadership and organization framework in.

In 1950, a village in Punjab receives the first generous monsoon after Partition, recording 620 mm rainfall (IMD data). Children, freed from the immediate anxieties of refugee camps, spend days bathing in temporary ponds and flying kites made from recycled cloth. Adults, meanwhile, are occupied with implementing the Land Reform Act 1950, redistributing 12 acres of cultivable land per household and attending night‑school literacy drives (literacy rate ≈ 18 %). The poem “irax” describes a child’s unrestricted play in monsoon‑laden fields, the sudden call of an adult to herd cattle, and the fleeting imagination that turns rain‑drops into silver boats. Using this scenario, students must identify the secondary themes in the poem, locate textual evidence, and explain how the historical land‑reform context and monsoon geography intensify each theme.

(E) Synthesize all four secondary themes to explain how they collectively enrich the primary theme of childhood freedom in the poem, taking into account the monsoon’s ecological role (groundwater recharge ↑ 15 % post‑1950 reforms) and the socio‑economic shift toward owner‑cultivation.

The WTO’s Agreement on Agriculture (AoA) requires member countries to reduce trade‑distorting domestic support (the “Amber Box”) by specified percentages over implementation periods. India, a major producer of wheat and rice, currently reports Amber‑Box support of US$12 billion annually, largely due to minimum support prices (MSPs) for wheat and rice, input subsidies (fertilizer, power, irrigation), and crop‑specific incentives. India argues that its support is necessary for food security and livelihood protection, invoking the “Peace Clause” (Article 13 of the AoA) which temporarily shields developing‑country members from legal challenges if they meet certain transparency and notification requirements. The Peace Clause is set to expire at the end of 2025 unless renewed. Historically, India’s Green Revolution (mid‑1960s) introduced high‑yielding varieties (HYVs) of wheat and rice in the Punjab‑Haryana region, dramatically increasing yields but also leading to groundwater depletion and soil salinity. Geographically, the Indo‑Gangetic plains (IGP) account for ~55 % of India’s cereal production, while rain‑fed drylands (e.g., Rajasthan, Maharashtra) contribute ~30 % and are more vulnerable to climate variability. Relevant data:  
- Average MSP for wheat: ₹2 200 per quintal (≈US$26/q).  
- Average market price: ₹1 800 per quintal (≈US$21/q).  
- Subsidy per quintal = MSP – market price = ₹400 (≈US$5/q).  
- India’s annual wheat production: 110 million tonnes (≈11 million quintals).  
- Fertilizer subsidy contributes an additional US$3 billion to Amber‑Box.  
- Power‑irrigation subsidy adds US$2 billion.  
The WTO’s Committee on Agriculture has requested India to justify its Amber‑Box levels and outline a roadmap for compliance post‑2025.

(B) Calculate the annual Amber‑Box contribution (in US$) from the wheat minimum support price subsidy alone, using the data provided.

The Joint Parliamentary Committee on State Reorganisation (JPCSR) was constituted in 2023 to evaluate a fresh demand for bifurcation of a hypothetical state ‘Pradesh’ into two regions: Region A (coastal) and Region B (inland). The committee received the following socio‑economic data: Region B’s average annual per‑capita income is ₹1,80,000, while Region A’s is ₹2,40,000. Region B hosts 30 % of the state’s irrigation projects but receives 45 % of the total water allocation. Historical records show that during the 18th‑19th centuries, coastal ports accounted for 78 % of the state’s external trade, leaving the inland region largely agrarian (Trade, Commerce and Long-Distance Exchange in Mesopotamia (c). Cultural‑linguistic surveys indicate a 0.62 similarity index between the dialects of Region B and the state’s official language, compared with 0.88 for Region A. Public‑sector employment in Region B is 22 % of total state jobs versus 35 % in Region A. Central fiscal transfers per capita are ₹12,000 for Region B and ₹18,000 for Region A. The committee must decide whether economic disparity, historical trade patterns, and cultural distinctiveness jointly satisfy the criteria for statehood under Article 3 of the Constitution.

(B) Compute the water‑allocation efficiency index for Region B, defined as (actual water allocation %) ÷ (irrigation‑project share %).

The Geomagnetic Polarity Time Scale (GPTS) shows that the Cretaceous Normal Superchron (CNS, chron C34n) lasted from 121 to 83 Ma — a remarkably long 38 Myr interval with no reversals. A magnetic profile across the Pacific Plate shows the CNS anomaly (a broad, smooth positive anomaly) is 1,140 km wide on one flank. Calculate the half-spreading rate during the CNS. Then, explain why the CNS anomaly is often used as a "keystone" for identifying Mesozoic magnetic lineations and reconstructing Pacific plate tectonics, despite the lack of internal reversal boundaries within it.

Pochampally weavers face existential threats from climate-induced cotton yield volatility and powerloom competition. A Telangana NGO proposes forming producer cooperatives that cultivate climate-resilient cotton (HS-6 variety) using drip irrigation, coupled with common facility centres for solar-powered dyeing and digital marketing. The cooperatives would mandate traditional pit-loom weaving and natural dyes to maintain GI eligibility. However, elders argue that drip irrigation alters soil microbiota critical for cotton fibre quality, and solar dyeing lacks the microbial diversity of open-vat indigo fermentation needed for authentic colour depth. Field data shows HS-6 cotton has 25% higher yield but 18% lower staple length variability (more uniform) than local rain-fed cotton, while solar indigo vats operate at 32°C average vs traditional 28°C. Analyze whether this model preserves the textile's cultural essence and GI viability, considering fibre science, dyeing microbiology, cooperative economics, and regional agro-climatology.

(A) Determine if HS-6 cotton's 18% lower staple length variability (coefficient of variation reduced from 0.22 to 0.18) sufficiently compensates for its 15% shorter average staple length (23.8mm vs local 28mm) to maintain yarn evenness adequate for Pochampally Ikat's resist-dyeing process, given that yarn CV must be <0.12 for precise ikat patterning.

A patient with hyperthyroidism is prescribed oral Iodine‑131 (^131₅₃I) for targeted beta‑radiation therapy. The nuclide decays with a half‑life of 8.02 days, emitting beta particles (average energy 0.19 MeV) and gamma photons (364 keV). The treatment protocol requires calculating (i) the decay constant and mean life, (ii) the activity of a 150 MBq administered dose after 48 h, (iii) the energy deposited per decay assuming 80 % of beta energy is absorbed in tissue, (iv) the number of ^131I atoms initially present, and (v) the mass of iodine needed, using the molar mass of iodine (≈126.9 g mol⁻¹). The problem binds radioactive decay laws, exponential functions (math), and stoichiometric mole‑mass conversion (chemistry) to assess therapeutic efficacy and safety.

(A) Determine the decay constant λ (in s⁻¹) and mean life τ (in s) for ^131I given its half‑life t₁/₂ = 8.02 days.
Fill in the blank: This happens because natural chlorine is a mixture of isotopes ³⁵Cl (______) and ³⁷Cl (25%).

Compare and contrast the contamination risk profile of using (a) 10% heat‑inactivated fetal bovine serum (FBS) versus (b) a chemically defined, serum‑free, protein‑free medium for a GMP‑grade CHO cell line producing a therapeutic monoclonal antibody. Include in your answer the impact on downstream purification and regulatory compliance.
A cylindrical juice container has a radius of 7 cm and a height of 20 cm. Calculate its volume in cm³. (Use π = 22/7)

In early 2025 a deepfake video falsely showing a prominent politician endorsing a extremist ideology goes viral on a major short‑form video platform. The platform’s trust‑and‑safety team responds by implementing DNS sinkholing: all domains identified as hosting the deepfake or facilitating its redistribution are redirected to a sinkhole server that serves a warning page and logs request metadata. The sinkhole uses IPv6 addresses from the 2001:db8:dead::/48 block and employs anycast with nodes in six metropolitan hubs (New York, London, São Paulo, Lagos, Tokyo, Sydney). Platform analytics reveal that 68 % of users who encounter the warning page abandon further sharing, while 12 % attempt to bypass the block via VPNs or alternate DNS resolvers. Sociological surveys indicate that communities with low media‑literacy scores are twice as likely to believe the deepfake despite the warning. Psychological studies show that repeated exposure to corrected information reduces belief persistence by 0.3 per exposure (on a 0‑1 scale). Students must evaluate the technical, sociological, and psychological effectiveness of the DNS‑based mitigation, consider legal implications of mandatory DNS filtering, and propose improvements.

(D) Analyze whether a government mandate requiring all ISPs to implement DNS sinkholing for domains hosting deepfake content satisfies the proportionality principle under Article 19(3) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR).

In a metropolitan city, a survey of residents aged 60+ shows that 27 % are underweight (BMI < 18.5) and 34 % have deficiencies in vitamin D and B12. Simultaneously, 41 % are overweight/obese (BMI ≥ 25), indicating a double burden of malnutrition. Traditional joint families are giving way to nuclear households, reducing intra‑familial food sharing. The municipal health department plans to launch a community‑based meal programme combined with regular health check‑ups and social engagement activities. As a public health nutrition specialist, you are to analyse the implications across developmental domains and propose a holistic intervention.

(B) Apply Erikson’s psychosocial stage of “integrity vs despair” to predict how chronic vitamin D deficiency may affect psychosocial outcome in late adulthood.

A low‑Earth‑orbit satellite uses solar panels that feed an inverter producing a sinusoidal voltage of V_rms = 200 V at f = 50 Hz. To enable short radar bursts, the inverter charges a capacitor bank which then discharges into the transmitter. Each burst requires 5 kW for 10 ms. The capacitor must store enough energy to meet this demand while the inverter continues to supply the average load. Assume ideal capacitor, negligible ESR, and that the voltage across the capacitor follows the inverter voltage (i.e., V_c(t) = V_m sin ωt). The cost of the dielectric material is $0.02 per µF, and a design safety factor of 1.2 on capacitance is required. Using the data, determine the required capacitance, its reactance, the rms and peak currents, the phasor relationship, the average power dissipated, and the final cost of the capacitor bank.

(C) Find the peak current I_peak and state the phase relationship between current and voltage in this pure capacitive circuit.

A village in Punjab has 8,000 residents spread over 20 sq km, with 65% of workers in agriculture. A nearby settlement has 12,000 residents over 5 sq km, with 30% in agriculture. Using the textbook's criteria, classify each settlement and justify your classification.

In September 2025 a viral video on platform X (formerly Twitter) showed a digitally altered clip of Isaac Asimov delivering a lecture in which he warned that “by 2030, autonomous AI will surpass human intellect and decide the fate of civilization.” Fact‑checkers traced the footage to a deep‑fake generated by an open‑source model fine‑tuned on Asimov’s public speeches and writings. The video amassed 4.2 million views in 48 hours, prompting a wave of posts claiming Asimov had “predicted” the AI takeover. A coalition of science‑communicators launched a counter‑campaign, quoting Asimov’s essay “On Science Fiction” where he employs a witty, self‑deprecating tone to dismantle prescientific myths and emphasizes that true science fiction rests on the premise that *science and technology shape the future*, not on mystical prophecy. They also cited a 2024 Pew Research survey showing that 61 % of adults who encountered the deep‑fake later expressed heightened anxiety about AI, versus 38 % who saw a corrective clip featuring Asimov’s actual essay excerpts. Using Asimov’s wit‑driven critic persona, his demarcation of science fiction from prescientific speculation, and his historical view of scientific progress, assess the efficacy of humor‑based rebuttals in combating AI‑generated misinformation.

(C) From the humor‑effects literature in , predict how a witty rebuttal (e.g., a meme that jokes “Asimov never said AI would rule us; he said we’d *invent* the rulers”) influences belief revision in individuals exposed to the deep‑fake, and specify the underlying mechanism.

In early 2025 a parliamentary committee drafts the “Right to Truth and Transparency Act” (RTTA) promising citizens access to all government files, including security‑related documents. The bill’s emblem features an open book superimposed on a shattered chain, symbolising liberation of knowledge. However, a concealed clause permits the executive to classify any document as “national‑security secret” without judicial review, effectively allowing blanket secrecy. A psychologist’s study shows that citizens exposed to RTTA’s publicity exhibit heightened cognitive dissonance when later denied access, measured by a 22 % increase in self‑reported stress scores. A constitutional lawyer argues the clause violates Article 21’s procedural fairness, while an economist estimates the secrecy provision could save ₹ 3 000 crores in potential litigation costs. Using irony, symbolism, legal reasoning, psychology, and economics, evaluate the RTTA’s internal consistency.

(C) Using the psychology node c11_psy_cbse_01_007, calculate the expected increase in stress‑related healthcare utilization if 1 million citizens experience the cognitive dissonance described, assuming a baseline utilization rate of 5 visits/1000 persons/year and a 22 % rise in stress translates linearly to healthcare visits.

Three women scientists from a Home Science background launch a start‑up producing plant‑based protein isolates using waste from local fruit‑processing units. They secured ₹2 crore seed funding under the “Women Entrepreneurship Platform” (WEP) and aim to scale to ₹50 crore turnover in five years. Each founder works 70 hrs/week, reports occasional insomnia, and scores high on Maslow’s self‑actualization drive (ps11_psy_cbse_03_001). Their lab generates bio‑hazard waste requiring strict containment; they incur ₹15 lakh/year for biomedical waste management (b11_bio_cbse_05_004). The venture aligns with the UN SDG 12 (responsible consumption) and the National Policy on Women’s Empowerment, which emphasizes “meaningful work” and “social responsibility” (c12_hs_cbse_01_010, c12_hs_cbse_01_011). Sociologically, the founders challenge traditional gender norms in STEM, noting a 30 % increase in female enrollment in allied health courses since the start‑up’s launch (s11_soc_cbse_03_005).

(B) Using the work‑gender node (c12_hs_cbse_01_008), explain how the founders’ venture challenges traditional gender stereotypes, citing two specific evidences from the scenario.

In the desert belts of Rajasthan, a collective of women artisans runs “Rang‑Barot”, a cooperative that produces hand‑embroidered wall hangings inspired by Aunt Jennifer’s tigers. Each panel replicates the tigers’ “bright topaz” hue using locally sourced silk, while the border motifs mimic the “ivory needle” struggle. The women describe how middlemen traders, often men, take 70 % of the sale price, leaving them with meagre earnings—a modern echo of the “massive weight of Uncle’s wedding band”. Recent government reports show a 12 % rise in rural‑to‑urban migration among young women seeking factory jobs, yet the cooperative’s income has increased 18 % after receiving a state‑run marketing grant linked to the “Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao” initiative. The cooperative’s leader invokes the historical role of women in textile guilds during the Mughal era (c11_his_cbse_01_003) and cites sociological studies on patriarchy in rural labor markets (c11_soc_cbse_02_006). Visitors to an urban exhibition are asked to assess whether the art truly liberates the creators or merely aestheticizes their subjugation.

(B) Infer why the cooperative’s earnings remain low despite increased sales, using two textual clues from the poem that parallel the economic exploitation described.

China’s proposed “Motong” dam on the upper Brahmaputra (Yarlung Tsangpo) aims to generate 60 GW and regulate flow for downstream agriculture. Satellite‑based snow‑cover data show a 9 % decline in winter snowfall over the Tibetan plateau (mean 450 mm water equivalent, σ=60 mm) between 2000‑2020, potentially reducing spring melt contribution. India’s Arunachal Pradesh government fears reduced dry‑season flow affecting the 2.7 lakh ha irrigated area of the Ranganadi project and the 1,300 MW Lower Subansiri HEP. Historical treaties: the 1906 Anglo‑Chinese Convention recognized India’s right to “reasonable use” of Brahmaputra waters, while the 2006 Framework Agreement on Hydrological Data Sharing (non‑binding) mandates annual data exchange. The affected area includes 12 tribal groups (e.g., Adi, Galo) whose livelihood depends on shifting cultivation (jhum) and river‑based fishing, with average household income of ₹7,200/month. Environmental impact assessments warn of altered sediment transport threatening the Kaziranga National Park’s grassland ecosystems. India has raised the issue at the UN Watercourses Convention platform, citing equitable and reasonable utilization under Article 5.

(E) Propose a three‑layered mitigation framework addressing (i) reduced dry‑season flow, (ii) sediment starvation downstream, and (iii) tribal livelihood insecurity, specifying one legal instrument, one technical measure, and one socio‑economic scheme for each layer.

AgriSense Technologies Pvt. Ltd., launched in early 2024, offers a subscription‑based AI platform that analyses drone‑captured hyperspectral imagery and IoT soil‑sensor data to prescribe variable‑rate fertilizer application for wheat farmers in Punjab. The platform charges INR 500 per acre per season. Initial investment includes INR 120 crore for drone fleet, INR 80 crore for AI‑server infrastructure, and INR 40 crore for sensor kits. The company expects to cover 2 million acres in Year 1, growing at 25 % p.a. GST on SaaS services is 18 %; the government provides a 20 % subsidy on capital expenditure for agri‑tech startups under the Sub‑Mission on Agricultural Mechanisation (SMAM). Farmers’ price elasticity of demand for fertilizer is –0.6, and a 10 % reduction in fertilizer use (due to AI optimisation) raises average wheat yield by 4 %. Using this information, evaluate opportunities/threats across the five business‑environment dimensions, compute the tax and subsidy impact on cash flows, assess the elasticity‑driven revenue effect, and recommend strategic actions.

The Apatani tribe of Arunachal Pradesh traditionally practiced clan exogamy (marriage outside one’s clan) with limited endogamy. Survey data show pre‑shift marriage patterns: 80% clan exogamous, 10% endogamous, 5% hypergamy (woman marries higher‑income man), 5% hypogamy. In 2021, the state of **Punjab** amended its tenancy act to grant sharecroppers (batai) permanent heritable rights, security against eviction, and a fixed rent of 20 % of produce. The Madhya Pradesh government proposes linking the Narmada and Shipra rivers (2025-2035) to divert surplus Narmada water to the drought-prone Malwa region, promising: (1) Irrigation for 20 lakh hectares of farmland, (2) Drinking water security for 100 lakh urban residents, (3) Revival of 500 traditional water bodies. Historical context: Past interlinking projects (e.g., Periyar in Kerala, 1895) increased agricultural yield by 25% but caused 15% loss in riparian biodiversity (per ICAR 2010); the Narmada-Shipra link requires tunneling through Vindhyachal hills, risking seismic instability in Zone II. Geographical constraint: Malwa region has black cotton soil (vertisol) with high shrinkage-swelling potential, making canal lining prone to cracks; average annual rainfall is 800mm (vs. Narmada basin's 1200mm). Recent data shows: 60% of Malwa farmers rely on groundwater (declining at 1m/year); only 20% have access to canal irrigation; Shipra river's ecological flow requirement is 15% of lean season flow (per NGT order). Environmental groups warn: Linking will alter Narmada's sediment transport, reduce Shipra's dilution capacity, and increase waterlogging in Malwa by 30% (per IIT Madras study).
**Task:** Analyze the assumption that river linking will solve water scarcity without significant ecological cost, using evidence from the scenario, then evaluate if the proposal adheres to the precautionary principle.

(D) Using historical project data and soil mechanics principles, calculate the approximate percentage of canal seepage loss in the Narmada-Shipra link attributable to Malwa's vertisol soil, and justify why this undermines the irrigation promise.

Estimate the reduction in average annual defence expenditure (as % of GDP) for Bandung states if the non‑alignment stance led to a 15 % cut in military spending, given that pre‑Bandung average defence spend was 4.2 % of GDP.

The City Metropolitan Authority (CMA) of Megalopolis proposes a “Heritage Transit Loop” – a replica 1920s‑style tram line operating alongside the modern metro to boost tourism and reduce commuter stress. In 2023 a wealthy Mumbai businesswoman, Ms. Ishani Desai, files a suit in the Supreme Court claiming half of her paternal ancestral property (a ₹ 2,200 crore real‑estate portfolio) based on two grounds: (1) she retained her natal gotra (Desai) after marriage, contrary to the patrilineal gotra‑exogamy norm, and (2) she received stridhana‑type gifts (jewelry, shares) from her mother’s family that were never accounted for in the partition. The Government of Rajasthan launches “वृद्ध‑स्मृति धरोहर” (Vriddha‑Smriti Dharo­har), a scheme to digitally record oral histories of villagers aged 60+ in the Shekhawati region. Using the secondary themes from “नवलिक नसोंनकल” (erosion of traditional family values, resilience of the human spirit, ancestral home as memory repository, communication gap) and the cross‑subject concepts listed, answer the following sub‑parts.

(E) Using the psychological concept of resilience in later life, predict the likely mental‑health outcome for elders who actively participate in the oral‑history interviews versus those who decline, assuming equal baseline depression scores.

Mr Lamb decides to replant part of his garden with dwarf apple trees that yield fruit after three years. Design the evening snack (≤ ₹8/child) that meets the remaining nutrient deficits (Energy 550 kcal, Protein 5 g, Fe 3.2 mg, VA 100 µg) using the ingredients bajra, ragi, arhar dal, spinach, oil, and iodized salt (negligible cost). The Uttar Pradesh Tourism Department plans to promote the Braj region (Mathura‑Vrindavan) as a global spiritual‑tourism hub. In a semi‑arid region, prolonged drought has reduced crop yields by 55% over three years. The state government proposes a “Smart Coastal Hub” on a 150 km² plain adjacent to the sea. A consortium aims to establish a green hydrogen production hub in the Great Lakes industrial region (USA‑Canada border) to supply steel plants transitioning from coal‑based to hydrogen‑based reduction. The hub will use offshore wind farms (capacity 2 GW) on Lake Erie, electrolyzers (efficiency 70 %), and storage caverns. Sixteen‑year‑old Meera spends upwards of five hours daily on a short‑video platform, chasing viral trends. In 2026, the Government of India approves the formation of a new state, “Vidarbha”, carved out of eastern Maharashtra. The state’s planners must prepare a five‑year fiscal plan (2027‑2032). They have the following census data:

The Ministry of Tourism, Government of Saudi Arabia, is assessing the **economic contribution of Hajj and Umrah** to the national GDP. In early 2025 a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) is filed before the Supreme Court challenging Rule 4(2) of the IAS Examination Regulations, which mandates a minimum of 60 % marks in the English language paper for eligibility. In 2025, the United Nations Permanent Forum on Indigenous Issues (UNPFII) and the International Dalit Solidarity Network (IDSN) co‑host a virtual summit titled “Voices of the Marginalised: Memory, Resistance, and Reparation.” Delegates from the Lakota Nation (USA), the Adivasi communities of central India, and Tamil Dalit activists present case studies. The Lok Sabha Secretariat deployed an AI translation system in 2024 to provide real-time Hindi-English interpretation during debates. Initial audits reveal a 22% higher error rate in translating Opposition members' speeches compared to Treasury benches, particularly with idiomatic expressions and sarcasm. For instance, a Treasury member saying "यह नीति जितनी स्पष्ट है, उतनी ही अस्पष्ट है उसकी नीयत" (The policy is as clear as its intent is unclear) was translated literally as "The policy is as clear as its intent is unclear" – missing the ironic reversal.
