The state government proposes to develop “Aurora Smart City” on the outskirts of an existing notified town area committee, “Shantinagar.” The proposed smart city spans 25 km² and currently houses a population of 450,000 (density 18,000 persons/km²). Of the 200,000 male main workers recorded, 150,000 are engaged in non‑agricultural activities (IT services, finance, tourism). The area overlaps partially with a cantonment board jurisdiction (covering 5 km² of the smart city). The project aims to achieve smart‑city status under the Government of India’s Smart Cities Mission, which requires the area to be classified as an urban settlement per Census criteria and to have a unified urban local body (ULB) for project financing. However, the plan faces two challenges: (i) a group of farmers claims the land acquisition violates the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013; (ii) existing slum settlements (occupying 2 km²) need rehabilitation under the Slum Rehabilitation Authority. Using geographic, political‑science, accounting, and sociogeographic concepts, assess the feasibility of the proposal.

(E) Assess the two major challenges to the proposal—(i) land acquisition under the 2013 Act and (ii) slum rehabilitation—by identifying the relevant political‑science principle and socio‑geographic concept, and suggest one accounting‑based mitigation measure for each.

Propose a mixed‑methods study to test whether increased code‑mixing causally raises reader engagement, specifying the independent variable, dependent variable, control variables, and the statistical model; then predict the expected change in average comments if code‑mixing rises from 10 % to 20 % assuming a linear regression coefficient of 0.45 comments per percent point of mixing.

GenomeThera LLP, a biotech firm, has partners Priya (40%), Rohan (35%), Samir (25%) under **Fixed Capital** method. Deed: 15% interest on capital, ₹2 lakh quarterly salary to Priya, 7.5% commission to Rohan on net profit after salary. Samir retires on 31-Dec-2024. Terms: Goodwill valued at 4 years' purchase of weighted average profit (weights 1,2,3 for 2022,23,24). Profits: 2022 ₹50L, 2023 ₹70L, 2024 ₹90L (9 months). Normal return 18% on capital employed ₹10Cr. Assets: Lab equipment (book ₹4Cr, fair ₹5Cr), IP rights (book ₹2Cr, fair ₹6Cr), Deferred clinical trial expenditure ₹3Cr (to be written off over 3 years). Liabilities: Bank loan ₹4Cr, Contingent liability ₹1Cr (probable). Priya and Rohan continue in new ratio 5:3. Deed requires continuing partners' capitals proportionate to new ratio via Current Accounts. Samir's loan account to be settled in 4 quarterly installments with 10% interest. Samir guaranteed minimum profit ₹25L p.a. (pro-rata for 9 months).

(C) Adjust goodwill for Samir's retirement without raising goodwill account. Priya and Rohan adjust in gaining ratio.

In January 2026, **Globex Dynamics**, a multinational conglomerate headquartered in Singapore, announced an AI‑driven “Unified Communication Protocol” (UCP) across all its regional offices. The protocol, enforced by an internal language‑monitoring AI, mandates that, effective July 2026, all official written communication (emails, reports, presentations) must be in **Globex Standard English (GSE)**, a tightly controlled variant derived from corporate‑style American English. Employees using any other language or dialect—including regional Englishes, Mandarin, Hindi, or even informal GSE—receive automatic flags and must complete remedial training.  

Data show that Globex’s workforce of 240 000 spans 40 countries, with significant linguistic clusters: 35 % native Mandarin speakers (mainly in Shanghai and Shenzhen offices), 20 % Hindi‑speaking employees (Bengaluru and Hyderabad), 15 % speakers of regional English variants (Singapore, Johannesburg, Lagos), and the remaining 30 % primarily GSE‑users (North America, Europe).  

Mira, a 28‑year‑old software engineer at the Bengaluru campus, awakens late on the first day of the UCP rollout after a night debugging a microservice. She recalls her team lead announcing a surprise code‑review quiz on GSE‑specific terminology—a topic she skimmed while watching a meme about the upcoming IPL final. She thinks of skipping work to join friends at Cubbon Park, where kite‑flying preparations are underway. The morning is warm; distant traffic honks blend with the scent of jasmine from roadside stalls. Despite the urge to stay home, Mira logs in, dreading a public reprimand from the AI‑monitor.  

In the virtual stand‑up, her manager, Alex, wearing a crisp Globex polo, announces that this is the last meeting where regional English phrases (e.g., “prepone,” “batchmate”) will be tolerated; from tomorrow, only GSE will be accepted. He reads a passage from the corporate style guide in a monotone voice, his eyes flicking to the AI‑notification panel. Mira, who previously viewed GSE as “boring corporate jargon,” feels a tightness in her chest as she struggles to rewrite a simple sentence using the prescribed lexical constraints. She notices Alex carefully saving a screenshot of the style guide, noting the old world map on the virtual background and the notifications of flagged messages popping up like digital fireflies. After the meeting, Mira walks to the cafeteria, the usual chatter of multilingual banter now sounding like a subdued, filtered hum.  

Using the scenario, answer the sub‑parts.

(C) Evaluate whether Globex’s UCP infringes upon employees’ linguistic rights as framed by the political‑science node on global governance and corporate soft power. Cite the relevant normative guideline and apply it to the scenario.

In 2026 the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) drafts a “Hill Forest Conservation and Livelihood Bill” (HFCLB) for the Rajmahal‑Santhal‑Paharia landscape. The bill proposes:  
- Designation of 8 000 ha as “Core Conservation Zone” (CCZ) where all extractive activities, including shifting cultivation, are prohibited.  
- Allocation of the remaining 4 000 ha to “Community Forest Management Units” (CFMU) where Paharias and Santhals may practice regulated jhum (max 2 years cultivation followed by 3 years fallow) and collect NTFP (mahua, silk cocoons).  
- Provision for carbon credit sales: each hectare of CCZ is expected to sequester 2.5 t CO₂ yr⁻¹; CFMU hectare sequesters 0.8 t CO₂ yr⁻¹ due to cyclic disturbance.  
- A legal safeguard: any CFMU decision requires prior informed consent of the Gram Sabha under PESA, and violations attract penalties under the Forest Conservation Act, 1980 (FCA).  
Using the data, evaluate the trade‑off between carbon sequestration potential and tribal livelihood security, and determine which legal doctrine (the “Doctrine of Essential Religious Practice” or the “Doctrine of Sustainable Development”) would most likely be invoked by the tribes to challenge the CCZ prohibition on jhum.

(E) Which legal doctrine is more likely to be successfully invoked by the Paharia and Santhal communities to challenge the CCZ prohibition on shifting cultivation, and why? Base your answer on the relationship between the doctrine, the constitutional protection of tribal customs under Article 244/ PESA, and the ecological rationale of the CCZ.

Finova Technologies, a Bangalore‑based AI‑driven lending platform, has ₹1,200 cr of EBITDA and ₹4,800 cr of net assets. The promoters hold 60 % equity. To fund a ₹2,500 cr expansion into Southeast Asia, the board considers three options: (a) Fresh IPO of new shares at a price to be determined via book‑building; (b) Offer for Sale (OFS) of 20 % of promoter holdings; (c) Rights issue of 1 new share for every 4 held at ₹150 per share. Current market price is ₹180. SEBI mandates minimum public shareholding of 25 % post‑issue. The company’s cost of equity (CAPM) is 14 %, risk‑free rate 6 %, market premium 8 %. Assume flotation cost 2 % for IPO, 0.5 % for OFS, 1 % for rights. Calculate the post‑issue equity structure, dilution, and effective cost of capital for each option. (Use the accounting equation to verify balance‑sheet impact.)

(B) For the OFS option, compute the number of promoter shares to be sold to achieve 25 % public shareholding post‑issue, given current public holding is 15 %.

An environmental monitoring unit modifies a standard compound microscope into a portable spectrometer. A diffraction grating (500 lines/mm) is placed immediately after the eyepiece. The objective has \(f_o = 3.5\text{ mm}\); eyepiece \(f_e = 20.0\text{ mm}\). The tube length is fixed at 180 mm. The instrument is used to measure the wavelength of the prominent green emission line of mercury (λ≈546 nm) by observing the angular position of the first‑order diffraction maximum formed by the grating after the eyepiece. The eye is positioned at the eyepiece’s exit pupil, and the final virtual image is at the near point (25 cm) for comfortable viewing. Using the grating equation \(d\sin\theta = m\lambda\) (with \(d = 1/(500\text{ lines/mm}) = 2.0\;\mu\text{m}\)), answer the following. (Assume paraxial approximation, small angles, and that the eyepiece produces an angular magnification as per simple microscope theory.)

(E) Suppose the piezoelectric actuator fails and the tube length remains fixed at the 20 °C value (165 mm). Determine the new linear magnification of the objective and the angular magnification of the eyepiece at 26 °C, and comment on whether the final image can still be viewed at infinity.

OrbitalLaunch Aerospace Ltd. issues 1,00,000 9% Secured Debentures of ₹1,000 each on 1st April 2024 at par, as collateral security against a term loan of ₹80 cr from a consortium of banks. The debentures are redeemable at par after 7 years. The company creates a Sinking Fund (SF) for redemption, investing annually in 10-year G-sec bonds yielding 7.1% (current). The SF policy: invest an amount each year such that the fund accumulates to ₹100 cr (face value) at redemption. The sinking fund investments are designated at FVTPL. The term loan carries floating rate = Repo + 2% (current repo 6.5% → 8.5%). RBI hikes repo by 50 bps on 1st Oct 2024 and another 50 bps on 1st April 2025. The company's revenue is USD-denominated (satellite launch contracts), with 40% hedged. INR depreciates 3% in 2024-25. Tax rate 25%. The debenture trust deed requires DRR of 25% of face value. Assume 360-day year.

(D) Compute the effective cost of debenture debt (post-tax) for Year 1, considering the collateral arrangement reduces the term loan interest rate by 50 bps (from 8.5% to 8.0% for first half). Compare with standalone debenture cost (9% coupon, no tax shield on premium redemption? Redemption at par). Assume tax rate 25%.

A poultry entrepreneur considers two pure‑line breeds for egg production: Breed X (high‑yield) and Breed Y (robust). Genetic marker data indicate that 60 % of Breed X chicks carry a favorable allele conferring 10 % higher egg number, while only 20 % of Breed Y chicks possess it. The baseline egg production per hen per cycle (52 weeks) is 260 eggs for Breed X and 240 eggs for Breed Y. Feed conversion ratio (FCR) for egg mass is 2.2 kg feed per kg egg for both breeds. Feed cost is ₹ 24 kg⁻¹. Chick cost is ₹ 30 for Breed X and ₹ 22 for Breed Y. Egg selling price is ₹ 4.5 per egg. Metabolizable energy (ME) of the feed is estimated using a bomb‑calorimetry‑like approach: the feed consists of 65 % carbohydrate (ΔHc = ‑17 kJ g⁻¹), 20 % protein (ΔHc = ‑23 kJ g⁻¹), and 15 % fat (ΔHc = ‑39 kJ g⁻¹). Assume 80 % of gross energy is metabolizable. The entrepreneur wishes to decide (a) the expected egg number per hen for each breed accounting for marker prevalence, (b) the metabolizable energy per kg of feed, (c) the optimal proportion of Breed X chicks in a mixed flock (0 ≤ f ≤ 1) that maximises annual profit per hen, (d) the sensitivity of profit to a 5 % change in feed cost, and (e) the impact on profit if the metabolizable efficiency drops from 80 % to 70 % due to heat stress. Use calculus to find the optimum of the profit function.

(E) Assess the impact on optimal profit (from Part C) if the metabolizable efficiency drops from 80 % to 70 % due to heat stress, assuming that feed intake must increase proportionally to meet the same energy requirement for egg production.

A research team prepares competent *E. coli* cells using the classic CaCl₂ method. Cells are harvested at OD₆₀₀ = 0.4, washed in cold 0.1 M CaCl₂, and resuspended to 2 × 10⁹ cells mL⁻¹. They mix 100 µL of this suspension with 50 ng of a 3 kb plasmid (kanamycin‑resistant) and incubate on ice for 15 min, then give a heat shock at 42 °C for a variable time tₛₕ, followed by 2 min on ice. Recovery is in SOC for 45 min before plating on LB‑kanamycin plates.  
Empirical data suggest the fraction of cells that become competent (F_c) follows an Arrhenius‑type dependence on heat‑shock temperature T (in Kelvin):  
F_c = A·exp(−Eₐ/(R·T))·(1−exp(−k·tₛₕ)),  
where A = 0.8 (dimensionless pre‑exponential factor), Eₐ = 45 kJ mol⁻¹, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, and k = 0.12 s⁻¹ (rate constant for membrane permeabilisation during heat shock).  
Transformation efficiency (TE) is defined as colonies per µg DNA: TE = (F_c·N_cells·P_uptake)/DNA_µg, where N_cells = 2 × 10⁸ cells in the 100 µL aliquot, P_uptake = 0.6 (probability a competent cell takes up DNA), and DNA_µg = 0.05 µg.

(A) Calculate the fraction of cells that become competent (F_c) for a heat‑shock duration tₛₕ = 30 s at 42 °C.

A pharmaceutical company produces human insulin in *E. coli* using a pET‑based plasmid. Insulin concentration in the supernatant is measured by a competitive ELISA (anti‑insulin antibody coated plate, HRP‑insulin conjugate). The plasmid integrity is checked by quantitative PCR (qPCR) targeting the antibiotic resistance gene. The process must: (i) generate a standard curve from ELISA absorbance vs. known insulin concentrations to quantify unknown samples, (ii) determine plasmid copy number per cell from Ct values assuming 100 % efficiency, (iii) model insulin expression as a function of IPTG inducer concentration using a Hill equation, (iv) estimate the rate of substrate (glucose) diffusion into spherical bacterial pellets of radius 0.5 mm, and (v) perform a simple cost‑benefit analysis comparing two induction strategies (low‑IPTG long‑duration vs. high‑IPTG short‑duration) using linear programming.

(D) Estimate the steady‑state diffusive flux (J, mol m⁻² s⁻¹) of glucose into a spherical bacterial pellet of radius r = 0.5 mm, given external glucose concentration C₀ = 5 mM, intracellular concentration Cᵢ ≈ 0 (consumption fast), diffusion coefficient D = 6.7×10⁻¹⁰ m² s⁻¹ (water at 25 °C). Use Fick’s first law for a sphere: J = D·(C₀−Cᵢ)/r.

Fill in the blank: Transport of carbon dioxide in blood occurs through three mechanisms: (1) dissolution in plasma (7%), (2) formation of carbamino compounds with haemoglobin (20-25%), and (3) conversion to bicarbonate ions (HCO₃⁻) via carbonic anhydrase catalysis in ______ (70%), with the latter two being reversible and dependent on partial pressure gradients and the Haldane effect.

To contain rising edible‑oil prices (global palm‑oil up 18 % YoY), the Government of India announces a **subsidy of Rs 12,000 per tonne** on imported palm oil for six months. Estimated palm‑oil import volume for the period is **2.5 million tonnes**. The subsidy is financed by drawing down the **contingency fund** (treated as an expense) and adding to the **fiscal deficit**. (C) Pass the journal entry to record the subsidy expense in the government’s accounts (assume payment from the contingency fund).
What are the two subunits of a eukaryotic 80S ribosome and their respective Svedberg values?

In an economy, consumption expenditure is ₹120 crore when income is ₹200 crore, and ₹180 crore when income is ₹300 crore. Find the consumption function, MPC, and autonomous consumption. Calculate APC at both income levels.

A clay tablet excavated at Ur (southern Mesopotamia) and dated to ≈ 2300 BCE bears **four** distinct seal impressions. Each impression shows the classic Harappan “unicorn” motif and a short line of the Indus script (right‑to‑left, average 5 signs). The tablet’s cuneiform inscription records a trade transaction: “120 shekels of silver received for carnelian beads delivered by Dilmun merchants.” Archaeologists have established that the Harappan weight system used binary fractions with a base unit of **13.6 g** (the smallest weight found at Mohenjo‑Daro). The Mesopotamian shekel of the period is standardized at **8.33 g**. Using this information, answer the following sub‑parts.

(C) Compare the political implication of Harappan seal usage on the Mesopotamian tablet with the contemporary Mesopotamian city‑state model. Identify ONE similarity and ONE difference concerning authority over trade.

Nexus Digital LLP (partners X, Y, Z sharing 5:3:2) faces a dispute. Partner Z claimed guarantee of minimum ₹2,00,000 p.a. for FY2020-21 to FY2023-24 (4 years). The deed: Interest on capital @10% p.a. (fixed capitals: X ₹10,00,000; Y ₹6,00,000; Z ₹4,00,000); Interest on drawings @12% p.a. (product method); Salary to X ₹1,20,000 p.a.; Commission to Y @5% of net profit after all appropriations including commission. Guarantee to Z: deficiency borne by X and Y in 5:3. Reported profits (before any appropriations): FY21 ₹8,00,000; FY22 ₹9,50,000; FY23 ₹11,00,000; FY24 ₹12,50,000. Drawings (product method): X: ₹5,00,000 (avg 6 months); Y: ₹3,00,000 (avg 6 months); Z: ₹2,00,000 (avg 6 months). The accountant omitted all appropriations for 4 years. Arbitrator orders rectification via Profit & Loss Adjustment Account. Firm valued for acquisition at 4x EV/EBITDA (Enterprise Value / EBITDA). EBITDA = corrected PAT + Interest on loan (none) + Tax + Depreciation (assume ₹0). Tax 30%. Acquisition price split among partners per final adjusted capitals. Use c11_acc_cbse_02_005 (Accounting Period Concept) for period separation.

(A) For each year, compute the correct divisible profit after all appropriations (interest on capital, drawings, salary, commission) and determine Z's guarantee deficiency. Show the allocation of deficiency between X and Y.

GreenTech manufactures mono‑crystalline solar panels. The industry is perfectly competitive. Each firm’s long‑run total cost (LRTC) is given by
\[
\text{LRTC}(q)=0.1q^{3}-3q^{2}+30q+100,
\]
where \(q\) is annual output (in MW). From this, derive LAC and LMC. The market demand for panels is
\[
Q^{D}=800-20P,
\]
with \(Q^{D}\) in MW and \(P\) in ₹ per MW. Firms depreciate their plant on a straight‑line basis over 10 years with zero salvage value. The initial plant cost (included in the constant 100) is ₹1,000 thousand. GreenTech is considering a government‑linked green bond that would reduce the effective interest cost on debt by 2 percentage points. The raw material (silicon) is sourced from mines whose environmental impact is evaluated using the biology concept of “Diversity in the Living World” (Classification) to assess opportunity cost of land use.

Answer the following:

(E) Suppose a government subsidy reduces the effective constant term in LRTC by 30 % (i.e., the 100 becomes 70). Determine the new long‑run equilibrium price and discuss the impact on the number of firms.

A laboratory receives unidentified solid samples that may contain the radioactive isotope Iodine‑131 (half‑life 8 days) or only its stable counterpart Iodine‑127. A Geiger‑Müller tube is used to screen each sample. When a sample truly contains I‑131, the tube registers a click (count) with probability 0.90 (detector efficiency). When the sample contains only stable I‑127, background radiation and electronic noise cause a false click with probability 0.05. Prior data show that 40 % of the received samples actually contain I‑131. Assume that successive readings on the same sample are independent conditional on the true composition of the sample. Using this information answer the following.

(E) In a batch of 10 independent samples, each with prior probability 0.4 of containing I‑131, what is the expected number of samples that will produce a click?

A 2023 WHO report on mental health notes a 38 % rise in “time‑blur” symptoms among remote workers post‑COVID‑19. Researchers provide: (i) Milton’s “On Time” (full text), (ii) a graph showing average perceived duration of an 8‑hour workday (pre‑pandemic = 7.9 h, pandemic = 9.2 h), (iii) definitions from cognitive psychology: *prospective time estimation* (predicting future duration) and *retrospective time estimation* (judging past duration), (iv) sociological concept of *time‑poverty* (feeling insufficient discretionary time despite adequate clock time), measured via a Likert scale (1‑5). Students must write a 170‑word analysis that (a) identifies the poem’s attitude toward Time, (b) explains how two poetic devices shape that attitude, (c) connects the attitude to prospective/time‑poverty phenomena in remote work, and (d) evaluates whether the poem offers a coping strategy or exacerbates anxiety. All data are supplied; no external literature needed.

(B) Analyse how the metaphor “heavy Plummets pace” (line 3) and the symbol “individual kiss” (line 10) contribute to the poem’s attitude toward Time.

In 2026, satellite imagery reveals that extensive land‑reclamation activities by State X in the South China Sea have destroyed 1,200 km² of coral reefs, violating the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea. A coalition of ASEAN states drafts a UNSC resolution demanding an immediate halt to reclamation, compensatory restoration funded by State X, and authorization for a UN‑led monitoring mission. The resolution is classified as substantive. Current UNSC membership: P5 (USA, UK, France, Russia, China) plus ten elected members. Recent voting records show: on similar environmental sanctions, China vetoed 3 times, Russia vetoed 2 times, USA abstained once, UK and France voted yes. The draft resolution has the support of 11 members (including France, UK, USA, and 8 non‑permanent). China indicates it will vote “no”; Russia signals abstention; USA signals yes. The UN peacekeeping budget for 2026 is $6.5 billion; a monitoring mission would add 0.4 % of the budget per month. Accounting principles require that contingent liabilities be disclosed when probable and estimable.

(E) Critically evaluate the argument that the P5 should adopt a “veto restraint” initiative for environmental sanctions, drawing a parallel to the Roman Senate’s use of *intercessio* (veto) as described in your history readings, and discuss how reform proposals in The Reform Of The Un Security Council address this concern.

GeneTech Partners, a biotech research firm (profit-sharing ratio 3:2:1 for Dr. A, Dr. B, Dr. C), dissolves on 31-Mar-2025. The partnership deed states: "All realisation expenses shall be borne by the firm." However, Dr. A (the managing partner) orally agrees to personally bear the ₹4.2 lakh cost of autoclaving and certified disposal of genetically modified organisms (GMOs) as mandated by the Environment Protection Act, 1986 — a public facility regulation ensuring ecological safety (c10_eco_cbse_01_005). The firm’s books show: Land ₹50L, Lab Equipment ₹30L, Patents (unrecorded) ₹20L, Creditors ₹15L, Dr. B’s Loan ₹10L, Dr. C’s Capital ₹5L (Dr. A ₹12L, Dr. B ₹8L). Realisation yields: Land ₹55L, Equipment ₹22L, Patents ₹18L. Additional realisation expenses: auctioneer’s commission ₹1.5L (paid by firm), legal fees ₹0.8L (paid by Dr. A on firm’s behalf). Dr. C is insolvent (deficiency ₹3L). Garner v Murray applies (c12_acc_cbse_04_008). The GMOs belong to Kingdom Monera (c11_bio_cbse_02_001) and require BSL-2 containment.

(B) Prepare the Realisation Account incorporating all realisation expenses (auctioneer ₹1.5L, legal ₹0.8L, GMO ₹4.2L) and asset realisations. Calculate profit/loss on realisation.

A jagirdar is transferred from a rich kharif-rabi (two-crop) jagir in the Punjab (jama: 2 crore dams, hasil typically 85%) to a single-crop Deccan jagir (jama: 1.5 crore, hasil typically 50% due to conflict). His salary claim is 1.6 crore. Trace his likely actions over the 3-year tenure and the impact on peasants in both jagirs.

"Despite numerous regulations, delay in decision-making, and oligarchic management, the Joint Stock Company remains the dominant form for large-scale enterprises." Evaluate this statement by weighing any three merits against three limitations, and conclude whether the trade-off is justified for a business aiming for ₹500 crore turnover.

In the district of Marusthali, average annual rainfall has declined from 600 mm to 420 mm over the past decade, increasing the frequency of droughts. The state government has introduced a subsidy for drip‑irrigation systems, covering 50% of installation costs, targeting smallholder farmers. Survey data shows that 70% of male‑headed households have adopted the technology, whereas only 30% of female‑headed households have done so, largely due to limited access to credit and land ownership rights. The district’s agricultural GDP has risen by 8% since the subsidy began, but the fiscal outlay on the subsidy has reached 4% of the district’s annual budget, prompting a review. A committee is tasked with evaluating whether to expand the subsidy, modify eligibility criteria, or shift focus to rainwater harvesting. Using concepts of Economic Geography, Gender Geography (a sub‑field of Social Geography), and basic accounting, assess the policy.

(A) Identify the major field of human geography that studies the spatial patterns of agricultural productivity and the impact of the drip‑irrigation subsidy.

A 35-year-old woman, Meera, presents with a 2-year history of multiple somatic complaints: chronic back pain, headaches, fatigue, and intermittent nausea. She has seen 7 specialists, undergone 3 MRIs, 2 endoscopies, and countless blood tests — all normal. She spends 3 hours daily researching symptoms, checks her pulse 20 times/day, and avoids exercise fearing "heart damage." Her husband says she "lives in hospitals." She denies mood symptoms. Diagnose and explain why it is NOT Illness Anxiety Disorder or Conversion Disorder.

In 1904, the British colonial government imposed a cess on Indian raw cotton exports to protect Lancashire mills, reducing the incentive for Indian farmers to cultivate long‑staple varieties. By 2023, a multinational apparel brand sources cotton from three Indian regions: Region A (historically high‑cess area, average micronaire 4.8, maturity 0.72, staple 22 mm), Region B (low‑cess area, micronaire 3.9, maturity 0.84, staple 30 mm), and Region C (organic tract, micronaire 4.1, maturity 0.78, staple 28 mm). The brand needs to produce a 60s Ne combed yarn for premium shirts. Processing losses: blowroom 1.5 %, carding 2.5 %, spinning 4 % (total 8 %). Raw cotton prices: A ₹110/kg, B ₹135/kg, C ₹150/kg. Processing cost = ₹28/kg input. The brand also faces a new EU regulation requiring ≥70 % biodegradability within 30 days (soil burial test). Using the same biodegradation model k = 0.02 × (1‑MR) day⁻¹, assess which region(s) meet yarn quality, cost, and eco‑criteria, and recommend an optimal sourcing mix (by weight) to minimise cost while satisfying all constraints.

(A) For each region, compute the expected yarn count (Ne) using Ne ≈ 0.05 × L × T, where tenacity T (g/tex) can be approximated from micronaire (MI) and maturity (MR) via T ≈ 2.5 + 0.3×(MI‑3.5) + 1.2×(MR‑0.7). Identify which regions can achieve ≥60s Ne.

The Ministry of Education wants to estimate the Gross Enrolment Ratio (GER) at secondary level (Classes 9-10) for 2024-25. Available sources: (a) Census 2011 age-specific population (14-15 years), (b) NSSO 75th round (2017-18) "Social Consumption: Education" with enrolment status by age and level, (c) UDISE+ 2023-24 administrative school enrolment data, (d) Projected population 2024 from Census 2011-based projections. Design a step-by-step estimation procedure and identify the major source of uncertainty.

An oxygen cylinder of volume 30 L has initial gauge pressure 15 atm at 27°C. After some oxygen is used, gauge pressure drops to 11 atm at 17°C. Estimate the mass of oxygen withdrawn. (Atmospheric pressure = 1 atm, M_O₂ = 32 g/mol, R = 8.31 J/(mol·K)). [NCERT Exercise 12.4 adapted]

A rectangle has length 12 cm and breadth 8 cm. Student A increases both dimensions by 4 cm. Student B multiplies both dimensions by 1.5. Which student produces a rectangle similar to the original? Explain why the other method fails.

In 2025, the Punjab government deploys an AI‑driven satellite‑monitoring system (IndusWatch) to track real‑time flow of the Sutlej and Beas rivers. Data reveals that downstream states (Haryana and Rajasthan) are receiving 18 % less water than the 1981 Ravi‑Beas Tribunal allocation, while upstream usage in Punjab has risen due to a shift toward high‑value horticulture. Protests erupt in Punjab’s Malwa region, with the Akali Dal demanding an immediate renegotiation of water‑sharing agreements, citing the Anandpur Sahib Resolution’s call for “bolbala” (dominance) of the Sikh community over Punjab’s natural resources. The Union Government invokes Article 262 of the Constitution and sets up a new tribunal, while also referencing the 1985 Rajiv Gandhi–Longowal Accord’s water‑sharing clause. Simultaneously, a civil‑society group files a PIL arguing that the satellite data violates the right to privacy under Article 21. The scenario requires students to trace the historical evolution from the Punjabi Suba movement to the present water dispute, evaluate constitutional mechanisms, and assess the role of technology in federal negotiations.

(D) Compare the Belgian consociational power‑sharing model with India’s federal mechanism for resolving the Punjab water dispute, highlighting where each succeeds or fails.

PharmaNova Ltd., a large pharmaceutical firm, acquires 100 % of BioGenix Ltd. for an enterprise value of ₹2 500 crore, paying ₹1 800 crore in cash and assuming ₹700 crore of debt. As part of the deal, it obtains BioGenix’s patent portfolio (fair value ₹400 crore) and a‑cGMP manufacturing plant (fair value ₹900 crore). PharmaNova also upgrades its existing R&D laboratory by purchasing new analytical equipment for ₹250 crore and capitalizing ₹30 crore of interest incurred during the installation period (qualifying asset). It disposes of old lab equipment for ₹40 crore (book value ₹25 crore). Additionally, PharmaNova invests ₹150 crore in a special purpose vehicle (SPV) that will conduct Phase‑III clinical trials; the SPV is treated as a long‑term investment. The company receives a milestone payment of ₹60 crore from a partner for achieving a pre‑clinical target (treated as a capital grant). Assume no financing or operating cash flows are considered. Using AS‑3, compute net cash flow from investing activities, prepare relevant ledgers, and discuss the impact of foreign‑exchange fluctuation if the SPV investment were made in euros at 1 EUR = ₹90, later moving to 1 EUR = ₹95.

(B) Calculate net cash flow from investing activities using: cash paid for acquisition, R&D equipment purchase, interest capitalized, disposal of old lab equipment, SPV investment, milestone grant.

In early 2025, a sudden surge in Chinese construction demand lifts international hot‑rolled coil prices by 35 % within three months. Simultaneously, the Indian rupee depreciates from 82 ₹/$ to 88 ₹/$ due to rising US treasury yields. The Visakhapatnam (Vizag) steel plant, a 7.5 Mtpa coastal integrated facility reliant on imported coking coal (Australia) and exporting ~40 % of its output to Southeast Asia, faces a mixed impact: higher sales revenue in rupee terms but increased import coal cost. The plant’s environmental clearance mandates a 20 % reduction in specific CO₂ emissions by 2030, pushing management to consider a shift to natural‑gas‑based DRI and scrap‑based EAF for 30 % of capacity. Using concepts of market access (Weber), exchange‑rate pass‑through, and environmental regulation, assess the plant’s short‑term profitability and long‑term strategy.

(D) Evaluate the feasibility of replacing 30 % of the plant’s BF‑BOF capacity with natural‑gas‑based DRI and scrap‑EAF to meet the 20 % CO₂‑reduction mandate, considering gas availability and cost.

The Battle of Talikota (1565) resulted in the sacking of Vijayanagara’s capital, Hampi, and the fragmentation of the empire into successor nayaka kingdoms. Contemporary Portuguese factory records from Cochin show a sudden 40 % drop in horse imports from the Vijayanagara‑controlled port of Bhatkal in the year following the battle, while Arab traders report a 25 % increase in horse shipments to the Malabar coast, citing safer routes avoiding Vijayanagara territory. Simultaneously, tax registers from the newly formed Madurai Nayaka kingdom indicate a 15 % rise in revenue from textile exports, attributed to displaced weavers relocating from Hampi’s ruined workshops. A sociological survey of migrant laborers in the Tungabhadra basin notes a 30 % decline in hereditary kudirai chetti merchant families engaged in horse trade, with many shifting to agrarian labor.  
Using this data, answer: (a) What was the approximate annual loss in state revenue (in ₹ lakhs) for the Vijayanagara successor states if the pre‑battle horse import duty was 12 % on a landed cost of ₹ 1 80 000 per horse and the pre‑battle import volume was 3 000 horses/year? (b) How does the shift in horse trade routes illustrate the concept of “trade diversion” in political‑science theory? (c) What geographic factor explains why Arab traders could redirect shipments to the Malabar coast more easily than to the Coromandel coast after the battle? (d) How did the influx of weavers into Madurai affect the traditional amara‑nayaka revenue‑sharing model between the centre and local nayakas? (e) If the kudirai chetti merchant decline reduces the effective tax base for horse‑related duties by 30 %, what should the successor states do to maintain pre‑battle revenue levels, assuming they cannot change the duty rate?

(C) What geographic factor explains why Arab traders could redirect shipments to the Malabar coast more easily than to the Coromandel coast after the battle?

The assay is performed at 22 °C instead of the optimal 37 °C. Assuming the HRP‑luminol reaction follows Arrhenius behavior with E_a = 50 kJ mol⁻¹, calculate the relative reaction rate at 22 °C compared to 37 °C.

In Rajasthan’s Barmer district, a nonprofit launched “Swasthya Vani,” an FM educational programme (92.1 MHz, 5 W) targeting rural women’s maternal health. Broadcasts occur twice daily, featuring expert interviews in Marwari, interactive phone‑in Q&A, and serial dramas depicting antenatal care, institutional delivery, and postnatal nutrition. The programme is funded by a Union Ministry of Health grant but airs on a private FM station licensed under the 2002 FM Policy (Phase II), which bars news but allows “educational” content. The Rajasthan State Women’s Commission seeks to replicate the model statewide, arguing health is a State List subject, while the Union contends that radio frequencies fall under the Union List (Posts and Telegraphs, 1880). Analyze the sociological impact of such developmental radio on health behaviour, trace the lineage of AIR’s post‑independence health campaigns, and evaluate the constitutional‑federal conflict over jurisdiction of educational FM content.

(D) Explain how Swasthya Vani’s serial dramas influence health behaviour through the sociological concepts of modelling and self‑efficacy.

To develop rice (*Oryza sativa*) lines tolerant to drought, the transcription factor DREB2A (900 bp) is cloned into the binary vector pCAMBIA1300 (6.2 kb) carrying a hygromycin phosphotransferase (hpt) selectable marker. The construct is mobilized into *Agrobacterium tumefaciens*, which co‑cultivates with rice embryogenic callus. Transformants are selected on medium containing 50 mg L⁻¹ hygromycin. Putative positives are screened by Southern blot using a DIG‑labeled 25‑mer probe complementary to the transgene. To estimate the likelihood of obtaining homozygous T₁ plants, 30 T₀ seeds (each hemizygous for a single‑copy insertion) are self‑pollinated. Off‑target integration risk is evaluated using binomial statistics, while the probe’s melting temperature (Tm) is calculated via the nearest‑neighbor model to ensure specific hybridization under stringent conditions.

(C) From the plate, 500 colonies are picked and screened with a DIG‑labeled 25‑mer probe. The probe hybridizes specifically to the transgene with probability 0.85 per colony, while nonspecific binding gives a false‑positive signal with probability 0.001 per colony. What is the expected number of positive signals (true + false) observed?

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are a school health ______ reviewing two students: Rohan (11 years, 55 kg, 145 cm) from a private urban school who brings packaged snacks daily, and Meena (10 years, 22 kg, 128 cm) from a government rural school who often skips breakfast.

In 2024, 22‑year‑old Maya launches an AI‑driven fintech startup in Bangalore. She secures ₹2 crore seed funding via convertible notes, personally guaranteeing ₹50 lakhs of the debt. Her paternal uncle was diagnosed with Generalised Anxiety Disorder (GAD) at age 30; her mother reports high trait neuroticism. Six months post‑launch, Maya experiences persistent worry about cash‑flow, insomnia, muscle tension, and recurrent panic attacks triggered by investor meetings. She avoids social media, fearing negative publicity will affect her company’s valuation. Financial statements show a monthly burn rate of ₹12 lakhs, with projected breakeven in 18 months if user acquisition meets 10 % month‑over‑month growth. Maya’s therapist notes she exhibits catastrophic thinking (“If I miss this pitch, I’ll lose everything”) and uses safety behaviours (rehearsing pitches for hours). Using the diathesis‑stress model, biological vulnerability (family history, putative GABAergic deficit), and socio‑cultural stressor (personal debt, investor pressure), answer the following.

(B) Using the biological node, explain how a putative GABAergic deficit could contribute to Maya’s anxiety symptoms.

In the industrial production of chloroform (CHCl₃), methane is chlorinated sequentially: CH₄ → CH₃Cl → CH₂Cl₂ → CHCl₃ → CCl₄. The reaction is run with excess methane to minimize polychlorination. Given that the relative reactivity per H for chlorination is CH₄:CH₃Cl:CH₂Cl₂:CHCl₃ = 1 : 0.33 : 0.07 : 0.01 (decreasing due to -I effect of Cl), calculate the molar ratio of CH₄:Cl₂ needed to achieve 80% conversion of Cl₂ to CH₃Cl with <5% of chlorinated products being CH₂Cl₂. Assume each Cl₂ reacts with one RH to give RCl + HCl.

A care label shows: "Hand wash, cold water, mild detergent, dry flat, do not bleach, iron low with steam." The garment is a wool-acrylic blend (70% wool, 30% acrylic). Evaluate whether this label correctly addresses the care needs of BOTH fibres. Cite specific property conflicts from Table 2.

A square loop of side 20 cm and resistance 2 Ω is placed with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. The field is reduced to zero uniformly in 0.4 s. Calculate the magnitude of induced emf and the induced current in the loop.

In early 2025, a multinational consortium secured a 30‑year lease to extract rare‑earth elements (REEs) from the biodiverse Eastern Ghats, home to 4 million Adivasis belonging to the Kondh, Saora, and Gadaba tribes. The project promises ₹85 000 cr in export revenue but requires clearing 1 200 km² of forest, displacing an estimated 250 000 tribal households and threatening sacred groves. Four response coalitions emerged: (i) **Reformist NGOs** demand a strengthened Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) with mandatory free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC) and a revenue‑sharing trust fund; (ii) **Revolutionary Eco‑Socialists** call for the abolition of private mining, advocating community‑controlled stewardship of the Ghats under a constitutional “Ecological Commons” amendment; (iii) **Resistance Groups** (traditional tribal councils) seek to defend existing forest rights under the Forest Rights Act 2006 (FRA) and block further encroachment by setting up vigilance patrols; (iv) **Reactionary Traders’ Association** argues for maintaining the status‑quo of state‑led mineral licensing, claiming that tribal opposition hinders national technological sovereignty and urging stricter anti‑terrorism laws to curb protests. Satellite data shows forest cover loss of 3.2 % per year in the lease area since 2022, while the national average is 0.4 %. The Ministry of Environment issued a draft order allowing “conditional clearance” contingent on compensatory afforestation elsewhere, which tribes contend violates the FRA’s prohibition on non‑forest‑land compensation.

(E) Forecast the probable trajectory of the tribal‑environmental coalition using insights from New Social Movements (New Social Movements (Nsms)), focusing on framing, alliances, and resource constraints.

A Bihar‑based startup, “SwaShakti Khadi,” procures organic cotton from Dalit farmer cooperatives, spins and weaves it using revived charkha units, and sells finished garments online. The venture received ₹20 crore seed funding (equity + debt) and projects ₹120 crore annual turnover by year 5, employing 5,000 artisans (80 % Dalit, 20 % OBC). Baseline per‑capita monthly income of Dalit households in the region is ₹8,000; the enterprise promises a 15 % increase via fair‑wage piece rates. Preliminary data show a projected reduction in the state’s Gini coefficient from 0.48 to 0.44 over five years due to increased rural wages. The initiative cites Gandhi’s Constructive Programme (khadi, Harijan uplift) and the Poona Pact (1932) as ideological anchors, while invoking Directive Principles (Art. 41 – right to work, Art. 46 – promotion of educational/economic interests of weaker sections). Satellite‑derived night‑light intensity shows a 12 % rise in the operational districts, suggesting broader economic spill‑over.

(D) Which sociological concept best explains why the enterprise’s emphasis on Dalit ownership of the value chain may lead to broader changes in caste‑based occupational segregation?

A newspaper editorial states: "The Supreme Court's 2023 judgment striking down the electoral bonds scheme is a victory for transparency. Data shows 95% of bonds went to the ruling party. Therefore, the judgment strengthens Indian democracy." Deconstruct this argument into descriptive premises, normative premises, and the conclusion. Identify any missing normative premise.

A multinational tech firm plans to build a new hyperscale data centre in India to support its AI‑driven services. The firm’s sustainability pledge requires that 80 % of the centre’s electricity come from renewable sources within five years. The government’s latest *National Renewable Energy Policy* offers a 15 % tax credit for firms that locate facilities in states with ≥ 30 % renewable‑energy grid share and mandates annual reporting of Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE). The firm’s engineering team has identified three candidate sites:  
- Site A (Gujarat): current grid renewable share 28 %, projected to reach 35 % in 3 years; land cost ₹ 1 200 / sq m; average ambient temperature 32 °C.  
- Site B (Karnataka): grid renewable share 42 % (already above threshold); land cost ₹ 1 500 / sq m; ambient temperature 27 °C.  
- Site C (Maharashtra): grid renewable share 22 %, projected 30 % in 5 years; land cost ₹ 1 300 / sq m; ambient temperature 30 °C.  
Each site’s expected IT load is 150 MW. The firm’s internal model estimates that cooling power = 0.45 × IT load × (T_ambient – 20) / 10 (in MW), where T_ambient is in °C. The base PUE (without cooling) is 1.2. The firm must also plan for e‑waste: servers have a 5‑year lifespan, and the firm aims to recycle 90 % of discarded hardware via certified e‑waste recyclers, as per *E‑Waste Management Rules 2022*.  

Using the data above, answer the following.

(A) Calculate the annual cooling power (in MW) required for each site, assuming the IT load runs at full capacity 24 × 365 h.

A state government runs a midday meal (MDM) programme for 12‑year‑old adolescents in a drought‑prone district of Rajasthan. The prescribed menu provides 450 kcal, 12 g protein, 4 mg iron, 200 mg calcium and 150 µg vitamin A per child per day. ICMR RDA for adolescents (12‑14 yr, moderate activity) is: Energy 1900 kcal, Protein 40 g, Iron 16 mg, Calcium 800 mg, Vitamin A 600 µg.  
Recent monsoon failure reduced local millet yield by 30 %, forcing procurement of rice at higher cost; the program now uses polished rice (lower micronutrient density). Additionally, a prevalent caste‑based food taboo prevents consumption of eggs and dairy among 35 % of children.  
Using the data, assess whether the MDM meets the adjusted RDA after accounting for (i) reduced millet micronutrient content (assume 20 % lower iron and calcium in polished rice vs. millet), (ii) 35 % children unable to consume egg/dairy (which normally contribute 30 % of protein and 50 % of calcium in the menu), and (iii) seasonal energy deficit due to lower crop yield (assume 10 % lower energy density of the ration). Recommend one policy intervention.

(C) Estimate the protein and calcium shortfall for the 35 % of children who avoid egg/dairy, given that these foods normally contribute 30 % of the menu’s protein and 50 % of its calcium.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) releases the 30-year climate normal (1981–2010) for Pune: June mean maximum temperature = 35.2°C, June mean rainfall = 145 mm. In June 2023, Pune recorded a mean maximum of 37.8°C and total rainfall of 80 mm. Calculate the anomalies and classify each as weather or climate.

HealthTech Ltd. has obtained CE‑marked certification for a disposable ECG patch that records cardiac rhythm for 24 hours and transmits data via Bluetooth to a smartphone app. The firm plans a pan‑India launch in Q4 2025. The total promotion budget is **₹4 crore**. Market testing (n = 5 000) yielded the following expected outcomes per rupee spent on each promotion tool:

| Tool | Expected impressions per ₹1 | Click‑through rate (CTR) | Conversion rate (click → purchase) | Average revenue per user (ARPU) in Q4 (₹) |
|------|-----------------------------|--------------------------|------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| Advertising (YouTube pre‑roll + health‑blog banners) | 1500 | 0.6 % | 1.2 % | 1800 |
| Personal Selling (trained medical reps visiting clinics) | 25 | 4 % | 18 % | 1800 |
| Sales Promotion (₹200 cash‑back on first purchase, limited to first 50 000 units) | 8000 | 1.0 % | 6 % | 1800 |
| Public Relations (medical‑journal op‑eds, health‑camp sponsorships) | 900 | 0.3 % | 0.8 % | 1800 |

Additional data:  
- The price‑elasticity of demand for the patch with respect to the net price after cash‑back is –1.5.  
- HealthTech’s advertisement claims the patch “detects atrial fibrillation with 99 % accuracy in all age groups”. A validation study showed 99 % accuracy in ages ≥ 40 years, but only 85 % accuracy in ages 18‑39 years.  
- Under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 (as amended), a medical device claim must be substantiated by clinical evidence relevant to the **intended population**.  
- The firm wishes to allocate the ₹4 crore promotion budget to **maximise expected revenue** in Q4, subject to: (i) at least 15 % of the budget must be spent on PR for credibility, (ii) no single tool may exceed 30 % of the total budget, (iii) the expected number of units sold must be at least 80 000 to achieve economies of scale in manufacturing.

(A) Determine the expected **revenue per rupee spent** on each promotion tool (i.e., ARPU × impressions × CTR × conversion). Identify the tool that yields the highest revenue per rupee.

A political research NGO has gathered constituency‑level results from the latest state assembly election in three states (Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh). For each of the 120 constituencies they have: total votes polled, votes for Party A, votes for Party B, votes for Party C, and percentage of voter turnout. The raw data exist as three parallel NumPy arrays: `votes_total` (int64), `votes_A` (int64), `votes_B` (int64), `votes_C` (int64), and `turnout_pct` (float64). Additionally, they have a list of constituency names and a list of district names (each constituency belongs to a district). The NGO wishes to (i) build a DataFrame from the NumPy arrays, (ii) assign constituency names as the row index, (iii) add a multi‑level index consisting of (state, district), (iv) compute the vote share for each party, and (v) identify constituencies where the winning margin is less than 5% of total votes.

(E) Identify constituencies where the winning margin (difference between highest and second‑highest party votes) is less than 5% of total votes. Return the count of such constituencies.

A student observes that the Brahmaputra in its Assam reach carries a huge sediment load (∼730 million tonnes/year) yet the channel bed is not rapidly incising. Using the concepts of stream power, sediment tools, and alluvial cover effect, explain this apparent paradox. How would the erosion mechanisms change if the sediment supply were suddenly reduced by 50% due to upstream dam trapping?

Rising sea levels and increased cyclone intensity have rendered 12 % of the Sundarbans delta (area ≈ 4 000 km²) uninhabitable. Approximately 1.8 million residents live in the affected zone, of which 55 % are in the working‑age group (15‑59 years). The overall sex ratio in the Sundarbans is 950 females per 1000 males, but among children (0‑14 years) it is 980. Migration trends show that 70 % of displaced persons move to nearby urban centres (Kolkata metropolitan area), while 30 % relocate to other rural districts within West Bengal. Migrants exhibit a higher literacy rate (82 %) than the origin population (68 %). The destination urban centres currently have a population of 15 million, with an age‑structure: 25 % under 15, 62 % 15‑59, 13 % 60+, and a sex ratio of 902. The state’s disaster‑rehabilitation policy promises cash compensation of ₹2 lakhs per household and skill‑training vouchers, invoking the Directive Principle of securing livelihood (Art. 41). Historical precedents: colonial land‑revenue surveys in Bengal were used to extract resources, paralleling modern displacement for climate adaptation. Using the data, assess the demographic impact on both origin and destination regions, the effectiveness of rehabilitation measures, and the legal challenges under the right to life (Art. 21) and the principle of non‑refoulement in international climate‑refugee discourse.

(C) Compute the expected increase in the urban centre’s literacy rate after the influx, assuming the migrant literacy is 82 % and the original urban literacy is 71 %. Use a weighted‑average approach.

In 2026, a UN advisory panel debates the “Neuro‑Storytelling Ethics Treaty,” which proposes limits on brain‑computer interface (BCI) technologies that allow users to compose novels directly via neural signals, bypassing manual input. The panel cites Lawrence’s essay, especially the passage:  
> “My hand… slips gaily along, jumps like a grasshopper to dot an i, feels the table rather cold, gets a little bored if I write too long, has its own rudiments of thought, and is just as much me as is my brain, my mind, or my soul.”  
A neuroscientist on the panel argues that BCIs could exacerbate the “dehumanisation of an industrial society” by further divorcing cognition from embodiment, referencing data from early trials: users reported a 28 % reduction in perceived physical fatigue but a 19 % increase in feelings of detachment from their own thoughts (source: NeuroTech Trials Report, 2025). A legal scholar notes that any restriction would engage Article 21 (right to life and personal liberty) and must satisfy the proportionality test under Article 19(2).  
Using only the information above, answer the following.

(D) Which constitutional right does the legal scholar invoke as potentially affected by BCI‑novel restrictions, and what test must the state satisfy to justify any limitation?

From the following Trial Balance extract, calculate the provision for doubtful debts and pass the necessary journal entries:
Sundry Debtors: ₹80,000; Bad Debts: ₹2,000; Provision for Doubtful Debts (old): ₹3,000.
Additional Information: (i) Further bad debts ₹1,000; (ii) Provision to be maintained at 5% on debtors.

In State Z (a Himalayan hill state), glacial retreat has increased the frequency of landslides, prompting seasonal out‑migration of working‑age males (≈ 12 % of the 15‑59 cohort) to urban centres for construction work. Simultaneously, improved healthcare has raised life expectancy, increasing the 60+ share from 8 % (2011) to 13 % (2021). The 2021 age‑sex distribution is: 0‑14 = 20 %; 15‑59 = 57 %; 60+ = 23 %; sex ratio = 940 females per 1,000 males. Using concepts of population distribution , growth , demographic transition , and incorporating insights from environmental geography (Climate Change impacts on mountain ecosystems) and psychology (Stress and coping in displacement), answer the following.

(E) Based on the dependency ratios, sex ratio, and environmental stressors, recommend the most appropriate policy mix for State Z: (a) expand elderly care infrastructure, (b) promote women’s skill development and micro‑enterprise, (c) implement climate‑resilient livelihood programmes for males, or (d) provide psychosocial counselling for displaced populations. Justify your choice using at least two quantitative indicators.

Researchers aim to enhance seed set in the submerged angiosperm *Vallisneria spiralis* by modifying pollen mucilage to alter its density in response to water pH. Male flowers release pollen grains (diameter 30 µm, base density 1.25 g cm⁻³) that acquire a hydrophilic mucilaginous coat whose swelling changes effective density ρ_eff = ρ_p + Δρ·(pH‑pK_a)/(1+10^(pH‑pK_a)), with pK_a = 6.5 and Δρ = 0.2 g cm⁻³. Water temperature is 20 °C (viscosity η = 1.0×10⁻³ Pa·s, density ρ_f = 998 kg m⁻³). Pollen must rise from the sediment floor (depth 0.8 m) to the water surface where the female flower floats. Using Stokes’ law for upward motion (buoyant rise) and first‑order kinetics for pH‑dependent germination (k = k₀·10^(pH‑7), k₀ = 0.02 s⁻¹), calculate (A) effective density at pH = 5.5 and 8.0, (B) terminal rise velocity, (C) time to reach surface, (D) fraction of pollen germinating before arrival assuming exponential decay, and (E) optimal pH maximizing product of rise speed and germination fraction.

(B) Determine the terminal rise velocity vᵣ of a pollen grain (diameter 30 µm) at pH = 5.5 and pH = 8.0 using Stokes’ law for buoyant rise.

A NITI Aayog task force is drafting a 5‑year vision document for Vidarbha. The team decides to use Robert Frost’s “A Roadside Stand” as a cultural audit tool. They compile a multidisciplinary dataset:  

| Indicator | Value | Source |
|-----------|-------|--------|
| Poem’s secondary theme intensity (expert rating, 0‑10) – False Promises | 8.2 | Literary panel |
| – Exploitation | 7.5 | |
| – Migration | 6.9 | |
| – Loss of Voice | 7.1 | |
| – Helplessness | 7.8 | |
| Land‑reform distribution efficiency (actual/ceiling surplus) | 0.12 | Ministry of Rural Development |
| Article 46 expenditure on SC/ST agri‑development (₹ crore/yr) | 340 | Finance Accounts |
| Monsoon anomaly index (2022) – (Actual‑LTA)/LTA | –0.18 | IMD |
| Farmer suicide rate (per 1 00 000 agri‑workers) | 22 | NCRB |
| Average institutional debt per household (₹ lakhs) | 5.8 | NABARD |
| Percentage of smallholders (<1 ha) that are tenants | 55 | NSSO |
| Share of SC/ST among landless labourers | 0.42 | SECC |
| State agri‑livelihood expenditure per farmer (₹/yr) | 4 500 | State Budget |
| Out‑migration rate of rural youth (15‑29) (%/yr) | 9 | PLFS |
| Institutional credit‑to‑deposit ratio for rural banks | 0.38 | RBI |

The task force must:  

1. **Identify** which secondary theme is most sensitive to changes in land‑reform distribution.  
2. **Quantify** the expected change in helplessness score if land‑reform distribution improves from 0.12 to 0.40, assuming a linear relationship where each 0.1 increase in distribution reduces helplessness by 0.6 points (on a 0‑10 scale).  
3. **Evaluate** whether the current Article 46 expenditure suffices to offset the exploitation theme, using a benchmark that exploitation drops by 0.5 points for every ₹ 100 crore increase in Article 46 spending (baseline exploitation =7.5 at ₹ 0 spend).  
4. **Predict** the migration theme score after a policy that raises agri‑livelihood expenditure to ₹ 9 000/farmer/yr, given that each ₹ 1 000 increase reduces migration score by 0.3 points (baseline migration =6.9 at ₹ 4 500 spend).  
5. **Synthesize** a single composite index (CI) that aggregates the five secondary themes (weights: False Promises 0.2, Exploitation 0.2, Migration 0.2, Loss of Voice 0.2, Helplessness 0.2) after applying the projected changes from Q2‑Q4, and state whether the CI crosses the “critical distress” threshold of 6.0.  

Answer the sub‑questions.

(C) Determine whether the present Article 46 expenditure (₹ 340 crore/yr) reduces the exploitation theme to below the critical level of 5.0, given the benchmark.

In early 2025, a sophisticated ransomware campaign encrypts critical healthcare databases in Germany, demanding payment in Bitcoin traced to wallets linked to a Russian‑based cybercrime syndicate. Simultaneously, a coordinated disinformation surge on social media platforms amplifies anti‑NATO narratives in Poland and the Baltics, using deep‑fake videos of NATO officials allegedly endorsing territorial concessions to Russia. The German government attributes the ransomware to “state‑sponsored proxies” and invokes Article 5 of NATO, while Poland requests EU‑wide sanctions on entities facilitating the disinformation campaign. Intelligence reports indicate the Russian Main Directorate of the General Staff (GRU) has allocated $120 million to its “information operations” division, a figure comparable to the Soviet KGB’s annual budget for active measures during the 1980s (~$150 million adjusted). Meanwhile, India, a long‑standing member of the Non‑Aligned Movement, issues a statement urging restraint, emphasizing that cyber conflicts should not escalate to kinetic exchanges and offering its Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT‑In) to assist in forensic analysis. The scenario notes that both the US and Russia retain nuclear arsenals capable of mutual assured destruction, with US strategic bombers on heightened alert in response to the cyber incidents.

(E) Evaluate the claim that the current US‑Russia nuclear alert posture in response to cyber incidents mirrors the brinkmanship seen during the Cuban Missile Crisis, and argue whether the risk of unintended escalation is higher, lower, or comparable.

Using Table 4.1 data, calculate the Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of Real Per Capita Income from 1951 (₹7,651) to 2018-22 (₹94,054) over 67 years. Then calculate CAGR of Male Literacy Rate from 16.67% to 78% over same period. Compare and explain why income growth (CAGR ~3.8%) vastly exceeds literacy growth (CAGR ~2.3%) despite education being a driver of growth.

Design a sampling plan to estimate the average daily wage of construction workers in a metropolitan city. The workforce comprises three categories: skilled (15%), semi-skilled (35%), unskilled (50%). You have a budget for 400 interviews. Specify: (a) the sampling method, (b) sample allocation across strata, (c) how you would select workers within each stratum, and (d) one practical challenge you might face in implementing this plan.

A pilot project in Maharashtra equips 5,000 soybean farmers with a low‑cost AI smartphone app that analyses leaf images for early signs of *Rhizoctonia* fungal infection. Historical data shows average yield of 20 quintal/ha with a 30 % loss to disease when detected late. The AI model detects infection 7 days earlier, reducing avoidable loss by 15 % of the total potential yield. Smartphone penetration among farmers is 60 %; of those, only 50 % have reliable 4G connectivity. The state offers a Minimum Support Price (MSP) of ₹4,200/quintal, but only farmers receiving AI alerts qualify for a 5 % input subsidy. Monsoon variability creates three agro‑climatic zones: high rainfall (40 % area), moderate (35 %), low (25 %). The AI model was trained primarily on images from high‑rainfall zones, leading to a 10 % lower detection accuracy in low‑rainfall zones.

(D) If the state raises MSP by ₹100/quintal only for farmers receiving AI alerts, calculate the additional income per hectare for an alerted farmer, assuming yield from Part A.

In early 2025, the national party “Lok Samanvay” faces an internal revolt. Its senior leaders, citing the party’s drift toward corporate‑friendly policies, demand a return to the original socialist platform, including a wealth tax, stricter labour laws, and renationalisation of key infrastructure. The party’s high command, backed by affluent urban cadres, resists, warning of electoral losses. The dissidents threaten to form a parallel bloc, echoing the 1969 Congress split where Indira Gandhi confronted the “Syndicate”. Historians draw a parallel to the Late Roman Republic, where the Populares (led by the Gracchi) challenged the Optimates’ senatorial elite over land reform and grain subsidies. The Lok Samanvay faction cites rising Gini coefficient (0.38 → 0.45 in five years) and declining real wages (‑8 % since 2020) as justification. Students must analyse the ideological, organisational, and historical dimensions of this intra‑party conflict, comparing it to both the 1969 Congress split and Roman Popular‑Optimate struggles.

(B) Using the 1969 Congress split as a model, forecast the probable electoral impact if the Lok Samanvay dissidents form a new party contesting the next general election, assuming they secure 12 % of the national vote share.

In early 2026, a developing nation faces a sudden surge in cyber‑attacks targeting its power grid, allegedly sponsored by a foreign state amid an ongoing regional conflict. The government responds with sweeping internet shutdowns, invocation of the National Security Act, and detention of suspected hackers without trial. Simultaneously, war‑driven inflation pushes staple prices up 40 %, triggering spontaneous protests in industrial towns. A coalition of university students, ex‑military coders, and rural activists forms an encrypted messaging network to coordinate “digital satyagraha” – spreading awareness, organising peaceful sit‑ins at data centres, and launching non‑destructive data‑leaks to expose governmental corruption. Intelligence warns that splinter groups may shift to disruptive cyber‑sabotage if repression continues. Using the Quit India Movement’s underground socialist networks (JP Narayan, Aruna Asaf Ali) and the wartime economic strain of 1942‑44 as lenses, analysts must determine (a) whether the current protest is likely to stay non‑violent, (b) what conditions would push it toward underground sabotage, and (c) how economic distress influences the durability of the movement.

(C) Evaluate the likely effectiveness of the government’s internet shutdowns and detentions under the National Security Act, drawing a parallel with the Defence of India Act used in Quit India, and state which political‑science principle justifies such measures temporally.

The rate constant for a reaction is \(k = 4.5 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{L}\ \text{mol}^{-1}\ \text{s}^{-1}\) at 300 K. (a) What is the overall order of the reaction? (b) If the reaction is \(\text{A} + \text{B} \rightarrow \text{Products}\) and is first order in A, what is the order in B? (c) Calculate the initial rate when [A]₀ = 0.15 M and [B]₀ = 0.20 M. (d) If the volume of the reaction mixture is doubled (diluting both concentrations by half), what is the new initial rate? Express as a fraction of the original rate.

A multinational corporation (MNC) preparing its 2024 ESG report wishes to benchmark caste‑based diversity in its Indian operations against Al‑Biruni’s comparison of Indian varnas with Persian social categories. The MNC’s workforce data for its Indian plants show: Brahmins 12%, Kshatriyas 10%, Vaishyas 18%, Shudras (SC/ST/OBC) 60%. Al‑Biruni noted that Persian society had four comparable classes: nobles (equivalent to Brahmins), priests (Kshatriyas), merchants (Vaishyas), peasants (Shudras). The MNC also tracks land‑holding patterns of employee households: Brahmins 8%, Kshatriyas 6%, Vaishyas 22%, Shudras 64%. The ESG team must (a) compute a **Varna‑Persian Alignment Score (VPAS)** measuring similarity between Indian workforce distribution and Persian ideal equal‑share (25% each), (b) adjust VPAS using the household land‑holding distribution as a proxy for socioeconomic status (weight = land %/25%), (c) evaluate the impact of a new reservation‑linked hiring policy that raises Shudra hiring by 10 percentage points (reducing Brahmin and Kshatriya proportionally), (d) compute a **Diversity‑Gap Index (DGI)** comparing post‑policy workforce to the Persian ideal, and (e) allocate a ₹5 crore CSR budget for skill‑training across three regions (A, B, C) inversely proportional to their DGI (after land‑weight adjustment) using the accounting concept of cost‑benefit analysis.

(C) A new policy raises Shudra hiring by 10 percentage points (taken equally from Brahmin and Kshatriya). Compute the new workforce percentages and the resulting **Post‑Policy VPAS**.

In 2026 the UN General Assembly adopts the **International Data Treaty (IDT)** to harmonise rules on cross‑border personal data transfers, data localisation, and algorithmic accountability. The Treaty creates a **Data Governance Council (DGC)** with seats allocated to UNESCO (ethics & culture), WTO (trade‑related data provisions), and the UN Office of Drugs and Crime (cybercrime). Contributing states must adopt the **UN Model Law on Electronic Transactions** (based on the 1996 UNCITRAL text) and submit annual compliance reports audited by the International Federation of Accountants (IFAC). Legal historians note that Roman *contractus* (especially *stipulatio*) required (i) a clear verbal formula, (ii) witness presence, and (iii) *pacta sunt servanda* (agreements must be kept) – principles echoed in the IDT’s emphasis on explicit consent mechanisms, independent audits, and sanction regimes for breaches. The Treaty also establishes a **Data Compensation Fund** financed by a levy on global digital advertising revenue, projected to raise $15 bn over a decade with a 3 % real return. Students must evaluate the Treaty’s design through political‑science theories of international law, historical analogues of contractual enforcement, and accounting standards for revenue recognition.

(B) Which element of Roman *stipulatio* (clear formula, witnesses, pacta sunt servanda) is most directly mirrored in the IDT’s requirement for explicit consent mechanisms, and why?

A fertility clinic wishes to vitrify oocytes using a solution containing ethylene glycol (EG) and sucrose. The protocol involves equilibrating oocytes in increasing concentrations of cryoprotectant (CPA) followed by rapid plunging into liquid nitrogen (‑196 °C).  

Key data:  
- Oocyte approximated as a sphere of radius **rₒ** = 50 µm, membrane hydraulic conductivity **Lₚ** = 0.5 × 10⁻¹² m/(s·Pa).  
- The intracellular water volume **V_w** ≈ 4/3πrₒ³ ≈ 5.24 × 10⁻¹³ m³.  
- During CPA addition, water efflux follows **dV_w/dt = –Lₚ A Δπ**, where **A** = 4πrₒ² is the surface area and **Δπ** is the osmotic pressure difference across the membrane.  
- Osmotic pressure of ideal dilute solution: **π = iCRT**, with van’t Hoff factor **i** = 1 for EG, **C** in mol/L, **R** = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K), **T** = 298 K.  
- The vitrification solution finally contains **C_EG** = 4 M and **C_sucrose** = 0.5 M. Sucrose is non‑permeating, contributing to extracellular osmotic pressure only.  
- The cooling rate **Ṫ** (°C/s) must be high enough to avoid ice nucleation; empirical relation: **Ṫ_min** = k · (C_total)ⁿ, where **k** = 0.5 °C·s⁻¹·M⁻ⁿ, **n** = 1.2, and **C_total** = ΣC_i (all solutes).  

The clinic can control the flow rate of CPA solution, thereby adjusting the time **t_eq** oocytes spend in each equilibration step.  

**Answer the following.**

(A) Calculate the **osmotic pressure difference Δπ** (in bar) across the oocyte membrane when the extracellular solution contains 4 M EG (permeating) and 0.5 M sucrose (non‑permeating), assuming intracellular EG concentration has equilibrated to 2 M and intracellular sucrose is negligible. Use π = iCRT with R = 0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K), T = 298 K.

A solid cylinder of mass 2.0 kg and radius 0.10 m rolls without slipping down a 30° incline of length 2.0 m. Calculate its linear acceleration, final speed at the bottom, and time taken. (g = 9.8 m/s²)

A camel and a horse each weigh 5,000 N. The camel's four feet have a total contact area of 0.2 m². The horse's four hooves have a total contact area of 0.04 m². Which animal sinks less into soft sand, and what is the pressure exerted by each?

VoltEdge, a Singapore‑based EV startup, plans to set up a lithium‑ion battery manufacturing hub in Gujarat (India) with an initial capacity of 2 GWh/yr. The project involves: (i) 150 technicians for cell‑assembly (specialised task), (ii) 80 engineers for process‑optimisation, (iii) 50 logistics coordinators for inbound raw‑material (lithium, cobalt) handling, and (iv) 30 quality‑audit officers. The plant will be a 100 % wholly‑owned subsidiary (WOS) of VoltEdge Pte. Ltd. Under Indian GAAP (Ind AS) the subsidiary must present separate financial statements. The company expects a learning‑curve effect: after the first 6 months, labour‑hour per kWh drops by 15 % due to specialisation. The market price of battery packs is projected at ₹ 8,500/kWh, with a price‑elasticity of demand of –1.2. The corporate tax rate in India is 25 % plus a surcharge of 7 % and cess of 4 % (effective 30 %).

(A) Calculate the expected reduction in labour‑hour per kWh after 6 months and the new labour‑hour per kWh if the initial labour‑hour per kWh is 0.45 h/kWh.

A 34‑year‑old male assistant commissioner, recently promoted to deputy secretary in the Ministry of Rural Development, presents with a 10‑day history of decreased need for sleep (averaging 3 h/night), inflated self‑esteem (“I can single‑handedly redesign the national irrigation scheme”), increased goal‑directed activity (drafting three policy papers simultaneously), pressured speech, and grandiose ideas about launching a startup to solve agrarian distress. He reports feeling “euphoric” and denies fatigue, though colleagues note irritability when his suggestions are challenged. He admits to occasional risky investments in cryptocurrency based on “insider tips.” A collateral interview reveals his father was diagnosed with bipolar I disorder and had two hospitalizations for mania. His recent performance appraisal awarded him an “outstanding” rating, increasing workplace stress. He denies depressive symptoms, psychotic features, or substance use beyond occasional caffeine. The employee handbook allows up to 15 days of sick leave for mental health, but he fears being perceived as unfit for promotion.  
Using the information above, answer the following sub‑parts.

(A) Which symptom cluster most specifically distinguishes the presented episode from a hypomanic episode according to DSM‑5‑TR criteria for Bipolar I Disorder?

A NITI Aayog task force examines the effectiveness of street‑vendor rehabilitation schemes in Tier‑2 cities. They select the quarter depicted in “फकीर के क्वार्टर” as a pilot site because the text describes the fakir’s informal barter economy (exchange of grain for cloth, services for shelter) and notes that residents often reject formal‑sector job offers due to distrust of bureaucratic processes. Recent field data show 70 % of households earn income through informal tasks (average ₹8,200/month), while only 22 % have taken up formal apprenticeships offered under the SVAMITVA scheme. Behavioral economists attribute this to confirmation bias – residents selectively recall past negative experiences with government officials, reinforcing preference for informal arrangements. The task force proposes a ₹1.5 crore intervention combining mobile grievance redressal units and skill‑upgradation workshops, expecting a 30 % shift to formal income within 18 months. Students must analyze the chapter’s depiction of informal economy, connect it to psychological concepts of confirmation bias, and evaluate the policy’s likelihood of success using economic‑behavioral reasoning.

(B) Using the chapter’s description of the fakir’s informal barter economy, explain how confirmation bias leads residents to overvalue past negative experiences with government officials.

A biotech startup aims to clone a 1.2 kb human insulin gene into the plasmid pBR322 (4.3 kb) for high‑level expression in *E. coli*. Two restriction enzymes are available:  
- **Enzyme X** recognizes 5´‑G^AATTC‑3´ (EcoRI) generating 5´‑overhangs CTTAAG (sticky ends).  
- **Enzyme Y** recognizes 5´‑CCC^GGG‑3´ (SmaI) generating blunt ends.  

The insulin amplicon is produced by PCR adding the appropriate sites. The ligation mixture contains vector (50 ng) and insert (variable mass) in 20 µL total volume with T4 DNA ligase (1 U/µL) at 25 °C. The standard free‑energy change (ΔG°) for phosphodiester bond formation is –5.0 kcal mol⁻¹ for sticky‑end ligation and –2.0 kcal mol⁻¹ for blunt‑end ligation (derived from base‑pairing and enzyme‑DNA contacts). Transformation efficiency of competent *E. coli* is 1 × 10⁶ CFU µg⁻¹ plasmid DNA. Assume ligation rate ∝ [Insert][Vector]·e^(–ΔG°/RT).  

Answer the following sub‑parts.

(A) Given the recognition sequences above, which enzyme produces sticky ends and which produces blunt ends? State the polarity (5´‑ or 3´‑overhang) of the sticky end generated by Enzyme X.

In a village in Rajasthan, a Patel (land‑owning Vaishya jati) farmer claims that a neighboring Bhil (Scheduled Tribe) family has encroached upon his ancestral plot. The Bhils counter that the land was granted to them under a 1950s state resettlement scheme for tribals displaced by a dam. The village’s jati panchayat (dominated by Patel elders) convenes, citing customary norms of land inheritance tied to ritual purity (only “clean” jatis may own irrigable land). Simultaneously, the state invokes Article 15(4) and the Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 (PESA) to transfer dispute resolution to a Gram Sabha with reserved seats for STs. Legal scholars compare the situation to Mesopotamian temple‑controlled agrarian economies (c11_hist_cbse_01_005), where priestly elites allocated land based on ritual status, and to the Belgian consociational model (c10_civ_cbse_01_001), which guarantees minority veto over territorial decisions. The Gram Sabha’s deliberations reveal tensions between purity‑based land customs and constitutional egalitarianism.

(A) The Patel jati panchayat’s restriction that only “clean” jatis may own irrigable land relies on which caste‑system principle?

A interdisciplinary research team uses natural‑language processing to quantify the atmospheric tone of descriptive passages in “I Sell My Dreams” (Latin American magical realism) and in selected excerpts from Virginia Woolf’s “Mrs Dalloway” (European modernism). They collect sentiment scores (‑1 to +1) for sensory adjectives, tag each sentence with geographic coordinates of the described setting, and overlay historical annual GDP per capita (PPP) and average temperature data for those locations. The goal is to test whether magical realism correlates with higher climate volatility and lower economic stability, producing a distinctive “wonder‑foreboding” tone. Provided dataset (excerpt):  
- Passage A (Havana, 1950): adjectives “bright”, “crumbling”, “distant”; sentiment = +0.2; GDP = US$2 k; Temp = 27 °C.  
- Passage B (Vienna, 1948): adjectives “grey”, “solemn”, “tram‑bell”; sentiment = ‑0.1; GDP = US$4 k; Temp = 9 °C.  
- Passage C (Barcelona, 1952): adjectives “ochre”, “salty”, “lively”; sentiment = +0.3; GDP = US$2.5 k; Temp = 18 °C.  
- Passage D (Oporto, 1950): adjectives “misty”, “wine‑scented”, “clamorous”; sentiment = 0.0; GDP = US$1.8 k; Temp = 15 °C.  
- Passage E (London, 1925 – Woolf): adjectives “foggy”, “melancholy", “rustle”; sentiment = ‑0.2; GDP = US$6 k; Temp = 11 °C.  
Students must compute aggregate measures, assess correlation, and interpret how setting‑driven atmosphere links to socioeconomic and climatic variables, integrating English setting analysis with economic history and physical geography.

(E) If the ocean current influencing Oporto’s climate shifted from the warm Gulf Stream to a cold Labrador‑like current, predict the likely change in sentiment score for Passage D and justify using geographic reasoning.

AuroPharma, an Indian API manufacturer, acquires 70 % of BioNova GmbH, a German biotech firm, forming a joint venture (JV) named “AuroNova”. The acquisition agreement stipulates that the Indian parent will appoint a CEO for the JV, while the German partner retains control over R&D and regulatory affairs. Post‑merger, the German R&D head reports both to the JV CEO (India) and to the German parent’s Head of R&D (Germany), creating dual subordination. Simultaneously, the JV must consolidate financial statements under Ind AS 110 (Consolidated Financial Statements) and comply with the EU’s GDPR for patient‑trial data. The Indian corporate tax rate is 30 % (including surcharge & cess); German rate is 29.9 %. The JV expects synergies of ₹ 20 crore per annum from shared distribution, but anticipates additional compliance costs of ₹ 4 crore/year due to GDPR. Employee surveys indicate a 12 % drop in motivation scores where dual reporting exists.

(E) Draft a short journal entry (in ₹) to record the monthly GDPR compliance cost of ₹ 4 crore per year, assuming the cost is incurred evenly each month and paid in cash.

Seventeen‑year‑old Rohan from Hyderabad has always been good at mathematics. His parents, both engineers, enrolled him in a specialized IIT‑foundation coaching class when he was in 8th grade. Over the years Rohan has received consistent praise for solving problems quickly, and his teachers repeatedly tell him he is “meant for engineering”. He has never taken up any hobby unrelated to academics, rarely spends time with friends outside study groups, and feels uneasy when his cousins talk about pursuing art or sports. Rohan recently scored 95% in his mock JEE‑Main test and feels a quiet pride, yet he also notices a vague sense of emptiness when he imagines life beyond exams. He has not explored any alternative career paths, nor has he questioned whether engineering truly aligns with his deeper interests. His school counselor observes that Rohan displays high confidence in his chosen path but shows little evidence of personal exploration.

(D) Discuss two sociological mechanisms through which the coaching‑class environment could reinforce Rohan’s foreclosed identity, drawing on concepts from social media influence (even if not directly used).

Design a hypothetical federal arrangement for a diverse country (not India) with three major linguistic groups (A: 50%, B: 30%, C: 20%) and two religious minorities (X: 15%, Y: 5%) cutting across linguistic lines.
