The farm aims to maintain a free chlorine residual of 0.5 mg L⁻¹ at the point of use. Chlorine is added as sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl) solution containing 10 % available chlorine by weight. The reaction stoichiometry is: NH₃ + HOCl → NH₂Cl + H₂O (1:1 molar ratio). The molar mass of NH₃ is 17 g mol⁻¹; HOCl is 52.5 g mol⁻¹. Additionally, historical data shows that any given hen has a 0.0012 probability per day of contracting a contagious respiratory disease if the water chlorine residual falls below 0.3 mg L⁻¹. Assuming independence, calculate (a) the daily volume of water to be treated, (b) the mass of NaOCl required to neutralise ammonia and achieve the target residual, (c) the concentration of NaOCl solution to be dosed (in mL L⁻¹ of water), (d) the probability that at least one hen shows disease symptoms on a given day when the residual is exactly 0.3 mg L⁻¹, and (e) the expected daily cost of disease outbreaks (treatment cost ₹ 150 per affected hen) versus the cost of chlorine (₹ ₹ 45 kg⁻¹ of NaOCl). Use Avogadro’s number where needed, and assume 100 % reaction efficiency.

(D) Assuming the free chlorine residual is exactly at the threshold of 0.3 mg L⁻¹, compute the probability that at least one hen shows disease symptoms on a given day. Use the binomial distribution with n = 2,500 and p = 0.0012 per hen per day.

The weights (in kg) of 60 students are given in an exclusive frequency distribution: 40–45: 8, 45–50: 15, 50–55: 22, 55–60: 10, 60–65: 5. The school nurse wants to report this using inclusive class intervals of width 5 kg for a parent newsletter. Convert the distribution to inclusive form. Then calculate the class mark for the 50–55 kg class in both forms and explain any difference.
Explain why the boiling point of propanal (322 K) is higher than that of methoxyethane (281 K) even though both have nearly the same molecular mass (58 vs 60 g/mol).

A biotech start‑up, **VaxNova**, plans to spend ₹120 crore on R&D for a novel vaccine during FY 2024‑25 (ex‑ante investment). It expects the wage bill to rise, inducing consumption with an MPC of 0.75 and autonomous consumption of ₹200 crore. The firm finances the plan by issuing equity (₹70 crore) and taking a short‑term loan (₹50 crore). After six months, due to regulatory delays, the actual realised investment is only ₹100 crore (ex‑post investment). Assume no change in government spending, taxes, or net exports. The economy is initially at equilibrium with income Y₀. Using the simple Keynesian model, answer the following.

(A) Identify whether the ₹120 crore R&D plan and the ₹100 crore actual spend are ex‑ante or ex‑post values, and justify your answer in one sentence each.

Calculate the minimum leg height required to keep the seating surface at least 30 cm above the expected flood level of 1.2 m, given that the seat thickness is 5 cm and the desired seated eye level for grandparents is 110 cm from the floor when seated.

A space‑based insulin factory must operate within a strict launch mass ceiling of 25 kg for all hardware, media, and consumables. The bioreactor hardware (including pumps, sensors, and power subsystem) has a fixed mass of 12 kg. Media density is 1 kg L⁻¹, and each batch consumes 5 L of medium. Consumables (filters, tubing, refolding buffer) add 0.3 kg per batch. A 15 % mass contingency is required for structural supports and insulation. The selling price of insulin is ₹ 6000 g⁻¹. Upstream media cost is ₹ 180 L⁻¹, downstream purification cost is ₹ 250 g⁻¹ of insulin, and fixed R&D overhead is ₹ 200 000. The effective yield of active insulin per batch (accounting for cleavage, purification, and microgravity‑reduced disulfide correctness) is 0.42 mg L⁻¹ h⁻¹ × 4 h × 5 L × 0.60 × 0.85 × 0.78 × 0.65 (the last factor being the fraction of correct disulfide bonds from microgravity kinetics).  
Determine the optimal number of batches (integer) that maximizes profit while respecting the launch mass limit.  
Answer the following sub‑parts.

(B) Determine the total launch mass (in kg) as a function of the number of batches (n), incorporating hardware, media, consumables, and the 15 % contingency.

A research lab needs to visualize purified virus particles (≈ 100 nm diameter) using a compound microscope. The objective lens has focal length fₒ = 4.0 mm and the eyepiece has focal length fₑ = 25 mm. The tube length (distance between the objective’s back focal plane and the eyepiece’s front focal plane) is standardized at L = 160 mm. The specimen is placed just beyond the objective’s focal point so that the objective forms a real, inverted, magnified intermediate image. The eyepiece then acts as a simple magnifier to produce a final virtual image at the near point (D = 25 cm) for comfortable viewing. The lab manager must: (i) determine the object distance for the objective to achieve a lateral magnification of –40× (the minus sign indicating inversion), (ii) compute the angular magnification of the eyepiece when the final image is at the near point, (iii) find the overall magnifying power of the microscope, (iv) assess how a 0.2 mm increase in the tube length affects the required object distance, and (v) calculate the depreciation cost of the objective lens over 3 years if its initial price is US $1200 and it depreciates linearly to a salvage value of US $200. Use the Cartesian sign convention throughout (object distances negative, image distances positive for real images, focal lengths positive for converging lenses). Assume thin lenses and paraxial approximation.

(D) If the tube length L increases by 0.2 mm (from 160.0 mm to 160.2 mm) while keeping the objective focal length unchanged, determine the new object distance uₒ′ (in mm) required to maintain the same intermediate image position (i.e., same vₒ).

A cord blood bank receives a 80 mL unit of umbilical cord blood (UCB) with a total nucleated cell (TNC) count of 1.2 × 10⁹ cells. To isolate hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) enriched for CD34⁺ progenitors, the unit undergoes density‑gradient centrifugation using Ficoll‑Paquel (density 1.077 g mL⁻¹). The plasma layer (density ≈1.025 g mL⁻¹) and the mononuclear cell (MNC) layer at the interface are harvested. The MNC layer is then resuspended in a HEPES‑buffered saline (pH 7.4) to maintain cell viability during subsequent magnetic‑activated cell sorting (MACS). The final product must deliver ≥2 × 10⁶ CD34⁺ cells kg⁻¹ recipient weight. For a 70 kg patient, the required CD34⁺ dose is 1.4 × 10⁸ cells. Historical data show that the CD34⁺ fraction in UCB MNCs follows a normal distribution with mean 1.5 % and SD 0.4 %.  
Answer the following sub‑parts, showing all steps and units.

(B) The MNC layer is resuspended in 20 mL of HEPES buffer. To maintain pH 7.4, the buffer system uses HEPES (pKa = 7.55) and its sodium salt. Calculate the ratio [HEPES⁻]/[HEPES] required and the mass of sodium HEPES (MW = 260.3 g mol⁻¹) needed if the total HEPES concentration is 50 mM.

In early 2024 a Track II dialogue comprising Indian constitutional scholars, Pakistani historians, and international economists convened in Geneva to explore a “limited autonomy” model for Jammu & Kashmir inspired by the treaty‑based integration of Mesopotamian city‑states under the Akkadian Empire. The proposal seeks to revive a version of Article 370 that grants J&K control over internal administration while ceding defence, foreign affairs, and communications to the Union. Participants are asked to evaluate the proposal on three fronts: (i) its legal fidelity to the original Instrument of Accession (1947) and the constitutional mechanics of Article 370; (ii) its historical plausibility by comparing it to the ways Akkadian rulers incorporated city‑states through sworn treaties and tribute systems; and (iii) its fiscal viability, requiring a transparent accounting of Union‑to‑J&K transfers under the existing special package. The dialogue provides the following data: the 2023‑24 Union budget earmarked ₹30,000 crore for J&K’s special status package; J&K’s projected population for 2024 is 1.25 crore. Students must identify which constitutional, historical, and accounting concepts apply, and then answer a series of sub‑questions that test conceptual clarity, comparative reasoning, and basic numerical estimation.

(D) Compare the integration of the princely state of J&K (1947‑48) with the integration of Mesopotamian city‑states under the Akkadian Empire (c. 2334‑2154 BCE), focusing on the role of treaties, central authority, and local autonomy.

एक समकालीन हिन्दी कवि ने 2017 में वस्तु एवं सेवा कर (GST) के कार्यान्वयन पर एक कविता “कर का बोझ” लिखी। कविता के दूसरे stanza में कवि writes: “कर का जाल, जिसमें फँस गया है common man का सपना, उसकी जेब़ खाली, पर सरकारी खज़ाना भरता चला जा रहा है।” तीसरे stanza में irony से कहा गया है: “हमने तो ‘एक देश, एक कर’ का सपना देखा था, पर देखो, अब तो हर चालान पर नया कर लग गया है—सिर्फ़ नाम बदल गया, शोषण पुराना।” कविता में विस्तृत imagery (वित्तीय जाल, खाली जेब, भरता खज़ाना) और symbolism (कर = बेड़ियों की ज़ंजीर) का प्रयोग किया गया है। scenario में दिए गए आंकड़े: GST की 표준 दर 18%, छोटे व्यापारियों पर अनुपालन लागत पिछले वर्ष की तुलना में 22% बढ़ी, और कर संग्रह में 12% की वृद्धि हुई। छात्र को कविता के imagery, metaphor, irony, symbolism और theme का विश्लेषण करना होगा, साथ ही इन literary devices को accounting concepts—जैसे कि उपयोगकर्ताओं (internal/external) की जानकारी और लेखा की शाखाओं (financial, cost, management) से जोड़कर बताना होगा कि कवि की आलोचना किस प्रकार वित्तीय सूचना के उपयोगकर्ताओं पर प्रभाव डालती है।

(B) कविता के तीसरे stanza में प्रयुक्त irony की पहचान कीजिए और बताइए कि यह irony किस accounting principle—“पूर्ण प्रकटीकरण” (full disclosure) —के उल्लंघन को इंगित करती है।

A colloidal quantum dot (QD) of radius 2 nm hosts an exciton population N_X(t) and a biexciton population N_XX(t). Radiative recombination of excitons occurs with rate constant k_r = 1 ns⁻¹. Biexciton Auger recombination removes biexcitons with a rate proportional to N_XX², characterized by k_A = 5 × 10⁻³ ns⁻¹. The coupled rate equations are  

\[
\frac{dN_X}{dt} = -k_r N_X + 2k_A N_{XX}^2, \qquad
\frac{dN_{XX}}{dt} = -k_A N_{XX}^2 + G,
\]

where G is the generation rate of biexcitons from a pulsed laser (pulse width ≪ 1 ns). By eliminating N_XX using the quasi‑steady‑state approximation dN_{XX}/dt ≈ 0, we obtain a single differential equation for N_X:  

\[
\frac{dN_X}{dt} = -k_r N_X + \frac{2G^2}{k_A}.
\]

Students must analyse the order, degree, and validity of the approximation, linking the result to enzyme‑kinetics Michaelis–Menten (c12_chem_cbse_04_001) and to the logistic growth model in biology (c12_bio_cbse_08_001).

(D) Under high excitation, the generation term G becomes proportional to N_X (G = α N_X). Substitute and find the degree of the resulting DE for N_X.

Compare how a Gestalt therapist vs. a CBT therapist would conceptualize and treat "perfectionism" in a Class 12 student, Ananya, who says "I must score 95% or I'm a failure." Use the NCERT classification parameters (cause, method, relationship, benefit, duration).

An ed‑tech startup plans to launch a nationwide AI‑based career guidance platform for students aged 14‑18 years. The platform’s design follows the cephalocaudal direction of higher‑order cognitive development (abstract reasoning, future planning) while accommodating individual differences in intelligence, interests, and personality. Pilot data indicate that 65 % of adolescents achieve clear career orientation (a cephalocaudal cognitive milestone) after 4 months of platform use, whereas 80 % demonstrate improved decision‑making confidence (a proximodistal‑linked self‑efficacy milestone) in the same period. The heritability of IQ in adolescence is estimated at 0.55. Annual operating budget for the platform is ₹3 crore, with 70 % allocated to AI‑model development and the remainder to human‑counselor support. A particular polymorphism in the COMT gene increases the likelihood of career‑choice anxiety by a relative risk of 1.6 compared to the baseline anxiety probability of 18 % in the adolescent population. Using the principles of directionality and individuality, answer the following.

(E) For adolescents carrying the COMT polymorphism, what is the probability (in percent) of career‑choice anxiety?

In 2025 the State Government allocated ₹8 000 crore to the “Coastal Resilience Mission” (CRM) to protect 1 200 km of shoreline from sea‑level rise. The plan emphasized mangrove restoration and community‑based early‑warning systems. However, the Detailed Project Report (DPR) revealed that ₹5 600 crore (70 %) was earmarked for constructing a 300‑km concrete seawall, while only ₹800 crore (10 %) went to mangrove nurseries and ₹400 crore (5 %) to warning‑system kits; the remaining 15 % covered consultancy and contingencies. By 2027, satellite monitoring showed the seawall reduced erosion in protected segments but caused downstream scouring, increasing flood risk for adjacent villages. Local fishing communities, whose livelihoods depended on intertidal zones, began referring to the seawall as “bandh kamal” (concrete lotus) – a sarcastic nickname highlighting its beauty‑like appearance yet destructive ecological impact. The mangrove saplings, meant to symbolize natural resilience, struggled due to altered sedimentation; many died, turning into a symbol of failed adaptation. The warning‑system kits, distributed but never maintained due to lack of funds for battery replacement, became symbols of abandoned preparedness. Analyze this scenario using irony and symbolism from the Hindi chapter, together with concepts of public‑works accounting (capital vs revenue, maintenance provisions) and disaster‑management governance (subsidiarity, participatory planning).

(E) Craft a 150‑word integrated analysis linking the irony, symbolism, public‑works misclassification, and governance failure to the chapter’s central theme of education as a struggle against systemic neglect.

QuantumTrade Ltd. is a proprietary trading firm that runs high‑frequency algorithms on NSE‑listed large‑cap stock “AlphaCorp”. The firm maintains a long position of 50,000 shares of AlphaCorp. The current market price is ₹1,800 per share, daily volatility (σ) is 2%, and the exchange imposes a margin requirement of 20% of the position value for overnight positions. QuantumTrade also holds a short position in AlphaCorp futures equivalent to 30,000 shares (notional). The NSE has a circuit‑breaker rule: if the Nifty 50 index moves ≥10% in a single day, trading is halted for 15 minutes. The firm’s risk‑management policy limits one‑day Value at Risk (VaR) at 95% confidence to 1.5% of the position value. Assume normal distribution of returns. Using this information, answer the following sub‑parts.

(B) Compute the one‑day Value at Risk (VaR) at 95% confidence level for the long position, assuming normal distribution, daily volatility σ = 2%, and position value as above.

A researcher is studying the influence of Hollywood on Indian cinema in the 1950s using Asokamitran’s excerpt from *My Years with Boss*. The passage describes Gemini Studios (established 1940), its make‑up department housed in a building believed to have been Robert Clive’s stables, the brand “Pancake” make‑up bought in truck‑loads, and the narrator’s duty of filing newspaper clippings. The researcher must answer literal questions about the text, infer the meaning of idiomatic expressions (e.g., “blew over”, “struck dumb”), connect the studio’s functioning to post‑Independence cultural policies (History), and evaluate implications for freedom of expression and state censorship (Political Science). The task requires distinguishing literal from inferential questions, locating textual evidence, and constructing PEEL‑style responses that incorporate historical and political‑science insights.

(E) Which vocabulary‑in‑context strategy best helps determine the meaning of “a coat of mail” as used in the passage?
Calculate the absolute and relative increase in the proportion of tribal households accessing formal credit from 8 % (2018) to 15 % (2023).

Fill in the blank: Imagine you are the first person trying to build a sociology department in an ______ university in the 1920s — no textbooks, no trained colleagues, no funding, and the British colonial administration controls education policy.

A 55‑year‑old patient presents with a solitary hepatic sarcoma (mesenchymal origin) diagnosed by contrast‑enhanced MRI. Tumor volume at diagnosis V₀ = 12 cm³. Growth follows the Gompertz equation: dV/dt = r V ln(K/V), with carrying capacity K = 200 cm³ and growth rate r = 0.03 day⁻¹. The patient is scheduled for stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) delivering a total dose of 50 Gy in 5 fractions (10 Gy per fraction). The linear‑quadratic (LQ) model predicts surviving fraction SF = e^(–αD – βD²) with α/β = 10 Gy for sarcoma (α = 0.3 Gy⁻¹, β = 0.03 Gy⁻²). Normal liver tissue has α/β = 3 Gy (α = 0.15 Gy⁻¹, β = 0.05 Gy⁻²). The cost of SBRT planning and delivery is US$15 000, while the expected cost of managing radiation‑induced liver disease (RILD) is US$80 000 if the normal‑tissue complication probability (NTCP) exceeds 5 %.  
Answer the following sub‑parts.

(C) Estimate the probability of developing radiation‑induced liver disease (RILD) assuming NTCP follows a logistic model: NTCP = 1 / [1 + exp(–(t – t₅₀)/k)], where t is the BED_liver, t₅₀ = 180 Gy₃, k = 20 Gy₃.

In late 2024, a UN General Assembly special session debates expanding the Security Council’s permanent seats to reflect the post‑Cold‑War order. The G4 nations (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) advocate for new permanent seats with veto power, while the African Union pushes for two permanent seats without veto, citing historical under‑representation. The United States conditionally supports expansion but warns against diluting the veto’s effectiveness, proposing a “veto‑restraint” pledge for new members. China opposes any change that could weaken its strategic position, advocating instead for enhancing the role of regional organisations (AU, ASEAN, EU) in peacekeeping financing. Simultaneously, a World Bank report shows that peacekeeping missions funded through mixed contributions (assessed dues + voluntary grants) have a 23% higher success rate in mandate completion. Delegates must reconcile legal principles of sovereign equality, regional representation, and the practical financing of peace operations, while referencing historical precedents of UN charter amendments and the veto’s evolution since 1945.

(B) Using the historic analogy of long‑distance trade regimes (Trade, Commerce and Long-Distance Exchange in Mesopotamia (c), assess whether the AU’s proposal for two permanent seats without veto resembles the role of non‑hegemonic city‑states in ancient Mediterranean trade leagues.

"A manufacturing company, Precision Tools Ltd, faces three simultaneous situations: (i) The Managing Director wants to know if a new CNC machine costing ₹50 lakh will reduce per-unit cost enough to justify the investment. (ii) The bank requires audited financial statements to renew a ₹2 crore working capital limit. (iii) The Pollution Control Board demands a report on effluent treatment costs. For EACH situation, identify: (a) the user, (b) the user category (internal/external), (c) the PRIMARY role of accounting serving this need, (d) the specific accounting branch involved, and (e) the qualitative characteristic MOST critical for this use case."

A NITI Aayog consultant prepares a policy brief on the impact of rural‑to‑urban migration on the ageing population in Uttar Pradesh. The brief notes that 22 % of households in western UP have at least one member migrated to metros (Delhi, Mumbai, Bengaluru) for work, leaving behind elderly parents. Field interviews reveal caregivers’ guilt and anxiety, mirrored by physiological markers: average heart‑rate variability (HRV) dropped from 48 ms (baseline) to 29 ms in left‑behind children, indicating heightened stress. The consultant uses Kamala Das’s “My Mother at Sixty‑six” to illustrate the emotional toll, citing the poem’s imagery of “ashen face” and “sprinting trees”. Simultaneously, the brief references India’s demographic dividend: the working‑age population (15‑59 yr) is projected to peak at 68 % of total population by 2031, yet the old‑age dependency ratio is expected to rise from 10.5 % (2021) to 14.8 % (2031). The consultant argues that policies must address both economic gains and the hidden psychosocial cost of migration on elders, using the poem as a rhetorical anchor.

(B) Using the psychological concept of stress‑induced heart‑rate variability (HRV) reduction, quantify the percent change in HRV observed in left‑behind children and relate this physiological change to the poem’s metaphor of the mother’s face as a corpse.
Identify which agro‑climatic zones meet the temperature and rainfall requirements for pulse cultivation (temperature 20‑30 °C, rainfall 350‑500 mm during critical growth stage).
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are filling a ______ balloon with helium at a steady rate of 900 cm³/s.

A research group seeks to prepare (S)-1‑phenylethylamine, a potent inhibitor of monoamine oxidase B, via Gabriel synthesis using enantiopure (R)-2‑bromo‑1‑phenylethane (0.06 M) and potassium phthalimide (0.09 M) in acetone at 45 °C. The substitution proceeds with inversion of configuration (SN2). After hydrazinolysis, the amine’s optical rotation is measured: [α]ᴅ²⁵ = +6.20° (c = 1.0, water). Literature reports [α]ᴅ²⁵ for pure (S)-1‑phenylethylamine = –7.40° (c = 1.0, water). The mixture also contains (R)-amine from racemization during hydrazinolysis (first‑order, k_rac = 1.2×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹). The lab must (i) calculate the enantiomeric excess (ee) of the product, (ii) determine the rate constant for the Gabriel step given that 70 % conversion occurs in 2.0 h, (iii) predict the ee after 5 h of hydrazinolysis assuming racemization continues, (iv) explain why Gabriel fails with (R)-1‑bromo‑naphthalene, and (v) assess the effect of replacing K‑phthalimide with Na‑phthalimide on reaction rate (consider ionic size and solvation).

(C) Predict the enantiomeric excess after 5.0 h of hydrazinolysis if racemization follows first‑order kinetics with k_rac = 1.2×10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, starting from the ee calculated in Part A (83.8 % R).

The Ministry of Electronics and IT releases a Hindi circular dated 3 March 2024 titled “डिजिटल सेवा 접근िता सुनिश्चित करने के लिए दिशा‑निर्देश”. The circular (excerpt) states:  
> “सभी राज्यों को निर्देशित किया जाता है कि वे अपने ग्रामीण ब्लॉकों में कम से कम ६० % घरों तक ब्रॉडबैंड कनेक्टिविटी सुनिश्चित बनायें। साथ ही, डिजिटल साक्षरता प्रशिक्षण के लिए प्रति ब्लॉक दो प्रशिक्षण centres स्थापित किये जायें। इस लक्ष्य की पूर्ति की समीक्षा kwartली basis पर की जायेगी।”  
Accompanying the circular is a bar‑graph showing rural broadband penetration (%) for five states: MP (48), Rajasthan (52), Bihar (35), West Bengal (61), Odisha (49). Students must: (i) extract literal targets, (ii) infer the implied socio‑economic challenge, (iii) interpret the data to identify which states meet the target, (iv) apply a sociological concept of digital divide to explain disparities, and (v) suggest a policy tweak based on the data.

(B) Infer the primary socio‑economic issue that the circular seeks to address.

A research team proposes to use the high‑spin \(Fe^{II}\) complex \([\text{Fe}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{2+}\) as a spin‑qubit embedded in a silicon quantum‑dot array for quantum computing. The complex is octahedral, high‑spin \(d^6\) (S=2). The zero‑field splitting (ZFS) parameter \(D\) arises from spin‑orbit coupling and is approximated by \(D ≈ \frac{λ^2}{Δ_{oct}}\), where \(λ = 400\ \text{cm}^{-1}\) is the spin‑orbit coupling constant for Fe\(^{II}\) and \(Δ_{oct}\) is the crystal‑field splitting.  

The qubit operations rely on microwave transitions between the \(m_S = 0\) and \(m_S = ±1\) sublevels of the spin triplet (effective S=1 after considering Kramers degeneracy? Actually for S=2, the ground state is split by ZFS into three Kramers doublets; the lowest doublet can be treated as an effective pseudo‑spin‑½).  

Given:  

- The complex is in a solid matrix where the ligand field can be tuned by applying uniaxial strain, changing the Fe–O bond length by ±2 %.  
- The relationship between bond length \(r\) and \(Δ_{oct}\) follows \(Δ_{oct} ∝ r^{-5}\) (point‑charge approximation).  
- The equilibrium bond length \(r_0 = 2.00\ \text{Å}\) gives \(Δ_{oct}^{(0)} = 10{,}000\ \text{cm}^{-1}\).  
- The microwave resonator operates at frequency \(ν = 9.8\ \text{GHz}\).  
- The spin‑lattice relaxation time \(T_1\) is limited by phonon processes and scales as \(T_1 ∝ (Δ_{oct})^{-2}\).  
- The dephasing time \(T_2^*\) is inversely proportional to the distribution of D values: \(T_2^* ∝ 1/σ_D\).  

Using the data:  

1. Calculate the zero‑field splitting \(D\) (in MHz) for the unstrained complex.  
2. Determine the strain (±2 % in r) required to shift the resonance frequency of the \(|0⟩↔|+1⟩\) transition to match the 9.8 GHz microwave source. (Assume the transition frequency ≈ 2|D| for the effective doublet.)  
3. Estimate the ratio of spin‑lattice relaxation times \(T_1\) for the +2 % strained case relative to the unstrained case.  
4. If the inhomogeneous broadening leads to a Gaussian distribution of D with standard deviation σ_D = 0.5 MHz, compute the expected \(T_2^*\) (in µs) assuming \(T_2^* = \frac{1}{π σ_D}\).  
5. Discuss how replacing H₂O ligands with the stronger‑field ligand CN⁻ would affect D, T₁, and the feasibility of electrical gate control of the qubit.

(E) Discuss qualitatively how substituting H₂O ligands with the stronger‑field ligand CN⁻ would affect (i) the zero‑field splitting D, (ii) the spin‑lattice relaxation time T₁, and (iii) the feasibility of electrical gate control of the qubit’s spin state via the Stark effect.

**ANALYZE:** "Net investment = Gross investment – Depreciation. Capital stock at end of year = Capital stock at start + Net investment."  
If capital stock on 1st April 2023 = ₹200 lakh crore, gross investment during 2023-24 = ₹30 lakh crore, depreciation = ₹8 lakh crore, calculate capital stock on 31st March 2024. Explain why depreciation is subtracted from gross investment to get the flow that changes the stock.

In August 2024, India participates in the **Malabar 2024** naval exercise alongside the US, Japan, and Australia in the South China Sea, conducting **anti‑submarine warfare drills** and **joint logistics replenishment** at Singapore’s Changi Naval Base. The exercise involves **12 warships**, **2 submarines**, and **over 4,000 personnel**. Concurrently, the United States and India sign a **Semiconductor Manufacturing Agreement (SMA)** under which a US‑led consortium will invest **US $3.5 billion** to establish a **300 mm wafer fab** in Gujarat, with technology transfer for advanced nodes (5 nm) and a clause for **joint R&D on defence‑grade chips**. The agreement also includes a **workforce‑upskilling programme** targeting **10,000 Indian engineers** over five years.  

On the diplomatic front, India abstains from a UN General Assembly resolution condemning Russia’s annexation of Ukrainian territories, maintaining its **strategic partnership** with Russia for **crude oil imports** (≈ 18 % of India’s total oil bill) and **defence spares** (MiG‑29 upgrades, S‑400 spares). However, India joins the US‑led **Indo‑Pacific Economic Framework (IPEP)** focusing on supply‑chain resilience and agrees to **share maritime domain awareness (MDA) data** via a shared satellite‑based platform.  

Public opinion polls show **55 %** of Indians view the Quad positively as a counter‑balance to China, while **38 %** perceive the US as exerting undue pressure on India’s foreign policy.  

Using the above data, answer the sub‑parts below.

(E) Propose a **policy mix** that allows India to **leverage US structural power** (via the SMA) while **mitigating constraints** (public opinion pressure) and **preserving strategic autonomy**, citing the accommodation model and hedging concepts.

GlobalTech Ltd., an Indian‑headquartered IT services multinational, plans to establish a delivery centre in Poland to serve EU clients. The firm will transfer 120 senior engineers from India (expatriates) and hire 180 local engineers. The expatriate package includes: basic salary ₹25 lakhs p.a., housing allowance 30% of basic, children’s education allowance ₹2 lakhs p.a., and tax equalisation ensuring the expatriate pays tax equivalent to Indian rates (30% inclusive of surcharge & cess). The local hire salary is €35,000 p.a. (≈₹31.5 lakhs at 1 €=₹90). The company must: (i) recognise the expatriate cost in the consolidated Ind AS financial statements, (ii) compute the deferred tax liability arising from tax equalisation, (iii) hedge the EUR/INR exchange rate risk for the local payroll using a 6‑month forward contract at a forward rate of 1 €=₹88, and (iv) evaluate the impact on the firm’s ROE if the expatriate attrition rate is 10% per annum (replacement cost = 1.5× expatriate CTC). The CFO also needs to disclose the human‑asset value on the balance sheet as per the Narayana Murthy viewpoint (intangible asset amortised over 5 years). Students must identify which staffing step is being exercised at each stage, link it to international accounting (Ind AS 12, 21, 105), foreign‑exchange risk management, and macro‑economic factors (EU GDP growth 2.5% affecting local wage inflation).

(B) Determine the annual tax equalisation amount (in ₹ lakhs) the company must bear per expatriate to ensure the expatriate’s tax liability equals the Indian tax rate of 30% on gross salary (basic + housing + education).

In 2024, a report by the Central Pollution Control Board reveals that microplastic concentrations in the Ganges near Varanasi have increased by 120% over the past five years, threatening the livelihoods of traditional fisherfolk communities (mainly Mallah and Kevat castes) who rely on the river for fish, aquatic plants, and ritual water. These communities describe a growing sense of helplessness as plastic waste chokes their nets, reduces fish catch, and contaminates the sacred water used in daily puja. Their plight echoes the secondary theme of human‑nature interconnectedness portrayed in the story 'lk>k' from 'vlxj otkgr', where the protagonist’s reverence for the river sustains both material survival and spiritual identity. Historical analysis shows that post‑independence water‑sharing agreements (c12_his_cbse_03_005) repeatedly prioritized industrial irrigation over riparian rights, weakening community‑based governance. Sociological studies indicate that caste‑based occupational exclusion (c12_soc_cbse_02_003, c12_soc_cbse_02_004) limits fisherfolk access to alternative livelihoods and decision‑making platforms, exacerbating their vulnerability to ecological degradation. Analyze how the secondary themes of human‑nature interconnectedness and cultural resilience in 'vlxj otkgr' illuminate this contemporary river crisis, considering historical water‑policy failures and sociocultural patterns of exclusion.

(E) Evaluate whether the existing legal framework (Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974; Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016) adequately addresses the secondary theme of human‑nature interconnectedness highlighted in 'vlxj otkgr'. Justify your answer with reference to historical water‑policy failures (History) and sociocultural patterns of exclusion (Sociology).

Using the GIS data (68 % of tribal habitations within 5 km of plume, average excess PM2.5 = 22 µg/m³), compute a simple spatial‑justice index (SJI) defined as SJI = (% affected) × (average excess pollutant) / 100.

A northern hill state reports that only 22% of residents aged 60+ use smartphones for health‑info access, despite 78% owning basic mobile phones. The State ICT Policy (2023) mandates “digital inclusion of senior citizens” and allocates ₹3,20,000 per block for training. Geographic data shows: 45% of villages lie >5 km from the nearest broadband tower, 30% have intermittent electricity. Psychological screening reveals: 60% exhibit low self‑efficacy regarding technology (measured by Tech‑Self‑Efficacy Scale), 40% express anxiety about privacy. Sociological mapping indicates strong intergenerational co‑residence (80% live with children) but prevailing norm that “elders should not handle gadgets”. The extension team must: (a) conduct a needs assessment using PRA tools adapted for elderly, (b) set SMART objectives, (c) select appropriate teaching methods and AV aids, (d) devise a monitoring plan, and (e) evaluate cost‑effectiveness.

(C) Select the most suitable extension teaching method for delivering digital‑literacy training to elders with low self‑efficacy, considering the intergenerational living context.

The village of Mandi lies on the left bank of the River Ganga in Uttarakhand. Houses are arranged in a continuous line following the riverbank, with agricultural fields extending behind the dwellings. The village has 150 households. Traditionally, 120 households cultivated wheat and barley (average annual revenue ₹2.4 lakh per household, average cost ₹1.2 lakh). After the launch of the state‑funded “Himalayan Homestay Scheme”, 45 households converted part of their homes into guesthouses, earning an average annual revenue of ₹4.8 lakh per homestay household with average costs of ₹2.0 lakh (including renovation, hospitality, and permits). The remaining 15 households are engaged in handicrafts (not considered in the analysis). The village panchayat now receives a proposal from a private developer to build a small eco‑resort on 5 ha of riverbank land currently used for farming, which would require converting 5 farm plots (≈3.3 % of total cultivated area) into commercial use. Under the 73rd Constitutional Amendment, the panchayat must decide whether to approve the land‑use change, weighing economic gains, social impacts, and environmental concerns. Students are expected to (i) classify the village’s dominant function, (ii) identify its settlement pattern, (iii) compute net incomes from agriculture and homestay sectors using basic accounting concepts, (iv) determine which tier of local government has authority to approve the land‑use change, and (v) evaluate a simple sustainability index that integrates economic, social, and environmental dimensions.

(E) Compute a simple sustainability index (SI) for Mandi village using the formula:  
SI = 0.5×(Economic Benefit) + 0.3×(Social Benefit) + 0.2×(Environmental Benefit), where:  
- Economic Benefit = (Net profit per household) / (Maximum net profit per household among the two sectors)  
- Social Benefit = (Number of households engaged in non‑farm activity) / (Total households)  
- Environmental Benefit = (1 – Fraction of cultivated land converted to resort)  
Use the data: net profit from agriculture = ₹144 lakh, homestay = ₹126 lakh (from Sub‑Part C). Total households = 150. Non‑farm households = homestay (45) + handicrafts (15) = 60. Cultivated land assumed proportional to number of farming households (120). Resort would convert 5 farm plots out of 120 → fraction converted = 5/120.

Astra Industries Ltd. plans to set up a new plant with capital outlay ₹12,00,00,000 (equity ₹6,00,00,000, debt ₹6,00,00,000 @ 9% p.a.). Expected annual output: 1,50,000 units; selling price ₹1,200/unit; variable cost ₹700/unit. Fixed manufacturing overhead (excluding depreciation) ₹1,80,00,000/yr. Depreciation on plant (SLM, 10‑yr life) ₹1,20,00,000/yr. Expected corporate tax rate 30%. The nation’s GDP is projected to grow at 6.5% FY 2024‑25 (source: Development). The company expects its sales to grow in line with GDP. Prepare projected Statement of Profit and Loss for Year 1, compute operating leverage, and assess the effect of a 1% point increase in GDP growth on projected PAT using the concept of income elasticity of sales (elasticity = 1.2).

(C) Compute the Degree of Operating Leverage (DOL) at the projected level of output.

In early 2025, a multinational consortium secured a 30‑year lease to extract rare‑earth elements (REEs) from the biodiverse Eastern Ghats, home to 4 million Adivasis belonging to the Kondh, Saora, and Gadaba tribes. The project promises ₹85 000 cr in export revenue but requires clearing 1 200 km² of forest, displacing an estimated 250 000 tribal households and threatening sacred groves. Four response coalitions emerged: (i) **Reformist NGOs** demand a strengthened Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) with mandatory free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC) and a revenue‑sharing trust fund; (ii) **Revolutionary Eco‑Socialists** call for the abolition of private mining, advocating community‑controlled stewardship of the Ghats under a constitutional “Ecological Commons” amendment; (iii) **Resistance Groups** (traditional tribal councils) seek to defend existing forest rights under the Forest Rights Act 2006 (FRA) and block further encroachment by setting up vigilance patrols; (iv) **Reactionary Traders’ Association** argues for maintaining the status‑quo of state‑led mineral licensing, claiming that tribal opposition hinders national technological sovereignty and urging stricter anti‑terrorism laws to curb protests. Satellite data shows forest cover loss of 3.2 % per year in the lease area since 2022, while the national average is 0.4 %. The Ministry of Environment issued a draft order allowing “conditional clearance” contingent on compensatory afforestation elsewhere, which tribes contend violates the FRA’s prohibition on non‑forest‑land compensation.

(D) Evaluate whether the Ministry’s draft order allowing “conditional clearance” with compensatory afforestation elsewhere constitutes a reasonable restriction on the tribes’ right to conserve their culture under Article 29, using the Sri Lankan power‑sharing model (majoritarianism) (c10_civ_cbse_01_002) as a contrast to assess accommodation of minority interests.

A state government proposes a 45 km metro corridor connecting three districts (A, B, C) to reduce congestion. District A is governed by a party that demands 60 % of stations in its territory under a power‑sharing agreement. District B contains a heritage site (point data) and a wetland (polygon data). District C has industrial zones (line data for freight corridors). The planning team must: (i) collect spatial data (satellite imagery, cadastral maps) and attribute data (population density, land‑use cost, expected ridership); (ii) store them in a GIS using appropriate vector (points for stations, lines for tracks, polygons for land‑use) and raster (DEM for elevation) models; (iii) perform overlay analysis to identify suitable alignments avoiding wetlands and heritage sites, and buffer analysis to assess 500 m impact zones for noise and displacement; (iv) run a cost‑benefit analysis where capital cost = ₹200 cr/km, operating cost = ₹2 cr/km/yr, benefit = ₹5 cr/km/yr from time savings, using accounting principles; (v) ensure the final alignment respects the power‑sharing clause (≥60 % stations in District A). The team has hardware (high‑end workstations), software (ArcGIS/QGIS), data, trained personnel, and standard operating procedures ().

(E) Explain how the “people” component of GIS can resolve a conflict between the technical team (recommending Alignment X) and District A’s political leadership (demanding Alignment Y) using procedural fairness.

India aims to establish a permanent lunar base by 2035, requiring a skilled workforce of 1.2 million persons over the next decade (engineers, technicians, support staff). The current total population is 1.42 billion. Age‑structure data: 28 % under 15 years, 65 % in the working‑age group 15‑59 years, 7 % aged 60 and above. Fertility rate (TFR) is 2.0 children per woman and declining at 0.05 per year. Urban literacy is 85 %; rural literacy is 70 %. Among the working‑age population, 12 % hold a graduate or technical degree (engineering, IT, vocational). Net rural‑to‑urban migration is 10 million persons per year. The sex ratio (females per 1000 males) is 920 overall, but in the 15‑29 age cohort it is 940. Historical Five‑Year Plans (post‑Independence) emphasized industrial workforce training, linking to Malthusian concerns about resource pressure. The state’s obligation to provide work derives from Article 41 and Directive Principles. Technical institutes are concentrated along the Delhi‑Mumbai Industrial Corridor, reflecting geographic planning. Ancient urban craft centres provide an analogy for modern skill‑clusters. Using this information, assess whether India’s demographic dividend can meet the lunar‑base workforce demand.

(C) Using the current TFR of 2.0 and its annual decline of 0.05, project the TFR after 6 years and comment on its implication for future workforce size relative to Malthusian theory.

A national museum is digitising 12,000 fragile palm‑leaf manuscripts from the Indus Valley era. Each manuscript’s metadata (script, dating, provenance) and a high‑resolution image (stored as a BLOB) are inserted into a MySQL table `manuscripts`. A Python script using `mysql.connector` reads a CSV of metadata, opens a connection, creates a cursor, executes an `INSERT` for each row, fetches the auto‑generated `manuscript_id` to link the image, and then commits. The script must run unattended overnight. The museum’s digital preservation policy (derived from the 2016 National Heritage Act) requires that **no database connection remain open for more than 30 seconds after a transaction completes**, otherwise the system logs a violation and may trigger an audit. Additionally, the Political Science module on “Cultural Property Protection” states that any breach of data‑handling protocols can be construed as negligence under Article 51A(g) of the Constitution. Identify how to guarantee that both cursor and connection are closed promptly, even if an `INSERT` fails due to a duplicate key, and explain the legal ramifications of leaving them open.

(E) Cite the specific constitutional article that could be invoked to argue negligence if a data‑handling breach leads to loss of cultural heritage data, and explain how proper resource closure supports compliance with that article.

An implantable sensor consists of a glucose‑oxidase (GOx)‑modified polymer layer forming one arm of a Wheatstone bridge. Glucose in interstitial fluid reacts with GOx, producing gluconic acid that locally lowers pH and increases polymer conductivity, decreasing its resistance Rₛ. The other three arms are made of a temperature‑compensating reference polymer with identical TCR but no enzyme. The bridge is powered by a 3.0 V lithium‑ion micro‑battery. The polymer’s resistance varies with glucose concentration [G] (in mM) as Rₛ = R₀[1 – k·[G]/(K_M+[G])], where R₀=10 kΩ, k=0.4, K_M=5 mM (Michaelis‑Menten‑type saturation). Temperature coefficient α = 30 ppm/°C for both sensor and reference arms.  
(a) Derive the bridge output voltage Vₒ as a function of [G].  
(b) Calculate Vₒ for [G]=2 mM and [G]=8 mM.  
(c) Using the function concept, express [G] explicitly in terms of Vₒ and invert the relation to obtain a calibration curve.  
(d) Perform a break‑even analysis: fixed development cost $2 M, variable cost per implant $150, selling price $500. Find the minimum number of units N to be sold to avoid loss.  
(e) Provide a shortcut to estimate Vₒ for low glucose ([G]≪K_M) and compute the time saved versus the full Michaelis‑Menten evaluation.

(B) Using Rₛ = R₀[1 – k·[G]/(K_M+[G])] with R₀=10 kΩ, k=0.4, K_M=5 mM, compute the bridge output Vₒ for glucose concentrations [G]=2 mM and [G]=8 mM. Assume the reference arms have constant resistance R₀ and the bridge is excited by Vₛ=3.0 V.

A coastal state plans to designate a circular Marine Protected Area (MPA) of radius **R** km to protect a commercially important reef fish (*Lutjanus argentimaculatus*). Adult fish inside the MPA follow logistic growth with intrinsic rate r = 0.0005 day⁻¹ and carrying capacity K = 2000 kg km⁻² (uniform density). Larvae are released uniformly from adult biomass and disperse according to a 2‑D diffusion model with coefficient D = 10 km² day⁻¹. The probability that a larva settles inside the MPA is P_settle = 1 − exp(−αR²), where α = 0.02 km⁻² (captures retention due to boundary). Recruitment to the fishery outside the MPA follows a Beverton‑Holt model: R = (α_rec · SSB) / (1 + β·SSB), where SSB is spawning stock biomass (kg) outside the MPA, α_rec = 0.8, β = 0.0004 kg⁻¹. Fish are harvested outside the MPA at a constant effort yielding yield Y = q·E·B_out, with catchability q = 0.0001 kg⁻¹ effort⁻¹, effort E = 100 effort‑days yr⁻¹, and B_out the biomass outside the MPA (kg). Assume steady state where biomass inside (B_in) and outside (B_out) satisfy:  
- Diffusion flux from MPA to outside ≈ D·(B_in/πR²) · (2πR) ≈ 2D B_in / R (kg day⁻¹).  
- This flux equals the larval settlement loss from MPA: loss = B_in · (1 − P_settle) · γ, where γ = 0.001 day⁻¹ (conversion of biomass to larval equivalents).  
- Outside biomass grows by inflow flux and natural logistic growth (same r,K) minus harvest.  

Using these relations, answer the sub‑parts. (All logarithms are natural.)

(A) Derive the expression for the steady‑state biomass inside the MPA (B_in) in terms of R, D, γ, α, and the larval retention probability P_settle.

The Karnataka State Industrial Planning Board envisions a 15 km² satellite town adjacent to the upcoming ‘TechCity’ IT‑park on Bengaluru’s outskirts. The site presents three physical zones: (i) a 4 km‑long ridge running NNW‑SSE (elevated, rocky, low water table) – suitable for **linear** settlement along the ridge; (ii) a 3 km × 3 km plateau with deep alluvial soil and existing network of **tanks** (traditional water‑harvesting ponds) – amenable to a **rectangular** grid aligned with tank bunds; (iii) a 1.2 km‑diameter depression containing a perennial **lake** – ideal for a **circular** settlement around the lake for water security. The state’s **Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013** mandates consent of affected Gram Panchayats, akin to the vertical power‑sharing model in India’s federal structure (c10_civ_cbse_01_005). Economic analysis: projected per‑capita GDP contribution from IT‑services = INR 2.5 lakh/yr; construction cost per household: linear = INR 2.2 lakh, rectangular = INR 2.0 lakh, circular = INR 2.4 lakh (due to lake‑front landscaping). Environmental constraint: maximum permissible groundwater extraction = 0.8 MCM/yr; linear layout increases runoff recharge by 15 %, rectangular by 5 %, circular reduces recharge by 10 % due to lake evaporation. Students must determine the optimal settlement shape balancing economic output, water‑security, legal consent, and construction cost.

(D) Assess the impact of each shape on the **maximum permissible groundwater extraction** (0.8 MCM/yr) considering the recharge changes given. Which shape allows the highest sustainable withdrawal without exceeding the limit?
In a circle of radius 25 cm, a chord of length 48 cm is drawn. Find the distance of this chord from the centre.

During the 2023‑24 farmers’ protest against the Farm Laws, a Hindi protest song gained viral traction. Its chorus uses the river Yamuna as a recurring motif:  

“यमुना की धारा, अखंड wieं — जैसे हमारी मांग,  
जो रुक‑रुक कर बहती है, पर रुकती नहीं।  
उसके तट पर बैठे हैं हम, जैसे बच्चे माँ की गोद में,  
पर upstream की fábricheन से आता ज़हरीला धुआँ,  
जैसे राज्य की नीतियाँ, ज़हर घोल रही हैं।”  

Accompanying data:  
- Central Water Commission (CWC) 2022 report: Yamuna dissolved oxygen (DO) average 3.2 mg/L (below the 5 mg/L threshold for aquatic life).  
- The Farm Laws (repealed 2021) had been critiqued for undermining Minimum Support Price (MSP); the protest demanded a legal guarantee for MSP.  
- Historical note: The 1930 Salt March used the imagery of the sea as a symbol of freedom; protestors marched to Dandi to make salt, challenging British monopoly.  
- Geographical fact: Yamuna’s catchment covers 8 % of India’s landmass but supports >50 million people via irrigation and drinking water.  

Students must dissect the song’s imagery and metaphor, connect them to the historical Salt March, the legal demand for MSP (a polity issue), and the river’s water‑quality data (geography), then judge the song’s effectiveness as a protest tool.

(D) Assess how the imagery of “ज़हरीला धुआँ” from upstream factories supports a claim under Directive Principle of State Policy (Article 47) regarding public health, linking to the Yamuna’s DO levels.

The Congo Basin hosts the world’s second‑largest tropical rainforest. Recent FAO data indicate that shifting cultivation occupies roughly 12 million ha, rotating every 4 years (2 years cropping, 2 years fallow). Average pre‑cultivation forest carbon stock is 200 t CO₂e ha⁻¹; after two years of cultivation it falls to 40 t CO₂e ha⁻¹. The UN‑REDD+ programme has pledged $200 million over five years to support sustainable land‑use projects in the basin, aiming to reduce emissions from shifting cultivation by 30 % through improved fallow management and agroforestry. The Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is a federal state where natural‑resource management is constitutionally shared between the central government and provincial entities (vertical power‑sharing).

(D) Identify the constitutional article that governs vertical power‑sharing between the central government and provincial entities in the DRC regarding natural‑resource management, and explain how it relates to the REDD+ implementation framework.

Compare the occupational structure transition of Tamil Nadu and Bihar (1991-2011) using the "Lewis Turning Point" concept. Data: TN 1991: P-58%, S-20%, T-22%; TN 2011: P-38%, S-26%, T-36%. Bihar 1991: P-78%, S-10%, T-12%; Bihar 2011: P-68%, S-14%, T-18%. Which state crossed the Lewis Turning Point? Explain using surplus labour absorption, wage trends, and migration data.

A municipal corporation in a historic Indian city plans to replace three aging clocktowers with smart‑enabled bronze towers that chime every half‑hour. The project proposal cites A.K. Ramanujan’s poem “Time and Time Again” to argue that the new towers will reflect the city’s “seasonal alliances” of Hindu, Christian, and Muslim communities. Before approval, the finance department must conduct an audit: verify the projected cost (₹12 crore), allocate funds under the “Urban Heritage” head, and assess whether the poetic justification aligns with the actual budgetary heads (maintenance, energy, community outreach). Simultaneously, a cultural‑heritage NGO raises a petition claiming the poem’s imagery of “a maker’s shaking hand in Switzerland” and “mutual distances commemorating a donor’s whim” suggests the towers will become symbols of external influence rather than local faith. A crew of 4 astronauts is stationed on a lunar base for 180 days. The average galactic cosmic ray flux is 2.5 particles cm⁻² s⁻¹ with a mean energy of 1.2 GeV per particle. A state education board introduces an inclusive exam for gifted students, using a battery of tests based on the PASS model, Triarchic theory, and Multiple Intelligences. In 2023, Gemini Studios’ successor, “SouthFrame Productions”, releases a big‑budget historical epic *Veeratha*. In 2025, the European Commission prepares a feasibility report on accelerating EU accession for a Western Balkan state (State X) that has recently held competitive elections after a decade of authoritarian rule. A biotech startup aims to mass‑multiply a rare medicinal plant using stem cuttings. An indole‑3‑acetic acid (IAA) solution is applied to the cut surface and must diffuse through a 5 mm cortical layer to reach the vascular cambium where it triggers cell division. The diffusion coefficient of IAA in plant tissue is \(D = 1.2\times10^{-10}\ \text{m}^2\text{s}^{-1}\). Assuming one‑dimensional diffusion from a constant surface concentration \(C_0\), the concentration at depth \(x\) and time \(t\) follows  
\[
\frac{C(x,t)}{C_0} = \text{erfc}\!\left(\frac{x}{2\sqrt{Dt}}\right).
\]  
The cuttings are incubated in a growth chamber where temperature cycles between 20 °C and 30 °C. Shoot formation per explant follows a geometric progression with ratio \(r = 1.5\) per week, starting from 1 shoot at week 0. A misting system delivers water droplets of radius \(0.2\ \text{mm}\) at a rate of \(2\ \text{droplets}\,\text{s}^{-1}\,\text{cm}^{-2}\).

(B) Calculate the time required for the IAA concentration at a depth of 5 mm to reach 10 % of the surface concentration \(C_0\).

EduTech Innovations launches an AR‑based science kit for class 11‑12 students. During the Artemis‑III lunar landing, NASA’s Mission Control Center (MCC) in Houston operates two parallel teams: Team A performs routine telemetry checks (a well‑learned, simple task) while Team B prepares an emergency abort procedure (a novel, complex task). In July 2024, the Cauvery Water Dispute Tribunal reconvened to adjudicate a fresh complaint from Tamil Nadu regarding Karnataka’s release of water from the Krishnaraja Sagar dam during a deficit monsoon year. In 2023, the Sahel region experienced a 22% decline in rainfall, prompting 1.4 million pastoralists to migrate southward. A research team studying the Sundarbans delta collects oral testimonies from fishermen displaced by cyclonic surges. In a village of Bihar, a cooperative of 120 handloom weavers launches a roadside stand to sell plain‑cotton sarees directly to passersby, hoping to bypass exploitative middlemen who pay ₹150 per saree. In the ecologically fragile Zanskar valley, a ₹120 crore climate‑adaptation package is routed through the three‑tier Panchayati Raj system to fund afforestation, check‑dams, and solar micro‑grids. An e‑commerce firm based in Mumbai deployed a generative AI chatbot in early 2023 to handle customer inquiries about order status, returns, and product recommendations. The chatbot was fine‑tuned on a corpus of past customer‑service transcripts. Explain how the societal benefit of fostering gender‑inclusive digital experiences should influence the decision per c11_acc_cbse_01_007.

In early 2025, the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) released a report on “Land Grabbing and Climate Resilience” highlighting the case of the Sundarbans delta, where multinational aquaculture firms have leased 150 km² of mangrove fringe land for shrimp farming, displacing 8,000 traditional honey‑collectors and fishers.
