(C) Examine the grammatical use of imperative sentences in Ananda’s dialogues (e.g., “Take this water,” “Look into the mirror”) and discuss how imperatives can encode power relations, referencing sociological views on language and dominance.

In 2024 the Ministry of Rural Development launches a nationwide “Digital Gram” campaign to promote broadband access in villages. The campaign’s anthem is a newly composed Hindi folk‑style poem titled *“Gaon ki Dhar”* (The Village’s Pulse). The poem uses vivid agrarian imagery – “golden wheat swaying like promise”, “iron plough singing with data streams”, “wells filled with light‑bytes”. The Ministry claims the imagery bridges traditional values with modern technology, thereby reducing resistance to the initiative. A civil‑society group files a PIL alleging the poem manipulates public perception by oversimplifying the digital divide and masking infrastructural gaps. As a policy analyst, you must examine the poem’s imagery (आरोह भाग-2) to determine whether it constitutes legitimate persuasion or misleading symbolism, linking your analysis to the constitutional principle of freedom of speech (Article 19) and the geographic reality of broadband coverage (only 38% of villages have 4G as per TRAI 2023 data).

(D) Analyze the protagonist (the imagined “village farmer” voiced in the poem) as a construct representing rural agency. Identify two traits conveyed through the poem’s language and assess whether these traits empower or constrain the farmer’s ability to critique the Digital Gram policy.

A Singapore‑based FinTech MNC launches an AI‑driven hiring platform that sources software engineers from India’s Tier‑2 cities. Candidates upload coding profiles; the platform’s algorithm scores them on proficiency in specific languages (e.g., Rust, Go), problem‑solving speed, and “cultural fit” inferred from social‑media activity. Top‑scoring candidates receive offers for six‑month project‑based contracts with renewal contingent on real‑time performance metrics; lower‑scoring applicants are placed in a “talent pool” receiving micro‑task gigs (bug‑bounty, UI testing) paid per‑task. The MNC advertises the scheme as “upskilling India’s workforce”, yet reports show that 62 % of contract engineers experience non‑renewal after the first cycle, 48 % of pool workers earn below the local minimum wage, and 35 % lack any provident‑fund contributions. Historical British‑era engineering colleges in India created a cadre of railway engineers loyal to the colonial state; today the algorithmic platform creates a new loyalty to global skill‑markets, mediated by proprietary scoring rules. Using this scenario, analyse how globalisation produces skill‑based flexibilisation, exacerbates the digital divide, and generates new forms of informal work, linking to sociological theories of flexibility, historical education‑labor linkages, and political‑science debates on data‑governance and labour rights.

(B) Using the data that 62 % of contract engineers face non‑renewal after the first cycle, calculate the probability that a randomly selected engineer from the hiring pool will experience at least one non‑renewal over two consecutive cycles, assuming independence.

A manufacturer wants to set up a new cement plant. The limestone deposit is in a forested tribal area (Schedule V area) with no rail link, 200 km from the nearest coal block, and 300 km from the major urban market. The state government offers a 15-year tax holiday and free land. Using the seven location factors, evaluate the viability of this site. Which THREE factors are most critical and why?

A 2023‑24 study of Indian high‑school students in Jaipur reveals that 68 % of those from families earning < ₹4 lakh/annum aspire to careers in entertainment or entrepreneurship, despite only 12 % having access to relevant training or capital. Interviews show students frequently use words like “arcade”, “prodigy”, and “amber glow” when describing their future lives, borrowing metaphors from movies and social media. Researchers note that when confronted with structural barriers (college fees, lack of mentorship), students exhibit “pangs of doubt” but quickly revert to fantasising, a pattern interpreted as cognitive dissonance reduction. The study draws a parallel to Barton’s Sophie, whose repeated affirmations (“I’ll be like Mary Quant”) serve a similar psychological function. Using the vocabulary list from *Going Places*, answer the following.

(A) In the Jaipur study, the term “arcade” is used metaphorically to describe a student’s imagined future workspace. Which of the following best captures the intended connotation?

A 27‑year‑old male elite marathon runner with type 1 diabetes mellitus prepares for an upcoming international marathon (42.2 km) to be held in a hot, humid climate. He weighs 68 kg, height 180 cm, and trains intensely (≈ 2 h/day, 5 days/week). His current basal insulin regimen is 20 units/day of long‑acting insulin (glargine) and he uses rapid‑acting insulin (lispro) for meal coverage. To avoid hypoglycemia during the race and maintain performance, his sports nutritionist must design a carbohydrate‑loading protocol, intra‑race fueling strategy, and post‑race recovery nutrition. The plan must adhere to diabetic sports guidelines: pre‑race carbohydrate intake 8‑10 g/kg body weight over 24‑48 h, intra‑race glucose intake 30‑60 g/h from low‑to‑moderate GI sources, and post‑race carbohydrate‑protein ratio 3‑4:1 to replenish glycogen and support muscle repair. Total daily energy needs on training days are estimated at 3,200 kcal. The nutritionist has access to the following sports foods with their GI and nutrient content per 100 g: dates (GI 42, carb 75 g, fiber 8 g), banana (GI 51, carb 23 g, fiber 2.6 g), energy gel (GI 78, carb 25 g, fiber 0 g), oatmeal (GI 55, carb 66 g, fiber 10 g), whey protein isolate (carb 2 g, protein 80 g, fat 1 g), and peanut butter (GI 14, carb 20 g, protein 25 g, fiber 6 g). The athlete’s monthly sponsorship budget for nutrition supplements is INR 15,000. Using principles of therapeutic diet planning integrated with exercise physiology, calculate: (a) total carbohydrate needed for loading, (b) hourly intra‑race carbohydrate amount and suitable food choices, (c) post‑race recovery snack quantity and composition, and (d) estimated monthly cost of the proposed sports nutrition plan.

(A) Calculate the total grams of carbohydrate required for carbohydrate loading if the athlete follows the guideline of 9 g/kg body weight over 24 h.

A senior policy advisor in the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs must produce a National Urban Mobility Policy (NUMP) within three weeks. The advisor leads a team of four analysts, coordinates with two state governments, conducts three stakeholder consultations, writes a 50‑page draft, and prepares a ministerial presentation. Daily routine includes ministerial briefings, email/administrative work, 45 minutes of exercise, and seven hours of sleep. The advisor has 112 waking hours per week (16 h × 7). Estimated effort:  
1) Literature review & data analysis (high cognitive load) – 30 h  
2) Stakeholder meeting preparation & conduction (medium) – 20 h  
3) Draft writing (high) – 25 h  
4) Ministerial presentation prep (medium) – 10 h  
5) Routine emails & admin (low) – 12 h  
6) Personal health & family (low) – 21 h  
7) Contingency buffer – 10 % of total time.  
Using the Eisenhower matrix (Urgent/Important) and the Pareto principle (80/20), the advisor must prioritize tasks to meet the deadline while maintaining well‑being.

(E) After inserting a 10 % contingency buffer (based on total weekly time), compute the remaining slack time available for leisure or unexpected tasks.

Create a partnership deed clause for a new firm that includes: (a) Monthly salary to working partner, (b) Commission on profit after commission, (c) Interest on partner's loan at 8% p.a. (deed overrides Act). Write the clause in formal language and specify the accounting treatment for each.

SolarWave Ltd., incorporated on 1‑Apr‑2023, manufactures solar photovoltaic panels. Authorized capital is ₹5,00,00,000 (50,00,000 shares of ₹10 each). Subscribed capital is 30,00,000 shares; called‑up is 60 % of subscribed. Share premium is ₹3 per share. The company has a general reserve of ₹8,00,000 and surplus from P&L of ₹4,50,000. It obtained a foreign currency loan of USD 2,00,000 at 5 % p.a. interest; the exchange rate on the date of loan was 1 USD = ₹82, and the reporting date exchange rate is 1 USD = ₹85. The loan is to be repaid in 4 years, hence shown as a non‑current liability. Fixed assets: solar panel manufacturing plant cost ₹12,00,000 (life 10 years, salvage 5 %); land (held for production) cost ₹3,00,000 (non‑depreciable). Intangible assets: carbon credits earned from verified emission reductions, valued at ₹6,00,000 based on biology‑derived metric of CO₂ sequestered (average 0.5 t per panel per year). Preliminary expenses ₹2,00,000 are to be written off over 4 years. Current assets: inventory of panels ₹4,00,000; receivables from power purchase agreements ₹3,50,000; cash ₹1,50,000. Current liabilities: trade payables ₹2,00,000; short‑term bank overdraft ₹1,00,000; provision for tax ₹80,000. The income elasticity of demand for solar energy is 0.9 and projected real GDP growth is 5 %. Assuming sales are proportional to national income, estimate the effect on receivables. Using the above data, compute the relevant balance‑sheet figures and ratios.

(C) Using the data below, compute (i) annual depreciation of the solar panel plant (straight‑line), (ii) annual amortization of carbon credits (assuming nil salvage), and (iii) annual write‑off of preliminary expenses. Plant cost ₹12,00,000, life 10 years, salvage 5 %; Carbon credits value ₹6,00,000, life 5 years (based on biology‑derived verification period); Preliminary expenses ₹2,00,000, write‑off period 4 years.

A multidisciplinary research portal combines three datasets:  
1. `heritage` (as in Seed 1) – historical manuscripts, bills, surveys.  
2. `legislative` (as in Seed 2) – bills with voting data.  
3. `geo_survey` – geographic survey records with fields: `survey_id` (INT), `location_desc` (VARCHAR) containing strings like `"Lat: 12.9716, Lon: 77.5946, Alt: 915m"`, `survey_date` (DATE), `agency` (VARCHAR), `elevation_m` (INT).  
The portal must generate a unified report showing:  
- Cleaned agency name (trim, title case).  
- Extracted latitude, longitude, and altitude as separate numeric columns from `location_desc`.  
- Survey age in years (rounded down) relative to today.  
- A flag `is_recent_survey` (TRUE if survey date ≥ 2015‑01‑01).  
- A composite key `survey_ref` made from the first two letters of agency (upper case) + `-` + last two digits of survey year + `-` + zero‑padded 3‑digit `survey_id`.  
- Only include surveys where altitude > 500 m and the agency name contains the word “Survey” (case‑insensitive).  
Write a single SELECT statement that fulfills all requirements. Assume MySQL 8.0.

(B) Extract latitude (`lat`), longitude (`lon`), and altitude (`alt_m`) as DECIMAL(8,4) from `location_desc` (format `"Lat: <value>, Lon: <value>, Alt: <value>m"`).

A 22‑year‑old female fashion influencer with 1.8 million followers posts a reel critiquing fast‑fashion labor practices. Within 4 hours, the video is reshared 250 k times, attracting both supportive comments and a coordinated hate campaign. The campaign includes death threats, doxxing of her apartment address, and memes labeling her “anti‑national.” She receives an average of 120 hostile messages per hour, with peaks of 300 msg/hr during night‑time IST. She reports difficulty sleeping, intrusive thoughts about the threats, and a urge to delete all social media. A close friend offers to stay with her offline, while her manager advises a temporary hiatus and legal notice to the platform. Her salivary cortisol measured at 08:00 hr is 22 nmol/L (baseline 8 nmol/L). The platform’s community‑guidelines invoke the “Safe Harbour” clause under the IT Act, 2000, which mandates swift removal of hateful content upon receipt of a valid complaint.  
Using this scenario, answer the following sub‑parts.

(A) Identify the primary appraisal of the influencer when she interprets the death threats as a potential loss of personal safety.

A farmer‑led startup launches a blockchain‑based platform that records every grain transaction from farm to mandi, aiming to create transparent data for Minimum Support Price (MSP) revisions. The platform has onboarded 120 million farmer households, of which 45 % use smartphones and actively upload sales data. After six months, the system shows an average price realization 12 % below the current MSP for wheat and pulses. The Bharatiya Kisan Union (BKU), claiming to represent 2 million farmers, demands a 15 % MSP hike and threatens a nationwide sit‑in if ignored. Simultaneously, a corporate agribusiness interest group lobbies the Ministry of Agriculture to maintain the status quo, citing inflationary risks. The ruling party promises an incremental 5 % increase, while the opposition demands full implementation of the BKU’s demand. Activists invoke Article 39(a) (Directive Principle on equitable distribution of resources) and Article 14 (right to equality) to argue that the state must ensure fair remuneration. Historically, they compare their effort to Roman tribunes’ intercessio power (c11_hist_cbse_02_004) and to Hammurabi’s code fixing fair prices for grain (c11_hist_cbse_01_007). The Election Commission notes that no political party has filed expenditure reports related to this issue under the Representation of the People Act, 1951.

(D) Assess the impact of the blockchain platform’s transparency on political party funding disclosure norms under the Representation of the People Act, 1951.

A municipal corporation plans to retrofit the historic walled city of Jaipur into a “smart heritage zone” with IoT‑enabled traffic, waste‑management, and pedestrian‑friendly streets. The project budget is ₹2,200 crore, financed 60 % by equity (municipal bonds) and 40 % by a concessional loan at 6 % p.a. repayable over 15 years. The corporation cites Ibn Battuta’s 14th‑century notes on Delhi’s efficient postal (ulug) system and road‑maintenance, Bernier’s 17th‑century observations of Mughal city planning (wide avenues, segregated bazaars), and Al‑Biruni’s early 11th‑century measurements of city dimensions and water‑works as historical precedents for integrated urban services. Critics argue that Mughal cities lacked municipal budgeting and relied on imperial treasury, making historical analogues misleading. Using the travellers’ accounts, basic public‑finance accounting, and the Mughal administrative context, answer the following.

(A) According to Ibn Battuta, what two features of the Delhi postal (ulug) system contributed to its efficiency?
Calculate the effective annual depreciation charge (in ₹ lakhs) for the machinery after availing the 20 % capital subsidy.
Fill in the blank: The Lorenz ______ answers this by showing exactly what percentage of total income is earned by the bottom 20%, 40%, 60% of families.

You have a target protein (350 residues) and find two templates in PDB: Template A (2XYZ) with 40% identity over 85% coverage, and Template B (3ABC) with 55% identity over 60% coverage. Which template would you prioritise for MODELLER-based modelling of the full-length protein, and what additional step would be essential?

Future Retail Ltd (FRL) under CIRP (Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process) per IBC 2016. Admitted claims: Secured financial creditors ₹18,500 Cr (SBI-led consortium), Operational creditors ₹2,100 Cr. Primary security: FRL assets (fair value ₹14,200 Cr). Collateral security: 15,000 secured NCDs of ₹10 Lakh each (₹1,500 Cr face) issued at par to LIC, 9% coupon, redeemable at 103% after 7 years. NCDs carry second charge on same assets. Resolution Plan: Reliance Retail offers ₹16,000 Cr (₹14,200 Cr cash + ₹1,800 Cr equity in NewCo). NCD holders (LIC) dissent - argue collateral NCDs should be paid at face + premium before equity. Committee of Creditors (CoC) votes 66% in favor (SBI 55%, others 11%). LIC holds 34% voting share. NCLT approves plan with "fair and equitable" test. Liquidation value ₹10,500 Cr. TDS on interest accrued but unpaid: 10% u/s 194A. Discount on issue? Issued at par. Processing fee amortized.

(A) Determine recovery for collateral NCD holders (LIC) under approved Resolution Plan. Apply "fair and equitable" test (Sec 30(2) IBC): (i) Priority: Secured creditors get liquidation value of security; (ii) Dissenting creditors get at least liquidation value. Compute LIC recovery % on face value ₹1,500 Cr + accrued interest ₹180 Cr + redemption premium ₹45 Cr.

In a replication of LaPiere's study, researchers sent emails to 200 restaurants asking: "Would you serve a same-sex couple?" 80% said yes. Then a same-sex couple visited 50 of those restaurants; 45 were served. Calculate the attitude-behaviour consistency rate and interpret it using the five conditions.

PQR Ltd., a manufacturing company, needs ₹10 crore for a new plant (useful life 10 years). It has stable earnings, wants to retain control, and seeks tax efficiency. Evaluate three options: (A) Equity shares, (B) 10% Debentures, (C) Term loan from a financial institution at 11% interest. Assume tax rate 30%. Which source best balances the factors? Show your reasoning.

A Muslim woman is divorced by her husband via *Talaq-e-Ahsan*. She has no income, two minor children, and her *iddat* period (3 months) has ended. Her husband refuses maintenance beyond *iddat*, citing *Shah Bano* was "overruled" by the 1986 Act. She approaches you. Which law applies? What is her entitlement? Calculate a reasonable monthly amount if husband earns ₹1,20,000/month, has no other dependents, and they lived in a metropolitan city. Show steps.

Two traffic lights at a busy crossing in Delhi flash their yellow warning lights. The first light flashes every 4 minutes, and the second light flashes every 6 minutes. If they flash together right now, after how many minutes will they flash together again?

Compare the wind blowing across the Thar Desert of Rajasthan 200 years ago with the wind blowing there today. Analyze how the status of wind changed from a mere natural phenomenon to an important resource.

Compare the pollution load (kg/day) of Suspended Particulate Matter (SPM) from two cement plants: Plant A produces 3000 tonnes clinker/day with ESP outlet concentration 50 mg/Nm³ and gas flow 500,000 Nm³/hr. Plant B produces 2000 tonnes clinker/day with bag filter outlet 20 mg/Nm³ and gas flow 350,000 Nm³/hr. Which plant has lower *absolute* SPM emission? Which has lower *specific* emission (kg/tonne clinker)? Interpret for regulatory inspection.

A foreign‑based asset manager, “GlobalAlpha Fund”, wishes to invest ₹50 crores in Indian equity shares of “Solaris Ltd.” through the FPI route. The fund opens a demat account with a DP that is also a custodian. The DP charges an annual custody fee of 0.02 % of assets under custody (AUC) plus a per‑transaction fee of ₹100. The fund plans to make 12 equity purchases during the year, each averaging ₹4 crores. India‑Mauritius tax treaty reduces capital gains tax to 10 % (instead of 15 % domestic). The fund’s accountant must: (i) compute total annual DP charges, (ii) pass journal entries for custody fee accrual and transaction fees, (iii) evaluate the effective cost of investment after tax benefit, and (iv) comment on the impact on India’s capital‑market liquidity. Assume the fund holds the investments at year‑end.

(B) Pass the journal entry to accrue the custody fee for the year (assuming payment at year‑end).

In the kharif season of 2023, Vidarbha region received 40% below‑average rainfall, causing a sharp decline in soybean and tur (pigeon pea) yields. The state government announced a Minimum Support Price (MSP) for tur at ₹6,600 per quintal, but procurement agencies reported that only 30% of the harvest was purchased at MSP due to logistical bottlenecks. Farmers, especially those from Other Backward Castes (OBC) and Dalit communities, turned to informal moneylenders for immediate cash to buy seeds and fertilizers for the next rabi season. These lenders, often operating through weekly *haat* traders, charged interest rates of 24% per annum and accepted future crop produce as collateral. Simultaneously, a digital agri‑fintech platform launched a “Crop‑Insurance‑Linked Loan” product that used satellite‑derived vegetation indices to assess risk and offered loans at 12% interest, but required farmers to have a formal land title and a bank account—criteria many smallholder Dalit farmers lacked. By mid‑season, Dalit farmers reported higher loan defaults and loss of land tenure, while OBC farmers with partial land documentation accessed the fintech loans and reported better input access. A parliamentary committee is debating whether the state’s agricultural credit policy is sufficiently embedded in local social realities.

(C) Apply the land market node to explain why Dalit farmers’ lack of formal land title exacerbates their vulnerability in the credit crisis.

Assess whether the combined effect of the ban, subsidy, and awareness campaign meets the city’s dual goals of 80 % plastic‑waste reduction and 30 % GHG‑emission cut. Use the data from Parts B and D, assuming the campaign achieves the reach calculated in Part D and that 70 % of reached citizens adopt the alternative.

A bottle of wine label says "12% v/v alcohol". The density of ethanol is 0.789 g/mL and density of water is 1.00 g/mL. Assuming the wine is only ethanol and water, and volumes are additive, calculate: (a) mass by volume % of alcohol, (b) mass by mass % of alcohol. If 100 mL of this wine is heated to evaporate all alcohol, what mass of residue (mostly water) remains?

A 0.5 kg block is attached to a horizontal spring (k = 200 N/m) on a frictionless surface. The block is pulled 10 cm from equilibrium and released from rest at t = 0. Write the equations for x(t), v(t), a(t). Find the time when the block first reaches x = 5 cm and its velocity at that instant. Verify using energy conservation.

A 2023‑24 study by the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology links a 1.2 °C rise in average monsoon temperature over the Gangetic plains to a 22 % decline in cotton yield in Bihar’s Madhubani district. Consequently, household incomes from farming dropped by ₹ 3 500 per month, prompting 28 % of cultivator families to seek seasonal work in brick kilns of Uttar Pradesh. Simultaneously, a state‑run “Climate‑Resilient Craft” initiative provides subsidized solar‑powered looms and training in dye‑fast natural pigments to 12 % of weaver households, aiming to sustain traditional motifs despite climate stress. Ethnographic interviews reveal that elders now weave motifs depicting drought‑resistant crops (e.g., millet) alongside traditional peacocks, while children’s school projects increasingly illustrate flood‑affected villages. Using the poem’s secondary themes, students must evaluate how climate‑induced economic stress, adaptive migration, and state‑supported technological adaptation intersect with poverty, social inequality, folk culture preservation, and generational continuity in the poem’s world.

(E) Synthesize the poem’s secondary theme of poverty with Psychology node c12_psy_cbse_08_003 (Stress, Coping & Intergenerational Trauma) to explain how prolonged climate‑related economic strain could affect the mental well‑being of the mother figure depicted in the poem.

A satellite in a circular low‑Earth orbit (period T = 6000 s) carries a solar panel of area A = 10 m². The Sun’s irradiance normal to the panel is I₀ = 1361 W m⁻². Because of orbital motion, the angle of incidence varies as θ(t) = ωt, where ω = 2π/T. The instantaneous power received is P(t) = η A I₀ cos(θ(t)) when cos θ ≥ 0 (sunlit half‑orbit) and zero during eclipse (the other half). The panel’s conversion efficiency η depends on its temperature Tₚ, which rises linearly with absorbed power: η(t) = η₀[1 − α(P(t) − P₀)], with η₀ = 0.30, α = 2×10⁻⁴ W⁻¹, and P₀ = η₀ A I₀ (the nominal power at reference temperature).  
Using the definition of area under a curve, determine the electrical energy generated per orbit, the effect of eclipses, and the loss due to efficiency drop.

(C) Determine the excess energy (in joules) available above a minimum required power Pₘᵢₙ = 200 W (constant) during the sunlit half‑orbit.

A 38-year-old woman is diagnosed with a 1.8 cm grade 2 invasive ductal carcinoma, ER+, PR+, HER2-, Ki-67 15%. Sentinel lymph node biopsy is negative. Using TNM staging and St. Gallen/ESMO guidelines, determine the stage, risk category, and recommended adjuvant systemic therapy. Justify each component.

Medivac Pharma, an Indian multinational, has developed a novel antiviral drug “ViroBlock”. The firm seeks simultaneous regulatory approval in the United States (FDA), Europe (EMA), and India (CDSCO). Estimated R&D expenditure incurred to date is ₹2,400 crore. Additional costs for Phase‑III trials in each region are: US – ₹800 crore, EU – ₹600 crore, India – ₹200 crore. Post‑approval, the firm plans to launch the drug at a price of ₹15,000 per patient‑course in the US, €12,000 in Europe, and ₹8,000 in India. Expected patient‑course volumes over the first 3 years are: US – 150,000, EU – 120,000, India – 300,000.  

The firm’s CFO asks the management team to:  
1. Compute the overall break‑even patient‑course volume (aggregated across regions) needed to recover total costs (R&D + trial) assuming a uniform contribution margin derived from regional prices and a variable cost of ₹3,000 per course (manufacturing, distribution).  
2. Allocate responsibilities for preparing the regional dossier (planning), monitoring trial execution (controlling), and coordinating submissions (coordination) across the three levels of management.  
3. Assess whether pursuing approval in all three regions simultaneously is more effective (higher probability of market access) or more efficient (lower cost per approved market) compared with a sequential strategy (US first, then EU, then India). Use a simple expected‑value model: probability of approval in each region if pursued alone = 0.8; if pursued jointly, probability drops to 0.65 per region due to divided focus, but total time saved = 1 year (valued at ₹500 crore opportunity cost).

(D) For Medivac Pharma, identify which management function (Planning, Organising, Staffing, Directing, Controlling) is primarily involved in each of the following:  
(i) Setting the target of obtaining approval in all three regions within 24 months.  
(ii) Assigning project managers to lead the US, EU, and India dossier teams.  
(iii) Comparing actual trial expenditures against the budgeted amounts each quarter.

Evaluate the statement: "The 90th percentile of monsoon rainfall in Kerala is 3000 mm, so designing drainage for 3000 mm is sufficient for 90% of years." Consider geographical and statistical limitations.

The Uttar Pradesh government launches a “Digital Handloom Mission” to revive the Banarasi silk saree industry. Geo‑tagged looms are installed in 150 villages along the Ganges floodplain, where raw silk is sourced from Karnataka and mulberry cultivation is promoted under the National Sericulture Project. Each loom produces 2 sarees/day, selling at ₹12,000 each. Historically, the Mughal era (16th‑18th c.) patronized Banarasi weaving, establishing designs still used today. The state provides a 30 % subsidy on loom cost (₹80,000 per loom) and offers GI‑tagged Banarasi saree protection under the Geographical Indications Act, 1999. Export data shows 40 % of production goes to the UAE and USA, fetching ₹1,800 cr annually. A recent sociological study notes that 70 % of weavers are women aged 20‑45, many migrating from neighboring Bihar due to agrarian distress. Environmental norms require effluent‑free dyeing; plants must install zero‑liquid‑discharge (ZLD) units costing ₹15 lakh per cluster.

(C) Compute the effective cost per loom after the 30 % subsidy if the base loom price is ₹80,000.

CAR‑T cells targeting EGFR are infused intravenously to treat a metastatic lung tumor. Blood flow in a representative microvessel (radius r = 0.02 cm) is laminar and described by the Hagen‑Poiseuille law. Shear stress on the vessel wall is τ = 4ηQ/(πr³), where η = 0.035 g/(cm·s) (blood viscosity). CAR‑T cells become activated and release cytokines if τ exceeds a threshold τ_th = 10 dyn/cm². Margination (movement toward the vessel wall) enhances tumor extravasation and is modeled by an efficiency factor M = 1 − exp(−βτ), with β = 0.15 cm²/dyn. The therapeutic goal is to choose an infusion flow rate Q that maximizes M while keeping τ ≤ τ_th. Determine the maximum allowable Q, the corresponding margination efficiency, and discuss how altering blood viscosity (e.g., due to dehydration) affects the safe infusion rate.

(A) Calculate the wall shear stress τ (in dyn/cm²) for a blood flow rate Q = 0.01 cm³/s in a microvessel of radius r = 0.02 cm, given blood viscosity η = 0.035 g/(cm·s).

A municipal corporation plans to launch a millet‑based midday meal programme for 12,000 school children in an urban slum. The budget allocated is ₹180 lakhs per annum. Millet costs ₹30 per kg (including processing) and provides 350 kcal per 100 g. The current rice‑based scheme costs ₹22 per kg and delivers 360 kcal per 100 g. The corporation must ensure that each child receives at least 300 kcal per meal. Millet procurement faces seasonal variability: only 70 % of the required quantity is accessible during the monsoon months (June‑September) due to transport bottlenecks, while accessibility rises to 95 % in the rest of the year. The corporation can interchange millet with rice or purchase ready‑to‑eat fortified packets at ₹45 per packet (350 kcal). Using the concepts of utility, accessibility, and interchangeability, answer the following sub‑parts.

(B) During monsoon months, only 70 % of the required millet is accessible. Compute the additional daily cost (in ₹) if the shortfall is met by purchasing fortified packets at ₹45 each (each packet = 350 kcal).

A future Mars base plans to produce isopropanol (C₃H₈O) as a fuel additive by hydrating propene (C₃H₆) generated from the Sabatier reaction. The process uses two parallel pathways: (i) acid‑catalyzed Markovnikov hydration with dilute H₂SO₄ (rate‑determining step: protonation of the alkene) and (ii) hydroboration‑oxidation using BH₃·THF followed by H₂O₂/NaOH (anti‑Markovnikov). The base also has a limited supply of 2‑bromopropane, which can be converted to isopropanol via SN1 substitution with aqueous NaOH.  

Given:  
- Initial propene concentration = 0.50 mol L⁻¹, [H₂SO₄] = 0.10 M (constant).  
- Rate law for acid hydration: rate = k₁[propene][H⁺]; k₁ = 2.5 × 10⁻³ L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹ at 298 K.  
- Activation energy for the protonation step Ea₁ = 55 kJ mol⁻¹.  
- Hydroboration step follows pseudo‑first‑order kinetics with respect to propene (k₂ = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹).  
- SN1 reaction of 2‑bromopropane: rate = k₃[2‑bromopropane]; k₃ = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ s⁻¹ (water as nucleophile, [OH⁻] effectively constant).  
- Temperature on Mars habitat = 273 K.  

Assuming ideal gas behaviour, calculate the time required to achieve 80 % conversion of propene to isopropanol via each pathway, and determine which route gives the higher yield after 2 h. Use the Arrhenius equation to adjust k₁ to 273 K.

(B) Determine the time required for 80 % conversion of propene via acid hydration assuming [H⁺] remains constant at 0.10 M.

Compare the *drivers* behind the 1932 unification into "Home Science" versus the 2020s renaming to "Human Ecology and Family Sciences." Identify one key similarity and one key difference in the *problems each change tried to solve*.

A pilot‑scale bioreactor (working volume **V = 5 L**) is to be used for meristem‑derived banana shoot proliferation. The vessel employs a Rushton turbine impeller of diameter **Dᵢ = 0.10 m** rotating at **N = 60 rpm**. The culture medium has density **ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³** and viscosity **μ = 0.001 Pa·s**. The power number for the impeller is **Po = 5.0**. Oxygen transfer is described by the empirical correlation **kₗa = 0.026·(P/V)^{0.4}·(v_s)^{0.5}**, where **v_s = 0.01 m s⁻¹** is the superficial gas velocity. The saturated dissolved‑oxygen concentration is **C* = 0.008 mol L⁻¹**, the operating dissolved‑oxygen level is **C_L = 0.002 mol L⁻¹**, and the specific oxygen uptake rate per gram of fresh weight is **q_O₂ = 0.02 mol g⁻¹ h⁻¹**.  
Assume steady‑state, negligible oxygen limitation in the bulk, and that shear stress τ ≈ μ·γ̇ with average shear rate γ̇ ≈ (P/(μV))^{1/2}.  
Answer the following sub‑parts.

(B) Determine the average shear rate **γ̇** (s⁻¹) and shear stress **τ** (Pa) in the broth.

Combine scarcity with factors of production. A small garment factory in Tirupur has: 500 sq m factory space (land), 20 workers (labour), 10 sewing machines (capital), and 1 owner-manager (entrepreneurship). It receives orders for 5000 T-shirts (₹200 each) and 2000 hoodies (₹500 each) for the month. Each T-shirt needs 0.5 hrs labour + 0.2 hrs machine; each hoodie needs 1 hr labour + 0.5 hrs machine. Workers work 200 hrs/month. Machines run 300 hrs/month. Determine if scarcity exists and which factor is the binding constraint.

Case-based question (CBSE Board 2023 pattern):
"In the village of Rampur, the dominant Thakur caste (12% of households) owns 65% of cultivable land. The 1961 Land Ceiling Act sets a limit of 20 acres irrigated per family. The Thakurs respond by: (i) transferring 200 acres to their wives and unmarried daughters via gift deeds; (ii) evicting 40 Dalit tenant families claiming 'personal cultivation' on 150 acres; (iii) filing 15 fictitious family partitions in the revenue court.
A district-level Land Reform Tribunal is proposed with powers to: (a) invalidate transfers made after 1950 if benami is proven; (b) require biometric verification of 'personal cultivation'; (c) treat the joint family as a single unit regardless of paper partitions.
Analyse whether this Tribunal design would overcome the three evasion strategies. For each strategy, state the specific Tribunal power that counters it, and identify one implementation risk rooted in local caste power."

A state government launches a “Digital Saksharta Abhiyan” to train 5,000 rural women in basic smartphone use, e‑banking, and accessing government schemes over 12 months. The program will be delivered by home‑science extension workers posted in 50 Gram Panchayats. Baseline survey shows: 60 % of target women belong to Scheduled Castes (SCs), 30 % to Other Backward Classes (OBCs), and 10 % to General category. Literacy rates are 45 % (SC), 55 % (OBC), 70 % (General). Political leaders from the dominant OBC caste have expressed reluctance to allow SC women to attend training sessions held in the village panchayat building, citing “social harmony”. The budget is ₹2 crore (₹40,000 per trainee). Extension workers must (i) assess training needs, (ii) select appropriate teaching methods, (iii) ensure participation across castes, (iv) monitor learning outcomes, and (v) report to the district officer.
Using the scenario, answer the following sub‑parts.

(E) Design a three‑component professional development plan (knowledge, skills, attitude) for the extension workers to address the gaps revealed in this scenario, linking each component to a specific node from the primary subject.

A 22‑year‑old gig‑economy driver works 12 h/day, averaging 5 h of sleep per night. Genome‑wide polygenic risk score (PRS) for insomnia places him in the top 10 % of the population, assigned a diathesis weight of 0.6. His monthly income statement (gig platform) shows: base fare earnings ₹45 000, incentive bonuses ₹5 000, fuel expenses ₹8 000, platform commission ₹4 500, maintenance ₹2 000, and irregular “surge” payments averaging ₹3 000 but with a standard deviation of ₹2 000. Each ₹1 000 of net income deficit (expenses − earnings) contributes 0.04 stress units, while each hour of sleep loss below 8 h/night contributes 0.03 stress units. The threshold for insomnia disorder onset is 0.85 units. Using the diathesis‑stress model, calculate his net monthly stressor load and decide whether he is likely to develop clinical insomnia.

(E) Critique the assumption that stressor contributions from income deficit and sleep loss are linearly additive and independent in this scenario.

In 2024, a US‑based healthcare‑analytics firm shifts its medical‑claims processing to a newly‑established BPO centre in Tier‑2 city Mysuru, employing 3,000 workers, mostly women graduates from local colleges. The move is enabled by India’s 2020 liberalisation of data‑processing services under the Automatic Route and a state‑level subsidy for setting up SEZs in backward districts. Concurrently, the Karnataka government amends the Shops and Establishments Act to allow flexible night‑shift work for women, citing international competitiveness. A study by a regional university finds that 40% of the BPO workforce are first‑generation migrants from surrounding villages, sending remittances that have raised average household income by 18% in source villages. However, grassroots organisations report rising stress disorders, gender‑based harassment during night commutes, and a weakening of traditional caste‑based panchayat authority as young migrants adopt individualized lifestyles. The firm invokes the WTO’s General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS) and the state cites the constitutional principle of equality (Article 14) to justify the night‑shift amendment, while activists argue that the changes undermine protective labour legislation rooted in the post‑Independence welfare state model.

(D) Apply WTO GATS principles and constitutional equality (Article 14) to assess the state’s night‑shift amendment for women.

A satellite in a circular low‑Earth orbit (altitude 400 km) uses a star‑tracker to measure its yaw angle θ relative to a reference star. The tracker outputs the angle as θ = sin⁻¹( (v·r)/|v||r| ), where v is the satellite’s instantaneous velocity vector and r is the unit vector toward the star. For a given orbit, the magnitude of v is constant (v₀ = 7.7 km s⁻¹) and the star lies in the orbital plane, so the dot product reduces to v₀ cos ωt, where ω = 2π/T is the orbital angular speed (T = 92 min). Hence θ(t) = sin⁻¹( cos ωt ). The satellite’s attitude‑control system requires dθ/dt to compute the required torque. Simultaneously, the hydrazine thruster’s specific impulse I_sp varies with the yaw angle as I_sp(θ) = I₀ [1 + α sin²θ] (I₀ = 220 s, α = 0.15). The instantaneous thrust power P(t) = T·v₀, where thrust T = ṁ g₀ I_sp(θ) and ṁ is the mass‑flow rate (constant). Using the derivative of sin⁻¹, find dθ/dt and then determine the time‑averaged thrust power over one orbit. (Physics: orbital kinematics; Chemistry: thruster performance dependence on angle.)

(C) Compute the time‑averaged thrust power ⟨P⟩ over one full orbit (period T).

In July 2026, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) delivered an advisory opinion on the “Legal Status of Climate‑Induced Migration,” examining a case where 45,000 residents of the low‑lying island nation of Kiribati sought relocation assistance due to sea‑level rise inundating 30 % of arable land. The plaintiffs argued that their right to life and livelihood under international human‑rights law was being violated by major greenhouse‑gas emitters. The defense contended that adaptation measures (sea walls, land‑reclamation) could suffice, citing economic feasibility studies showing a cost‑benefit ratio of 1:4 in favor of relocation. Observers noted parallels with Gandhi’s Champaran struggle: a disadvantaged rural community confronting a powerful external force (British planters vs. industrialized nations) over control of essential resources (land for food vs. carbon‑rich atmosphere). They highlighted Gandhi’s statement from the Indigo excerpt: “It was in 1917… a peasant came up to me … ‘I am Rajkumar Shukla. I am from Champaran, and I want you to come to my district!’” as a exemplar of grassroots agency prompting elite intervention.  
Using the excerpt, the ICJ summary, and concepts of leadership, resource geography, human rights, and social motivation, answer the following.

(B) Explain how the theme of “justice and moral duty” in the Indigo excerpt (c12_eng_f_cbse_05_006) is reflected in the ICJ’s framing of climate‑induced migration as a human‑rights issue.

A university debate club is preparing a panel titled *“Poetry and Public Policy”* for a national youth festival. The panel will discuss the two poems from Chapter 5 (“olar vk;k” and “rksM+ks”) in relation to:
1. The **Theme** of resilience in adversity (as expressed in the poems).
2. Historical use of poetry during the **Quit India Movement (1942)**, where verses were circulated to mobilize masses (source: The Shramana Challenge).
3. **Article 19(1)(a)** of the Indian Constitution guaranteeing freedom of speech and expression.
4. Current **water‑scarcity data** from Rajasthan (average annual rainfall 450 mm, groundwater depletion rate 1.2 cm/yr) that mirrors the dry‑land imagery in the poems (Pastoralism).
Students must prepare spoken points that (a) cite specific lines from the poems, (b) connect them to the historical protest, (c) argue how the poems reinforce the constitutional right to free speech, and (d) suggest a localized water‑conservation initiative inspired by the poems’ imagery.

(D) Propose a one‑minute spoken action plan for a village in Rajasthan that uses the metaphor of “थकी हुई नदी” (weary river) from the poems to motivate rainwater harvesting, integrating theme, metaphor, and fundamental‑rights justification.

Using the literacy‑rate bar graph (48% → 62%) and the 2006 Rajasthan Right to Education Act timeline, assess whether the poem’s call “स्कूलों की दीवारें तोड़ो” aligns with the policy’s impact on marginalized communities.

The government imposes a heavy tax on sugary drinks, raising their price by 30%. A student argues: "This will increase demand for fruit juices because they are substitutes, so fruit juice producers will benefit." Evaluate this argument. Consider at least two other factors that might affect the outcome.

Read the following hypothetical scenario and apply the 'lessons from accommodation' (NCERT pp. 131-133) to propose a constitutional-political strategy:

"State 'X' (population 4 crore) has a distinct linguistic minority (30%) concentrated in its northern districts. This minority demands a separate state 'Y', citing: (i) neglect of irrigation/industry in north, (ii) cultural marginalisation (language not taught in schools), (iii) out-migration to south. The minority has launched a democratic mass movement (hunger strikes, electoral pressure) — no violence. The ruling party in State X opposes division; the Centre's coalition depends on State X's ruling party. Design a step-by-step accommodation strategy using *only* existing constitutional instruments (Articles 3, 371, Fifth/Sixth Schedule, Accords). Justify each step against the four NCERT lessons."

An online grocery platform sources fresh vegetables from farmers in three states—Punjab, West Bengal, and Tamil Nadu—and uses AI‑driven dynamic weighing scales at its regional hubs to pack 1 kg bags of spinach. Each hub displays a verification stamp issued by the respective State Legal Metrology Department. The stamp on the Punjab hub reads “LM‑PB‑2023‑045” and is valid for 2 years; the West Bengal hub stamp “LM‑WB‑2022‑012” expired 3 months ago; the Tamil Nadu hub stamp “LM‑TN‑2024‑078” is valid for 1 year. The platform advertises a “net weight 1 kg ± 2 %” guarantee. A consumer in Mumbai receives a bag labelled 1 kg that weighs 0.970 kg on a certified laboratory balance. The consumer files a complaint alleging short‑weighting and claims the platform violated the Legal Metrology Act, 2009 by using an expired stamp and exceeding the permissible error. Simultaneously, a competitor alleges that the platform’s dynamic pricing algorithm, which raises prices in West Bengal by 15 % during monsoon due to higher transport costs, constitutes an unfair trade practice under the Competition Act, 2002. Using the data provided, determine the legal and consumer‑rights implications, the permissible error limits, and the relevance of regional geography to pricing.

(E) Propose a compliance checklist the platform should implement to avoid future Legal Metrology and Competition Act violations, integrating verification, monitoring, and geographic pricing logic.

In a colony hybridization experiment using a nitrocellulose membrane, a student forgets to bake the membrane at 80°C after transferring colonies. What specific step fails, and why does this cause false negatives?

GlobalTech Inc., an Indian multinational, issues US$ 10 million denominated debentures at a fixed 5% annual coupon, redeemable after 3 years. The debentures are issued at par (US$1 = ₹75). To meet the sinking fund requirement, the company invests the annual sinking fund instalment in US Treasury bills yielding 2% p.a. (USD). The Companies Act requires a DRR of 25% of the face value of outstanding debentures, to be invested/in deposited in specified securities by 30th April each year; the company decides to meet this by investing in Indian government securities yielding 6% p.a. (INR). Assume the sinking fund instalments are made at the end of each year in USD, and the DRR transfer is made in INR at the prevailing rate. The spot rate at issuance is ₹75/US$. Expected spot rate at redemption is ₹78/US$. The company enters a forward contract to lock the redemption rate at ₹77.5/US$. Compute the effective cost of debt in INR, the sinking fund instalment in USD, the DRR amount in INR, and the journal entries for the first year’s sinking fund investment and forward contract settlement.

(B) Compute the Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) amount required in INR, and state the amount to be invested/deposited by 30th April each year (15% of face value maturing next year).

In the tribal district of Bastar, Chhattisgarh, a baseline survey shows that 45 % of pregnant women have haemoglobin <11 g/dl, and average dietary iron intake is 12 mg/day against the RDA of 27 mg/day for the second trimester. The district administration plans to launch a weekly iron‑folic acid supplementation programme alongside nutrition education. As a public health nutrition intern, you are tasked to analyse the developmental implications and design appropriate interventions.

(E) Evaluate how the Pradhan Mantri Matru Vandana Yojana (PMMVY) addresses the identified nutritional deficit and its potential impact on fetal development, referencing family welfare programmes and functions.

A bio‑energy startup aims to assemble a synthetic light‑harvesting complex (LHC) inspired by plant PSII, comprising three polypeptide subunits: PsaA (30 kDa), PsaB (30 kDa), and a small linker L (5 kDa). The functional unit is a trimer of heterodimers ( (PsaA–PsaB)₃ ) stabilized by inter‑dimer hydrophobic contacts (average –7 kJ mol⁻¹ per contact) and a network of inter‑subunit hydrogen bonds (average –3 kJ mol⁻¹ per bond). Each heterodimer binds two chlorophyll‑a molecules; excitation energy transfer efficiency η_ET depends on the distance R between chlorophylls via Förster theory: η_ET = 1 / [1 + (R/R₀)⁶], where R₀ = 3.2 nm for the Chl‑Chl pair. The linker L can be engineered to adjust R; wild‑type L gives R = 2.8 nm. Each amino‑acid substitution in L changes R by ±0.02 nm per residue and alters expression cost: wild‑type cost = ₹200 mg⁻¹; each substitution raises cost by 8 % due to lower solubility. The startup has a budget of ₹5 × 10⁵ for producing 15 mg of LHC. Determine whether a linker variant with three substitutions (increasing R) can achieve η_ET ≥ 0.85 while staying within budget.

(A) Calculate the total number of inter‑dimer hydrophobic contacts in the trimer of heterodimers if each heterodimer makes three contacts with each of the other two heterodimers.

In 2026 the World Literacy Consortium (WLC) launches the “Uniscript Initiative”, proposing to replace all national writing systems with a single phonetic script called “UniWrite” by 2035, asserting it will eradicate illiteracy, reduce printing costs by 55 %, and facilitate global AI‑driven education. The initiative is unveiled at a summit in Geneva, where delegates from the Federated States of Pacifica (FSP) – a microstate of 250 000 people whose cultural identity is tightly bound to its indigenous logographic script “Kāli” – protest. The FSP delegation presents a traditional Kāli‑inscribed stone tablet, chants a centuries‑old creation epic in Kāli, and projects a live feed of rising sea levels threatening their atoll homeland. Simultaneously, a delegation from the Eurasian Trade Union (ETU) displays a flowchart showing how UniWrite would streamline customs documentation across the Eurasian rail corridor, while a contingent of UN peacekeepers stands guard outside the venue. Using irony, symbolism, imagery/metaphor, theme, historical language‑policy precedents, international law on cultural heritage, and the geography of vulnerable island states, answer the sub‑parts below.

(E) Synthesize the irony, symbolism, imagery/metaphor, historical precedent, and legal analysis to draft a PEEL paragraph (max 150 words) arguing that the Uniscript Initiative constitutes a form of neo‑linguistic imperialism, and indicate how the island geography of FSP amplifies this critique.

Bharat Conglomerates Ltd (listed, NSE/BSE) announces buyback of 1 crore equity shares (FV ₹2) at ₹450 via tender offer (SEBI route). Pre-buyback: Equity Capital ₹200 Cr (100 Cr shares); Securities Premium ₹500 Cr; General Reserve ₹1,200 Cr; Retained Earnings ₹800 Cr; 9% Debentures ₹1,000 Cr; Term Loan ₹500 Cr. Market price ₹380. Buyback tax (Sec 115QA): 20% on distributed income (buyback price - issue price). Shareholders: Promoters (60%, tax-exempt trust), FIIs (25%, treaty benefits), Retail (15%, 10% LTCG >₹1L). Company uses General Reserve + Securities Premium. Economic concepts: Signaling theory , Tax clientele effect , Capital allocation efficiency vs. public facility investment. CFO must: (a) verify Sec 68/SEBI limits, (b) compute buyback tax, (c) pass entries with CRR, (d) analyze post-buyback leverage & EPS accretion/dilution, (e) evaluate if buyback destroys value vs. capex (NPV ₹2,000 Cr project available).

(E) Value destruction test: Capex project NPV = ₹2,000 Cr (IRR 18%). Buyback uses ₹450 Cr + ₹93.184 Cr tax = ₹543.184 Cr. Compare shareholder value: Buyback vs. Project. Assume WACC 12%, tax rate 30%. Use economic concept of opportunity cost and development goals.
Calculate the energy (in kcal) contributed by the carbohydrate fraction of a 50 g edible film that contains 80 % carbohydrate by weight.

LearnSmart Partners (profit-sharing 2:1:1 for P, Q, R) dissolves on 31-Dec-2025 due to new Data Privacy Act, 2025. Deed: "Realisation expenses borne by partner managing dissolution (Q)." Q pays: data deletion ₹30L, legal compliance ₹20L, employee severance (including unvested ESOPs valued ₹50L) ₹100L. Assets: Servers ₹200L, Customer Database (unrecorded) ₹300L, Brand ₹150L. Liabilities: Creditors ₹100L, P’s Loan ₹50L, Pending Lawsuits (unrecorded) ₹80L. R insolvent (deficiency ₹40L). Garner v Murray applies. ESOPs are non-monetary compensation. Q pays all expenses from personal funds. Realisation: Servers ₹180L, Database ₹250L, Brand ₹120L.

(B) Prepare Realisation Account showing all items. Calculate realisation profit/loss.

Fill in the blank: The electoral roll (voter list) is the official register of all eligible citizens in a constituency who are entitled to vote, prepared and periodically revised under the ______ of the People Act, 1950, and Article 326 of the Constitution, which guarantees universal adult franchise to every citizen aged 18 years and above unless disqualified by law.

Seventeen‑year‑old Arjun, a Class 12 science student in Kota, spends 4 hours daily scrolling TikTok, where a recent “#StudyUntilYouDrop” challenge glorifies 18‑hour study marathons. He consumes two energy drinks (each 80 mg caffeine) per night to stay awake. His paternal aunt has panic disorder; his mother reports high conscientiousness. Over the past month, Arjun experiences sudden episodes of palpitations, dyspnea, and fear of dying during online tests, lasting 10‑15 minutes, followed by exhaustion. He avoids mock tests, fearing embarrassment if his video shows him panicking. Saliva cortisol measured after a mock test is 22 µg/dL (reference 5‑25 µg/dL, upper‑normal). His school’s average JEE Main mock score is 180/360; Arjun’s score dropped from 210 to 150 after panic onset. Using concepts of anxiety disorder biology (GABAergic inhibition), socio‑cultural influence (social media contagion), and psychological appraisal (catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations), answer the following.

(B) Using the biological node c11_bio_cbse_01_001, explain how chronic caffeine intake could lower GABAergic inhibition and contribute to Arjun’s anxiety.

Using the ISRO rainfall anomaly (–22 %) and the TISS rumor impact (68 % of farmers reduced sowing by 15 %), calculate the combined expected reduction in sowing area assuming the two effects are independent and multiplicative.

A landless agricultural labourer in Bihar borrows ₹10,000 from a moneylender at 5% per month simple interest for 6 months to pay for his daughter's medical treatment. He repays ₹13,000 at harvest. The moneylender then says "interest is due on the full ₹10,000 for another 6 months" and rolls over the loan. Explain why this is a classic debt trap mechanism even though the stated rate is "only 5% per month."

Using the GIS‑derived agro‑ecological zoning (55 % flood‑prone alluvial plains, 30 % drought‑prone uplands, 15 % mixed), evaluate how the poem’s imagery of “bahut bei baarish” (abundant rain) and “sukhi mitti” (dry soil) corresponds to the spatial distribution of these zones.

A state government intends to develop a 10 km² smart‑city module on the banks of the Sabarmati River, aiming for LEED‑Gold certification and flood resilience. The site lies atop a palaeo‑channel of the Sabarmati that was active during the mature Harappan period (c12_hist_cbse_01_002). Archaeologists have uncovered a grid‑patterned layout of baked‑brick streets and a sophisticated covered‑drain network (c12_hist_cbse_01_003, c12_hist_cbse_01_004) reminiscent of Mohenjodaro. The city planners propose to adopt a modular grid (100 m×100 m blocks), centralized storm‑water tanks, and permeable pavements. However, environmental activists warn that the plan may alter the natural recharge zone of the river, affecting downstream agriculture. You are asked to evaluate (i) whether the Harappan grid offers a superior flood‑resilience model compared to modern radial layouts, (ii) the hydraulic efficiency of the Harappan‑style covered drains versus open‑channel swales under projected 2050 rainfall intensities (increase of 20 %), (iii) the impact on groundwater recharge if permeable pavement covers 60 % of the surface, (iv) the risk of upstream back‑flow if tidal influences increase due to sea‑level rise, and (v) an integrated design brief that merges Harappan techniques with modern smart‑city sensors.

(C) Projected sea‑level rise of 0.3 m by 2050 could increase tidal influence upstream in the Sabarmati estuary, potentially causing back‑flow into storm‑water outlets located 5 km inland. If the outlet invert is at 2.0 m above mean sea level (MSL) and the river bed slope is 1:5000, estimate the maximum tidal water surface elevation (in meters MSL) that would produce back‑flow at the outlet.

In the humid Pampas of Argentina, a 500‑ha cooperative mixed farm integrates cattle rearing with soybean and maize cultivation. The cooperative follows the classic mixed‑farming model: soybean residues feed cattle during winter, while cattle manure is applied to fields to maintain soil nitrogen. Each member contributes capital proportional to the land they allocate: 40% of members contribute cash for machinery (total $2 million), 30% contribute livestock worth $1.5 million, and 30% contribute land valued at $2.5 million. Profits are distributed according to a hybrid rule: 50% of net profit is shared equally among members, and the remaining 50% is distributed in proportion to capital contribution. The cooperative operates under a provincial power‑sharing statute that grants autonomous decision‑making over land use to local producer assemblies, subject to national environmental caps on deforestation. Last year, the farm generated gross revenue of $4.2 million from soybeans ($2.0 M), maize ($0.8 M), and livestock sales ($1.4 M). Input costs (seeds, feed, veterinary, machinery depreciation) totaled $2.6 M. The national environmental agency imposed a fine of $0.2 M for exceeding a temporary soybean‑area limit. Assuming the cooperative’s net profit is gross revenue minus input costs minus fines, calculate each member’s profit share under the hybrid rule and comment on how the power‑sharing arrangement influences the farm’s adherence to environmental caps.

(A) Identify two core characteristics of mixed farming demonstrated in the scenario that distinguish it from extensive commercial grain farming.

In the Western Ghats, a rare orchid species (Species X) reproduces exclusively by vegetative propagation (asexual) through rhizome fragmentation. A closely related species (Species Y) reproduces sexually via insect pollination. Climate models predict 3°C warming and altered rainfall patterns over 50 years. Predict which species has higher extinction risk and justify using metabolic, reproductive, and evolutionary principles.

A sociology student from Karnataka intends to study the socio-economic impact of the Cauvery water dispute on farmers in Mandya district (Karnataka-Tamil Nadu border). The village has 70% Karnataka-origin farmers (protesting water releases to TN) and 30% Tamil Nadu-origin farmers (accused of hoarding water). The student, a Karnataka native, plans to conceal their state identity during initial rapport-building to avoid bias, revealing it only after trust is established. They will conduct household surveys using a structured questionnaire (caste, landholding, crop loss) and informal interviews with panchayat members. The student argues disclosure would trigger defensive responses (Karnataka farmers seeing them as "anti-farmer"; TN farmers as "pro-TN spy"), compromising data validity. However, they face ethical dilemmas: hiding identity violates informed consent, and their latent loyalty might influence question framing or interpretation despite concealment efforts. They seek guidance on balancing positional authenticity with ethical fieldwork practices.

(D) Using c12_soc_cbse_07_003, formulate a revised research question that maintains scientific rigor while adhering to NCERT ethics. Justify why it avoids the leading-question trap inherent in the original implicit assumption ("water shortage causes economic loss").
Determine the fraction of probe‑target complexes that are hybridized at 65 °C, assuming probe (100 nM) and target (10 pM) are in large excess relative to each other.

In 2025, a Maharashtra-based tech startup launched "BhaktiBytes," an AI-driven app that curates personalized Abhang recitals for users based on biometric feedback (heart rate variability during listening) and geolocation. The app claims to democratize access to the Varkari tradition by generating real-time Marathi-Abhang remixes infused with electronic beats, targeting urban youth disconnected from rural pilgrimage routes. However, historians criticize it for decontextualizing Abhangs from their 15th-16th century agrarian-stress origins, while sociologists warn that algorithmic personalization may amplify caste-blindness by ignoring how Sant Eknath's message specifically addressed *ati-shudra* marginalization.  
   
   Key data includes:  
      - App analytics: 72% of users are aged 18-25 (65% urban, 35% rural); 41% skip the "historical context" audio snippet before listening.  
      - Historical records: Sant Eknath composed Abhangs during the Ahmadnagar Sultanate's land-revenue crises (1540-1560), where *mirasdars* (hereditary farmers) faced 60% revenue hikes, driving *ati-shudra* landless laborers toward the Varkari fold.  
      - Sociological surveys: 58% of app users believe Abhangs promote "universal love" without acknowledging caste-specific liberation; only 22% can name one *ati-shudra* saint contemporary to Eknath (e.g., Kanhopatra).  
      - Literary analysis: Original Abhangs used *deshvak* (regional dialects) and agricultural metaphors (*kulith*, *jowar*) to resonate with peasantry—elements stripped in BhaktiBytes' "neutral" Marathi.  
   
   Assess whether BhaktiBytes fulfills or betrays Sant Eknath's intent to make devotion accessible to the marginalized, considering the tension between technological democratization and historical specificity.

(A) Using the land-revenue crisis data (60% hikes on *mirasdars*) and Sant Eknath's focus on *ati-shudra* inclusion, explain why algorithmic stripping of agricultural metaphors (*kulith*, *jowar*) in BhaktiBytes undermines the Abhangs' original socio-political function as a tool for landless laborer mobilization.

A state government wants to decide the Minimum Support Price (MSP) for wheat for the next crop year. They have data on: (i) cost of cultivation per hectare for last 5 years, (ii) market prices in different mandis, (iii) farmers' income levels, (iv) global wheat prices. Identify which specific statistical application from the textbook is being used at each step: (a) calculating average cost of cultivation, (b) comparing mandi prices to find the highest, (c) estimating next year's cost using past trend, (d) presenting the final MSP as a single number instead of a 50-page report.

Compare the decimal expansions of \( \frac{3}{8} \) and \( \frac{3}{80} \). Both have denominators with only 2s and 5s. How many decimal places does each terminate after? What pattern do you notice about the relationship between the denominator's prime factorization and the number of decimal places?

A student writes: "My plan is to study 4 hours every day from today until exams." Using the planning framework, identify three specific missing elements that make this an incomplete plan, and explain what resource analysis should have been done for each.

GreenGrid Ltd. is a social enterprise that installs solar‑plus‑battery microgrids in off‑grid villages of Jharkhand. Each microgrid serves 150 households, providing 5 kWh/day per household for lighting, phone charging, and small‑scale irrigation pumps. Capital cost per microgrid is ₹1.2 crore (solar panels ₹0.7 cr, batteries ₹0.3 cr, installation ₹0.2 cr). Annual operating and maintenance (O&M) cost is ₹8 lakh. The enterprise expects to recover costs through a combination of:  
- A service fee of ₹150 per household per month (affordability‑based).  
- A government subsidy of ₹30 lakh per microgrid (capital grant).  
- Revenue from selling excess solar power to the nearest grid at ₹4/kWh (estimated 100 kWh/day excess).  

The enterprise’s dual objectives are:  
1. **Effectiveness** – achieve a social impact score of at least 80 / 100 (measured by hours of study enabled, income‑generating device usage, and reduction in kerosene use).  
2. **Efficiency** – achieve a financial internal rate of return (IRR) of at least 12 % on equity invested after accounting for subsidies.  

The board asks the management team to:  
(a) Compute the equity IRR assuming the enterprise finances 40 % of the capital cost through equity (rest via zero‑interest debt) and the remaining 60 % is covered by the government subsidy (treated as a non‑repayable grant).  
(b) Determine which level of management (Top, Middle, Lower) should set the social impact target, monitor O&M expenses, and coordinate with village committees for load‑management.  
(c) Using a simple linear‑programming model, find the optimal mix of service fee (x) and excess‑power price (y) that maximises the social impact score (SI = 0.4·x + 0.6·y, where x and y are in ₹ units) subject to a budget constraint that the total annual revenue must cover O&M plus a 5 % return on equity.  
(d) Propose a coordination mechanism that ensures the effectiveness goal (high social impact) does not lead to financial inefficiency (excessive subsidies or low tariffs).  
(e) Classify the following statements as effective/ineffective and efficient/inefficient:  
 (i) “We will keep the service fee at ₹100/household/month to maximise adoption, even if it means needing a larger subsidy.”  
 (ii) “We will set the excess‑power price at ₹6/kWh to boost revenue, even if it discourages grid‑interconnection and reduces overall renewable utilisation.”

(B) Assign each of the following responsibilities to the appropriate level of management (Top, Middle, Lower) in GreenGrid Ltd.:  
(i) Setting the social impact target of SI ≥ 80.  
(ii) Monitoring monthly O&M expenses against the budgeted ₹8 lakh.  
(iii) Coordinating with village committees to decide daily load‑shedding schedules during low‑sun periods.

A Bengaluru‑based incubator assesses a pitch from 17‑year‑old Ananya, who proposes “The Tide Boutique” – a sustainable fashion outlet on the renovated Mangalore wharf. The pitch deck includes excerpts from *Going Places* (Sophie’s dialogue, Jansie’s doubts, references to wharf, solitary elm, pangs of doubt) alongside market data: (i) Wharf footfall increased 35% after arcade installation (c12_geo_cbse_01_004); (ii) Government coastal‑zone policy offers 15% tax rebate for eco‑retail (c12_pol_cbse_01_004); (iii) Historical analysis shows wharf districts transition from cargo handling to leisure hubs post‑2000 (c12_his_cbse_01_005). Evaluators must infer the meanings of six highlighted words to critique the pitch’s realism, risk factors, and branding tone. They have 18 minutes to produce a scored rubric that correctly uses each inferred word in a comment.

(D) Ananya says, “I’ll be chuffed if the boutique gets a green certification.” Which inference best captures the meaning of **chuffed**?
Using sociological reasoning, explain how the documentary’s code‑switching and visual imagery contributed to the observed 18 % rise in demand for crop‑insurance schemes.

Dr. Meera, a 32‑year‑old virologist, works in a high‑containment lab studying SARS‑CoV‑2 variants. Since the lab switched to 12‑hour shifts and mandatory double‑gloving, she reports spending **≈45 min** each entry and exit performing hand‑washing with antimicrobial soap, followed by **three** cycles of alcohol‑based rub, even when her gloves appear intact. She describes intrusive thoughts: “If I miss a spot, I could transmit a lethal strain to my family.” These thoughts cause **marked anxiety (8/10 on a visual analogue scale)** and she feels compelled to repeat the ritual until it “feels right.” Over the past 8 weeks, she has missed **2 data‑collection sessions** per week, delaying her project timeline. Her salivary cortisol measured **pre‑shift** is **0.18 µg/dL** and **post‑ritual** is **0.34 µg/dL**. Lab colleagues note she avoids shared equipment and eats lunch alone, citing fear of contamination. Her mother has a diagnosed OCD (washing subtype). Using the information, answer the following.

(B) Calculate the percent increase in salivary cortisol from pre‑ to post‑ritual.

A rectangular garden is to be designed such that its area is 180 m². The length and breadth are positive integers. The perimeter of the garden is to be minimised to save fencing cost.  
(a) Form a quadratic equation whose roots are the possible values of the breadth (in metres) if the length is 3 m more than the breadth.  
(b) Find the dimensions that minimise the perimeter.  
(c) If the cost of fencing is ₹50 per metre, calculate the minimum fencing cost.

A state government passes a law allowing preventive detention of 'suspected troublemakers' for 90 days without trial. A journalist is detained under this law for reporting on corruption. She files a habeas corpus petition under Art. 32. The state argues: (a) preventive detention is permitted under Art. 22; (b) the law was passed by legislature, so 'procedure established by law' is satisfied. Using Maneka Gandhi and Hussainara Khatoon, explain why the detention is unconstitutional.

A 30-year-old woman, 2nd trimester, pre-pregnancy BMI 18.5 (underweight), sedentary, Hb 9.5 g/dL, vegetarian. Her current intake: 1800 kcal, 45 g protein, 12 mg iron, 400 mg calcium. Using ICMR 2020, calculate her nutrient deficits. Propose two specific dietary modifications (with gram quantities) that address the largest deficits without worsening nausea. Justify each modification physiologically.

India imports over 90% of its copper concentrate demand despite having reserves. Evaluate the three most critical factors causing this import dependence, using geological and infrastructural reasoning.

A widely circulated editorial cartoon depicts a stern-looking politician gripping an hourglass whose upper bulb is a melting glacier dripping into seawater, while the lower bulb is filled with coins. From the politician’s coat pocket, a factory chimney exhales smoke that forms the shape of dollar signs. The caption reads: “TIME IS MONEY – LET THE FUTURE PAY”. Below the cartoon, a small inset shows a graph: global CO₂ emissions rose from 35.3 Gt in 2010 to 36.6 Gt in 2023, while the average annual temperature anomaly increased from +0.72°C to +1.20°C over the same period. The cartoon appeared in a national newspaper during a parliamentary debate on delaying the net‑zero target from 2050 to 2070. Students are asked to apply Milton’s treatment of time and eternity in “On Time” to decode the cartoon’s ironic stance and symbolic language, and to evaluate its persuasive power using concepts from political science (policy delay), geography (climate data), and history (environmental movements).

(C) Analyze how the combined use of irony and symbolism in the cartoon critiques the policy of delaying climate action, using concepts from political science (policy delay) and history (environmental movements).

Integrate chemical evolution with the first metabolic pathways. Given that glycolysis is nearly universal and anaerobic, and that FeS minerals catalyse acetyl-CoA synthesis from CO, CO₂, and CH₃SH (methyl mercaptan) at 100°C, construct a stepwise argument for how a protocell could couple FeS-driven carbon fixation to substrate-level phosphorylation.

A neuro‑research lab in Bangalore studies how haptic feedback in virtual‑reality (VR) storytelling influences subjects’ sense of self‑embodiment. Participants read a short literary passage (either a descriptive paragraph from a classic novel or a factual exposition) while wearing VR gloves that simulate texture and pressure corresponding to the narrative. fMRI scans show that during novel passages, the somatosensory cortex and the default‑mode network (DMN) co‑activate 23 % more than during expository passages. Self‑report scores on the “Presence and Agency” scale rise from 3.2 to 4.7 (out of 7) after novel‑based VR. The lab proposes that Lawrence’s claim—that the novel captures the whole man alive through the body’s own “rudiments of thought”—is neurologically plausible.  
Students must integrate Lawrence’s literary concept, neuroscientific findings on embodied cognition, geographical notions of mental maps of urban space, and psychological theories of mind‑body dualism to evaluate the claim.

(D) In what way does the concept of cognitive maps (c12_geo_cbse_05_003) help explain why novel‑based VR enhances sense of agency more than expository VR?

A university library is digitising the original manuscript of Emily Dickinson’s “Trees” for an open‑access portal. The project team must (a) tag each stanza with precise contextual meanings of difficult words, (b) ensure the digital surrogate meets ISO 18926 preservation standards (temperature ≤ 18 °C, RH ≤ 45 %), (c) assess whether the poem, unpublished in Dickinson’s lifetime, is now in the public domain under the U.S. Copyright Act of 1976 (life + 70 years, but unpublished works receive a different term), and (d) evaluate the risk of paper‑based original degradation given current regional climate data (average summer temperature = 28 °C, RH = 70 %). The team receives a set of five annotated images showing marginal notes, each containing a key word from the poem. Students must interpret the words, link them to preservation and legal considerations, and propose actionable steps.

(B) How does the imagery of “Miniature Creatures / Accompanying the Sun –” function as a metaphor for the poem’s theme of fleeting vitality? Identify the literary device and explain its effect.

During a nationwide vaccination drive, the government allocates 10 million doses to be administered over 180 days through 5000 vaccination centres. Each centre uses a single FIFO queue to manage beneficiaries awaiting injection. Beneficiaries are categorized into four priority groups: (1) frontline health workers, (2) elderly ≥ 60 yr, (3) comorbid individuals 18‑59 yr, (4) general public 18‑59 yr. The central logistics system pushes daily shipments to centres based on real‑time stock levels; each centre can store at most 200 doses (buffer size). To promote equity, the policy mandates that no centre may serve more than 30 % of its daily injections from group 4 unless the average waiting time for groups 1‑3 exceeds 2 hours. Historical data shows that arrival rates (beneficiaries per hour) follow: group 1 = 0.5 × N, group 2 = 1.2 × N, group 3 = 0.8 × N, group 4 = 2.5 × N, where N is the centre’s service rate (doses per hour). The vaccine has a shelf‑life of 6 hours at ambient temperature; doses unused after this period must be discarded.

(D) Assuming vaccine doses lose potency after 6 hours at ambient temperature, and a centre receives a shipment of 200 doses at time t=0, what is the maximum number of doses that can be administered without wastage if the centre’s administration rate follows a linear decline from 20 doses/hr at t=0 to 5 doses/hr at t=6 hr due to staff fatigue?

A biotech startup wants to clone the human pre‑proinsulin gene (0.5 kb) into a plasmid backbone (3.0 kb) to express insulin in *E. coli* BL21. The plasmid must maintain a copy number of ~15–20 per cell to achieve a target intracellular insulin concentration of 50 mg L⁻¹ after 6 h induction. The host culture is grown in a 5 L shaken flask at 37 °C with a doubling time of 20 min. After transformation, plasmid DNA is isolated and analysed by agarose gel electrophoresis (1 % agarose, 100 V, 40 min run) to confirm insert size. The restriction enzyme EcoRI (recognising GAATTC) works optimally at pH 8.0 and 37 °C; its activity halves for every 5 °C deviation. The ligation reaction uses T4 DNA ligase requiring ATP (2 mM) and Mg²⁺ (10 mM).  
Using the data above, answer the following sub‑parts.

(B) Determine the expected band position (distance from the well) of the linearized plasmid (insert + backbone) on the agarose gel, given that the gel length is 10 cm, the voltage is 100 V, the run time is 40 min, and the mobility (µ) of a 3.5 kb DNA fragment under these conditions is 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ cm² V⁻¹ s⁻¹.

In early 2025 ASEAN launches the “Southeast Asian Renewable Energy Grid (SAREG)” to interconnect solar farms in Vietnam, wind corridors in Laos, and geothermal plants in Indonesia, targeting a 40 % regional renewable share by 2035. The project mirrors the EU’s European Green Deal, requiring cross‑border electricity trading, harmonised grid codes, and a green‑bond financing mechanism worth US$25 bn. Analysts note that the SAREG’s success depends on predictable monsoon‑driven hydro‑generation patterns, reminiscent of historical reliance on seasonal rains for agrarian surplus along the Mekong and Chao Phraya rivers. Meanwhile, a group of Japanese investors requests clarity on accounting treatment for green‑bond proceeds, specifically whether issuance costs should be amortised over bond life or expensed immediately. Environmental NGOs warn that without a supranational enforcement body, member states may prioritise national coal projects, undermining the grid’s reliability. The ASEAN Secretariat must decide: (1) whether to adopt EU‑style supranational grid governance, (2) how to leverage historical monsoon‑based water management for reservoir operation, (3) what accounting standard to apply to green‑bond issuance, (4) how the ASEAN Way affects enforcement of renewable commitments, and (5) whether SAREG can serve as a counterweight to US‑China competition over clean‑energy technology.

(A) Compare ASEAN’s proposed supranational grid authority (modeled on the EU’s Agency for the Cooperation of Energy Regulators) with the existing ASEAN Way of consensus‑based energy cooperation. Which feature would most likely improve compliance with renewable targets, and why?

An electric oven draws a current of 10 A when connected to a 220 V supply. The oven is used for 2 hours daily. (a) Calculate the charge passing through the oven in one day. (b) If the oven's heating element is made of nichrome wire of length 5 m and cross-sectional area 2 × 10⁻⁶ m², and the number density of free electrons in nichrome is 9 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, estimate the drift velocity of electrons in the element. (Use e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C). (c) Explain why the oven heats up almost instantly when switched on, even though drift velocity is very small.

GreenBite Foods plans to launch two snack variants targeting urban millennials who increasingly prefer healthy, plant‑based, and locally sourced foods. Variant A is a millet‑energy bar; Variant B is an oat‑honey bar. Social‑environment research shows: (i) 35 % of urban consumers now check ingredient lists for “no artificial additives”; (ii) 28 % prefer snacks labelled “vegan”; (iii) during festive seasons, demand for traditional‑taste snacks rises by ~15 %.  
Resource limits per week: millet 500 kg, oats 300 kg, honey 200 kg. Unit resource requirements:  
- Variant A: 0.20 kg millet, 0.10 kg oats, 0.05 kg honey.  
- Variant B: 0.10 kg millet, 0.20 kg oats, 0.10 kg honey.  
Profit contribution (after variable cost) before any regulatory cost: A = ₹15 per unit, B = ₹12 per unit.  
Market‑survey imposes weekly demand ceilings due to cultural preferences: max A = 4,000 units, max B = 3,000 units.  
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) recently mandated that any product bearing a “vegan” label must display allergen‑information in a prescribed format, adding an estimated extra labeling cost of ₹2 per unit for any product that carries the vegan claim. Only Variant A can be marketed as vegan (Variant B contains honey).  
Formulate and solve the optimization problem to maximize weekly profit.

(D) Determine the shadow price (dual value) of millet based on the optimal solution.

On 10 May 1857, sepoys in Meerut mutinied, seized the bell of arms, and marched ~70 km to Delhi, arriving at the Red Fort gates on 11 May. They cut the telegraph line to Delhi, proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar as their leader, and were joined by urban artisans and peasants. Simultaneously, in Kanpur, Nana Saheb took control of the artillery magazine after the British garrison surrendered, while in Lucknow, Begum Hazrat Mahal rallied taluqdars and sepoys.
