To ensure ≥95 % completion of agglutination, the residence time t_res in each antibody zone must satisfy 1 − e^(−kt_res) ≥ 0.95. The chip must also handle a worst‑case scenario where the donor’s blood group is O (universal donor) and the recipient is AB (universal recipient). In a population, the allele frequencies are p(I^A)=0.25, p(I^B)=0.15, q(i)=0.60. Assume Hardy‑Weinberg equilibrium.

(B) Determine the minimum residence time t_res (in seconds) required in each antibody zone to achieve ≥95 % agglutination, given k = 2.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹.

A fintech startup “CrediSwift” uses an AI model that analyses alternative data (mobile recharge frequency, social‑media activity, utility‑payment timeliness) to approve personal loans. In a pilot of 100,000 applicants, the AI approved 68 % of urban applicants and 44 % of rural applicants. Traditional bank scoring approved 55 % of urban and 50 % of rural applicants. The AI model’s default rate is 4 % versus 6 % for traditional scoring. However, explainability audits reveal the model heavily weights “frequency of online shopping” – a variable strongly correlated with urban income and negatively with rural internet access. Sociological studies indicate rural users perceive the system as “elitist” (c12_soc_cbse_01_005). The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has issued a discussion paper on “Fair Lending in the Digital Era” requiring disparate impact analysis and mitigation plans (c12_pol_cbse_01_002).

(D) According to RBI’s discussion paper on fair lending, a disparate impact analysis must show that a neutral practice does not disproportionately harm a protected group unless justified by business necessity. State whether the AI model’s reliance on online shopping frequency meets the business‑necessity defense, giving one reason for and one against.

A consortium of elite private schools in Bengaluru launches a metaverse campus where students attend immersive VR lessons, interact via avatar‑based social spaces, and earn blockchain‑verified credentials. The platform offers optional “Cultural Enrichment Modules”: (1) a Sanskrit‑language chanting circle led by a Brahmin scholar, (2) a Western‑style debate club coached by an Oxford alumnus, and (3) a digital‑art workshop using NFT tools. Enrollment data shows that 68 % of students from upper‑caste (Brahmin, Bania) families opt for the Sanskrit chanting circle, while 54 % of the same group also join the debate club, indicating simultaneous participation. In contrast, 82 % of students from Scheduled Caste (SC) backgrounds enroll exclusively in the NFT art workshop; only 12 % of SC students attempt the Sanskrit circle, citing “cultural alienation” and “lack of perceived utility.” Avatar customization reveals that upper‑caste students frequently choose avatars with fair skin tones, blonde hair, and Western attire, whereas SC students predominantly select avatars reflecting traditional Indian attire and darker skin tones, despite the platform’s neutral design. Historical records note that Bengaluru’s rise as an IT hub was fueled by state‑led investments in electronics parks during the 1990s, which attracted a predominantly upper‑caste, English‑educated workforce, creating a self‑reinforcing elite enclave. Political scientists observe that the Karnataka State Education Act mandates 25 % reservation for SC/ST in private unaided schools, yet enforcement is weak in elite institutions due to loopholes around “minority status” and “curricular autonomy.”

(D) Apply the lessons from Sri Lankan power‑sharing (majoritarianism and accommodation failure, c10_civ_cbse_01_002) to evaluate why the 25 % SC/ST reservation in Karnataka’s private unaided schools remains ineffective in elite institutions, and how this ineffectiveness manifests in the metaverse cultural‑participation patterns observed.

A draft bill seeks to establish a National Digital Library (NDL) offering free access to digitised manuscripts, including Sanskrit epics, regional literatures, and government reports. The bill’s preamble invokes India’s “long tradition of argumentative discourse” citing the Mahabharata’s Shanti Parva debates and the colonial‑era Vernacular Press Act debates as historical setting. It then adopts a scholarly yet inviting atmosphere, urging “thoughtful exploration” and “open‑minded critique.” The accompanying financial statement estimates a one‑time digitisation cost of ₹8 000 crore (classified as capital) and annual operational costs of ₹1 200 crore (revenue). A public‑opinion poll reveals that respondents’ attitudes towards the NDL resemble Lencho’s faith in “Lencho’s Faith in God”—a confident belief that the library will democratise knowledge. A parliamentary standing committee, tasked with evaluating the bill, must determine whether the bill’s setting and atmosphere are sufficiently robust to justify its financial outlay, using Sen’s framework, basic accounting classifications, and literary‑character analysis.

(D) The poll comparing public attitudes to Lencho’s faith underscores which literary‑character trait?

In 2024, offshore natural gas discoveries in Cyprus' Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) have reignited tensions between the Greek Cypriot administration and Turkish Cypriot leadership, with Turkish naval vessels escorting seismic surveys in disputed waters. UNFICYP (established 1964), currently deploying 850 personnel along its 180km buffer zone, faces pressure to expand its mandate beyond ceasefire monitoring to facilitate resource-sharing negotiations. Historical analysis reveals Roman provincial governors in the Mediterranean managed similar resource conflicts through *concilia provinciae* (provincial councils) incorporating local elites, while Belgium's consociational democracy resolved linguistic conflicts via segmental autonomy and mutual veto powers. The UN Secretary-General proposes modifying UNFICYP's mandate to: (1) establish a joint technical committee for EEZ resource management, (2) deploy civilian experts to monitor hydrocarbon activities, and (3) facilitate power-sharing talks based on the Belgian model. However, permanent members P2 (France) and P3 (Russia) veto the proposal, citing concerns over mandate creep and impartiality, while P1 (USA) and P5 (UK) support it as conflict prevention. P4 (China) abstains, emphasizing sovereignty. Concurrently, reports indicate Turkish Cypriot factions reject power-sharing without security guarantees, and Greek Cypriot nationalism opposes any resource compromise. Using UN Peacekeeping principles and historical/civic analogies, evaluate the feasibility of this mandate adjustment.

(C) Using the Roman *concilia provinciae* model, propose one specific mechanism UNFICYP could adopt to enhance impartiality in resource talks, and explain why it addresses the P2/P3 veto concern about mandate creep.

A bio‑engineering lab wants to sort fluorescently tagged DNA fragments (average length 2 kb, effective charge –30e) flowing through a straight microchannel (width 100 µm, height 20 µm) by exploiting lateral deflection in a non‑uniform electric field. Two parallel strip electrodes run along the channel walls: the left electrode is held at +V₀ = +15 V, the right electrode at –V₀ = –15 V. The medium is aqueous buffer (relative permittivity ε_r ≈ 80). The goal is to achieve a lateral displacement of at least 30 µm over a channel length L = 2 cm for the target DNA, while ensuring that field lines never cross (to avoid undefined field direction) and that the field line density correctly reflects the local field magnitude for accurate force estimation.  
Using the given geometry, assume the potential varies linearly between the electrodes (V(x) = V₀·(2x/w – 1), where x measures distance from the left wall, 0 ≤ x ≤ w). The electric field is **E** = –∇V.  
Students must: (i) find the field direction at any point via the tangent to field lines, (ii) justify why field lines cannot intersect, (iii) relate field line spacing to |**E**|, (iv) determine where field lines originate/terminate, and (v) sketch the qualitative field line pattern for the electrode pair, noting any regions of high field intensity that could cause particle trapping.

(D) Identify where electric field lines originate and terminate in the electrode configuration described.

A cooperative society in Punjab has 50 hectares to grow wheat and mustard. Wheat profit = ₹10,500/ha, Mustard profit = ₹9,000/ha. Wheat needs 20L herbicide/ha, Mustard needs 10L/ha. Maximum herbicide allowed = 800L (to protect a nearby lake). Formulate the LPP to maximize profit. Then, explain why this is a Manufacturing Problem and not a Diet Problem, referencing the constraint structure and objective direction.

A mixture contains 10 mL of ethanol and 10 mL of ethanoic acid. A few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid are added, and the mixture is heated gently for 10 minutes. A sweet, fruity smell is detected. The reaction mixture is then poured into a beaker containing sodium hydrogen carbonate solution. Effervescence occurs. Identify the organic product formed in the first step, write the balanced equation for both steps, and explain why effervescence occurs in the second step. (Density of ethanol = 0.789 g/mL, ethanoic acid = 1.05 g/mL; molar masses: ethanol = 46, ethanoic acid = 60, ethyl ethanoate = 88 g/mol).

A cognitive‑neuroscience lab conducts an fMRI study on 30 healthy volunteers listening to a recited reading of *Kubla Khan*. Researchers measure BOLD signal changes in the default mode network (DMN), dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), and ventral tegmental area (VTA). Results show: DMN activation ↑ 42 % (p < 0.01), DLPFC activation ↓ 18 % (p < 0.05), VTA activation ↑ 27 % (p < 0.01). Participants also complete the Creative Achievement Questionnaire (CAQ) before and after the session; post‑session CAQ scores rise by a mean of 6.3 points (SD = 2.1). The lab hypothesizes that the poem’s visionary content induces a transient altered state akin to dreaming, boosting dopaminergic reward and loosening executive control, thereby facilitating creative insight. Students must evaluate this hypothesis using concepts of poetic theme, altered states of consciousness, and neurobiological correlates of creativity, while also considering how such a state might relate to charismatic political leadership (e.g., leaders who claim visionary inspiration).

(E) Synthesize the findings from Parts A‑D to assess whether exposure to *Kubla Khan* could be used as a tool in leadership‑training programs aimed at fostering visionary thinking. Provide a reasoned argument that weighs poetic theme, neuro‑creative evidence, and charismatic authority theory.

A 2023 graphic novel “Nagar Ka Darpan” depicts a megacity where every streetlamp doubles as a facial‑recognition camera. The recurring visual motif is a cracked mirror reflected in the glass of each lamp, showing fragmented faces of passersby. The author states in an interview that the mirror “represents the shattered self under constant watch”. Sales data show the novel sold 2.4 lakhs copies in metros but only 12 k in towns with < 5 lakh population, where CCTV density is 0.2 per km² versus 4.8 per km² in metros. Using irony and symbolism concepts, analyse how the cracked‑mirror motif operates as a symbol and whether the novel’s reception exhibits situational irony regarding its intended audience.

(C) Using the sociology node , argue how the cracked‑mirror motif exemplifies the concept of “panoptical internalisation” in a surveillance society.

A person standing on the ground looks up at the top of a 30 m tall tower. The angle of elevation is 45°. Draw the diagram, identify the line of sight, and find the distance from the person to the base of the tower.

A start‑up designs a microfluidic chip to isolate motile spermatozoa using **dielectrophoresis (DEP)**. The chip has a rectangular channel (width = 200 µm, height = 50 µm, length = 2 cm) with planar electrodes generating a non‑uniform AC field (frequency = 10 MHz, peak‑to‑peak voltage = V₀ V). Sperm cells are modeled as spherical shells (radius = 3 µm) with cytoplasm conductivity σᵢ = 0.5 S/m, membrane capacitance Cₘ = 0.01 F/m², and external medium conductivity σₒ = 1.5 S/m. The Clausius‑Mossotti factor for the sperm at this frequency is Re[f_CM] ≈ 0.4.  

Simultaneously, the female partner receives a bolus of LH (luteinising hormone) that triggers ovulation. LH plasma concentration follows first‑order elimination: C(t) = C₀ e^(–kt), with C₀ = 30 IU/L and k = 0.15 min⁻¹. Ovulation occurs when C(t) ≥ 10 IU/L.  

After sorting, the chip delivers N = 2 × 10⁵ motile sperm per insemination. The probability that a single sperm fertilises the oocyte is p = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴ (based on in‑vitro data).  

Assume temperature rise in the channel due to Joule heating is ΔT = (σₒ E² τ)/(ρcₚ), where E ≈ V₀/(2d) (d = electrode gap = 100 µm), τ = pulse width = 10 µs, ρ = 1000 kg/m³, cₚ = 4180 J/(kg·K). Viability requires ΔT ≤ 2 °C.  

**Using the data above, answer the following.**

(D) Assuming each sperm acts independently, what is the probability **P_success** that at least one fertilisation occurs in a single insemination delivering N = 2 × 10⁵ sperm, given per‑sperm fertilisation probability p = 1.2 × 10⁻⁴?

Consider an urban economy where the government invests ₹50 crores in building public parks (providing leisure services) versus ₹50 crores in building a new cargo railway terminal (providing freight transport services). How do these two types of services impact the production of other goods in the economy differently?

Partners A, B, C share profits 4:3:3. On 1 Oct 2023, they change ratio to 3:3:4. Deed: Interest on capital @10% on fixed capitals (A ₹8,00,000, B ₹6,00,000, C ₹4,00,000); Salary to A ₹1,00,000 p.a.; Commission to B @5% on net profit after commission; Guarantee to C: total appropriation ≥ ₹2,50,000 p.a., deficiency borne by A and B in 3:2. Interest on drawings @12% p.a. (avg period 6 months). Drawings: A ₹2,00,000; B ₹1,50,000; C ₹1,00,000 (evenly). Past adjustment: Previous year (2022-23) interest on capital calculated @12% instead of 10% (capitals same). Net profit before appropriations 2023-24: ₹15,00,000. Partner A’s loan ₹5,00,000 @12% interest (paid). Government introduces “inclusive income policy” (c10_eco_cbse_01_002) capping partner’s total income from firm at ₹10,00,000; excess taxed at 30% (not in NCERT, but for economic analysis). Partners assess “income beyond money” (c10_eco_cbse_01_002).

(D) Prepare Profit & Loss Appropriation Account and Partners’ Capital Accounts (fixed capital) for 2023-24 incorporating all adjustments.

In 2024, the Canadian government launches the “Atlantic Tech Stay” scheme offering fast‑track permanent residency to skilled IT workers who agree to reside in Newfoundland for three years and contribute to local digital infrastructure. A second‑generation Irish‑Canadian woman, Siobhan (24), has received a job offer from a Silicon Valley startup that would double her salary and allow remote work from anywhere. Her widowed mother, who relies on Siobhan’s weekly visits for medication management and companionship, insists she stay to honor the family’s promise made after her father’s death. Siobhan recalls her grandmother’s stories of the 1950s Irish emigration wave, when many left for England and the US despite familial pressure. She feels torn between pursuing professional growth and fulfilling perceived familial duty. The scenario invites analysis of Eveline’s paralysis, the historical context of Irish migration, gendered expectations of care work, and the psychological impact of decision fatigue when faced with high‑stakes, value‑laden choices.

(C) Analyze the symbolism of dust in *Eveline* and propose a comparable symbol in Siobhan’s scenario that conveys stagnation.

A small kirana store records daily sales (in ₹) for 7 days: 4200, 4500, 4300, 4400, 4600, 4350, 12000. The owner wants to tell a supplier his "typical daily sales" to set a regular delivery quota. Which measure should he use? Calculate all three and justify.

In 2032, Colebrook installs an AI‑driven video‑analytics system to monitor illegal fishing within its EEZ, funded by a ₹120 crore smart‑port initiative. The system uses facial‑recognition‑style vessel identification, predicts optimal patrol routes, and alerts authorities in real time. While official reports show a 40 % drop in illicit catches, ethnographic fieldwork reveals rising unease among fishers: they report feeling “constantly watched,” experience sleep disturbances, and speak of a phantom “AI‑ship” that will arrive “tomorrow” to vindicate their innocence. The town’s council cites the National Digital Security Act (NDSA) 2029, which permits surveillance for maritime safety, while civil liberties groups invoke Article 21 (right to privacy) of the Constitution and the Supreme Court’s *Puttaswamy* judgment. Historically, Colebrook’s earlier reliance on manual look‑outs fostered communal trust; the shift to algorithmic oversight has eroded that solidarity, mirroring Conrad’s theme of isolated individuals clinging to an imagined redemption. Psychological surveys indicate a 22 % increase in anxiety scores, correlated with perceived surveillance intensity.

(A) Identify two technological details from the scenario that establish the modern setting of Colebrook’s surveillance regime.

A mass‑spring‑damper system models a micro‑scale sensor immersed in a fluid. The displacement obeys x(t) = A e^(−γt) cos(ω_d t), where A = 5 mm, γ = 0.2 s⁻¹ (damping coefficient), and ω_d = √(ω₀²−γ²) with natural frequency ω₀ = 10 rad s⁻¹. The viscous drag force is F_d = −b v, with b = 2γm (m = 0.01 kg). The instantaneous power dissipated is P(t) = F_d·v = −b v². Engineers need the total energy dissipated from t = 0 to t = T = 5 s, given by E = ∫₀ᵀ b v(t)² dt. Because v(t) = dx/dt contains a product of exponential, sine, and cosine terms, v² expands to e^(−2γt) multiplied by a trigonometric polynomial. Evaluating ∫ t·e^(−2γt) cos²(ω_d t) dt (after using identities) requires repeated integration by parts and the special exponential‑trigonometric form. Students must derive v(t), square it, simplify using trigonometric identities, set up the integral, apply integration by parts twice, and compute the numeric energy loss. They should also verify energy conservation by comparing with the loss of mechanical energy (initial − final).

(D) Evaluate I_c = ∫₀ᵀ e^(−2γt) cos(2ω_d t) dt using integration by parts twice (or the complex exponential method) and give its expression in terms of γ, ω_d, T.
A cyclist rides 3 km east, then 4 km north in a total of 30 minutes. What is the magnitude of the cyclist's average velocity? (Give answer in km/h with direction.)

Using Census 2011 data, State X has: Total population = 72.6 million, Net sown area = 18.5 million hectares, Net cultivable area = 22.1 million hectares, Total workers = 31.2 million, Cultivators + Agricultural labourers = 18.7 million. Calculate crude density (area = 307,000 km²), physiological density, and agricultural density. Which density best reflects the pressure on food production? Why?

In an experiment, detached leaves of *Brassica* are floated on solutions of (a) water, (b) 10 ppm kinetin, (c) 10 ppm GA₃, (d) 10 ppm kinetin + 10 ppm GA₃. After 10 days in light, chlorophyll content is measured. Predict the ranking of chlorophyll retention from highest to lowest and justify using the specific molecular functions of each hormone.

A think‑tank developing an urban‑planning simulation packages data processing, demographic forecasting, and policy impact analysis into a Python package `urbansim`. The package contains subpackages `data` (handles CSV/JSON census files), `model` (implements cohort‑component population projection), and `policy` (evaluates effects of zoning, transit, and tax changes). The `data/__init__.py` uses `__all__` to expose `load_csv` and `load_json`. The `model` subpackage imports `numpy` for matrix operations and `random` for Monte‑Carlo runs, while `policy` uses `datetime` to schedule policy roll‑outs. The team must comply with the Right to Information Act (RTI) when publishing simulated datasets, ensuring no personally identifiable information is leaked. Geographic coordinates of wards are stored as (lat, lon) tuples; the simulation needs to compute ward‑wise population density using `math.sqrt` for area calculations. A junior developer attempts to call `load_json` from `policy/evaluate.py` via a relative import.

(D) A ward has an area of 2.25 km² and a simulated population of 9000 persons. Using only the `math` module, compute the population density in persons per km² (rounded to the nearest integer).

A public‑private partnership launches an advisory mobile app for farmers across India, offering crop‑specific guidance in 12 regional languages. The app’s backend uses sub‑domains like `advisory.agri.in` with language‑specific prefixes (e.g., `hi.advisory.agri.in` for Hindi, `ta.advisory.agri.in` for Tamil). To reduce latency, the service employs latency‑based DNS (LDNS) that routes users to the nearest regional server farm based on measured round‑trip time (RTT). Monsoon‑induced cloud cover increases RTT variability in the western ghats, while trust studies show farmers are 35 % more likely to follow advice presented in their mother tongue. You must analyse how DNS resolution interacts with linguistic preference (sociology), monsoon‑affected network performance (geography), and user trust (psychology) to ensure effective service delivery.

(C) Explain how monsoon‑induced atmospheric conditions can increase RTT variability between a farmer’s device in the Western Ghats and the central server farm, and propose a DNS‑based mitigation strategy that does not involve changing the application logic.

A research team wants to over‑express a thermostable lipase (MW ≈ 50 kDa) in E. coli BL21(DE3) for industrial biodiesel production. The gene is cloned into a pBR322‑derived plasmid (copy number ≈ 50) containing a T7 lac operator promoter, a Shine‑Dalgarno sequence, a C‑terminal His₆ tag, and a rho‑independent terminator. Induction is performed with IPTG. The lipase activity follows Arrhenius behaviour with activation energy Eₐ = 50 kJ·mol⁻¹. The culture is grown to OD₆₀₀ ≈ 0.6 (≈ 1 × 10⁹ cells·mL⁻¹), induced with IPTG, and incubated for 4 h at 30 °C. mRNA half‑life is 2 min, translation initiation rate is 20 proteins·mRNA⁻¹·min⁻¹, and protein degradation is negligible over the induction period. Purification via Ni‑NTA gives 80 % recovery. Using the data below, answer the sub‑questions.

**Given:**  
- T7 promoter strength = 100 transcripts·plasmid⁻¹·min⁻¹  
- Basal leak of T7 lac promoter = 1 % of maximal activity  
- Hill coefficient for IPTG binding (n) = 2, dissociation constant Kd = 0.1 mM  
- Avogadro’s number Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹

(E) Adjust the yield from part D for temperature‑dependent activity using the Arrhenius equation (Eₐ = 50 kJ·mol⁻¹) to find the active lipase yield at 30 °C relative to 37 °C, and express the final concentration in µg·mL⁻¹ for a culture density of 1 × 10⁹ cells·mL⁻¹ (MW = 50 kDa, purification recovery = 80 %).

A cooperative of 250 small‑holder tea growers in Upper Assam seeks Fairtrade certification to access premium EU markets. The region receives 2 200–2 800 mm annual rainfall, mean temperature 18‑24 °C, and has lateritic soils. Recent land‑reform acts have transferred 15 % of erstwhile plantation land to tribal cooperatives, but 8 % of plots remain under disputed tenure. The cooperative plans to invest ₹45 lakh in organic certification, shade‑tree planting, and worker welfare. Current average green leaf yield is 1.2 t ha⁻¹; Fairtrade premium adds ₹20 kg⁻¹ to the sale price of processed tea (sold at ₹180 kg⁻¹). Fixed costs for certification and overheads are ₹12 lakh. Variable costs per ha (plucking, transport, organic inputs) are ₹25 000. The cooperative holds 180 ha under cultivation. Using the above, answer the sub‑parts.

(C) Assess whether the land‑tenure situation (15 % transferred to tribals, 8 % disputed) satisfies the political‑science principle of “equitable power sharing” as outlined in Vertical Division Of Power (vertical division of power). Provide a brief justification (≤ 80 words).

In June 2024, a coalition of Dalit student groups launched a Twitter‑storm using the hashtag #Laal Haath (Red Hand) to protest a recent state‑government order diluting the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act. Participants changed their profile pictures to a red‑filled fist graphic and tweeted verses from the poem “fujkyk” that evoke the colour red as a sign of resistance. The campaign generated 4.8 million impressions, with 1.1 million unique users, 68 % aged 18‑25. A concurrent offline rally in Jaipur saw 8,000 protesters, 55 % of whom were women. Police registered three FIRs under Section 153A (promoting enmity) against activists alleging “hurting religious sentiments”. Legal experts cited Article 17 (abolition of untouchability) and Article 21 (right to life) as constitutional backing. Sociological analysts noted the campaign’s alignment with “new social movement” theory, emphasizing identity‑based mobilisation rather than class‑based. Psychological studies showed that exposure to the red‑fist image increased feelings of solidarity by 23 % (measured via Implicit Association Test).

(A) Identify the poem’s theme of revolutionary awakening and explain how the #Laal Haath hashtag operationalises this theme in the digital campaign.

In July 2025, a sophisticated ransomware strain named “BlackOut” infiltrated India’s National Power Grid Control Centre through a zero‑day exploit in a widely used SCADA software vendor’s update package. The malware encrypted real‑time load‑balancing servers across the northern and western grids, causing a cascading blackout that left over 120 million people without electricity for up to 18 hours. Hospitals relied on diesel generators, leading to increased particulate emissions and temporary disruption of cold‑chain vaccine storage. A video released by the attackers showed a masked figure claiming allegiance to a trans‑national jihadist network, demanding payment in 50 BTC to restore services and threatening to leak classified grid schematics if unpaid. The group’s manifesto cited grievances over India’s alleged occupation of Kashmir and its support for Israel, framing the attack as a “digital jihad” to compel policy change. Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT‑IN) coordinated with the National Technical Research Organisation (NTRO) and allied agencies under the Quad Cyber‑Security Initiative, while the Ministry of Power activated emergency protocols and began gradual restoration using micro‑grids. Analysts debate whether the incident constitutes terrorism, its impact on human and environmental security, the adequacy of cooperative security responses, and what lessons can be drawn from historical attacks on urban infrastructure (e.g., Roman aqueduct sabotage) for protecting modern critical assets.

(A) Based on the scenario, does the BlackOut ransomware attack satisfy the definitional criteria of terrorism from? Focus on the target (civilian infrastructure), the actor (non‑state), and the intent (to coerce a government).

Read the following Hindi excerpt (original composition) inspired by ISRO’s Chandrayaan‑3 landing (23 August 2023):  

> “चाँद की सिल्की सतह पर पैर रखते ही,  
>  शून्य की गहरी खामोशी ने कानों को चूम लिया,  
>  जैसे कोई पुराना वादा थामे खड़ा हो,  
>  silenzieux वादे की तरह, ठंडी हवा ने चुम्बन दिया.”  

The poem uses visual (silky surface), auditory (deep silence), and tactile (cold wind) imagery. The line “जैसे कोई पुराना वादा थामे खड़ा हो” functions as a metaphor, comparing the moon’s stillness to an old promise.  

Contextual data:  
- Launch site: Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh (13.73° N, 80.20° E), a flat coastal plain with lateritic soil.  
- Mission budget: ₹ 615 crore (≈ US $75 million), a 23 % increase over Chandrayaan‑2.  
- Historical link: The poem’s metaphor echoes the Cold‑War era “Space Race” where the USA’s Apollo 11 (1969) framed the Moon as a “promise of peace”.  
- Political context: India’s 2023‑24 Space Budget raised ISRO’s allocation to ₹ 13 000 crore, reflecting a strategic shift toward lunar‑based resource exploration.

(E) Write a 4‑sentence PEEL paragraph (Point‑Evidence‑Explanation‑Link) analyzing how the poem’s imagery and metaphor together reinforce India’s contemporary space policy of peaceful lunar exploration.

Sanjay, a 28‑year‑old cyber‑security analyst, prevented a major ransomware attack on a national bank in March 2024, but during the incident he witnessed confidential patient data being exfiltrated. Two weeks later he began experiencing **intrusive images of the data breach** (flashback‑like) and **compulsive checking of firewall logs** every 10 minutes, fearing he missed a subtle indicator. He reports **average 3 hrs/day** spent on checking, causing him to miss project deadlines. Salivary cortisol measured **baseline** 0.10 µg/dL, rises to **0.35 µg/dL** during checking episodes. He also reports **avoidance of team meetings** (fear of being blamed) and **social withdrawal** (eats lunch alone). A standardized PTSD checklist yields a score of 22/40 (cut‑off ≥ 20 suggests PTSD); an OCD‑YBOCS score is 24/40 (cut‑off ≥ 16 suggests OCD). His sister has diagnosed OCD (checking subtype). Using this rich dataset, answer the following.

(A) Based on the YBOCS and PTSD checklist scores, state whether each disorder meets diagnostic threshold and compute the combined probability of comorbidity assuming independence (P(OCD) × P(PTSD)).

Rising temperatures and erratic rainfall in the Satpura‑Maikal range have reduced mahua flowering by 40 % over the past decade, threatening the livelihood of Gond forest‑dependent communities. A state‑run “Climate Resilient Livelihoods” programme (₹8 crore) proposes to relocate 2 000 families to nearby urban fringes, providing skill‑training in textile weaving. Tribal leaders resist, arguing that relocation severs the link between the Gond baiga’s storytelling and the forest ecosystem that supplies metaphors (river, mahua, tiger). The programme’s environmental impact assessment cites a 2022 IPCC report projecting a 2 °C rise by 2050 for the region. Students must analyse the primary theme of the storyteller in light of ecological loss, evaluate the protagonist’s role as ecological interpreter, decode key metaphors, assess the displacement policy against constitutional safeguards for tribal rights, and suggest an ecologically sensitive alternative using geographical data on forest cover and migration corridors.

(D) Evaluate the proposed relocation policy against the constitutional safeguards for tribal communities, citing the relevant political‑science node and a historical displacement case.

A 29-year-old woman with PCOS (polycystic ovary syndrome) presents with oligomenorrhea (cycles 45-60 days) and infertility for 18 months. Her husband's semen analysis is normal. HSG shows bilateral patent tubes. She has BMI 32 kg/m². Explain the pathophysiological basis of her infertility and the stepwise management plan including first-line ART.

In 2024, the Department of Information and Broadcasting in Bharatvarsha introduced 'Vidyaloka', a cloud‑based content‑moderation platform that automatically flags any artistic work deemed “against national ethos”. All online art portals must integrate Vidyaloka; flagged works are demonetised and creators receive a notice to remove or alter the piece within 48 hours. A celebrated photographer, Meera Singh, known for her black‑and‑white series on migrant labourers, uploaded a photo‑essay titled “Tracks of Hope”. Vidyaloka flagged it as “showing distress incompatible with national optimism”. Her account was temporarily suspended, and she received a summons under the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines) Rules, 2021, to appear before a grievance committee. Simultaneously, a meme page “Sarkari Satire” used Vidyaloka’s own API to generate ironic posters (e.g., a smiling statue made of e‑waste) that went viral. The government cited Section 69A of the IT Act to block the meme page, alleging it threatened “public order”. This scenario parallels the tension in 'इग्योकु की छाया' where the protagonist navigates royal patronage versus personal vision, now reframed through algorithmic gatekeeping, intermediary liability, and the chilling effect on artistic expression.

(E) Examine how the metaphor of the 'algorithmic gate' in the scenario (state's 'Vidyaloka' tool) functions as a literary device (c12_hin_ar_cbse_13_008) to reinforce the secondary theme of 'tradition-modernity transition' (c12_hin_ar_cbse_13_007). Contrast this with one instance of imagery from 'इग्योकु की छाया' that depicts a similar tension, explaining why the metaphor is more effective than literal description in conveying the theme's complexity in the digital age.

India’s decision to adopt a single Indian Standard Time (IST) in 1906 created a temporal fault line with its northeastern states, where solar noon can lag IST by up to 90 minutes. In 2024, a proposal emerges to introduce a second time zone (IST‑II) for the seven‑sister states to improve productivity and align work hours with daylight. The debate draws on Ramanujan’s poem: supporters cite the lines “each slightly off the others’ time… deeper or lighter in its bronze… out of the accidents of alloy” as a celebration of natural temporal diversity; opponents argue that a unified time signal is essential for national integration, invoking the poem’s later image of a “knocked‑out clockwork… after a riot… a peace‑march time bomb” to warn that temporal disunity could precipitate social unrest. The discussion involves historians recalling the colonial imposition of IST, political scientists analysing the impact on federalism and Article 1 (territorial integrity), and geographers examining the longitudinal spread (68°E–97°E) and its effect on solar irradiance, agricultural cycles, and energy consumption.

(C) Analyse how the poem’s celebration of “different sequence each half‑hour” can be applied to the debate over introducing IST‑II, especially in terms of agricultural productivity and energy consumption in the northeastern states.

In 2028 a successive failure of monsoon rains leaves 60 % of India’s districts facing acute water scarcity. The Union government, citing a threat to national security, proclaims a **National Water Emergency** under Article 352. Ordinances are issued permitting (a) inter‑state diversion of river waters without state consent, (b) criminalisation of groundwater extraction beyond a fixed quota, and (c) postponement of all pending State Legislative Assembly elections. To insulate these measures from judicial challenge, Parliament passes three amendments modeled on the Emergency‑era changes:  
1. **38th‑type amendment** – makes the proclamation of a water emergency and any related ordinance **non‑justiciable**.  
2. **39th‑type amendment** – removes the jurisdiction of courts to hear disputes concerning the election of the Chief Minister, Governor (appointed) and Speaker of State Legislative Assemblies.  
3. **42nd‑type amendment** – amends the Preamble to insert “water security” and adds a new clause to Article 31C stating that any law enacted to secure equitable water distribution (a Directive Principle) shall **prevail over** Fundamental Rights relating to property (Art 31) and trade (Art 19‑g).  
A group of agrarian states approaches the Supreme Court contending that the amendments destroy the federal balance and the basic structure. Using historical precedents from ancient Mesopotamian water‑management codes (c11_hist_cbse_01_009) and the centralising tendencies of the Roman Empire’s provincial administration (c11_hist_cbse_02_004), assess the validity of the amendments.

(E) Compare the Indian Water Emergency amendments with (i) ancient Mesopotamian water‑management inscriptions that granted the king authority to allocate river waters during drought, and (ii) the Roman Empire’s provincial edicts that allowed the emperor to requisition water supplies for the army. Which constitutional value is most at risk in all three instances?

In July 2024, a Sri Lankan parliamentary committee reviews the Hambantota Port lease agreement with a Chinese state‑owned enterprise, amid public protests over alleged “debt‑trap” diplomacy. The committee seeks to determine whether the loan structure mirrors historical monsoon‑wind‑driven trade patterns, where Indian Ocean merchants extended credit based on seasonal cargo returns, and whether the accounting of the loan adheres to the effective interest rate method under IFRS 9. Data provided: initial loan ¥30 billion (2015), effective interest rate 5.8 % p.a., moratorium 5 years, repayment schedule begins 2021 with annual installments of ¥4.2 billion, and a final balloon payment of ¥12 billion in 2030. The committee also notes that, similar to ancient monsoon traders who adjusted credit terms based on voyage outcomes, the loan includes a clause allowing repayment extension if port throughput falls below 8 million TEU for two consecutive years. Using these facts, members must judge the economic rationale, assess the accounting treatment, and relate the arrangement to broader regionalism trends.

(E) Using the distinction between book‑keeping and accounting (c11_acc_cbse_01_001), argue why evaluating the Hambantota deal solely on cash‑flow statements would be insufficient for assessing its long‑term strategic impact.

A topographic map (1:50,000, contour interval 20 m) shows a river valley. You are asked to determine the intervisibility between two points A (1,100 m) and B (1,300 m) separated by a hill with a summit at 1,350 m. The horizontal distances: A to summit = 1.2 km, summit to B = 0.8 km. The line of sight just grazes the summit. Calculate the minimum height of a tower needed at A so that the line of sight clears the summit by 5 m.
Why did the autonomous women's movement of the 1970s-80s deliberately distance itself from political parties, and what was a major consequence of this autonomy?

GramVikas Bank, a regional cooperative bank serving 150 villages, faces a rumor‑driven run after a poor monsoon season. Depositors withdraw ₹180 crore in cash over three days, reducing its demand deposits. The bank’s NDTL after the run is ₹9,000 crore. It must maintain CRR = 3 % and SLR = 20 %. The bank approaches the RBI for LOLR support. The RBI agrees to lend ₹250 crore at the Bank Rate (penalty rate) of 6.5 % p.a., accepting the bank’s gold collateral (market value ₹300 crore). The loan is for 90 days. The bank also simultaneously sells ₹100 crore of government securities to the RBI under an Open Market Operation (OMO) sale, receiving cash. Assume no other transactions. Answer the following.

(A) Compute the LOLR interest expense (in ₹ lakh) for the ₹250 crore loan at 6.5 % p.a. for 90 days.

A national museum is digitising its collection of ancient Sanskrit and Prakrit manuscripts. Each record must store: ManuscriptID (unique integer), Title (up to 200 characters), Language (e.g., Sanskrit, Prakrit, up to 50 chars), Date of creation (only year‑month‑day needed), Material (palm leaf, birch bark, paper – up to 30 chars), Length and width in centimetres (measured to one decimal place, max 200 cm), Estimated market value in Indian Rupees (up to ₹99,99,99,999.99 with paise precision), Holding institution name (up to 100 chars), and free‑form Notes (unlimited length). The museum also wants to query: average value per institution, manuscripts created after a certain date, and to concatenate Title and Language for catalogue display. Identify the most suitable MySQL data types for each column, justify choices, and write SQL snippets for the required queries.

(E) List manuscripts created after 01‑01‑1500 CE, ordered by EstimatedValue_INR descending, showing only Title, DateCreated, and EstimatedValue_INR.

In FY 2023‑24, India exported 1.2 million tonnes of Alphonso mangoes. 68 % by value went via air cargo from Bengaluru International Airport to the UAE, fetching an average FOB price of USD 2 200 per tonne. The remaining 32 % by value moved by road through the Petrapole ICP (Bangladesh) to Nepal, averaging USD 1 400 per tonne. Simultaneously, India imported 0.9 million tonnes of raw cashew nuts from Côte d’Ivoire, all via air cargo to Mumbai at USD 1 800 per tonne. A new India‑UAE Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) reduced the import duty on mangoes from 5 % to 0 % and increased the export duty on cashews from 2 % to 4 %. Using the data, compute the net change in India’s trade balance (in USD million) attributable to mango and cashew trades after the CEPA, assuming volumes unchanged.

(E) Which of the following statements is correct regarding the suitability of air cargo for mangoes versus land route for cashews?

In 2024, a leading global semiconductor firm, **AstraChip**, headquartered in a neutral European state, is accused by the United States of embedding covert back‑doors in its 5G chips that could be exploited by a rival power’s military. The U.S. invokes an updated version of the Cold‑War‑era **COCOM** (Coordinating Committee for Multilateral Export Controls) regime, threatening secondary sanctions on any third‑party country that continues to purchase AstraChip’s advanced nodes. Simultaneously, a bloc led by a resurrected **Eurasian Security Union (ESU)**—comprising Russia, several Central Asian states, and a re‑aligned China—offers AstraChip a lucrative partnership, promising technology transfer and market access in exchange for establishing a joint R&D centre in Minsk. The ESU frames the offer as a “new non‑aligned” initiative, echoing the Cold‑War Non‑Aligned Movement, while the U.S. warns that accepting the deal would violate the **Truman Doctrine**‑style commitment to contain technological espionage. AstraChip’s board must decide whether to (a) comply with U.S. demands and shift production to allied fabs, (b) accept the ESU partnership, or (c) pursue a hybrid strategy. The firm’s CFO prepares an impact assessment using accounting information on users (investors, creditors, governments) and qualitative characteristics (relevance, reliability). The board also consults a historian who draws a parallel between the current bifurcation of technology blocs and the historic division of the **Roman Empire** into Eastern and Western halves, noting how the Byzantine Empire survived longer by adapting to shifting alliances.

(D) AstraChip’s CFO must present an impact assessment to investors. Using the users of accounting information and qualitative characteristics , identify which two user groups would prioritize **relevance** over **reliability** in this context, and explain why.

A university psychology department is conducting a study on how memoir writers reconstruct workplace trauma and nostalgia. They select Asokamitran’s *My Years with Boss* as a case study, focusing on the “Poets and Pancakes” chapter. Researchers note the author’s rambling, anecdotal style, his shifting tone from amused detachment to sudden poignancy when recalling the make‑up department’s monotony, and his use of fragmented memories (e.g., recalling specific clippings but forgetting exact dates). The study aims to map these narrative techniques onto concepts of selective memory, cognitive dissonance, and the therapeutic function of humor. Simultaneously, the history faculty wants to link the memoir’s depiction of Gemini Studios to the broader socio‑economic landscape of 1950s Madras, including labor migration, the rise of patronage networks, and the influence of American cinematic technology. The interdisciplinary team must produce a joint report that explains how the memoir’s structure serves both as a psychological coping mechanism and a historical artifact revealing informal economies within the film industry.

(A) Identify the primary narrative technique used in the excerpt’s shifting tone from amused detachment to sudden poignancy and explain its psychological function.

A spherical implant of radius R = 5 mm releases a drug at a first‑order rate constant kᵣ = 0.1 h⁻¹ into blood volume V = 5 L. The drug is eliminated from plasma by first‑order clearance with rate constant kₑ = 0.15 h⁻¹. The plasma concentration C(t) (mg L⁻¹) follows dC/dt = (kᵣ M₀/V) e^{−kᵣt} − kₑC, where M₀ = 100 mg is the initial drug load.  
Using the area under the concentration‑time curve (AUC) concept, determine total drug exposure, the time above a therapeutic threshold, and the influence of pH‑dependent release and patient weight.

(B) Evaluate the AUC analytically and verify the numerical value from part A.

A commercially important pelagic fish species (*Sardinella longiceps*) inhabits the Arabian Sea. Baseline sea‑surface temperature (SST) is **27 °C**. Climate projections indicate a **+2 °C** rise by 2050. The fish’s standard metabolic rate (SMR) follows a Q₁₀ = 2.5 relationship: SMR₂ = SMR₁ × Q₁₀^((T₂−T₁)/10). Oxygen solubility in seawater at 27 °C, 35 ‰ salinity is **6.5 mg L⁻¹**; at 29 °C it drops to **5.9 mg L⁻¹** (approx. linear). The fish’s critical oxygen tension (P_crit) is **20 %** of ambient saturation. Assume the population follows exponential decay when ambient DO falls below P_crit, with mortality rate μ = 0.001 day⁻¹ per % deficit of DO below P_crit. Initial stock is **10⁶** individuals. Using these data, answer the sub‑parts.

(C) Assuming the fish population experiences mortality only when ambient DO falls below P_crit, calculate the daily mortality rate (μ_eff) at 29 °C if the measured ambient DO is **5.0 mg L⁻¹**. Use μ = 0.001 day⁻¹ per % deficit of DO below P_crit.
Fill in the blank: Should you lease it (pay rentals, return after 3 years) or opt for hire purchase (pay ______, own it at the end)?

In mid‑2025, a severe drought reduces North Korea’s grain output by 40 %, threatening famine for 10 million people. The World Food Programme (WFP) prepares an emergency aid package of 500 000 tons of rice, funded largely by the EU and Japan. China offers to transport the aid through its rail network but insists on monitoring distribution to prevent diversion to the military. The United States, citing concerns over aid legitimizing the regime, proposes linking any assistance to verifiable steps toward denuclearization and threatens to block the WFP funding unless such conditions are met. South Korea offers to contribute humanitarian goods directly across the DMZ, but North Korea refuses, fearing espionage. The UN Security Council debates a resolution urging unhindered humanitarian access; Russia supports the resolution, while China urges a “human‑first” approach without political strings. The episode revives debates about whether humanitarian aid in the Korean context functions as a tool of soft power, how non‑aligned states historically navigated similar dilemmas during the Cold War, and what the implications are for the contemporary NAM’s relevance.

(D) Determine how the scenario influences the contemporary relevance and activities of the Non‑Aligned Movement (NAM).

A designer selects acetate fabric for a formal evening gown lining. The gown will be dry-cleaned. During production, the lining is accidentally pressed with an iron set at 200°C. Predict the damage, explain the molecular reason, and propose a remediation that does not require replacing the lining.

A 1:50,000 toposheet is photocopied at 150% linear enlargement. A student measures a road on the enlarged copy as 9 cm and calculates ground length using original RF 1:50,000, getting 4.5 km. Another student argues the RF has changed. Who is correct? Derive the new effective RF of the enlarged copy and explain why graphical scale (bar scale) would have avoided this confusion.

A newly launched snack brand “CrunchLite” markets its product as “0% trans fat, high fibre (5g per serving)” on front‑of‑pack labels. An independent NGO, “Consumer Health Watch (CHW)”, purchases 200 samples from retail outlets across five states (Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, West Bengal, Karnataka) and sends them to a NABL‑accredited lab. Lab results show average trans‑fat content of 0.8 % per serving (exceeding the 0.2 % limit set by FSSAI) and fibre content of only 2.1 g per serving. CHW files a complaint with the District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (DCDRC) of Mumbai seeking refunds and compensation for 1,500 affected consumers who bought the product at ₹50 per pack. Simultaneously, CHW files a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in the Bombay High Court alleging violation of Article 21 (right to health) and misleading advertising under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. CHW also lobbies the Ministry of Consumer Affairs for mandatory third‑party verification of nutrition claims. The NGO’s annual report shows ₹1.2 crore funding, 70 % from individual donations, 30 % from grants; its financial statements follow accrual basis and are audited by a CA firm.

(D) Calculate the total expenditure incurred by the 1,500 consumers on CrunchLite packs and determine the average excess trans‑fat intake per consumer assuming each pack contains one serving.

In 2024, a coastal Gujarat community revives the traditional salt‑pan industry, aiming to improve workers’ welfare through a cooperative model. The cooperative’s leadership wishes to launch a **monthly “Silent Shore” ceremony**, inspired by Neruda’s lines where the salt‑gatherer looks at his hurt hands, to foster workers’ reflection on occupational hazards and solidarity. They seek to (a) justify the ceremony using the poem’s imagery of hurt hands and the historical context of 1930s Salt Satyagraha, (b) assess potential economic impact using basic accounting concepts (cost‑benefit of lost work‑time vs. expected reduction in accident‑related medical expenses), and (c) design a Speaking‑and‑Listening activity for cooperative members that links the ceremony to the poem’s call for “brothers in the shade, doing nothing”. The cooperative provides: average daily wage ₹450, average monthly medical expense due to salt‑related injuries ₹12,000 per worker, proposed silent ceremony duration 15 minutes per shift (reducing effective work‑time by 0.25 hr/shift), and 120 workers. Determine which poetic, historical, and accounting concepts apply, then calculate the **net monthly monetary impact** of the ceremony (considering wage loss and medical‑expense saving).

(C) Compute the monthly wage loss due to the 15‑minute silent ceremony per shift, assuming one shift per day and 26 working days in a month.

Suppose in 1957, a private industrialist wanted to increase the production capacity of their existing textile mill from 10,000 meters to 15,000 meters per month. Under the provisions of IPR 1956, explain the exact regulatory step the industrialist had to take, and calculate the percentage increase in capacity that required this regulatory approval.
In an age problem, if the present age of A is x years and present age of B is y years, how do you express "A's age 5 years ago" and "B's age 3 years hence" in terms of x and y?

A biochemical engineer models the concentration \(C(t)\) (mol/L) of a substrate in a well‑mixed bioreactor where an enzyme catalyzes its conversion to product. The reaction follows Michaelis–Menten kinetics approximated by a first‑order decay when substrate concentration is far below the Michaelis constant: \(\displaystyle \frac{dC}{dt} = -k(T) C\), where the rate constant \(k(T)\) obeys the Arrhenius law \(k(T)=A e^{-E_a/(RT)}\). The reactor is heated linearly with time: \(T(t)=T_0 + \beta t\), with \(T_0=300\) K and heating rate \(\beta=0.5\) K/s. Initial substrate concentration is \(C(0)=2.0\) mol/L. After 200 s, the measured concentration is \(C(200)=0.5\) mol/L.  
Using this data, determine (a) the activation energy \(E_a\), (b) the pre‑exponential factor \(A\), (c) the general solution for \(C(t)\) under the time‑varying temperature, (d) the particular solution satisfying the initial condition, and (e) the time required for the substrate to drop to 0.05 mol/L. Assume the gas constant \(R=8.314\) J mol\(^{-1}\) K\(^{-1}\). All intermediate results must be retained in exact form where possible, and final numerical answers given to three significant figures.

(A) Determine the activation energy \(E_a\) (in kJ mol\(^{-1}\)) using the concentration data at \(t=0\) and \(t=200\) s.

Fill in the blank: Limits and Achievements of Popular Movements in India refers to the critical assessment of the tangible outcomes (policy changes, social awareness, empowerment of marginalized groups) and structural constraints (lack of ______, dependence on charismatic leadership, state repression, co-option by political parties) that characterize non-party political mobilizations such as the Chipko Movement, Dalit Panthers, Bharatiya Kisan Union, Anti-Arrack Movement, Narmada Bachao Andolan, and broader women's and environmental movements in post-1970s India.

A new AI‑driven marketplace, “BharatBazaar”, uses machine‑learning models to dynamically price handicraft items based on real‑time demand, competitor listings, and artisan reputation scores derived from past transaction reviews. The platform operates across India, the USA, and the UAE. To curb potential algorithmic collusion, the Competition Commission of India (CCI) proposes mandatory explainability reports for pricing algorithms, while the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) requires disclosure of any “dark patterns” that manipulate consumer choice. Simultaneously, the UAE’s Data Protection Law mandates data localisation of personal data of UAE‑resident buyers. Historically, medieval Indian guilds fixed prices through collective agreements; today, AI algorithms perform a similar function but lack transparency. Psychologically, artisans exhibit “automation bias”, overtrusting the AI‑suggested price even when it undervalues their work. Sociologically, the platform’s gig‑model exacerbates income inequality, as top‑10 % of artisans capture 55 % of total revenue due to algorithmic visibility bias. The platform must also address the digital divide: 25 % of artisans lack smartphones capable of running the ML‑based app, relying instead on SMS‑based order notifications.

(B) The CCI’s explainability requirement draws parallels with historical guild price‑fixing. Identify one similarity and one difference between medieval guild price‑setting (c11_hi_cbse_01_005) and AI‑driven dynamic pricing in BharatBazaar with respect to (i) decision‑making transparency, and (ii) enforcement mechanism.

A family in Bengaluru booked a holiday package worth ₹12 lakh through a travel agency. The agency cancelled the trip at the last moment without refund. The family incurred additional expenses of ₹3 lakh for last-minute alternative bookings and claims ₹5 lakh for mental harassment. They want to file a complaint. Which forum should they approach? If the District Commission dismisses their complaint, what is the next step?

A square sheet of metal of side 30 cm is to be used to make two identical square bases for a model. The squares must be cut from the sheet with minimal waste. The designer proposes cutting the sheet along lines joining the midpoints of the sides, yielding a central square and four corner triangles. The central square is used as one base, and the four triangles are reassembled to form the second base. Verify that both bases have equal area and find the side length of each base.

SolarFlux LLP (India) partners: Ravi (50%), Priya (30%), Anil (20%). Capital: Ravi ₹40 Cr, Priya ₹24 Cr, Anil ₹16 Cr. Assets: Solar farms ₹100 Cr (USD 12 Mn at ₹83.33/USD), Batteries ₹20 Cr, Cash ₹10 Cr. Liabilities: USD loan $5 Mn (₹41.67 Cr), INR loan ₹15 Cr. On 1-Jul-2024, Helios GmbH (Germany) admitted for 20% share. Helios brings €10 Mn (₹90 Cr at ₹90/€) + carbon credits worth €2 Mn (₹18 Cr). Agreement: (a) USD loan restated at ₹85/USD, (b) Solar farms revalued to USD 15 Mn (₹127.5 Cr), (c) Carbon credits recognised at fair value, (d) Accumulated losses ₹5 Cr written off, (e) Capitals made proportionate to new ratio (Ravi:Priya:Anil:Helios = 5:3:2:4) via current accounts, (f) Hidden goodwill computed via capitalised value method. Helios's capital account credited with his share of hidden goodwill. Exchange differences on USD loan routed through P&L per Ind AS 21. The firm uses hedge accounting for USD revenue (80% of sales).

(A) Compute hidden goodwill and Helios's goodwill share. Show capitalised value derivation with dual-currency adjustments.

A student calculates the lateral surface area of a cuboid of dimensions 10 cm × 8 cm × 6 cm as $2 \times 6 \times (10 + 8) = 216 \text{ cm}^2$. Another student says the answer should be $2 \times (10 \times 8 + 8 \times 6 + 6 \times 10) = 376 \text{ cm}^2$. Who is correct? Explain why the other formula gives a different value.

A sugar mill in Uttar Pradesh processes 5000 tonnes of sugarcane daily (sucrose content 12%). Sugarcane loses 70% weight during crushing (bagasse, molasses, water vapor). Sugar recovery is 10.5% of cane weight. Calculate: (a) weight-loss ratio, (b) daily sugar output, (c) bagasse produced (assume 30% of cane weight), (d) why sugar mills must locate within 30 km of cane fields.

You are annotating a newly sequenced bacterial genome. You find a gene with 85% amino acid identity to a known antibiotic resistance gene in a distantly related species, but the genomic neighbourhood (flanking genes) is completely different. The gene is also flanked by insertion sequences. What does comparative genomics suggest about the origin of this gene, and what analysis would you perform to test your hypothesis?

A pilot telemedicine project is launched in 12 remote villages of Uttarakhand, each situated >2,000 m above sea level. The initiative provides solar‑powered tablets, 4G‑enabled micro‑cells, and free video‑consultation slots with specialists in Dehradun. Baseline survey shows: (i) 68 % of households own a basic mobile phone, (ii) only 22 % have ever used the internet, (iii) among internet users, 74 % are men aged 18‑35, while women >45 % report low confidence in using apps, (iv) after 6 months, 41 % of patients completed follow‑up consultations, and maternal‑infant morbidity dropped by 18 %. The state government proposes scaling the model to all 150 high‑altitude villages, allocating ₹12 crore for infrastructure and ₹3 crore for digital‑literacy workshops targeting women’s self‑help groups. Identify which aspects of the digital divide are illustrated and evaluate the policy’s likely impact on usage and outcome levels.

(E) The state’s plan to allocate ₹15 crore (₹12 crore infrastructure + ₹3 crore literacy) for scaling the project is an example of which type of policy intervention, and which political‑science node evaluates its feasibility?

In 2024 the Ministry of Rural Development launched the **“Smart Village Initiative”** in 120 drought‑prone districts. Each village receives a fleet of solar‑powered AI drones that scan fields every two hours, sending real‑time moisture and pest data to a central portal. The government claims the programme will **increase yields by 35 %**, **reduce water waste by 22 %**, and **ensure food security for all**, projecting it as a symbol of **inclusive nationalism**—technology bridging the urban‑rural divide.  

Field‑level data after the first kharif season show:  
- Average yield rose **28 %** in villages with full drone coverage.  
- **18 %** of smallholder farmers (≤2 ha) reported loss of access to traditional grazing lands because drone no‑flight zones were set over commons.  
- **7 %** of those farmers filed grievances alleging that the drones “watch over the crops but ignore the farmers”.  
- Satellite imagery reveals that the drone flight paths form a **grid pattern** resembling a **chakra** (wheel) over the cultivated area.  

Students must analyse the scenario for **irony** (the promise of inclusion vs. exclusion of marginal farmers) and **symbolism** (drone grid as a chakra, fields as a living nation).

(D) Evaluate the **effectiveness** of using the drone grid as a symbol to convey the message of inclusive nationalism, referring to imagery‑metaphor techniques.

A popular fitness influencer with 2 million followers signs a contract to promote a new sugar‑laden energy drink, receiving ₹1.5 crore for a series of posts. The influencer privately follows a strict low‑sugar diet and believes the drink contradicts her health advocacy, potentially misleading followers who trust her expertise. After posting the first endorsement video, she notices a surge of comments questioning her credibility and experiences mild anxiety. To alleviate discomfort, she decides to run a marathon for a charity supporting diabetes awareness, posting about her training regimen. Using cognitive dissonance theory, analyze how the influencer’s attitude toward the drink may evolve and identify the dissonance‑reduction strategies employed.

(E) From a sociological standpoint, discuss how the influencer’s endorsement might reinforce or challenge existing social stratification regarding health‑conscious lifestyles.
At timestamp 22 min, why does the undo stack signal overflow? State the exact condition.

A multinational firm’s HR department launches a “Caste‑Sensitivity” module after an internal audit reveals 34% of employees report caste‑based microaggressions at work (2022 survey). The module uses selected scenes from *Chandalika*: Prakriti’s character arc (from shame to divine self‑assertion), the recurring forest and mirror imagery, and the grammatical pattern of imperative sentences in Ananda’s dialogues (“Take this water,” “Look into the mirror”). HR data: mirror imagery appears in 3 of 5 acts; imperative sentences constitute 22% of Ananda’s lines; forest setting frames 40% of the play’s action. Participants must analyze how character development, visual symbols, and sentence types reinforce or challenge power dynamics, and propose improvements to the training using sociological and psychological theories.

(E) Using critical‑thinking criteria, evaluate whether the use of *Chandalika* in corporate training risks essentializing caste experiences, and suggest a safeguard based on the play’s own narrative complexity.

In a 2024 Public Interest Litigation (PIL) filed in the Supreme Court, petitioners cite the poem *cukjl* as sociocultural evidence to argue that the State failed its constitutional duty to provide timely disaster relief during the 2023 Vidarbha drought. The Court considers the poem alongside official data: rainfall deficit (‑30 %), farmer suicides, debt levels, and the status of the Zamindari Abolition Act’s implementation. The case raises questions about how literary works can inform legal reasoning—specifically, the principle‑application test in CLAT’s Legal Reasoning module—and whether poetic description of setting and atmosphere can satisfy the “facts” and “reasoning” stages of IRAC (Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion). Students must analyze the poem’s setting, imagery, theme, and critical‑analysis dimensions, then map them to legal principles such as the Public Trust Doctrine, the duty of the State under Article 21, and the principle of reasonable classification.

(E) Synthesize the above analyses to formulate a legal conclusion (IRAC) regarding whether the State breached its duty under Article 21 and the Public Trust Doctrine by failing to provide timely disaster relief, using evidence from all four domains (Hindi, History, Political Science, Geography) and the CLAT Legal Reasoning principle‑application skill.

In 2023, a coalition of Dalit women’s groups in Maharashtra’s Vidarbha region launched a campaign linking land‑rights struggles (inspired by the 1946 Tebhaga movement) with demands for gender‑justice within the autonomous feminist movement. Survey data from five districts shows: (i) 61% of Dalit women households cultivate less than 1 acre; (ii) 48% report seasonal migration of male members for sugarcane cutting; (iii) 34% have participated in at least one peasant protest in the last three years; (iv) 55% support linking land‑rights demands with demands for stricter enforcement of the Domestic Violence Act; (v) Only 22% feel represented by national‑level feminist NGOs headquartered in Mumbai. Historical notes: The 19th‑century social reform movement opposed child marriage but largely ignored caste‑based agrarian exploitation; Ambedkar’s 1930s advocacy for separate electorates highlighted political empowerment but not economic land reform. Using this information, assess how regional peasant dynamics shape Dalit feminist activism and its alliance with broader women’s movements.

(B) Using the concept of relative deprivation, explain why 34% participation in peasant protests is higher than the 22% feeling represented by national feminist NGOs, despite similar economic marginalization.

An online fashion retailer “TrendHub” tracks weekly inventory of three SKUs (A, B, C). Initial stock (units) in B2:D2 = 500, 300, 200. Weekly sales (units) are recorded in rows 5‑16 (columns B‑D). Reorder level is 100 units (cell G2). Lead time is 2 weeks (cell G3). Holding cost per unit per week is ₹5 (cell G4). Stock‑out cost per unit is ₹50 (cell G5). In column E, compute ending stock = previous ending + receipts – sales (receipts = order quantity if week ≥ lead time). In column F, compute holding cost = ending stock × ₹5. In column G, compute stock‑out cost = max(0, –ending stock) × ₹50. In column H, total weekly cost = holding + stock‑out. In cell B18, compute economic order quantity (EOQ) using formula √(2DS/H) where D = annual demand (sum of weekly sales ×52), S = ordering cost ₹1000 (cell G6), H = holding cost per unit per year (₹5×52). In cell B19, compute reorder point = (average weekly sales × lead time) + safety stock (safety stock = 0.5× weekly demand std dev). All inputs are highlighted. The student must use relative/absolute references, SUM, AVERAGE, STDEV.P, IF, MAX, and SQRT.

(D) Which formula computes total annual demand D in cell B18 using weekly sales in columns B:D (rows 5:16)?

An equilateral triangle has a side length of $(2y + 1)$ cm, and its perimeter is given as 21 cm. Formulate an equation representing this geometric property and test whether $y = 3$ or $y = 4$ is the correct solution.

The Supreme Court is hearing a petition challenging a state scheme that offers an additional ₹50 000 cash grant exclusively to Hindu refugees from the 2024 displacement, arguing it violates secularism. The petition cites Article 25 (freedom of religion) and Article 14 (equality). The state defends the grant as compensatory for “historical injustice” akin to the “eye‑for‑an‑eye” principle in Hammurabi’s Code , claiming it restores balance. Simultaneously, the state’s finance department seeks to account for the grant under the evolving accounting framework which emphasizes substance over form. Using the data: total Hindu refugees = 1.44 lakh; total scheme outlay = ₹720 crore.

(D) Using the evolving accounting framework (substance over form), classify the ₹720 crore outlay: is it an expense, a liability, or equity? Justify.

An environmental biotech startup aims to use a genetically tolerant line of *Chlorella vulgaris* to remove lead (Pb²⁺) from industrial wastewater. The algae are cultivated in a flat‑panel photobioreactor where light is supplied by LED arrays. The system must satisfy three constraints: (i) provide sufficient photon flux for photosynthesis to drive ATP synthesis needed for Pb²⁺ uptake via a Pb‑ATPase pump, (ii) maintain temperature within 20‑28 °C to keep enzyme kinetics favourable, and (iii) keep the lead concentration below 0.5 mg L⁻¹ in the effluent to meet discharge norms.  

The following data are available:  
- The specific Pb²⁺ uptake rate (q_Pb, in mg Pb g⁻¹ DW h⁻¹) follows Michaelis‑Menten kinetics with respect to intracellular ATP concentration: q_Pb = V_max·[ATP]/(K_m + [ATP]), where V_max = 2.5 mg Pb g⁻¹ DW h⁻¹ and K_m = 0.8 mM ATP.  
- ATP production rate is proportional to photosynthetic rate, which in turn depends on incident PAR (I) according to the model: r_ATP = α·I/(I + I_k), with α = 5 mM ATP h⁻¹ per (µmol m⁻² s⁻¹)⁻¹ and I_k = 100 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹.  
- Temperature affects V_max via the Arrhenius relationship with activation energy Ea_ATPase = 60 kJ mol⁻¹. At 25 °C, V_max,25 = 2.5 mg Pb g⁻¹ DW h⁻¹.  
- The reactor volume is 500 L, inflow lead concentration is 5 mg L⁻¹, and the desired residence time is τ = 4 h (plug‑flow approximation).  
- Mixing is achieved by sparging air; the power input per unit volume (P/V) must exceed 0.02 W L⁻¹ to avoid sedimentation, and the corresponding shear stress τ_s (in Pa) is approximated by τ_s = η·(P/V)^{2/3}, where η = 0.001 Pa·s·(W L⁻¹)^{−2/3}. Cells suffer damage if τ_s > 0.15 Pa.  

Using the above, answer the sub‑parts.

(B) Using the Arrhenius equation, calculate V_max at 20 °C and 28 °C for the Pb‑ATPase, given Ea = 60 kJ mol⁻¹ and V_max,25 = 2.5 mg Pb g⁻¹ DW h⁻¹.

GreenTech Ltd. issued 10,000 8% debentures of ₹100 each at par on 01‑04‑2023, redeemable at par after 5 years. Interest is paid annually. By 01‑04‑2025 the market yield on similar debentures has risen to 10% due to tightening monetary policy, causing the debentures to quote at ₹80. The company’s articles permit purchase of own debentures from the open market for cancellation and also allow conversion of debentures into equity shares at a fixed conversion price of ₹20 per share (i.e., 5 shares per debenture) if the market price of the share exceeds ₹25. On 01‑04‑2025 GreenTech decides to buy back 4,000 debentures from the open market at ₹80 each and cancel them immediately. Simultaneously, it evaluates converting the remaining 6,000 debentures into equity shares. The current market price of GreenTech’s equity share is ₹28. Assume no transaction costs and that the company wants to minimise its debt‑equity ratio while preserving earnings‑per‑share (EPS). Relevant accounting standards require any profit or loss on cancellation to be transferred to Capital Reserve.
Using the data above, answer the following sub‑parts.

(C) Assuming the company opts to convert the remaining 6,000 debentures into equity shares at the agreed conversion price, pass the journal entry for conversion and compute the number of shares issued.

In early 2025, Walt Disney Studios (a U.S.–based transnational corporation) announced that its Indian OTT platform Disney+ Hotstar would stream the entire Phase 5 of the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) simultaneously worldwide. The deal grants Disney+ Hotstar exclusive streaming rights for 3 years, with a projected subscriber base of 52 million in India by the end of 2025. Revenue sharing is structured as 70 % to Disney (U.S.) and 30 % to the Indian partner (Jio Platforms). To comply with India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, Disney+ Hotstar must self‑classify each MCU title, provide Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, and Bengali dubs, and appoint a grievance officer resident in India.
Critics argue that the heavy promotion of Hollywood franchises undermines regional cinema, while supporters point to the historical precedent of cultural exchange along the Silk Road, where goods, ideas, and artistic motifs travelled across borders and were locally adapted. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has also issued a notice requiring that at least 30 % of prime‑time slots on OTT platforms carry Indian‑origin content.
Using this scenario, answer the following sub‑parts.

(C) Using the concept of glocalisation, analyse how Disney+ Hotstar’s dubbing and subtitle strategy represents a balance between global media flows and local cultural adaptation.

A 10 g sample of an unknown ionic compound XY (molar mass 100 g/mol) is dissolved in 200 mL water. The solution conducts electricity. When 5 g of XY is heated in a crucible, it melts at 800°C and the melt conducts. However, XY does not dissolve in 200 mL ethanol. Based on this, identify the likely charges on X and Y, and justify using lattice energy and solvent polarity concepts.

A pendulum clock uses a brass rod (αₗ = 1.9×10⁻⁵ K⁻¹) as the pendulum shaft. The clock keeps correct time at 20°C. If the temperature rises to 35°C, will the clock run fast or slow? Calculate the fractional change in time period and the time error per day. (g = 9.8 m/s², T = 2π√(l/g))

A tech startup proposes to use generative AI to create an immersive, multisensory recreation of Xanadu (Shangdu) for a global digital heritage platform. The AI draws on three data streams: (1) satellite‑derived DEMs and Landsat imagery of the Ordos Basin, (2) transcribed excerpts from Marco Polo’s *Il Milione* and Yuan dynasty gazetteers, and (3) the full text of Coleridge’s *Kubla Khan*. The platform will offer subscription‑based virtual tours, educational modules, and NFT‑based collectible “views” of the pleasure‑dome. Projected first‑year metrics: 250 000 unique users, average session length 18 min, subscription fee $4.99/month, estimated gross revenue $14.97 million. Legal scholars raise concerns about copyright of the poem (public domain in most jurisdictions but with potential moral‑rights claims in certain EU states) and the use of historical texts (some still under national heritage laws). Sociologists warn that AI‑mediated reconstructions may alter collective memory, privileging a romanticized, poet‑centric narrative over the multicultural reality of Yuan‑era Shangdu (which included Tibetan, Muslim, and Chinese artisans). Students must evaluate the proposal using concepts of poetic theme, imagery, symbolism, tourism economics, intellectual property law, and sociological theories of cultural memory.

(C) Explain how the imagery of “gardens bright with sinuous rills” and the symbolism of the “sunless sea” could be emphasized by the AI to evoke a romanticized, poet‑centric memory of Xanadu, and discuss the sociological risk of such emphasis eclipsing the historical multicultural fabric of Yuan‑era Shangdu.
A shop gives a 10% discount on purchases above ₹1000. Write a program that reads the purchase amount (float) and prints the net amount payable after discount.

A fintech startup launches a “Love‑Option” product: investors can purchase a call option that pays off if a couple’s relationship duration exceeds a preset threshold (e.g., 5 years). The marketing copy borrows Donne’s shadow conceit, claiming “True love, like the noon sun, offers constant payoff; morning shadows represent early‑stage uncertainty, afternoon shadows signal decay”. Behavioral economists warn that investors may exhibit the **confirmation bias**, overweighing early positive signals (morning shadows) and ignoring later deterioration. Legal counsel questions whether the option contract’s payoff clause, tied to an amorphous “relationship duration”, satisfies the certainty requirement under Indian contract law (Section 29, Indian Contract Act, 1872). Using concepts of financial derivatives (eco11_cbse_02_004), cognitive psychology (psy12_cbse_01_009), and legal principles of contractual certainty (clat_legal_03_011), evaluate the product’s viability across three axes: financial soundness (35%), behavioral risk (30%), legal enforceability (35%).

(C) Explain how confirmation bias could lead investors to overestimate the Love‑Option’s expected payoff, and propose one debiasing technique grounded in the scenario.

A consortium aims to establish a green hydrogen production hub in the Great Lakes industrial region (USA‑Canada border) to supply steel plants transitioning from coal‑based to hydrogen‑based reduction. The hub will use offshore wind farms (capacity 2 GW) on Lake Erie, electrolyzers (efficiency 70 %), and storage caverns. Key considerations: (i) wind capacity factor 45 % yields annual electricity generation; (ii) water availability from the lakes (abundant, negligible cost); (iii) cross‑border governance: the Boundary Waters Treaty of 1909 requires joint approval for water‑related projects, adding a regulatory review period of 10 months; (iv) financing via a green bond with coupon 3 % and tax‑exempt status, reducing effective interest rate to 2.2 %; (v) depreciation of electrolyzers (straight‑line, 12‑year life, zero salvage). Using the data, evaluate the levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH) and assess whether the hub meets a target LCOH of $3/kg H₂, considering also the potential carbon credit revenue of $50/ton CO₂ avoided (each kg H₂ avoids 9 kg CO₂ when replacing coal in steel). Assume electrolyzer CAPEX $800/kW, OPEX 2 % of CAPEX/yr, and that the hub operates at 80 % of wind‑generated electricity due to curtailment.

(C) Compute the annual OPEX (USD) for the electrolyzer plant given CAPEX $800/kW, total electrolyzer capacity equal to 80 % of wind farm capacity (to match utilization), and OPEX rate 2 % of CAPEX per year.

A 30‑year‑old marketing professional shifted to full‑time remote work during the pandemic. She reports a sharp rise in online shopping triggered by promotional emails and bouts of boredom during breaks. Over the past three months she averages 3 hours/day browsing retail sites, makes ≈5 purchases/week, spends about ₹4,000 per transaction, and has accrued ₹60,000 in credit‑card debt. Her essential monthly expenses are ₹50,000 against a net income of ₹80,000. She describes a rapid heart‑beat surge (≈20 bpm increase) and mild sweating when seeing “flash sale” notifications, followed by a temporary reduction in anxiety after completing a purchase, but later feels guilt and financial strain. She wishes to curb this behaviour to build an emergency fund of ₹2,00,000 within six months while maintaining her job performance.

(B) Propose two antecedent operations (stimulus‑control strategies) to reduce the online shopping behaviour, justifying each with a learning principle.

A quantum processor stacks three superconducting qubit chips to reduce cross‑talk. Chip A lies in the plane \(x + 2y - 2z = 4\) mm, Chip B in \(2x - y + 3z = -6\) mm, and Chip C is to be inserted such that its plane is parallel to the line of intersection of Chips A and B and makes a \(45^\circ\) angle with Chip A. The processor operates at 15 mK; any residual magnetic flux trapped in the chips induces decoherence proportional to the sine of the angle between the chip’s normal and the applied magnetic field \(\vec{B}=0.1\hat{i}+0.2\hat{j}+0.3\hat{k}\) mT. Additionally, the chip material’s critical current density depends on strain, which varies with the distance of the chip’s centre from the processor’s mounting point at \(O(0,0,0)\). Determine: (i) the angle between Chips A and B, (ii) the equation of Chip C satisfying the given constraints, (iii) the decoherence factor for Chip C, (iv) the distance of Chip C’s centre from \(O\) if its centre is constrained to lie on the line of intersection of A and B, and (v) how a 10 % increase in critical current (due to reduced strain) would affect the allowable angle tolerance before decoherence exceeds a threshold.

(B) Find the equation of Chip C’s plane given that it is parallel to the line of intersection of A and B and makes a \(45^\circ\) angle with Chip A.

In a coastal reclamation project, you must choose between planting Casuarina (she-oak) and Avicennia (mangrove) for stabilising newly deposited tidal mudflats. Compare their root adaptations for (a) anchorage in fluid sediment, (b) oxygen supply to roots, and (c) salt tolerance mechanism. Which genus would you select for the first 5 years and why?

A streaming platform commissions a limited series adaptation of Umberto Eco’s medieval mystery *The Name of the Rose*.
