In 2022 a field study of Firozabad’s glass‑bangle industry recorded 4,500 child workers aged 8‑15, of whom 70 % belonged to Scheduled Castes, 20 % to Other Backward Classes, and 10 % to General categories. Average daily wage was ₹30, with 12‑hour shifts in furnaces exceeding 1,200 °C. 55 % of families had migrated from rural Uttar Pradesh due to agricultural distress (successive droughts 2018‑2021). Mukesh, the protagonist of *Lost Spring*’s second story, dreams of becoming a motor mechanic yet continues to bangles, saying, “I will become a motor mechanic… I have seen cars in the city.” The nearest vocational training centre is 8 km away, with no subsidised transport. The scenario supplies all data needed to analyse Mukesh’s character, connect his aspirations to educational policy, evaluate industrial labour laws, assess rural‑push migration, interpret occupational psychology, and examine caste‑based labour segmentation.

(A) Identify Mukesh’s key character trait evident in his aspiration to become a motor mechanic and support it with two textual evidences, explaining how the trait relates to occupational aspiration theory.

A High Court Chief Justice recommends Lawyer Y for appointment as a High Court judge. The State Governor and Chief Minister object. The Supreme Court Collegium (CJI + 2 senior-most judges for HC appointments) clears the name. The Union Law Ministry delays processing for 14 months. A PIL is filed in the Supreme Court seeking a mandamus to compel appointment. Analyze the legal position.

In May 2024, a severe cyclonic storm struck the Odisha‑Andhra coast, prompting the evacuation of 1.2 million people. The State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) relied on a hybrid communication setup: (i) satellite‑based VSAT terminals (providing 10 Mbps uplink) deployed at 150 relief camps, (ii) GSM‑based mobile towers (restored within 6 h using diesel generators), and (iii) a network of amateur radio (ham) operators coordinating ground‑to‑ground messages. Simultaneously, the Indian Railways ran 30 special freight trains carrying relief material from Vishakhapatnam to Bhubaneswar, utilizing the dedicated freight corridor (DFC) laid parallel to the NH‑16. Historical analysis shows that during the 1999 Odisha super‑cyclone, the lack of redundant communication delayed relief by 48 h, whereas the 2013 Phailin cyclone benefited from early GSM restoration. The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) now mandates that all district headquarters maintain a minimum of 30 % redundant communication capacity (satellite + ham) and that critical transport routes (rail and road) have optical fibre laid alongside for real‑time tracking.  
Given the following data: each VSAT terminal costs ₹2.5 lakh, each GSM tower restoration costs ₹8 lakh, each ham operator kit costs ₹12,000, the railway DFC length is 420 km with OFC laying cost of ₹1.8 lakhs/km, and the total budget allocated for communication redundancy in the affected districts is ₹180 crore, answer the sub‑questions below.

(B) Determine the expenditure for restoring GSM towers if 45 towers were damaged.

After electrophoresis of a restriction digest, a 1.2 kb band is excised from a 0.9 % agarose gel. The gel slice weighs 80 mg. DNA is eluted into 50 µL TE buffer. The eluate’s absorbance at 260 nm (A₂₆₀) measured in a 1 cm cuvette is 0.45. The standard conversion for double‑stranded DNA is 1 A₂₆₀ unit = 50 µg/mL. Agarose residues cause light scattering, reducing the accurate absorbance by ~10 % (correction factor = 0.9). The eluted DNA will be used to transform competent *E. coli* cells (transformation efficiency = 1×10⁶ CFU/µg DNA). Blue‑white screening will be employed; the vector’s multiple cloning site has an insertion efficiency of 70 % (i.e., 70 % of ligated plasmids contain the insert) while the remaining 30 % are self‑ligated vector.  

The student must (i) calculate the diffusion coefficient of the 1.2 kb fragment in the elution buffer, (ii) determine the corrected DNA concentration and yield, (iii) compute the elution efficiency assuming theoretical maximum DNA content of 1 µg per mg gel slice, (iv) estimate the number of transformant colonies expected, and (v) predict the proportion of white colonies (insert‑containing) among total colonies.

(B) Calculate the DNA concentration (µg/mL) in the eluate from the measured A₂₆₀ = 0.45, path length = 1 cm, and correction factor = 0.9 for agarose scattering.

A multinational technology firm launched a “Neurodiversity Inclusion” program in 2023, publishing internal surveys where 78 % of employees expressed favourable attitudes toward hiring autistic and ADHD‑talented individuals. Six months later, HR data showed only 4 % of new hires were neurodivergent, despite open positions. Concurrently, an internal wellness study measured salivary cortisol (a stress biomarker) before and after interview panels; panels with higher average cortisol showed a 3‑fold drop in actual neurodiverse offers compared to low‑cortisol panels. The firm’s annual CSR report highlighted “robust inclusive hiring practices,” yet the accompanying financial statements (prepared per Ind AS 1) disclosed only ₹0.8 cr spent on accommodation tools, far below the ₹5 cr budgeted in the CSR narrative. Using LaPiere’s classic attitude‑behaviour gap as a reference, answer the following.

(E) Using the accounting concept of “users of accounting information” (Users Of Accounting Information), identify which stakeholder group would most likely detect the CSR‑spending discrepancy and why.

A multidisciplinary research team collects screenshots of alleged COVID‑19 hoaxes from Twitter, WhatsApp forwards, and Facebook posts. Each item is stored as a JSON line file (`hoax_001.jsonl`) containing fields: `platform`, `timestamp`, `text`, `image_url`, `fact_check_status`. The team must (a) append new entries to a master log file each night, (b) quickly retrieve the 10 most recent entries for a given platform using `seek()` and `tell()` to avoid loading the whole file, (c) detect duplicate hoaxes by computing an MD5 hash of the `text` field and logging duplicates to a separate file, and (d) generate a weekly summary CSV of hoax counts per platform. The project operates under the IT (Intermediary Guidelines) Rules, 2021, which require platforms to remove misinformation within 24 hours of notice, and sociological studies show that confirmation bias amplifies hoax spread in homogeneous groups. Students must write Python scripts using `with` statements for safe file handling, binary mode for hash computation, and text mode for CSV generation, integrating exception handling for malformed JSON.

(C) Design a duplicate‑detection routine: for each new entry, compute MD5 hash of its `text` field, and if the hash already appears in `hashes.log`, append the entry to `duplicates.log`; otherwise, append the hash to `hashes.log`. Use `with` blocks for both files, ensuring each is closed after its operation.

A district education office runs a midday meal scheme for 1,500 government school children aged 6‑12 years. The sanctioned budget is ₹25 per child per day. The meal must provide approximately 650 kcal and 20 g of protein (ICMR norms for this age group). Current market prices (₹/unit) are: rice ₹40/kg, dal (pigeon pea) ₹120/kg, mixed vegetables ₹30/kg, refined oil ₹150/L, milk ₹45/L, eggs ₹6 each. The proposed menu per child is: 100 g cooked rice, 30 g dal, 50 g vegetables, 5 g oil, and 100 ml milk.  
Recently, dal prices have risen by 20 % due to a poor harvest. The office must (i) verify if the existing menu fits the budget, (ii) redesign the menu using food exchange lists to keep cost ≤ ₹25 while meeting the protein target, (iii) assess the impact on child growth and satiety (linking to biological growth metrics), and (iv) suggest a simple psychological nudge to improve meal acceptance without extra cost.  
Students must identify relevant concepts from meal planning, food groups, balanced diet, exchange lists, low‑cost diet planning, basic accounting for cost tracking, and growth‑related biology.

(B) Determine whether the sanctioned budget (₹25/child/day) is sufficient for the proposed menu. If not, compute the shortfall or surplus per child.

Consider a simplified model of a super‑Earth exoplanet with a metallic liquid‑iron core of radius R_c = 2000 km, electrical conductivity σ = 1.0×10⁶ S m⁻¹ (resistivity ρ = 1.0×10⁻⁶ Ω·m). The core rotates with angular velocity ω = 2π / T, where T = 10 h is the rotation period. A dipolar magnetic field B₀ = 0.5 T is anchored in the core and rotates with it, causing a time‑varying magnetic flux in the conducting fluid as seen by an inertial observer. This induces eddy currents that dissipate heat, contributing to the planet’s internal energy budget. Assume the magnetic field varies sinusoidally with frequency f = ω/2π at any fixed point in the core, and the induced emf per unit length is ε = B₀ ω r sinθ (r = distance from rotation axis, θ = colatitude). (a) Derive the volume‑averaged rms emf 〈ε_rms〉 over the core. (b) Estimate the effective resistance of a representative eddy‑current loop approximated as a circular path of radius r ≈ R_c/2 and cross‑sectional area A ≈ π δ², where skin depth δ = √(2ρ/μ₀ω). (c) Compute the volume‑averaged rms power dissipation per unit volume 〈P〉. (d) Using the planet’s mass M = 5×10²⁴ kg and average specific heat c ≈ 800 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, estimate the temperature increase ΔT_core after 1 × 10⁹ s of heating if all eddy‑current power goes into raising the core temperature uniformly. (e) Discuss qualitatively how this internal heating could affect the planet’s habitability, linking to the concept of the circumstellar habitable zone (requires knowledge of stellar flux).

(A) Derive an expression for the volume‑averaged rms emf 〈ε_rms〉 in the rotating conducting core, given ε(r,θ) = B₀ ω r sinθ.
Find the curved surface area of a frustum with radii 9 cm and 4 cm, and slant height 13 cm. Use \(\pi = \frac{22}{7}\).

Design a **two-pronged policy framework** to simultaneously: (a) raise agriculture's GDP share by 2 percentage points in 5 years, and (b) reduce agriculture's workforce share by 3 percentage points in the same period. Specify one supply-side and one demand-side measure for each goal, with geographical targeting (name specific regions/crop zones).

A student solves a composite rod problem and gets a junction temperature of 150°C when the hot reservoir is at 100°C and cold at 0°C. They claim "the junction is hotter because heat accumulates there." Evaluate this claim and identify the error.

In the mountainous district of Kiphire, Nagaland, a tribal community practices jhum (shifting cultivation) on steep slopes averaging 30° inclination. A recent climate‑impact study shows that the average monsoon rainfall has increased from 2 200 mm to 2 800 mm yr⁻¹ over the past decade, shortening the fallow period required for soil regeneration from 8 years to 5 years. The community has registered its forest land under the REDD+ mechanism, expecting to earn carbon credits based on avoided deforestation. Each hectare of preserved secondary forest is estimated to sequester 4.2 t CO₂ yr⁻¹, valued at US $5 t⁻¹CO₂ in the voluntary market. The community cultivates 120 ha under jhum, rotating plots every 2 years (i.e., 60 ha under cultivation, 60 ha fallow at any time). The government’s Forest Rights Act (FRA) 2006 grants them legal ownership of the forest produce, but mandates that any carbon‑credit revenue be shared 70 % to the community and 30 % to the state forest department. The task is to (i) confirm that jhum remains a primary activity, (ii) compute the annual carbon‑credit revenue per hectare and for the whole community, (iii) apply the FRA revenue‑sharing rule, (iv) evaluate how increased rainfall affects soil erosion risk (a physical‑geography factor), and (v) decide whether the community should expand cultivation area given the carbon‑credit incentive.

(C) Apply the Forest Rights Act 2006 revenue‑sharing rule to the carbon‑credit income and determine the amounts received by the community and the state forest department.

During the 2023 monsoon, Marathwada received only 58 % of its long‑period average (LPA) rainfall (average 720 mm → actual 418 mm). The region’s groundwater table declined by 2.3 m in the hard‑rock aquifer, affecting 1.2 million ha of sugarcane and cotton farms. The National Green Tribunal (NGT) issued a suo‑motu order restricting groundwater extraction to 60 % of the existing withdrawal limit, citing declining water levels and rising salinity. Simultaneously, ISRO’s VEDAS (Versatile Energy and Drought Assessment System) provided monthly soil‑moisture anomalies showing a −0.25 m³/m³ deficit over the region. The Maharashtra State Disaster Management Authority (MSDMA) must decide whether to (i) enforce the NGT order via metered borewells, (ii) promote micro‑irrigation (drip/sprinkler) with subsidies, or (iii) invest in watershed‑based recharge structures (check dams, percolation tanks). Using the data below, evaluate the hydrological, legal, and technological dimensions.

**Data:**  
- Pre‑drought groundwater withdrawal = 1.8 km³/yr (≈ 60 % for irrigation, 30 % for domestic, 10 % for industry).  
- NGT‑ordered withdrawal cap = 1.08 km³/yr (60 % of current).  
- Average sugarcane water requirement = 1.8 m/ha/yr; cotton = 0.9 m/ha/yr.  
- Current irrigated area under sugarcane = 600 000 ha; cotton = 400 000 ha.  
- Micro‑irrigation saves 40 % water vs. flood irrigation; subsidy covers 50 % of capital cost (₹ 40 000/ha).  
- One check dam (10 ha catchment) recharges ≈ 0.05 hm³/yr; cost = ₹ 12 lakh.  
- Discount rate = 6 %; project life = 15 yr.  
- VEDAS soil‑moisture anomaly correlates with a 10 % yield drop per −0.05 m³/m³ deficit.

(C) Estimate the annual water volume saved (in hm³) if micro‑irrigation is adopted on 50 % of the current sugarcane area, assuming a 40 % reduction in water use per hectare.

A rectangular wooden block (density 650 kg/m³) of dimensions 0.4 m × 0.3 m × 0.2 m floats in water (density 1000 kg/m³). The block is oriented with the 0.4 m × 0.3 m face horizontal. Find: (a) the depth of submersion (draft), (b) the volume above water, (c) the maximum additional mass that can be placed on top before the block sinks, and (d) the apparent weight of the block when pushed down until its top face is just at the water surface. Use g = 9.8 m/s².

Write the complete balanced chemical equation for the preparation of 1-iodobutane from 1-butanol using the best laboratory method. Include all reagents, conditions, and byproducts. Calculate the theoretical yield of 1-iodobutane (in grams) if 15.0 g of 1-butanol (M = 74.12 g/mol) is used with excess KI/95% H₃PO₄. (Molar mass of 1-iodobutane = 184.02 g/mol)

A state electricity distribution company (DISCOM) must decide whether to sign a long-term Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with a new solar plant. They have 10 years of hourly data on: (i) Peak demand (MW), (ii) Solar generation potential (MW) at their location, (iii) Exchange price (₹/kWh) on the power exchange. The solar plant offers a fixed tariff of ₹2.50/kWh for 25 years. Explain how statistics helps in this decision using three distinct applications from the chapter.
Calculate the 3rd trimester RDA for energy, protein, iron, folic acid, and calcium for a 25-year-old pregnant woman, pre-pregnancy weight 52 kg, moderate activity level. Use ICMR 2020 values.

A state government plans to allocate ₹12 crore annually for a grand “Ramotsav” festival celebrating Tulsidas’ Ramcharitmanas, featuring processions, tableaux, and cultural performances. A public interest litigation (PIL) is filed alleging that the scheme violates Articles 25‑28 (freedom of religion and state neutrality) and Article 14 (equality) by favoring a specific Hindu sect, marginalising minorities, and diverting funds from minority‑community welfare. The state defends the festival as a secular cultural event promoting national integration, citing historical precedent of state patronage of Bhakti movements under medieval sultanates and Mughals. The court must examine (i) whether the festival is religious or cultural, (ii) the historical extent of state support for Bhakti‑Sufi traditions, (iii) the fiscal impact on minority welfare schemes, and (iv) the applicability of the doctrine of “positive secularism” under Articles 25‑28. Relevant data: minority population in the state = 18 % (majority Muslims = 10 %, Christians = 5 %, Sikhs = 3 %). Current annual budget for minority welfare = ₹30 crore. The proposed festival would consume 40 % of that budget if fully diverted.

(C) Applying the doctrine of positive secularism (state can promote all religions equally), which constitutional article primarily enables the state to fund a festival claimed to be *cultural* rather than *religious*?

The National Manuscript Mission (NMM) proposes to digitize all extant 17th‑century manuscripts of Raskhan’s *Jake Panjrekul* using AI‑based optical character recognition (OCR) trained on Perso‑Arabic and Devanagari scripts. The project budget is ₹8 crore, spanning 24 months, with deliverables: searchable PDFs, metadata tags (theme, raga, linguistic features), and an AI‑generated commentary linking verses to Bhakti sociopolitical contexts. A coalition of scholars from Aligarh Muslim University and Banaras Hindu University raises concerns: (1) OCR may misinterpret Persianized Hindi, altering theological nuance; (2) AI commentary could inadvertently impose modern secular biases, misrepresenting the poet’s devotional intent; (3) Data sovereignty—who holds the digital rights? The NMM cites Article 51A(h) (scientific temper) and the IT Act, 2000 (data protection) to argue that technological preservation serves public interest. A parliamentary committee must decide whether to approve funding, impose oversight, or reject the project.

(E) Predict the effect on Muslim youth’s perception of their religious‑cultural identity if the AI‑generated commentary consistently frames Raskhan’s devotion as a “precursor to modern secular nationalism,” using and.

A 2023 study in Tamil Nadu's Tiruppur garment cluster finds that 55% of young Dalit women workers (ages 18-25) live in factory hostels, send 60% of wages to natal villages, return for festivals, and have marriages arranged by parents. Meanwhile, 30% of upper-caste women in the same factories live in nuclear family apartments, keep full salaries, and choose partners via dating apps. Using the concepts of "joint family functions," "caste-class intersectionality," and "gendered migration," explain this divergence in 5 analytical steps. What does it reveal about the "decline of joint family" thesis?

A research team uses satellite‑derived night‑light data and census records to map occupational shifts in three industrial corridors (Bengaluru‑ Hosur, Ahmedabad‑Vadodara, Delhi‑Meerut) over 2000‑2020. They focus on two jatis: the “Patidar” (traditionally Vaishya, agrarian/trading) and the “Mala” (traditionally Dalit, agricultural labour).  
Findings:  
- In Bengaluru‑Hosur corridor, Patidar share in IT‑services jobs rose from 4 % (2000) to 18 % (2020); Mala share in same sector rose from 0.5 % to 3 %.  
- In Ahmedabad‑Vadodara corridor, Patidar share in manufacturing remained stable at ~12 %; Mala share in manufacturing increased from 2 % to 7 %.  
- In Delhi‑Meerut corridor, Patidar share in construction fell from 15 % to 9 %; Mala share in construction rose from 6 % to 11 %.  
Overall night‑light intensity (proxy for economic activity) grew 65 % in Bengaluru‑Hosur, 40 % in Ahmedabad‑Vadodara, and 30 % in Delhi‑Meerut.  
The team hypothesizes that varna‑based occupational ideals are weakening, but jati‑based network effects still channel migration.  
Using this dataset, evaluate the hypothesis and its implications for the varna‑jati distinction.

(C) The Mala (Dalit‑jati) share in construction work in the Delhi‑Meerut corridor rose from 6 % to 11 %. Using the overall night‑light growth of 30 % in this corridor as a proxy for economic expansion, assess whether the Mala’s occupational shift is proportional to economic growth.

A drone flies from point A(1, 2, 0) to B(4, 6, 0) and then to C(2, 9, 0). (i) Write the displacement vectors \(\vec{AB}\) and \(\vec{BC}\) in component form. (ii) Find the resultant displacement \(\vec{AC}\) using vector addition. (iii) Verify that the triangle law holds by showing \(|\vec{AC}|^2 = |\vec{AB}|^2 + |\vec{BC}|^2 + 2|\vec{AB}||\vec{BC}|\cos\theta\), where \(\theta\) is the angle between \(\vec{AB}\) and \(\vec{BC}\). (iv) If the drone’s speed is constant at 10 m/s, find the time taken for the whole journey.

A federal government proposes a digital tax system inspired by the Ain-i-Akbari, dividing tax domains into five digital daftars (central, state, local, tribal, and international). They must allocate revenue sources (agriculture, manufacturing, services, digital, natural resources) and ensure accountability through double‑entry bookkeeping. Provided data: total GDP = ₹20 lakh crore; agriculture share = 15 %; manufacturing = 20 %; services = 30 %; digital = 10 %; natural resources = 5 %; remaining 20 % untaxed. Zamindar‑like local bodies collect 40 % of agricultural tax, retain 10 % of that collected amount for local militia, and remit the rest to the state. Students must synthesize Ain‑i‑Akbari structure, zamindar military power, land‑revenue measurement, jagirdari transferability, and accounting principles (users, qualitative characteristics, role in society) to evaluate the feasibility of the model.

(D) If a digital jagir (right to collect a portion of digital service tax) is granted for 5 years and the state expects ₹2 crore annual revenue from it, what is the annual amortization expense assuming straight‑line method over the grant period?

A frog is aestivating in a burrow during peak summer (40°C, dry). Predict the functional state of each major organ system and explain how the frog survives without food/water for months, referencing tissue-level adaptations.

A patient receives an intravenous injection of a Technetium‑99m (^99mTc) labelled phosphonate compound for bone scintigraphy. The nuclide decays radioactively with a physical half‑life \(T_{1/2}^{\text{phys}} = 6.01\ \text{h}\). Simultaneously, the compound is cleared from the bloodstream by renal excretion, which follows first‑order kinetics with a biological half‑life \(T_{1/2}^{\text{bio}} = 12.0\ \text{h}\). The observed disappearance of radioactivity is governed by the sum of the two independent first‑order processes.  

Using this information answer the following sub‑parts.

(D) Derive the integrated rate law for the activity \(A(t)\) of the ^99mTc‑phosphonate and show that a plot of \(\ln A\) versus time yields a straight line. State the slope and intercept in terms of the given parameters.

A research lab intends to use fructose as a non‑penetrating cryoprotectant for preserving red blood cells at –80 °C. They prepare an aqueous fructose solution and measure its freezing point depression. The cryoscopic constant of water is K_f = 1.86 K kg mol⁻¹. Fructose does not dissociate (i = 1) but can form up to five hydrogen bonds with water molecules (three hydroxyl donors, two acceptors). The lab wants the solution to freeze at –5 °C (ΔT_f = 5 K) to avoid ice‑induced damage during storage. Additionally, they need to know the osmotic pressure at physiological temperature (37 °C) to assess cell shrinkage/swelling.  
Answer the following sub‑questions.

(B) Calculate the osmotic pressure (π) of the fructose solution from Part A at 37 °C. Use R = 0.0831 L bar mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

In early 2025, the Delhi government, in collaboration with a fintech startup, launched “Shramik‑ID”, a blockchain‑based digital identity card for migrant construction workers. Each worker receives a QR‑coded card linked to a decentralized ledger storing verified proof of address, skill certifications (e.g., welding, formwork), banking details, and grievance‑redressal history. Employers scan the card to auto‑generate contracts, track attendance, and transfer wages directly to the worker’s linked wallet, reducing cash‑handling delays. Within six months, 1.2 million workers registered; average wage‑payment delay fell from 12 days to 2 days, and disputes over non‑payment dropped by 35 %. However, only 22 % of registrants are women, and many workers report difficulty updating skill certificates due to limited smartphone literacy. The system integrates with the Union Ministry of Labour’s e‑Shram portal, aiming to port data nationwide. Traditional informal networks—such as the “maal‑gaadi” (goods‑vehicle) referral system for job finding and the “panchayat‑like” elder mediation for wage disputes—have seen declining use. Activists argue that the system may exacerbate exclusion of older, less‑tech‑savvy workers and that data centralisation raises surveillance concerns. The initiative cites the National Policy on Skill Development 2020 and the Directive Principles of State Policy (Article 41) on right to work as its constitutional basis.

(B) Using the nodes on westernisation and secularisation , determine whether the decline of the “maal‑gaadi” referral system reflects westernisation, secularisation, or a combination.
Fill in the blank: You can also test the ______ rule by placing a toy 10 cm from the mirror and observing that the image appears exactly 10 cm behind the glass.

During a closely contested state assembly election, a 45‑second deepfake video showing a prominent candidate allegedly accepting bribes circulates rapidly via WhatsApp forwards and TikTok shares. The video, generated using open‑source AI tools, reaches an estimated 12 million viewers within 48 hours, influencing voter perception in three key districts. Fact‑checkers label it as manipulated, but the video persists in echo chambers due to confirmation bias and algorithmic amplification. The Election Commission invokes Section 66D of the IT Act (cheating by personation) and proposes mandatory labeling of AI‑generated content on social platforms. Meanwhile, the candidate’s party alleges defamation under IPC 500 and seeks damages, while civil society groups warn that over‑broad regulation could chill legitimate political satire. Using concepts of mass media effects, psychological belief formation, economic incentives for disinformation, legal regulation, and historical propaganda parallels, analyse the episode.

(D) Assess the legality and proportionality of using Section 66D of the IT Act and IPC 500 to address the deepfake, referencing principles of freedom of expression.

EcoPower Ltd. issues 5,000 9% debentures of ₹2,000 each to finance a solar‑wind hybrid plant. The debentures are issued at a 5 % discount, payable in cash. Holders have the option to convert each debenture into 25 equity shares of EcoPower (face value ₹10) at any time after 2 years. Interest is payable quarterly. TDS on interest is 7.5 %. The company must create a DRR of 20 % of nominal value before redemption and invest the amount in 8 % government securities. After 3 years, 30 % of the debentures are converted into equity, 40 % are redeemed by draw of lots at par, and the remaining 30 % are purchased in the open market at ₹1,850 (ex‑interest). The plant’s expected annual EBITDA is ₹12 crore with a 60 % probability of achieving full capacity; otherwise EBITDA is ₹4 crore. Corporate tax rate is 25 %. Using the data, pass journal entries for issue, interest, conversion, redemption, and compute the cost of debt and expected EBITDA coverage.

(A) Pass the journal entry for the issue of the debentures at a 5 % discount, including cash received and discount on issue.
Calculate the simple interest on ₹12,000 at 7.5% per annum for 2 years and 6 months.
Fill in the blank: Product A gives ₹______ profit per unit but requires 2 hours of machine time; Product B gives ₹300 profit per unit and requires 1 hour.

A federal agency seeks to design a backup communication backbone for a region prone to earthquakes (annual fault‑rupture probability p = 0.02) and floods. The backbone must interconnect three state capitals using a mix of twisted‑pair (TP), coaxial (coax), and fiber‑optic (fib) links, each 150 km long. Engineering data: TP suffers crushing damage with probability 0.8 per event, coax suffers corrosion damage 0.5 per event, fib suffers bending damage 0.1 per event. Repair costs: TP $20 k/link, coax $35 k/link, fib $50 k/link. Political authority: under the Disaster Management Act, the federal agency can override state decisions after a national emergency declaration; otherwise, each state retains veto power over links crossing its territory. Societal factor: community trust in technology influences adoption; trust score T (0–10) follows logistic adoption A = 1 / (1 + e^(‑0.5·(T‑5))). Current trust scores: TP = 4, coax = 6, fib = 8.

(E) Propose a hybrid link strategy (choice of media for each of the three state‑capital links) that minimizes total expected annual repair cost while ensuring societal adoption ≥0.6 for each link. Justify your answer.

Two neighboring states, **State A** and **State B**, share the **River X** basin. State A hosts the megacity **Capitalis** (population 12 million) and State B hosts the rapidly growing metropolitan city **Industrica** (population 3.5 million). A new inter‑state metro rail link is proposed to connect Capitalis and Industrica, aiming to reduce vehicular pollution and integrate labour markets.  
Relevant data:  
- River X average annual flow at the inter‑state boundary: **15 billion cubic metres (BCM)**.  
- Existing water‑use allocation (based on a 1980 treaty): State A = 60 % of flow, State B = 40 % of flow.  
- Current consumptive use: State A uses 55 % of its allocation (mostly domestic & industrial in Capitalis); State B uses 35 % of its allocation (agriculture‑dominant).  
- The metro rail project will increase Industrica’s population by **0.8 million** over the next decade, raising its domestic water demand by **0.12 BCM/year** (assuming 150 litres per capita per day).  
- Under the Inter‑State Water Disputes Act, 1956, a tribunal can modify allocations if “material change in circumstances” is proved.  
- Constitutional provisions: Article 262 allows Parliament to provide for adjudication of inter‑state water disputes; Article 245 gives Parliament legislative power over water‑resources (Union List).  
Assume no return flow changes. Answer the sub‑questions that follow, integrating geography, political science, and legal reasoning.

(C) Applying the doctrine of “material change in circumstances” under the Inter‑State Water Disputes Act, 1956, argue whether the projected increase in Industrica’s domestic water demand constitutes sufficient grounds for the tribunal to revisit the 1980 allocation.
Why can we separate a mixture of acetone (boiling point 56°C) and water (boiling point 100°C) by simple distillation, but not a mixture of salt and water by the same method to recover both?

Using the concepts of labour productivity, capital intensity, and skill requirements, explain why manufacturing (secondary) failed to become the main absorber of surplus agricultural labour in India, unlike in China or South Korea."

A multinational IT company headquartered in Bengaluru conducts an internal diversity audit. Data shows: 68% of employees identify as upper‑caste (General), 22% as OBC, 8% as SC, and 2% as ST. In the cafeteria, separate drinking water dispensers labelled “General” and “Reserved” are observed, though no signage enforces use. The firm’s HR policy cites the Constitution (Articles 15 & 16) and provides reservation‑based promotions for SC/ST/OBC cadres. An internal whistle‑blower alleges that senior project leads (mostly upper‑caste) routinely exclude lower‑caste teammates from informal networking events held at private clubs that enforce dress codes linked to traditional caste attire. The company’s legal team invokes the Power‑Sharing model (Belgium) to argue for accommodations, while citing the Mesopotamian invention of written records as a precedent for maintaining caste‑based ledgers in ancient trade guilds.

(B) Explain how the firm’s reservation‑based promotion policy reflects the *secular* dimension of caste and cite one constitutional article that enables it.

A village in the Awadh suba (c. 1650) contains four land parcels:  
- **Parcel A** (Polaj): fertile, cultivated every year, area 80 bigha, average yield 2.0 maund/bigha of wheat.  
- **Parcel B** (Parauti): left fallow one year in two, area 60 bigha, yield in cultivated year 1.5 maund/bigha of wheat.  
- **Parcel C** (Chachar): fallow for 3–4 years, area 40 bigha, when cultivated yields 0.8 maund/bigha of millet.  
- **Parcel D** (Banjar): barren, uncultivable, area 20 bigha, yields zero.  
The amil‑guzar uses the Zabti system: revenue demand = one‑third of the average produce (in kind) valued at prevailing market prices. Market prices: wheat = 1.8 dam/maund, millet = 1.2 dam/maund. The village also pays a **nazrana** (tribute) of 50 dam to the zamindar for maintenance of the local fort.

(E) Discuss how the inclusion of Parcel C (Chachar) influences the progressivity of the village’s land revenue burden compared to a scenario where only Polaj and Parauti exist.

In 2023, the state of Vidarbha inaugurated a mega‑industrial corridor along its border with neighboring State X, attracting 600,000 migrant workers (mostly young males aged 20‑35) from poorer districts. The corridor’s total population rose from 4.2 million to 4.8 million. Vital statistics for the corridor (post‑migration, one year) are:  
- Live births: 55,000  
- Deaths: 22,000  
- Age‑specific fertility rates (per 1,000 women) for resident women 15‑49: 15‑19 = 8; 20‑24 = 60; 25‑29 = 90; 30‑34 = 55; 35‑39 = 30; 40‑44 = 10; 45‑49 = 1  
- Infant deaths: 825  
- Maternal deaths: 55  
- Life expectancy: 66.0 years  
- Pre‑migration (baseline) data for the same area: live births 48,000; deaths 20,000; infant deaths 720; maternal deaths 48; life expectancy 64.8; TFR (baseline) 2.05.  
Students must evaluate how the influx of young male migrants altered fertility and mortality measures, compute pre‑ and post‑migration TFR, IMR, and CDR, and discuss the socio‑political implications using concepts of ethnic power‑sharing (Belgium) and historical patterns of labor‑migration‑driven demographic change (e.g., 19th‑century European industrial zones).

(A) Calculate the Crude Death Rate (CDR) before and after migration. Express per 1,000 population.

In a lab test, a sample of pancreatic juice is added to three test tubes: (A) starch solution, (B) egg albumin (protein), (C) oil. After 30 minutes at 37°C, which tube(s) will show digestion? What additional substance is needed for tube C to show digestion, and why?

A consignment of 500 kg of certified organic cumin seeds arrives at Mumbai port from Ethiopia, labelled “Net Weight 500 kg ± 0.5 %”. The importer’s weighbridge shows a reading of 497 kg, while the port authority’s calibrated scale records 498.5 kg. The importer claims the discrepancy arises from moisture loss during transit (estimated 0.3 % weight loss) and seeks clearance. The customs officer suspects short‑weighting and invokes the Legal Metrology Act, 2009. Simultaneously, an environmental NGO argues that the long‑haul transport (Ethiopia → Djibouti → Mumbai) incurs 0.04 t CO₂ per ton‑km, contributing to climate impact, and demands a carbon‑offset fee under India’s National Clean Energy Fund. A trade association cites the WTO Agreement on Technical Barriers to Trade (TBT), asserting that India’s domestic weight tolerance (±0.5 %) must not be more restrictive than international standards (ISO 22000 allows ±1 %). Using the data, assess the legal metrology compliance, the validity of the moisture‑loss defence, the WTO TBT implication, and the environmental liability.

(E) Using basic statistical reasoning, calculate the probability that the true mean weight of the consignment lies below 498 kg assuming the observed measurements (weighbridge 497 kg, port scale 498.5 kg) are independent estimates with a standard deviation of 1 kg each.

In 2023, a delayed monsoon in western Rajasthan caused a 35 % drop in bajra (pearl millet) yield, pushing its market price from ₹ 22/kg to ₹ 30/kg. Elderly farm‑households (average age 68 y, primarily dependent on home‑grown bajra for meals) traditionally consume bajra‑roti with lentil dal and buttermilk, providing ~ 600 mg calcium/day from millet (≈ 150 mg/100 g) and dal. The state’s Public Distribution System (PDS) offers wheat‑based fortified flour at subsidised rates, but many elders reject it due to taste preference and chewing difficulty.  

A state‑level nutrition task force must evaluate whether the price shock will push calcium intake below the ICMR‑2020 RDA (1000 mg/day) for this demographic and propose a cost‑effective, culturally acceptable intervention that also aligns with the National Food Security Act, 2013 (NFSA) and the Rajasthan State Policy for Senior Citizens, 2019.  

You are asked to:  

1. Calculate the expected daily calcium intake from bajra before and after the price increase, assuming households adjust quantity purchased to keep expenditure constant at pre‑shock levels.  
2. Estimate the shortfall in calcium and suggest a locally available, low‑cost calcium booster (e.g., garden‑grown moringa leaves, sesame seeds, or amaranth) that can meet the deficit without exceeding a 10 % increase in food budget.  
3. Explain how the intervention respects NFSA’s entitlement to “nutritious meals” and the State Senior Citizens Policy’s clause on “promoting locally sourced, age‑appropriate foods.”  
4. Discuss the psychological effect of perceived food insecurity on appetite in the elderly and how the proposed intervention mitigates it.  
5. Outline a monitoring framework using process (price, distribution) and outcome (serum calcium, dietary diversity) indicators.

(C) Suppose the household’s calcium intake from bajra + dal falls to 850 mg/day after adjusting for lower bioavailability (only 70 % of ingested calcium is absorbed). Calculate the absorbed calcium and the additional absorbed calcium needed to meet the absorbed‑RDA of 700 mg/day (assuming 70 % absorption efficiency applies to all sources).

The chapter presents two "foreign" visitors to Gemini Studios: the Moral Re-Armament Army (MRA) and Stephen Spender. Compare how the studio staff responds to each. What does this comparison reveal about the cultural politics of the Indian film industry in the 1950s?

A tech startup develops a conductive yarn for wearable ECG patches by wrapping a stainless‑steel filament (diameter 0.1 mm) around a cotton core (linear density 15 Tex). The yarn must achieve an electrical resistance ≤ 5 Ω/m, have a twist multiplier between 2.5 and 3.5 to minimize electromagnetic interference, and be classified as a novelty yarn due to its core‑spun structure. Production cost is to be estimated using activity‑based costing (ABC): activity pools are “filament winding” (₹200/kg) and “twisting” (₹80/kg), with a combined yield of 70% from raw inputs to final yarn. Biocompatibility is assessed by measuring bacterial growth on the yarn surface; the growth follows logistic kinetics with carrying capacity K = 10⁶ CFU/cm² and intrinsic rate r = 0.3 day⁻¹. The design goal is to keep surface CFU below 10⁴ after 3 days to avoid skin irritation.

(D) The bacterial growth on the yarn surface follows logistic kinetics: dN/dt = rN(1 − N/K), with r = 0.3 day⁻¹ and K = 10⁶ CFU/cm². Assuming initial surface density N₀ = 10² CFU/cm², estimate the surface CFU after 3 days. Does it satisfy the design goal of < 10⁴ CFU/cm²?

The atmosphere holds about 12,900 km³ of water. The average residence time of a water molecule in the atmosphere is 9 days. Assuming steady state, calculate the global average evaporation rate (which equals precipitation rate) in km³/day and in km³/year.

A construction contract between a government agency and a private builder contains an arbitration clause. A dispute arises over delay penalties (₹10 crore). The builder initiates arbitration. The government agency objects, claiming: (i) the dispute involves 'sovereign function' so not arbitrable; (ii) the arbitration clause is invalid because it wasn't signed by the authorised officer. As the arbitrator, how do you rule on jurisdiction? Cite relevant principles.

Combine Accounting Period, Going Concern, and Matching Concepts. M/s Patel Manufacturing purchased a machine on January 1, 2024 for ₹12 lakh (estimated life 10 years, residual value ₹2 lakh). The firm follows the financial year April–March. Calculate: (a) Depreciation expense for the first accounting period (Jan 1 – Mar 31, 2024). (b) Carrying value at March 31, 2024. (c) Depreciation expense for FY 2024–25 (full year). (d) Explain how the three concepts interact in this calculation.

A group of Home Science graduates plans to launch a social enterprise, “EcoFiber”, that converts banana stem agro‑waste into natural fibre for apparel. The venture aims to employ 120 rural women (aged 20‑45) in a processing unit located in a drought‑prone district. Initial capital required is ₹48 lakhs (₹30 lakhs for machinery, ₹12 lakhs for working capital, ₹6 lakhs for training). Projected annual production is 15 000 kg of fibre sold at ₹250/kg. Variable cost per kg (raw material, utilities, wages) is ₹130. Fixed annual overheads (rent, salaries of supervisors, marketing) are ₹9 lakhs. The team conducts a SWOT: Strength – abundant local waste & women’s tailoring skills; Weakness – limited access to credit; Opportunity – growing eco‑fashion market; Threat – competition from synthetic fibres. They must map personal aptitudes (identified via SWOT) to career roles, assess entrepreneurship feasibility, compute basic financial viability, and explain why the fibre is biodegradable from a biological perspective.

(E) Explain, using the biological definition of a living organism, why the banana‑stem fibre produced by EcoFiber is biodegradable.

A high‑school delegation is preparing for a Model United Nations conference on the Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education). The delegate must deliver a **speech** (2‑3 minutes) that uses *Lost Spring* as a primary case study to illustrate barriers to education faced by urban poor children in India. The speech should reference Saheb’s scavenging, the “perpetual state of poverty”, lack of schools in his neighbourhood, and the imposed burden of supporting the family. Additionally, the delegate must integrate: (a) the historical British Education Act of 1870 (c12_hist_cbse_01_005) showing early state responsibility for schooling, (b) the UNESCO Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) Article 28 (c12_polsc_cbse_01_010) as an international benchmark, and (c) geographical data on migrant slum growth in Mumbai and Chennai (c12_geo_cbse_01_008) to show spatial dimensions of the problem. The speech needs a strong opening, logical progression, use of rhetorical devices, and a concluding appeal for policy action. Students must choose the speech format, extract relevant textual evidence, employ chapter‑specific vocabulary, structure the speech with proper salutation, body, and conclusion, and weave in cross‑subject references to substantiate the argument.

(D) Outline the speech structure with salutation, three body paragraphs (each containing one piece of evidence, one vocab item, and one cross‑subject reference), and a concluding call‑to‑action.

A new fintech platform “SevaPay” allows citizens to donate as little as ₹10 to any registered political party via UPI, with real‑time public disclosure of donor‑party matches. In the first quarter, SevaPay recorded ₹2.4 crore in donations: 45 % to Party A (a national party with 38 % Lok Sabha seats across 12 states), 30 % to Party B (a regional party concentrated in State X with 7 % Lok Sabha seats but 55 % of Assembly seats in State X), 15 % to Party C (a newly registered party with <1 % vote share in any state), and 10 % to independents. The Election Commission (EC) uses two criteria for national party recognition: (i) minimum 6 % of valid votes in any four or more states in the last Lok Sabha election, OR (ii) minimum 2 % of Lok Sabha seats (i.e., 11 seats) from at least three states. For state party recognition: (i) minimum 8 % of valid votes in the state Assembly election, OR (ii) minimum 6 % of Lok Sabha seats from that state. Historical analogy: In the late Roman Republic, wealthy patrons (patricians) provided *munera* (games, grain) to clients, creating informal patronage networks that later influenced formal political offices (e.g., consulship). Assume SevaPay donations are treated as “political contributions” under the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and must be reflected in parties’ annual accounts per Accounting Standard AS‑1 (Disclosure of Accounting Policies). Using the data above, answer the following.

(E) If SevaPay’s transaction data must be reflected in Party A’s annual accounts per AS‑1, what qualitative characteristic of accounting information (c11_acc_cbse_01_001) ensures that donors can rely on the disclosed figures for decision‑making?

After a vasectomy, the severed vas deferens ends may heal and reconnect (recanalization), restoring fertility. Histology shows fibroblast‑mediated scar formation whose tensile strength σₛ(t) increases with time t (days) according to σₛ(t) = σ₀[1 – e^(‑αt)], where σ₀ = 1.5 MPa (ultimate tensile strength of mature scar) and α = 0.03 day⁻¹. Luminal pressure generated by seminal fluid flow during ejaculation can be approximated by Poiseuille’s law in a cylindrical tube of radius r = 0.2 mm and length L = 20 mm, with viscosity η = 1.2 × 10⁻³ Pa·s and average flow rate Q = 0.5 mL min⁻¹. Recanalization is assumed to occur when the instantaneous transmural pressure P exceeds the instantaneous scar strength σₛ(t). The hazard (instantaneous risk) of recanalization per day is modeled as h(t) = λ·[P – σₛ(t)]₊, where λ = 0.02 day⁻¹ MPa⁻¹ and [x]₊ = max(x,0).  
**Task:** Compute the pressure generated during ejaculation, determine the time window when recanalization is mechanically possible, and evaluate the cumulative probability of at least one recanalization event within the first 180 days post‑vasectomy.

(D) Derive the cumulative probability 𝒫(t) of at least one recanalization event by time t, assuming hazards are independent and using 𝒫(t) = 1 – exp[‑∫₀ᵗ h(u) du]. Compute 𝒫(180 days).

In the village of Shelgaon (Marathwada, Maharashtra), annual rainfall has declined from 750 mm to 450 mm over the past decade, causing repeated crop failures. The village relies on a 20‑year‑old hand‑pump system that now yields water only 2 hours per day. The Gram Panchayat has submitted a proposal to the State Rural Water Supply Department for a solar‑powered piped water scheme estimated at ₹1.8 crore. Under the 15th Finance Commission, the village is eligible for a tied grant of ₹1.2 crore (60 % of project cost) subject to submission of a Utilization Certificate (UC) within 12 months of fund release. The Panchayat’s accounts show a previous UC submitted for a road‑repair grant that was later flagged by the State Accountant General for mismatched expenditure (₹15 lac reported vs ₹9 lac verified). The village also faces out‑migration of youth to nearby towns due to inadequate water for livestock and domestic use. Using the concepts of rural settlement problems, Panchayati Raj fiscal devolution, and governmental accounting, answer the following.

(B) Which constitutional provision empowers the Gram Panchayat to prepare and implement the water‑supply scheme, and what is its relevance to the scenario?

A wearable biosensor employs a moving‑coil galvanometer to transduce minute bioelectric currents (≈ 10⁻⁹ A) generated by neuronal activity into a measurable needle deflection. The coil is rectangular (width = 2 mm, height = 5 mm), N = 30 turns, suspended in a radial magnetic field B = 0.2 T produced by a permanent magnet. The galvanometer’s spring constant k = 1.5 × 10⁻⁶ N·m/rad. The sensor must resolve angular deflections down to Δθ_min = 0.01 rad. Using set theory, the designer defines the set of detectable currents 𝕀_det as those producing a torque τ ≥ k·Δθ_min. The task is to compute the torque‑current relationship, determine the minimum detectable current, and evaluate whether the sensor can resolve single‑neuron signals, while applying set operations to combine tolerance bands from temperature drift (±5 % in B) and manufacturing tolerances (±10 % in N).

(B) Calculate the minimum detectable current I_min required to produce an angular deflection Δθ_min = 0.01 rad, given the spring constant k.

The River Brahmaputra basin spans State A (upstream) and State B (downstream). State A proposes a new industrial township on its floodplain, covering 200 km². Current land use: 120 km² of rural settlements (average density 300 persons/km², 80 % male workforce in primary activities) and 80 km² of wetlands. State B fears reduced water flow and demands a water‑sharing treaty. A joint technical committee suggests: (i) classify the township as a statutory town if it meets Census criteria; (ii) apply a power‑sharing mechanism akin to the Belgium model for water allocation; (iii) conduct a cost‑benefit analysis where the project cost is ₹3,600 crore, expected annual benefits (agriculture loss avoided, industrial revenue) are ₹540 crore, and the discount rate is 6 % over 20 years. Using settlement classification, power‑sharing, and accounting/economics, answer the sub‑parts.

(C) Applying the Belgium power‑sharing model (c10_civ_cbse_01_001), which institutional arrangement would give State B (downstream) a veto over water‑allocation decisions that affect its agriculture?

In Mumbai's stock exchange, co-located servers rely on ultra-low-latency network devices for sub-microsecond trading advantages. A recent SEBI audit found that legacy hubs in some brokerage firms' internal networks added 500ns jitter per hop, negating gains from expensive fiber upgrades. Meanwhile, a global bank's router misconfiguration caused asymmetric latency between NSE and BSE feeds, triggering erroneous arbitrage trades. The bank uses gateways to translate between proprietary trading protocols (FIX) and standard IP networks. Analyze how device-layer choices impact trading fairness, considering collision domains, queuing delays, and protocol translation overhead in the context of India's evolving market microstructure regulations.

(D) During high volatility, SEBI mandates circuit breakers that halt trading for 15 minutes. Explain how this market-level intervention interacts with network device buffers to prevent cascade failures, referencing queue management principles.

A textile dyeing unit in Tiruppur discharges 500 m³/day of effluent with BOD 800 mg/L, COD 1600 mg/L, and TDS 8000 mg/L. The local CETP has a design capacity of 20 MLD and treats mixed effluent to meet outlet norms: BOD <30 mg/L, COD <250 mg/L, TDS <2100 mg/L. The unit operates 300 days/year. Calculate: (a) annual pollution load (kg/yr) of BOD, COD, TDS from this unit; (b) percentage of CETP hydraulic and organic (BOD) load contributed by this unit if total influent BOD is 600 mg/L; (c) why TDS is not reduced significantly in a conventional biological CETP.

In the Eastern Ghats, a tribal community traditionally practiced hunting‑gathering across 1,200 km² of forest. Recent deforestation reduced viable forest to 600 km², pushing the group toward settled agriculture. The government plans to allocate 150 km² of revenue land for permanent villages, expecting a shift to a linear settlement shape along a river. The tribe’s Forest Rights Act (FRA) claims require recognition of customary over 300 km². Financial support includes a grant of ₹450 crore over 5 years, to be accounted as a deferred revenue grant. Using the concepts of settlement shape, function, tribal rights (civics), and grant accounting, answer the sub‑parts.

(E) If the tribal community’s customary claim of 300 km² is recognized, what percentage of the original forest area (1,200 km²) would remain under state control after allocating the 150 km² for villages?

A research team designs a probe where a benzenediazonium moiety is coupled to a phenolic fluorophore (λ_abs = 350 nm, λ_fl = 420 nm, Φ_fl = 0.65) via an azo bond. In the probe’s “off” state, the azo group quenches fluorescence via photoinduced electron transfer (PET). Upon enzymatic reduction of the diazonium group (by nitroreductase, NTR) to a hydrazine, the azo bond cleaves, releasing the free fluorophore and restoring fluorescence. The reaction follows Michaelis–Menten kinetics with K_M = 15 µM and k_cat = 120 s⁻¹ for NTR. The probe is used at 2 µM concentration in a cellular assay. The fluorescence intensity is measured after 60 s incubation. Using the data, answer the following sub‑parts, which require enzyme kinetics (biology), photophysics (physics), and numerical integration (math).

(A) Calculate the initial rate (v₀) of diazonium reduction by NTR under the assay conditions (probe = 2 µM, [NTR] = 0.1 µM). Assume enzyme concentration is constant and the probe concentration is far below K_M.

A new satellite town is developing 30 km south‑west of Delhi. The 2023 Census provisional figure puts its population at 78,000. Occupational survey shows: 32 % engaged in agriculture and allied activities, 24 % in small‑scale manufacturing (auto‑components, textiles), 28 % in wholesale/retail trade and transport services, and 16 % in education, health and other community services. The town proposes a property tax of ₹500 per capita per annum, with an estimated collection efficiency of 85 %. The state government follows the 74th Constitutional Amendment for urban local bodies, classifying towns with population < 1 lakh as Municipal Councils and ≥ 1 lakh as Municipal Corporations. Using the Census size‑class thresholds, determine the town’s classification, infer its dominant economic sector, estimate the annual property‑tax revenue, and discuss how a population rise to 1.2 lakh would affect its administrative status and fiscal devolution.

(A) According to Census size‑class thresholds, to which class does the town (population 78,000) belong?

A municipal corporation has deployed a fleet of mini‑drones (30 cm wingspan) to monitor traffic violations at intersections. Each drone records video streams and stores them locally for 24 hours before automatic deletion. An investigative journalist, Arun, discovers that the drones’ firmware contains a back‑door allowing the corporation’s security team to access live feeds from any drone without logging the access. The back‑door was allegedly inserted to enable rapid response to accidents, but it also permits unscheduled surveillance of private courtyards visible from the streets. Arun knows that exposing the back‑door will trigger a public‑interest litigation (PIL) under the Right to Privacy judgment, likely resulting in a ₹1.5 crore fine and a mandatory overhaul costing ₹80 lakhs. If he stays silent, the corporation saves the overhaul cost but continues the covert surveillance, which an independent study estimates could capture private activities of ≈ 5,000 residents per month, causing psychological distress valued at ₹3 lakhs per incident (based on willingness‑to‑pay studies). Simultaneously, a civil‑rights group cites the Tao Ying episode from “One Centimetre” as an analogy: a small, seemingly harmless intrusion (drone glitch) justified as a “minor saving” or “efficiency gain”, yet potentially eroding trust in public institutions. Arun must decide whether to publish the findings, report them anonymously to the regulator, or leak them to a foreign tech‑watchdog.

(E) Synthesize the theme of “small compromises eroding integrity” with the historical evolution of surveillance states (e.g., East Germany’s Stasi) to judge whether the corporation’s secret back‑door is a minor compromise or a step toward systemic intrusion.

Assuming the parent’s profit after tax for FY 2023 is ₹300 lakhs and the subsidiary’s profit after tax (in Euro) is €20 million, compute the group’s consolidated profit after tax (in INR lakhs) using the average rate method (assume average €/INR rate for the year is ₹82.5). Then compute the consolidated Return on Equity (ROE) using average equity (beginning + ending)/2.

In 2025, the federation of Avalon faces divergent demographic trajectories among its four provinces: Province A (industrialized) shows CBR = 12, CDR = 9; Province B (agrarian) CBR = 28, CDR = 6; Province C (tourist‑hub) CBR = 18, CDR = 8; Province D (resource‑rich) CBR = 22, CDR = 5. Total national population is 80 million, distributed as A = 20 %, B = 35 %, C = 25 %, D = 20 %. The central government collects a uniform tax of 15 % on provincial gross domestic product (GDP). Provincial GDPs (in billions of Avalon credits, AC) are: A = 250, B = 120, C = 180, D = 300. Tax revenue is redistributed via a formula that gives each province a share equal to (0.6 × its population share + 0.4 × its tax contribution share). The national finance ministry must project the impact of demographic trends on future tax bases and design a power‑sharing arrangement (based on the Belgian accommodation model) for the upper house, where seats are allocated according to each province’s share of the *eligible voter* population (citizens ≥ 18 years), assumed to be 65 % of each province’s total population uniformly.  
Using the data, answer the following.

(C) Determine each province’s eligible voter population (in millions) and its share of the national eligible voter base.

The State Urban Development Authority plans to deploy an AI‑based adaptive signal control system across 150 intersections in City Z (population ≈ 4.2 million, daily vehicle count ≈ 2.8 million). Before implementation, a baseline survey must capture: (i) current traffic flow volumes, (ii) commuter travel‑time variability, (iii) public opinion on privacy concerns related to license‑plate recognition cameras, and (iv) socioeconomic disparities in access to alternative transport (e.g., metro, ride‑share). The survey will combine roadside automatic traffic counters (ATCs), structured interviews with commuters at major bus depots, and an online questionnaire distributed via municipal wards. The team has access to 8 traffic engineers, 12 enumerators for face‑to‑face interviews, and a budget of ₹20 lakhs. They must decide on sampling frames for each method, assess reliability of the ATC data (calibration with manual counts), ensure validity of the opinion questionnaire (face‑validity, construct validity), and finally integrate the findings into a cost‑effectiveness analysis comparing the AI system against a conventional signal‑timing upgrade. Relevant secondary data include ward‑wise socio‑economic indices from the latest census and real‑time air‑quality monitoring stations (PM2.5 averages 45 µg/m³).

(A) For measuring traffic volume at intersections, justify whether to rely solely on ATCs, supplement with manual counts, or use a hybrid approach, considering calibration error and budget.

The National Manuscript Mission (NMM) proposes to digitize all extant 17th‑century manuscripts of Raskhan’s *Jake Panjrekul* using AI‑based optical character recognition (OCR) trained on Perso‑Arabic and Devanagari scripts. The project budget is ₹8 crore, spanning 24 months, with deliverables: searchable PDFs, metadata tags (theme, raga, linguistic features), and an AI‑generated commentary linking verses to Bhakti sociopolitical contexts. A coalition of scholars from Aligarh Muslim University and Banaras Hindu University raises concerns: (1) OCR may misinterpret Persianized Hindi, altering theological nuance; (2) AI commentary could inadvertently impose modern secular biases, misrepresenting the poet’s devotional intent; (3) Data sovereignty—who holds the digital rights? The NMM cites Article 51A(h) (scientific temper) and the IT Act, 2000 (data protection) to argue that technological preservation serves public interest. A parliamentary committee must decide whether to approve funding, impose oversight, or reject the project.

(A) Determine the time period (century) during which the majority of Raskhan’s manuscripts were likely produced, using evidence from रचनाकार-परिचय और पृष्ठभूमि एक चयनात्मक विवरण-कौशल है and The sacrificial tradition (yajna) in the Vedic period (c.

A research NGO launches a digital archive project to map the 1947 refugee flows using declassified satellite imagery, oral‑history testimonies, and GIS layering. The dataset includes 12,000 geo‑tagged points of refugee camps, train‑station departures, and violence hotspots from August 1946 to December 1948. The team overlays these points with (a) the Radcliffe Line awards, (b) locations of Gandhi’s fast‑unto‑death protests in Calcutta and Delhi, and (c) current India‑Pakistan border enclaves (e.g., Dahagram‑Angarpota). Using this, they assess (i) how Direct Action Day (16 Aug 1946) accelerated the timeline to the Mountbatten Plan (June 1947), (ii) whether Gandhi’s interventions correlated with localized reductions in violence hotspots, (iii) how the resulting migration patterns inform present‑day disputes over citizenship and minority rights under Articles 25‑30 of the Indian Constitution, and (iv) what geopolitical risks arise if historical migration corridors are ignored in modern border‑management policies. Students must evaluate the project’s methodology, interpret spatial‑temporal patterns, and link them to constitutional and political‑science concepts.

(D) Using Article 29 (Protection of Interests of Minorities) and the archive’s data showing 62 % of migrated Hindus settled in West Bengal, evaluate whether the state’s post‑1950 language policy (favoring Bengali) could be challenged under this article.

A 120 kg low‑Earth‑orbit satellite (altitude 500 km) experiences a constant disturbance torque of τ_dist = 1.0 × 10⁻³ N·m about its yaw axis due to solar‑radiation pressure. In a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanner, the transverse magnetization \(M_{xy}(t)\) (in arbitrary units) after a radio‑frequency (RF) pulse is modeled as the product of two processes: (i) the decay due to spin‑spin relaxation, described by \(R(t)=e^{-t/T_2}\) with \(T_2=80\;{\rm ms}\), and (ii) the phase‑accumulation from a linear gradient field, given by \(G(t)=\cos\bigl(\gamma G_x t\bigr)\) where \(\gamma=2.675\times10^8\;{\rm rad·s^{-1}·T^{-1}}\) is the gyromagnetic ratio and \(G_x=10\;{\rm mT/m}\) is the gradient strength. The detectable signal is \(S(t)=k\,M_{xy}(t)=k\,R(t)\,G(t)\) with proportionality constant \(k=1\).  
During a specific echo‑planar imaging (EPI) readout, a sudden RF re‑pulse is applied at time \(t=t_e=12\;{\rm ms}\) to refocus the spin echo. The re‑pulse instantaneously flips the sign of the transverse magnetization, which is mathematically represented by multiplying the signal by \(-1\) for \(t\ge t_e\). Hence the actual signal transmitted to the receiver is  
\[
\Sigma(t)=\begin{cases}
\; S(t), & t<t_e\\[4pt]
\; -S(t), & t\ge t_e
\end{cases}.
\]  
The imaging engineer requires that \(\Sigma(t)\) be **continuous** at the re‑pulse instant \(t=t_e\) to avoid artifacts, and that its derivative \(\Sigma'(t)\) be **continuous** for optimal edge‑preserving reconstruction. Using the algebra of continuous and differentiable functions, determine whether \(\Sigma(t)\) and \(\Sigma'(t)\) satisfy these conditions. If discontinuities exist, propose the minimal modification to the gradient strength \(G_x\) (or alternatively to the flip factor) that restores continuity of \(\Sigma(t)\) while keeping the echo time \(t_e\) fixed and the signal‑to‑noise ratio (SNR) loss below 3 %.

(A) Show that the relaxation factor \(R(t)=e^{-t/T_2}\) is continuous for all \(t\ge0\).
