Data: 2023‑24 film production – 1,200 titles total; language breakup – Hindi 38 %, Tamil 15 %, Telugu 12 %, Malayalam 9 %, Punjabi 6 %, Others 20 %. The CFCB received 84 objections, 62 % from South Indian producers. Historical note: The 1952 Cinematograph Act allowed regional language boards to certify films in their mother tongue; the 1983 amendment introduced a single‑language (Hindi/English) script requirement for central subsidies, later rolled back in 1999 after protests.

(A) Identify the secondary theme from *Poets and Pancakes* that best parallels the filmmakers’ resistance to the English/Hindi‑only script mandate and justify with one line from the text.

A 2025 Instagram campaign by the NGO “CityBridge” posts memes depicting rural‑to‑urban migration. One meme shows a silhouette of a farmer turning into a stream of tiny figures flowing into a skyscraper‑shaped funnel, captioned: “Fields are **veins**; cities are the **heart** that pumps hope.” Another meme overlays satellite night‑light data showing a 23 % increase in urban luminescence over five years, with the tagline: “Our arteries glow brighter.” The campaign cites World Bank data predicting a 35 % rise in India’s urban population by 2030. Students must identify imagery and metaphor in the memes, interpret the geographic data, apply sociological theories of place attachment and spatial fix, and evaluate the campaign’s effectiveness in shaping public perception.

(A) Identify the visual imagery in the “veins/heart” meme and specify the sense it targets.

A researcher wants to construct a genomic library for a 3 Gb mammalian genome. She can choose between a BAC library (average insert 150 kb) and a YAC library (average insert 500 kb). Calculate the minimum number of independent clones needed for each to achieve 99% probability of containing any given sequence (use the Clarke-Carbon formula: N = ln(1-P) / ln(1 - I/G), where P=0.99, I=insert size, G=genome size). Which vector requires fewer clones, and what practical drawback of YACs might still make BACs preferable?

The Ministry of External Affairs launches “Hindi Setu”, a program to teach Hindi to second‑generation Indian diaspora youths in the United States, United Kingdom, and UAE via online modules. The program aims to strengthen cultural ties and improve soft‑power influence. Linguists note that Hindi speakers abroad constitute roughly 8 million, with significant concentrations in the Gulf (2 M), North America (3 M), and Europe (1 M). Sociologists warn that without contextualization, language learning may lead to superficial identity formation, whereas educators argue that integrating regional literature (e.g., Prasad’s essays) enhances affective engagement. Geographers point out that language clusters follow migration corridors and economic hubs. The task: evaluate the program’s potential success by analyzing (a) the geographic distribution of Hindi speakers, (b) sociolinguistic theories of language and identity, and (c) the pedagogical value of incorporating literary texts from the chapter. Provide a structured answer (150‑200 words) using data from the scenario, at least two theoretical concepts (e.g., Fishman’s reversals, Bourdieu’s cultural capital), and a reference to Prasad’s use of भाषा‑सौष्ठव (linguistic elegance). Use PEEL format.

(B) Explain how Fishman’s theory of language reversals predicts the likely outcome of the “Hindi Setu” program if it focuses only on linguistic competence without cultural content.

Classify the following for a **textile manufacturing company** with justification: (1) Cash received from sale of fabric; (2) Cash paid for purchase of cotton; (3) Cash paid for new weaving machine; (4) Cash received from sale of old delivery van; (5) Cash received from issue of 10% debentures; (6) Interest paid on debentures; (7) Dividend paid to shareholders; (8) Cash paid for income tax; (9) Cash received as dividend on shares held as investment; (10) Cash paid for purchase of shares in another textile company (long-term investment).

Suppose the export price of cotton drops by 20 % due to a glut in Surat, while the local jowar price remains unchanged. Re‑calculate the state revenue demand and discuss the likely impact on the zamindar’s ability to guarantee peasant loans.

A case-study: "VaxGen India" is developing an inactivated viral vaccine using Vero cells (African green monkey kidney epithelial line). They currently use M199 medium + 5% FBS for virus propagation. For Phase III clinical trials, CDSCO requires: (a) Animal-component-free media, (b) Defined composition for lot release testing, (c) Scalability to 2000 L bioreactor. The process team proposes three strategies:
Strategy I: Switch to a commercial chemically defined, protein-free, serum-free Vero medium (e.g., VP-SFM).
Strategy II: Develop in-house serum-free medium by replacing FBS with recombinant human albumin, transferrin, insulin, and FGF-2 in M199 basal.
Strategy III: Continue with M199 + 5% FBS but implement viral clearance validation (nanofiltration, low pH hold) downstream.
As a regulatory affairs consultant, evaluate each strategy against the three CDSCO requirements. Create a 3×3 compliance matrix (Strategy vs Requirement) with Yes/No/Partial and a one-sentence justification per cell. Recommend one strategy with a risk mitigation plan.

COMPETENCY
Translating real-world regulatory constraints into media selection decisions with evidence-based justification
Identify the limiting reagent between sodium ethoxide (from part A) and methyl iodide (800 g).

A factory produces 480 toys in 8 hours with 5 machines running simultaneously. The owner wants to produce 810 toys in 6 hours. How many additional machines are needed, assuming each machine works at the same rate? Use the unitary method to find the production rate per machine per hour, then solve.

India imports ~70 % of its phosphate rock demand, primarily from Jordan and Syria. A new offshore phosphate deposit is discovered off the Gujarat coast (lat 20.5° N, long 70.2° E) within the exclusive economic zone (EEZ). The Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas proposes a joint venture with a foreign firm to extract 1 Mt/yr of rock phosphate. The Gujarat government seeks a share of royalty revenues, while the Ministry of Finance worries about fiscal deficit. Environmental groups warn of potential damage to coral reefs in the Gulf of Kutch. The current subsidy on diammonium phosphate (DAP) is ₹12 000/tonne, and the market price of DAP is ₹24 000/tonne. Using the phosphate occurrence map, answer the following.

(C) Link phosphate rock to its key end‑use industry: name two major fertilizer products derived from it and state their approximate annual consumption in India.

A 2024 NSSO survey reveals that 38 % of households in Vidarbha have at least one member who migrated to cities for work, yet 62 % of those migrants send less than ₹3 000 monthly remittances, insufficient to cover agricultural input costs. Simultaneously, state‑run “Agri‑Tech Parks” promise high‑yield seeds and drone‑spraying services to villages, requiring farmers to register online and pay a subscription fee. Many smallholders, unable to afford the fee, continue to rely on traditional roadside stands for survival. Using Frost’s irony and symbolism, answer the following.

(E) Apply the Economics concept of agricultural credit constraints to explain why smallholders avoid the Agri‑Tech Parks subscription despite potential yield gains.

A machine was purchased on 1st October 2022 for ₹2,00,000. The firm closes books on 31st March and charges depreciation @10% p.a. on original cost under the Provision for Depreciation method. Calculate the depreciation for the first year (2022-23) and show the journal entry on 31st March 2023.

Given a list `prices = [120, 45, 200, 80, 350, 60]` representing item prices in rupees, write a single list comprehension that produces a new list containing the discounted prices (10% off) only for items originally priced above ₹100. Show the output.

True or False: Weather refers to the day-to-day atmospheric conditions of a specific place, whereas climate represents the average weather pattern of a region calculated over a long period, typically 30 years or more.

In 2026, the Ministry of Rural Development deploys an AI‑driven platform “Samriddhi‑AI” to auto‑generate beneficiary lists for MGNREGA, PM‑KISAN, and food‑security schemes across 50 000 Gram Panchayats. The algorithm uses satellite‑derived land‑holding data, SECC‑2011 socio‑economic scores, and mobile‑phone usage patterns to predict eligibility. Pilot results show a 22 % reduction in inclusion errors (false negatives) but a 17 % increase in exclusion errors (false positives) among elderly, landless, and nomadic communities who lack digital footprints. Civil‑society groups file a writ petition alleging violation of Article 14 (right to equality) and Article 38 (State to promote welfare). The Government defends the tool citing efficiency gains and cites the Directive Principle of Article 46 (promotion of educational and economic interests of SC/ST/other weaker sections) as justification for targeting. Using the concepts of distributive justice (c12_soc_cbse_10_002), the tension between procedural and substantive democracy (c12_soc_cbse_10_001), and the constitutional status of Panchayats (c12_soc_cbse_10_004), assess whether Samriddhi‑AI advances or retreats from the constitutional goal of social justice.

(A) Identify which constitutional article(s) are most directly implicated when evaluating Samriddhi‑AI’s impact on *procedural* democracy.

In 2025, a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) is filed before the Supreme Court challenging the constitutionality of the "State‑Level Electoral Bond Scheme" (SLEBS), which allows anonymous corporate donations to state parties via bonds purchased at designated banks. The petitioners argue that SLEBS violates Articles 14 (equality before law), 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech and expression), and 21 (right to life) by enabling opaque funding that skews the playing field in favour of the ruling National Unity Party (NUP), which received 78% of total bond value in FY 2024‑25. The NUP contends that the scheme promotes clean money and protects donor privacy, citing the 1951‑52 First General Elections where covert funding led to black‑money inflation (as discussed in ). Historical parallels are drawn to the Roman Senate’s use of *sublicae* (private loans) to fund provincial governors, a practice later curtailed by the *lex Julia de vi publica*. Socio‑economic data shows that states with highest NUP bond receipts also exhibit the lowest Gini coefficients (0.28) and highest human development indices (0.78), whereas opposition‑strong states show higher inequality (Gini 0.38, HDI 0.62). Students must assess the constitutional validity of SLEBS, its impact on democratic competition, and whether the observed developmental outcomes justify the scheme under the doctrine of "reasonable classification".

(C) Compare the legal constraints on private financing in the Roman Republic (lex Julia de vi publica) with the current lack of explicit caps on electoral bond denominations in India. Identify two similarities in the rationale behind such restrictions and one difference in enforcement mechanism.

"In 2013-14, India experienced a 'taper tantrum' — FII outflows of $12 billion in a few months — while FDI inflows remained stable at $24 billion. The rupee depreciated 15% against the dollar. The RBI responded by raising interest rates and opening a special swap window for banks. Analyze this episode using the concepts of (a) capital flow volatility, (b) policy trilemma, and (c) sterilised intervention."

A district in Bihar's Kosi floodplain receives IMD's "Orange Alert" for extreme rainfall (200 mm in 24 hrs). As District Disaster Management Authority (DDMA) chair, list the SEQUENCE of 5 response actions you would trigger in the first 12 hours, justifying the ORDER.

Consider a firm with production function Q = 50L + 15L^2 - L^3. The firm is currently employing 8 units of labor. The manager says, "We are in Stage II because MP is positive." Evaluate this statement. If incorrect, determine the actual stage and the optimal labor range for a rational producer. Also, if the wage rate is ₹1000 and output price is ₹100, find the profit-maximizing labor (assuming the firm is a price taker in both input and output markets).

A flat‑panel photobioreactor (FPR) is employed to induce somatic embryogenesis from sugarcane meristematic cells. The reactor is illuminated by red LED arrays providing a photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD) of 150 µmol photons m⁻² s⁻¹ (PAR, 400–700 nm). The illuminated area is 0.25 m², and the culture volume is 2 L with a cell density of 1 × 10⁶ cells mL⁻¹. The medium’s optical path length is 2 cm, and the cellular absorption coefficient at 660 nm is 0.8 cm⁻¹ (i.e., 80 % of incident photons are absorbed by the biomass). Each absorbed photon at 660 nm carries energy E = hc/λ (h = 6.626×10⁻³⁴ J·s, c = 3.00×10⁸ m s⁻¹, λ = 660 nm). Excess energy not used in photochemistry is dissipated as heat and can generate reactive oxygen species (ROS); assume 1 % of the absorbed energy yields ROS, each ROS molecule scavenged by one molecule of ascorbate (Asc). The medium is buffered with MES (pKa = 6.10) to maintain pH ≈ 5.8 during embryogenesis. Metabolic acid production generates 0.02 mol H⁺ over the 4‑hour illumination period.  
Using the data, answer the following sub‑parts.

(A) Calculate the total number of photons absorbed per second by the culture.

A patient with hyperthyroidism is prescribed oral Iodine‑131 (^131₅₃I) for targeted beta‑radiation therapy. The nuclide decays with a half‑life of 8.02 days, emitting beta particles (average energy 0.19 MeV) and gamma photons (364 keV). The treatment protocol requires calculating (i) the decay constant and mean life, (ii) the activity of a 150 MBq administered dose after 48 h, (iii) the energy deposited per decay assuming 80 % of beta energy is absorbed in tissue, (iv) the number of ^131I atoms initially present, and (v) the mass of iodine needed, using the molar mass of iodine (≈126.9 g mol⁻¹). The problem binds radioactive decay laws, exponential functions (math), and stoichiometric mole‑mass conversion (chemistry) to assess therapeutic efficacy and safety.

(E) Using the molar mass of iodine (126.9 g mol⁻¹), find the mass of ^131I corresponding to the initial number of atoms from Part D.

HealthTech Ltd. launches “PulsePro”, a smartwatch marketed as capable of detecting atrial fibrillation (AF) with clinical‑grade accuracy. The device uses a proprietary optical sensor and an AI algorithm. After six months, a 58‑year‑old engineer from Bengaluru receives repeated false‑negative alerts (device shows normal rhythm while ECG confirms AF). He suffers a minor stroke attributed to untreated AF. He files a complaint against HealthTech Ltd. for defective product (sensor failure) and deficiency in service (inaccurate health advice). The claimed compensation includes: device cost ₹25,000, medical expenses ₹1,80,000, loss of earnings ₹2,00,000, and punitive damages ₹5,00,000. The total claim amounts to ₹9,05,000. Using the scenario, answer the following sub‑parts.

(E) Apply a basic cost‑benefit analysis (CBA) to decide whether the State Commission should impose a recall of all PulsePro units as a remedial measure, given the following: estimated recall cost ₹12 crore, expected avoidance of future medical costs ₹3 crore, and non‑monetary benefit (consumer trust) valued at ₹1 crore. Show your calculation and state whether the recall is economically justified.

In 2023 the Ministry of Labour released a report stating that 27 % of formal‑sector jobs in India required proficiency in Hindi as a core competency, while 18 % mandated English, and 55 % listed “any official language” as acceptable. Concurrently, the Supreme Court in *State of Karnataka vs. Praveen Kumar* (2022) upheld a state‑level rule that government recruitment exams could be conducted exclusively in Kannada, reasoning that linguistic accessibility is a facet of the right to equality under Article 14. A follow‑up PIL in 2024 challenged the central government’s Hindi‑preference in banking sector recruitment, arguing it violated Articles 14 (equality) and 16 (equal opportunity). The Court referred to the doctrine of “reasonable classification” and noted that any language‑based criterion must satisfy a clear nexus to job performance.  
Students must extract exact percentages (literal), infer the legal reasoning behind the judgments, and connect them to economic implications of language‑based employability (node c12_eco_cbse_05_008) and judicial principles of equality (node c12_ls_cbse_02_006).

(E) Draft a concise legal‑economic argument (max 120 words) that the central government’s Hindi‑preference in banking recruitment violates Article 14 unless it demonstrates a clear nexus to job performance, referencing the 2023 labour data and the *Karnataka* precedent.

In 2024, Rajesh, a former wire‑rattrap maker from Bihar, now designs low‑cost IoT‑enabled “crop‑rattraps” that alert farmers via SMS when pests enter their fields. He assembles these devices from salvaged electronic parts bought at urban scrap markets and sells them door‑to‑door in villages of Jharkhand and Odisha. Though his invention reduces pesticide use by 30 %, Rajesh earns only ₹150 per unit because middlemen take 70 % of the sale price. He lives in a rented shack, his diet is insufficient, and he often skips meals to keep his phone charged for orders. One evening, after a long trek through a forested route, he notices a signboard announcing a new government scheme under Article 21 that guarantees “right to livelihood” for rural artisans. He recalls a history lesson on Zamindari abolition (1950‑55) that aimed to break exploitative landlord‑tenant relations, and a geography map showing that only 18 % of households in his district have reliable 4G coverage. Rajesh wonders whether the scheme will truly free him from the exploitative “rattrap” of middlemen or merely replace one trap with another.

(A) Identify the literal statement in the scenario that directly explains why Rajesh’s earnings remain low despite his invention’s effectiveness.

In 2024 a student‑led collective “Bhasha‑Mitra” launches a pan‑India Instagram campaign demanding official recognition for Bhili, a tribal language spoken by ~10 million people across Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Maharashtra. The campaign’s poster shows two hands clasped—one holding a traditional Bhili drum, the other a smartphone—captioned in Hindi: “समान सम्मान, स्वतंत्र बोल” (Equal respect, free speech). Within 48 hours the post garners 2.3 lakhs likes, 1.1 lakhs shares and attracts a legal notice from the State Education Department alleging violation of the “Three‑Language Formula” under Article 29(2). The collective cites the story “HkfDru” where the protagonists recognize each other’s dignity beyond ownership, arguing that language is an extension of personal autonomy. Using the data:  
- Population of Bhili speakers: 10 million (≈0.75 % of India)  
- Instagram reach: 2.3 lakhs likes, 1.1 lakhs shares  
- Legal basis: Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of expression) and Article 29(2) (protection of minority interests)  
Answer the following sub‑parts.

(D) Identify the metaphor used in the campaign poster (hands holding drum & smartphone) and explain, using c12_hin_ar_cbse_10_008, how it reinforces the story’s theme of mutual dignity.
Calculate the normality of a solution prepared by dissolving 4.9 g of H₂SO₄ in 250 mL of solution. (Molar mass H₂SO₄ = 98 g/mol)

An IVF laboratory aims to optimize the culture medium for zygote development. The medium uses a HEPES buffer (pKa = 7.55) at 25 mM total concentration to maintain pH 7.40. Oxygen is supplied via a gas‑permeable membrane; the external O₂ partial pressure is 0.21 atm, and the solubility coefficient of O₂ in the medium at 37 °C is α = 1.3×10⁻³ mol L⁻¹ atm⁻¹. The membrane thickness is 50 µm, area 2 cm², and the diffusion coefficient of O₂ in the membrane is D = 2.0×10⁻⁵ cm² s⁻¹. Embryo development is monitored: out of 48 zygotes cultured, 36 reach the blastocyst stage (Day 5). Assume development follows a binomial distribution with probability p of normal development.  
Using the data, answer the sub‑parts below. Show all steps, state assumptions, and give final answers with correct units.

(D) Assuming embryo development follows a binomial distribution with n=48, estimate the maximum likelihood estimate (MLE) of the success probability p and construct an approximate 95 % confidence interval using the normal approximation.

In early pregnancy (weeks 5‑8), placental trophoblasts secrete VEGF in response to two stimuli: (i) hypoxia‑induced HIF‑1α stabilization (oxygen‑dependent degradation with half‑life t₁/₂,O₂ = 5 min at pO₂ < 40 mm Hg, negligible above 60 mm Hg), and (ii) shear‑stress‑activated PI3K/Akt pathway, where VEGF secretion rate S (pg h⁻¹ cell⁻¹) follows S = S₀ + σ·τ, with basal S₀ = 2 pg h⁻¹ cell⁻¹, shear sensitivity σ =0.05 pg h⁻¹ cell⁻¹ Pa⁻¹, and τ the wall shear stress (Pa) in fetal capillaries.  

Fetal capillary flow is modeled as a series of identical cylindrical segments: radius r_f = 3 µm, length L_f = 200 µm, blood viscosity η_f =0.0035 Pa·s, pressure gradient ΔP_f = 800 Pa. Maternal intervillous flow provides O₂ with inlet pO₂ =100 mm Hg; fetal capillary pO₂ rises linearly along the segment due to O₂ uptake, assuming a constant consumption rate per unit length Q̇_O₂ = 1.2×10⁻¹⁸ mol s⁻¹ µm⁻¹ (derived from fetal metabolic demand). Oxygen diffusivity in plasma Dₚ =2.0×10⁻⁵ cm² s⁻¹, solubility α =1.3 µmol L⁻¹ mm Hg⁻¹.  

Assume steady state, axial diffusion negligible compared to convection, and that VEGF released accumulates in the interstitial space with first‑order clearance k꜀,VEGF =0.1 h⁻¹ (half‑life ~6.9 h).  

Using the above, answer the following sub‑parts. Show all steps, keep units consistent, and indicate assumptions.

(D) Model the interstitial VEGF concentration C_V(t) (pg mL⁻¹) assuming secretion from N =1×10⁶ cells uniformly distributed in a placental interstitial volume V_int =0.5 mL, first‑order clearance k꜀ =0.1 h⁻¹, and using the average secretion rate ⟨S⟩ from Part C. Find the steady‑state concentration and the time to reach 90 % of steady state.

A contemporary NGO files a public‑interest litigation challenging the constitutional validity of certain state‑level land‑acquisition laws that allow eminent‑domain compensation below market rates, citing historical precedents from Mughal India where, according to François Bernier, the emperor held absolute proprietorship over all land, discouraging private investment. The defense counters by invoking Ibn Battuta’s account of his service as a qazi in Delhi, arguing that Islamic law recognized private property rights and that state appropriations were subject to Sharia‑based justification. The court must (a) assess the evidentiary weight of Ibn Battuta’s legal observations as a primary source for Mughal‑era property norms, (b) apply principles of Islamic jurisprudence (Sharia) concerning *mulk* (private ownership) and *khiraj* (land tax) to determine whether Bernier’s characterization holds, (c) compare these historical norms with modern fundamental rights under Article 300A (right to property) and the doctrine of eminent domain, (d) use geographical reasoning to explain how the fertility of the Gangetic alluvial plains influenced land‑revenue systems and thus the perception of property rights, and (e) formulate a hypothetical legal test balancing state developmental needs with individual property protections, drawing analogies from the *uluq* relay’s reliability standards. Use the following data: Ibn Battuta notes that Delhi’s land‑tax (kharaj) averaged 10 % of produce and that land could be bought, sold, and inherited subject to payment of tax; Bernier states that the Mughal emperor owned all land and could grant or revoke holdings at will; the Gangetic alluvial plain has an average soil fertility index of 0.85 (on a 0‑1 scale) and supports 2.5 times the crop yield of the Deccan plateau. Modern compensation law provides 100 % of market value plus 100 % solatium.

(E) Design a procedural test for state land‑acquisition that mirrors the reliability standard of the *uluq* relay system (i.e., minimal points of failure and timely communication), specifying two procedural safeguards and one performance benchmark.

StreamOn, a video‑streaming platform, experiences three simultaneous non‑price influences on demand: (i) a rise in expected future subscriber growth (expectation) increases current willingness to subscribe by 15% at every price; (ii) the number of potential buyers rises due to a successful partnership with a smart‑TV manufacturer, shifting demand outward by 20 million subscribers; (iii) a government budget deficit raises market interest rates, increasing the opportunity cost of capital and reducing firms’ willingness to invest in content, which shifts the supply curve leftward by 10 % at every quantity. Initially, demand (in millions of subscribers per month) is Qd = 120 – 0.5P and supply (in millions) is Qs = 20 + 0.3P, where P is the monthly subscription fee in ₹. The government deficit also leads to a temporary tax credit of ₹5 per subscriber for content creation, which shifts supply rightward by the credit amount (treated as a subsidy to producers). Using this data, answer the following.

(C) Journal entry to record the receipt of the government tax credit of ₹5 per subscriber for the months when the equilibrium quantity is realized, assuming the credit is received cash‑based at month‑end.

A private consortium has filed a proposal with the Bihar State Tourism Development Corporation to construct a five‑star eco‑resort on a 12‑acre plot situated 85 m north‑west of the Vishwa Shanti Stupa at Rajgir. The resort design includes glass‑facaded villas, a spa utilizing geothermal springs, and a conference centre capable of hosting 500 delegates. The project promises to generate ₹250 crore in investment and create 1,200 jobs. However, conservation activists have lodged a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in the Patna High Court alleging violation of the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 (AMASR Act), which prohibits any construction within 100 m of a protected monument without prior approval from the National Monument Authority. The activists further contend that the resort’s night‑time lighting and increased vehicular traffic will alter the tranquil, meditative atmosphere that has characterized the stupa’s environs for centuries, as described in travelogues and the NCERT excerpt’s depiction of “awe at the ancient ruins”. The GIS unit of the State Remote Sensing Centre has provided data: (i) the plot lies on a moderate‑risk seismic zone (zone III), (ii) soil liquefaction potential is 0.31 (moderate), (iii) the line‑of‑sight from the stupa to the surrounding hills is obstructed by the proposed resort’s height (18 m), and (iv) night‑time luminosity is projected to rise from 0.2 cd/m² (natural) to 1.8 cd/m² (artificial). As a legal‑heritage analyst, you must (i) dissect the setting layers evident in the activists’ PIL petition, (ii) explain how the author of the NCERT excerpt uses sensory details to construct an atmosphere of awe, and (iii) determine whether the resort project violates the AMASR Act’s spirit and letter, integrating geographical risk, legal thresholds, and atmospheric impact assessments.

(B) Identify the historical layer of setting by providing two references to past periods, events, or traditions linked to the stupa.

India’s Annual Market Support (AMS) for wheat and rice in FY 2022‑23 was estimated at USD 15 bn, calculated using the fixed‑external‑reference‑price (FERP) method. The WTO’s Agreement on Agriculture permits developing countries to exceed the de minimis level (10 % of AGVP) under the “Peace Clause” if the subsidy is tied to public stockholding for food security. India’s total agricultural GDP (AGVP) in FY 2022‑23 was USD 420 bn. The government proposes to increase the Minimum Support Price (MSP) for wheat by 6 % and for rice by 4 %, expecting a resultant rise in AMS of USD 0.9 bn. A group of WTO members challenges the legality of India’s stockholding program, arguing that it causes serious prejudice to their exporters. Using the data below and concepts of agriculture subsidies, AMS, Peace Clause, and basic arithmetic, answer the sub‑questions.

(D) Explain the “Peace Clause” in the WTO Agreement on Agriculture and state one condition under which a developing country may invoke it for public stockholding subsidies.

"The distinction between 'sex' and 'gender' is not merely academic — it determines whether policy targets biology or social structure." Using the case of maternity leave vs paternity leave policies in India, analyse this statement. In your answer: (a) define the sex/gender distinction in policy terms; (b) explain how the Maternity Benefit Act (26 weeks for women, 0 for men) reinforces gendered care division; (c) propose one gender-transformative reform with justification.

The trajectory of a projectile launched from a platform is modeled by h(t) = -5t² + 20t + 15 (height in meters, time in seconds). Find the equation of the tangent line to the height-time curve at t = 2 seconds. What does this tangent line represent physically? At what other time does the projectile have the same instantaneous velocity?

A metropolitan newspaper invites readers to submit letters (120‑150 words) addressing rising noise pollution in Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru. Contributors must draw on *Keeping Quiet* to argue that prescribed “quiet zones” can improve mental health and productivity. They receive: (i) WHO 2022 data showing 65 % of urban residents report stress from traffic noise; (ii) India’s Coastal Regulation Zone (CRZ) notification (2019) that designates silent zones near hospitals and schools; (iii) a sociological study (c12_soc_cbse_01_009) linking chronic noise to decreased community trust; (iv) a psychological model (c11_psy_cbse_01_012) stating that auditory breaks restore attentional resources. Writers must produce a letter that (a) quotes the poem’s opening lines, (b) identifies two literary devices, (c) notes the irony of advocating silence in a noisy city, (d) ties the argument to at least one sociological finding, one psychological mechanism, and one existing policy (CRZ), and (e) ends with a call for municipal action.

(D) Connect the letter’s argument to one sociological finding (c12_soc_cbse_01_009) on urban noise and community trust, and explain how quiet zones could mitigate the identified issue.
Using the nearest‑neighbor method (including initiation and 50 mM Na⁺ salt correction), compute the Tm (°C) for each primer. Determine if the ΔTm between the pair is ≤ 5 °C.

EcoThread is a startup launching a line of organic‑cotton T‑shirts marketed as “eco‑friendly”. Each shirt costs Rs 300 to produce (raw material, fair‑wage labour, eco‑dyes). The firm plans a premium price of Rs 800 per unit, targeting environmentally conscious urban millennials. Distribution will be through its own e‑commerce website and pop‑up stores in select malls (Place). Promotion relies on Instagram micro‑influencers, a “buy‑one‑give‑one” scheme (for every shirt sold, one is donated to a rural school), and highlight‑reels on sustainable fashion. The company expects to sell 15,000 shirts in the first year. Accounting policies: inventory is valued using FIFO; revenue is recognized at point of sale; shipping costs are treated as period expenses. A price‑sensitivity survey indicates that raising the price from Rs 800 to Rs 900 would reduce expected sales from 15,000 to 12,000 units. Legal concerns include avoiding green‑washing claims (must substantiate “eco‑friendly” with certifications) and protecting the brand name and logo under trademark law. Relevant data: variable cost per unit Rs 300, fixed marketing cost Rs 12,00,000, expected tax rate 25 %.

(D) Using the midpoint formula, calculate the price elasticity of demand for EcoThread’s T‑shirt when the price rises from Rs 800 to Rs 900 and expected sales fall from 15,000 to 12,000 units.

In 2024, the Union Ministry of Agriculture launches a real‑time satellite‑NDVI portal that predicts wheat yield at the block level. Farmers’ unions in Punjab, historically agitated over MSP (Minimum Support Price) procurement delays, use the portal to anticipate market gluts and demand pre‑emptive price floor adjustments. Simultaneously, sociologists note a rise in “rational protest” framing – protesters citing data‑driven forecasts rather than traditional moral claims about farmer distress. Historical records show that the Green Revolution (1960s‑70s) introduced high‑yield varieties (HYVs) and institutionalized procurement, while the 1991 liberalization reduced state intervention in agricultural markets.  

Students must integrate:  
- Sociological concepts of social movements, framing, and resource mobilization (c12_soc_cbse_01_001, c12_soc_cbse_01_002, c12_soc_cbse_01_003, c12_soc_cbse_01_004).  
- Historical concepts of institutional change, technological determinism, and policy continuity (c11_hist_cbse_01_005, c11_hist_cbse_01_009, c11_hist_cbse_01_010).  
- Political‑science concepts of policy feedback, interest‑group liberalism, and constitutional doctrine of property rights (Article 300A) (c11_pol_cbse_01_001, c11_pol_cbse_01_002).  

The question set requires students to decide whether the satellite tool amplifies existing political opportunities, alters the sociological basis of protest, or merely reflects a historical trajectory of technocratic state‑farmer interaction.

(E) How does the constitutional doctrine of property rights (Article 300A) influence the state’s ability to intervene in agricultural markets via tools like the satellite‑NDVI portal?

Tata Steel plans to acquire a European steel maker for an enterprise value of USD 12 billion. The acquisition is financed by: (i) USD 8 billion of 8% fixed‑rate debentures, (ii) USD 1 billion of 6% cumulative preference shares subscribed by Tata Sons Ltd., (iii) another USD 1 billion of 6% cumulative preference shares subscribed by Tata Steel, (iv) USD 1 billion of internal accruals, and (v) a fresh equity issue of USD 1 billion at a face value of ₹10 per share. The corporate tax rate is 30%. Post‑acquisition EBIT is expected to be USD 2 billion. The existing equity capital before the deal consists of 100 million equity shares of ₹10 each, and the new equity issue is priced at par.

(E) Calculate the degree of financial leverage (DFL) and the interest coverage ratio for the levered capital structure, and interpret their significance.

The Sharma family lives in a low‑lying village of Assam that experiences severe flooding every monsoon. Their annual household income is ₹6,00,000 (₹50,000/month). They own a pucca house valued at ₹12,00,000 on a 5‑decimal plot. The state government, under Article 39 of the Directive Principles (c11_pol_sci_cbse_01_004), offers a flood‑relief package: temporary shelter for up to 3 months and a one‑time cash assistance of ₹1,50,000 for households that voluntarily relocate to higher ground. Alternatively, the family can avail a low‑interest loan (6% p.a.) from a rural bank to raise the house foundation by 1.5 m, estimated cost ₹4,00,000, repayable in 5 years. The monsoon is expected to start in 45 days. The family has two earning members (father, mother), two school‑going children, and elderly parents requiring ground‑floor access. They have ₹2,00,000 in liquid savings and can allocate at most ₹30,000/month toward loan repayment without compromising children’s education. Using the disaster risk map (c11_geo_cbse_01_009), the probability of inundation >1 m in the next 5 years is 0.6. Identify the decision type, apply the decision‑making steps, and evaluate consequences if a step is omitted.

(A) Which decision‑making type (routine, strategic, crisis, technical) best describes the Sharma family’s choice between house elevation and government relocation?

In 2024 the Ministry of Housing launched a pilot in Bengaluru using an AI‑based natural‑language model to scan 12,000 online rental advertisements for caste‑biased phrasing (e.g., “prefer Brahmin families”, “no SC/ST tenants”). The model flagged 240 ads (2.0%). A parallel survey of 1,500 tenants showed that 48 households (3.2%) reported experiencing discrimination in the past year, of which 30 had encountered the exact phrasing flagged by the AI. The government claims the tool applies universal anti‑discrimination principles derived from the U.S. Fair Housing Act, while activists argue it ignores caste‑specific sensitivities embedded in Indian customary law and the Constitution’s Article 15. Data: flagged ads = 240; total ads = 12,000; discriminatory experiences reported = 48; exact‑match experiences = 30.

(B) Calculate the proportion of flagged ads that corresponded to actual discriminatory experiences reported by tenants.

Combine concepts from (Financial Management cycle: Plan → Control → Evaluate) with this node's resource classification. A Delhi family (dual income ₹1.2L/month, one child) has been "saving whatever remains" for 3 years — ₹12 lakh accumulated in savings account (3% interest). They now want to buy a ₹25 lakh car in 2 years. Current resource audit: Human — father's data analytics skill (unused), mother's HR certification (unused), child's coding hobby (human); Material — ₹12L savings, ₹50k/month potential surplus, old car worth ₹3L; Community — company car lease policy (father's firm), metro connectivity, free Coursera access via company. Apply the Plan-Control-Evaluate cycle to redesign their resource optimisation.

A multinational electronics firm plans to establish a 5 GW/year solar‑PV module fab in Rajasthan’s Jaipur district. The site offers access to high‑purity silica sand (SiO₂ ≥ 99.8 %) from the Thar Desert, average annual solar irradiance of 6.5 kWh m⁻² day⁻¹, and a semi‑arid climate with temperature range 5‑45 °C. The state government provides a capital subsidy of 20 % on plant machinery (₹ 4000 crore machinery cost) and a 10‑year tax holiday on profits. Labour laws require payment of minimum wages (₹ 18 000 per month) and provision of skill‑development cess of 2 % of wages. The firm must decide location based on (i) raw‑material transport cost (silica sand mining 150 km away, rail rate ₹ 1.2 ton⁻¹ km⁻¹), (ii) energy cost for the fab (electricity ₹ 5.5 kWh⁻¹, estimated consumption 2 MWh per ton of modules), and (iii) projected revenue (selling price ₹ 180 per Wp, capacity utilization 85 %). Using break‑even analysis, the firm needs to compute annual fixed cost (including depreciation of machinery over 10 years, zero salvage), variable cost per ton, and the annual profit after tax holiday period.

(E) Using variable cost per ton (raw material + electricity + labour) and the annual output from Part A, compute the break‑even selling price per Wp (assuming 1 Wp ≈ 1 g Si) after the tax‑holiday period, given that the firm requires a 12 % post‑tax profit margin on total cost.

In 2023, a coalition of Dalit and Adivasi NGOs files a Supreme Court PIL challenging the exclusion of fortified millet‑based PDS rations from certain tribal districts, arguing that the omission violates Article 21 (right to life) and the Directive Principle of improving nutrition. The PDS in these districts continues to distribute plain rice and wheat, while pilot programs in neighboring states distribute iron‑fortified pearl millet (bajra) and zinc‑fortified sorghum (jowar) developed under a public‑private biotech initiative. The NGOs present data showing a 18 % prevalence of anemia among women aged 15‑49 in the excluded districts versus 9 % in fortified‑pilot districts. The government counters that fortification raises procurement costs and that states have discretion under the National Food Security Act (NFSA) to choose commodities. The Court must decide whether the denial of fortified grains constitutes a denial of the right to adequate nutrition, and whether biotech‑fortified grains fall within the PDS’s statutory scope. Students must analyse the sociological (caste/tribe), technological (biotech fortification), legal (right to food), and economic (cost‑benefit) dimensions.

(E) Which biotechnological advancement enables the fortification of pearl millet with iron without altering its agronomic traits, and what sociological implication does this have for adoption in PDS?

A metabolic pathway contains two intermediates, X and Y, whose concentrations (in mol L⁻¹) jointly determine the rate of a downstream reaction according to the rate law \(v = k [X][Y]\), where \(k = 2.5×10^{3}\ \text{L}^2\text{mol}^{-2}\text{s}^{-1}\). The set of all possible positive concentrations forms a group under ordinary multiplication: the identity element corresponds to a concentration of 1 M (reference state), and the inverse of a concentration \(c\) is \(1/c\). The value of \(k\) is obtained from transition‑state theory, which depends on the activation energy \(E_a = 55\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) (chemistry). The pathway is regulated by a transcriptional feedback loop where the concentration of a protein product P evolves as \(\frac{dP}{dt}= rP\) with \(r=0.03\ \text{min}^{-1}\) (biology). Students must (i) identify the identity element for multiplication on \(\mathbb{R}^+\), (ii) compute the inverse of a given concentration, (iii) verify associativity and commutativity, (iv) calculate the concentration of X required to achieve a target reaction rate when Y is fixed, and (v) determine the time needed for the protein level to increase by a factor of \(e^{4}\).

(C) Prove that multiplication on \(\mathbb{R}^{+}\) is associative and commutative.

At a national youth poetry slam in Lucknow, a performer presents a piece titled “The Broken Ladder”. The poem opens with tactile imagery: “Cold iron rails bite my palms as I climb, each rung slick with oil of deceit.” Visual imagery follows: “Above, a gilded platform glows, inaccessible, while below, mud‑streaked feet shuffle in perpetual dusk.” The central metaphor runs through the poem: “Society is a ladder where the privileged stand on polished steel, the marginalized clutch at rotting wood.” The performer cites recent NSSO data: the top 10 % of households hold 57 % of national wealth, while the bottom 20 % survive on less than ₹1,200 per month. Using concepts of imagery (tactile, visual, olfactory), metaphor (simple, extended, mixed) and sociological theories of social stratification (The Growth Of The Working Class) together with economic indicators of poverty (Autonomous Transactions In The Balance Of Payments (Bop)), analyze how the poetic devices illuminate structural inequality and motivate audience reflection on redistributive policies. Relate the tactile imagery to the physical experience of low‑wage labour and the metaphor to the Weberian concept of life chances.

(C) Explain how the tactile imagery of cold, biting iron rails conveys the physical hardship of low‑wage labour, linking to the economic concept of poverty (Autonomous Transactions In The Balance Of Payments (Bop)).

In 2025, the Pacific Island nation of Kiribati faces imminent submersion due to sea‑level rise. The government launches a “Resettlement Rattrap” program: families receive cash incentives to relocate to higher‑ground inland plots, but the funds are disbursed only after participants complete mandatory reforestation workshops and sign contracts agreeing to labor on government‑run sea‑wall construction for two years. A UN‑commissioned study notes: (i) 60 % of households accepted the offer, citing “unwonted joy” at the prospect of secure land; (ii) 25 % dropped out after six months, reporting that the labor contracts felt like an “impenetrable prison”; (iii) among completers, average annual income rose from FJD 1,200 to FJD 3,500, yet 40 % reported renewed “hunger gleamed in his eyes” due to delayed wage payments; (iv) satellite imagery shows a 15 % increase in vegetation cover in resettlement zones. Using the concepts of plot and narrative structure, setting and atmosphere, and theme from “The Rattrap,” alongside relevant historical, political‑scientific, and geographical insights, evaluate whether the program constitutes a genuine humanitarian rattrap or a coercive one.

(E) Compose a one‑sentence thematic statement that links the program’s outcome to the central metaphor of the world as a rattrap, using textual evidence.

A drone flies with a velocity of 25 m/s at an angle of 53° above the horizontal towards the north-east. Resolve the velocity into eastward (x) and northward (y) components. Take cos53° = 0.6, sin53° = 0.8.

A sociologist surveys 1,000 workers in a metropolitan city: 300 in a public sector steel plant (permanent), 200 in a private auto ancillary unit (150 permanent, 50 contract), 300 home-based garment workers (piece-rate), 200 casual construction workers. Estimate the maximum potential union membership if: (a) all public sector permanents are unionised (typical density 80%), (b) private sector permanents at 40%, (c) contract workers at 5% (legal barriers), (d) home-based at 2% (no common employer), (e) casual at 1%. Show calculations and interpret the result for union density.

Given the following grouped data of annual rainfall (cm) for 30 years: 0-20: 3, 20-40: 5, 40-60: 12, 60-80: 7, 80-100: 3. Construct the "less than" cumulative frequency table and state the coordinates of the first two points to plot.

A nationwide survey by the Ministry of Health in early 2025 revealed that 22% of packaged “fortified” snack foods sold in urban markets contained undeclared allergens (peanut traces) due to cross‑contamination in shared manufacturing lines. The label claimed the product was “peanut‑free” based on supplier declarations, but testing showed detectable levels (>5 ppm). A parent from Jaipur filed a complaint after her child suffered an anaphylactic reaction, alleging violation of the Right to Safety (protection against hazardous goods). Simultaneously, a nutrition scientist argued that the fortification program aimed to combat micronutrient deficiencies (linked to biology concepts of metabolism) was being undermined by lax labeling enforcement. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) cited insufficient resources for random testing and relied on self‑certification by manufacturers. The case highlighted intersections of consumer rights, public health biology (nutrient metabolism, allergenicity), and accounting (cost of compliance vs. testing).

(D) Discuss how the fortification initiative’s goal (addressing micronutrient deficiency) creates a tension with the Right to Safety when labeling failures occur, referencing the biological concept of metabolism (Growth In Living Organisms).

A student attempts directed differentiation of hiPSCs to hepatocytes but gets <5% ALB+ cells at Day 20. Their protocol: Day 0-3: Activin A 100 ng/mL (DE); Day 3-6: FGF2 20 ng/mL + BMP4 10 ng/mL (hepatic specification); Day 6-20: HGF 20 ng/mL + Oncostatin M 10 ng/mL (maturation). Identify two likely errors in the *specification phase* (Day 3-6) based on developmental biology and propose corrected factors with concentrations.

In a school laboratory experiment, Rahul sets up three test tubes containing iron nails: Tube 1 has dry air, Tube 2 has water with dissolved oxygen, and Tube 3 has boiled water covered with an oil layer. Predict which tube will show rusting of the nail after 5 days and provide the chemical reasoning for why the other two tubes will not rust.

A 28‑year‑old woman in a remote village registers for the Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA) at 5 weeks gestation. She receives weekly folic acid (5 mg) tablets and is scheduled for an ultrasound at 8 weeks. The state has recently amended the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act, 1971 to permit termination up to 20 weeks for fetal anomalies diagnosed after 12 weeks. Baseline incidence of neural tube defects (NTDs) in the population is 1 per 1000 births. Folic acid supplementation reduces NTD risk by 70 % when taken periconceptionally. The embryo is currently undergoing organogenesis. Using this information, answer the following.

(E) A rural health worker lacks portable ultrasound devices. Discuss how this limitation affects early detection of congenital anomalies and propose a policy‑level solution linking to the PMSMA framework.

During a declassified NATO exercise, historians reveal that a covert WAN linked Washington, London, and Bonn in the 1960s used one‑time pad (OTP) keys distributed via diplomatic pouches. The network employed leased telephone lines (guided media) with analog modems, and each node ran a custom client‑server application that encrypted/decrypted messages using the OTP. Economists note that the OTP program consumed 0.3 % of the defense budget, reflecting a trade‑off between information security and fiscal constraints. Present‑day analysts propose replacing the OTP with AES‑256‑GCM over fiber‑optic links, citing lower operational cost and comparable security. Students must assess how historical network security practices (encryption, key distribution, media) intersect with Cold‑War political decisions and economic evaluation.

(C) Which network device would have been used at each node to convert digital OTP‑encrypted signals to analog for transmission over telephone lines, and what is its modern equivalent?

Using the outcome of the 1980s Chipko movement’s reliance on local dialects for mobilization, predict a likely community response if the podcast is produced exclusively in Hindi without local language adaptation.

In a state election, a sitting MLA publicly endorses a controversial infrastructure project that would displace a tribal community to make way for a highway. Privately, the MLA believes the project violates constitutional protections for tribal land (Article 244) and will exacerbate socioeconomic inequality. However, a real‑estate firm offers the MLA a ₹2 crore campaign donation contingent on public support. After delivering a televised speech in favor of the project, the MLA notices rising protests on social media and receives criticism from civil‑society groups. The MLA now feels uneasy about the inconsistency between the public endorsement and private beliefs, especially as the donation has not yet been transferred. Using Festinger and Carlsmith’s insufficient justification paradigm, predict how the MLA’s attitude toward the project is likely to shift and identify the psychological mechanisms at play.

(A) Identify the two dissonant cognitions experienced by the MLA after the public endorsement.

Design a hypothetical village-level survey to investigate why female literacy in a specific district lags 20 percentage points behind the state average. List three key variables you would measure, the social groups you would compare, and one qualitative method you would use to capture "hidden barriers" not visible in Census data.

A recent UN report (2024) projects that by 2050, 200 million people will be displaced due to climate‑related events, with the Indo‑Gangetic plain accounting for 45 % of this flow. The narrator‑protagonist, now a visiting professor at a Central University, is invited to chair a panel on “लिविंग हेरिटेज एंड क्लाइमेट पलायन” (Living Heritage & Climate Migration). During the panel, he shares a personal anecdote from his childhood in a flood‑prone village of Bihar, recalling how his grandmother’s oral stories (लोक कथाएँ) taught him resilience. He notes that 62 % of the audience are faculty from social sciences, 28 % are students, and 10 % are policymakers. A live poll shows that 54 % believe cultural narratives can motivate adaptation, while 31 % are skeptical. The protagonist reflects on his earlier self‑description in the text as “एक लेखक जो अपनी जड़ों से जुड़ा हुआ है”, questioning whether academic detachment dilutes that rootedness. Using this scenario, evaluate how the protagonist’s sense of identity, motivation, and relationship to cultural heritage shift when confronted with macro‑level environmental crises, integrating concepts of cultural geography, psychology of place attachment, and historical patterns of oral tradition preservation.

(C) Identify the psychological construct that explains the protagonist’s heightened sense of belonging when recalling grandmother’s stories, and describe one measurable indicator used to assess it in research.

A farmer in Punjab has 4 hectares of land. He wants to adopt drip irrigation (technological reform) and avail a loan under the Kisan Credit Card scheme (institutional reform). The drip system costs ₹1.2 lakh per hectare. The KCC offers a loan limit of ₹1.6 lakh for his land size at 4% interest (with interest subvention). Calculate the maximum area he can bring under drip irrigation using *only* the KCC loan, and state one reason why he might still not adopt it fully.

A multinational tech conglomerate adopts a “shared leadership” model where five senior executives (CEO, CTO, CFO, CMO, COO) jointly report to a single chief diversity officer (CDO) who oversees strategic decisions. The board argues this mirrors ancient polyandrous unions, claiming it reduces conflict, pools expertise, and ensures gender‑balanced governance. Internal data shows a 12% rise in innovation patents after adoption, but female employees report a 15% increase in perceived workload due to mediating between executives. Using concepts of patriarchy, kinship economics, and wealth inequality, assess whether this model genuinely advances gender equity or reproduces hierarchical control.

(E) If the corporation were sued under Article 15(1) of the Indian Constitution for gender‑based discrimination, which argument would most likely succeed for the plaintiffs?

Fill in the blank: Agriculture in the Indian economy refers to the primary sector activity encompassing crop cultivation, livestock rearing, forestry, and fisheries that contributes to Gross Value Added (GVA), provides employment to nearly 43% of the workforce (PLFS 2022-23), ensures food security for 1.4 billion people, and supplies raw materials to agro-based industries, while its declining share in GVA (from 35% in 1990-91 to 18.3% in 2022-23) signals structural ______ toward services and industry.

In 2024 UNESCO launches the “Dream Archives” project in Bogotá, collecting personal dreams from 1,200 conflict‑affected campesinos to craft narrative‑based peace‑building workshops. A Portuguese ambassador (analogous to the story’s ambassador) funds the initiative, a Viennese clinical psychologist (Frau Frieda analogue) conducts dream‑interpretation sessions, a celebrated Colombian poet (Pablo Neruda analogue) provides lyrical framing for the dream transcripts, and a skeptical investigative journalist (the narrator) probes whether the project genuinely fosters reconciliation or exploits vulnerable hopes for donor funding. Preliminary data show: 68 % of participants report increased hope, 22 % feel pressured to conform to optimistic narratives, and funding totals €4.2 million. The project draws on Colombia’s historic diplomatic ties with Portugal (1950s cultural exchanges), employs soft‑power strategies, operates in Andean migration corridors, relies on participants’ confirmation bias, and taps into rural superstition about prophetic dreams.

(D) Using the concept of cognitive bias (confirmation bias) from psychology, explain how the participants’ hope increase (68 %) can be interpreted as both a coping mechanism and a potential source of exploitation in the Dream Archives.

The central government launches “Awaas Mitra,” a rental‑subsidy scheme for inter‑state migrant construction workers. Units are 30 m², rent capped at ₹ 3,500/month, located in peri‑urban industrial corridors. The scheme’s guidelines state: “A house provided under Awaas Mitra becomes a home when the worker experiences safety, dignity, and a sense of belonging.” Psychological surveys of 1,200 beneficiaries show 54 % report improved belongingness, 30 % report no change, and 16 % report decreased belongingness due to overcrowding. Economic data: subsidy covers 40 % of market rent; average monthly income of beneficiaries is ₹ 12,000. Using Deshpande’s primary theme, Maslow’s belongingness tier, and housing‑affordability principles, evaluate whether Awaas Mitra succeeds in turning shelters into homes for migrant workers.

(A) Recall the primary theme of Deshpande’s essay and state, in one sentence, how it maps onto the scheme’s definition of a home (safety, dignity, belonging).
A 500 W motor lifts a 100 kg load at constant velocity of 0.2 m/s. Find the force exerted by the motor and verify if the power is sufficient (ignore friction).

VaxiGen, a mid‑size pharmaceutical firm, is conducting a Phase‑III trial of its mRNA vaccine across 15 sites in India. Each site employs Clinical Research Associates (CRAs) who verify informed consent, monitor adverse events, and ensure protocol compliance. A supervisor oversees the CRAs, performing functions such as: (i) confirming that every CRA has completed mandatory GCP training before site activation, (ii) reviewing weekly safety reports, (iii) coordinating logistics for sample shipments, (iv) motivating CRAs who face long travel and high workload, (v) fostering a collaborative leadership style to integrate site investigators, data managers, and regulatory affairs, and (vi) addressing communication barriers arising from varied site‑specific SOPs. The firm has capitalized Rs. 120 crore of R&D expenditure, to be amortized over 5 years. Per‑capita income data shows significant disparity between states, influencing vaccine price sensitivity.

(C) Using Herzberg’s two‑factor theory (extension of motivation), classify “recognition for successful patient enrollment” as a motivator or hygiene factor and justify.

A 10 L stirred‑tank bioreactor is used for a fed‑batch CHO culture producing a recombinant protein in serum‑free medium. The initial glucose concentration is 5 mM. Cells consume glucose at a specific rate q_glc = 0.5 mmol gDCW⁻¹ h⁻¹ (where gDCW is gram dry cell weight). The culture reaches a viable cell density of 5 × 10⁶ cells mL⁻¹ at 48 h, with an average cell dry weight of 300 pg cell⁻¹. Lactate is produced stoichiometrically at 1 mol lactate per mol glucose consumed, and ammonia is generated from glutamine at a rate q_amm = 0.05 mmol gDCW⁻¹ h⁻¹. The objective is to keep glucose ≤ 20 mM (to avoid osmotic stress) and lactate ≤ 30 mM (to avoid inhibition) while maintaining pH ≈ 7.2 via base addition. Assume perfect mixing, no cell death, and that the feed solution contains 500 mM glucose. Calculate the required feed rate and the resulting lactate and ammonia concentrations at 72 h.

Answer the following sub‑parts, showing all steps and stating any assumptions.

(C) Determine the feed rate (in mL h⁻¹) of 500 mM glucose solution required to maintain glucose at 15 mM (set‑point) in the 10 L reactor, assuming glucose consumption rate from part B remains constant and neglecting glucose accumulation in the feed.

A program calculates compound interest for a savings account. Principal = ₹50000, annual rate = 8% (0.08), time = 3 years. The formula is A = P(1+r)^t. Write code using chained assignment for initial values, then compute amount and interest. Show how reassigning the rate variable to a string for display affects (or doesn't affect) the computed interest.

A school stores cubical boxes of chalk. Each box is a cube of side 15 cm. The storage shelf is a cube of side 1.5 m. How many chalk boxes can fit on the shelf if they are packed perfectly without gaps? (Assume boxes cannot be cut.)

A state pollution control board plans to evaluate nitrate contamination in the alluvial aquifers of District Y, which has witnessed rapid expansion of sugarcane cultivation over the past two decades. The board deploys a team to collect primary data using portable ion‑selective electrode sensors at 45 tube‑well locations, recording nitrate concentration (mg/L) and GPS coordinates. Simultaneously, they acquire secondary data: (i) annual groundwater quality reports from the Central Ground Water Board (CGWB) for 2018‑2023 providing district‑average nitrate levels, (ii) historical land‑use maps from the Survey of India (1995, 2005, 2015) showing area under sugarcane, and (iii) census data on village‑wise population and livestock density (2011). The sensor readings reveal a spatial pattern: wells adjacent to fields with >70 % sugarcane cover average 42 mg/L nitrate, while wells in mixed‑cropping zones average 18 mg/L. The CGWB reports list district‑average nitrate as 24 mg/L (2022). The team notes that sensor calibration drift could affect readings by ±5 %, CGWB data are based on annual grab samples, and land‑use maps are at 1:50,000 scale with possible classification errors. They intend to store the integrated dataset in a spatial database for trend analysis.

(B) Assess the validity of using CGWB district‑average nitrate levels (24 mg/L, 2022) to represent nitrate exposure for the 45 sampled tube‑wells.

The Ministry of Rural Development launches “Digital Saksharta Abhiyan” in 200 selected Gram Panchayats of State X, providing free smartphones and six‑month training on e‑governance portals to women aged 18‑45. Baseline data show that only 12% of women attend Gram Sabha meetings, while 68% own a mobile phone but use it mainly for calls. The program aims to raise attendance to ≥30% within one year. As a Class XII sociology student, you are tasked with designing a small‑scale project to evaluate whether the digital literacy intervention causally influences women’s participation in local governance. You must (i) formulate a research question, (ii) choose an appropriate method (survey, observation, or mixed), (iii) decide on a sampling strategy feasible within a two‑week fieldwork window, (iv) consider how historical patterns of women’s exclusion from public assemblies (e.g., Roman *matrona* limitations vs. later medieval guild participation) might shape current attitudes, and (v) examine how constitutional provisions for women’s reservation in Panchayats (Articles 243D/243T) interact with digital access to affect outcomes. Identify which sociological concepts guide each step and justify your choices with reference to the provided nodes.

(A) Formulate a single, clear research question that isolates the effect of the digital literacy training on women’s Gram Sabha attendance, controlling for pre‑existing mobile phone ownership.

A rural primary health centre in Rajasthan serves a population of 12,000, of which 18 % are adults aged ≥ 60 years. Recent screening shows 22 % of these elderly have type 2 diabetes mellitus. The health worker must design a culturally acceptable, low‑cost therapeutic diet using locally available millets (bajra, jowar, ragi) and pulses (moong, urad) that can be procured through the Public Distribution System (PDS) at subsidized rates. The diet must meet the following criteria for a 68‑year‑old woman weighing 58 kg, height 152 cm, lightly active (household chores): total energy ≈ 1,800 kcal/day, carbohydrates 50‑55 % of kcal, protein 15‑20 %, fat 25‑30 %, fiber ≥ 25 g/day, and glycemic load kept low by favoring low‑GI millets (bajra GI 54, jowar GI 62, ragi GI 68) and pulses (moong GI 30, urad GI 43). PDS provides bajra at INR 22/kg, jowar at INR 20/kg, ragi at INR 25/kg, moong dal at INR 70/kg, urad dal at INR 65/kg, and subsidized rice at INR 32/kg (but rice is higher GI). The worker also needs to consider seasonal availability: bajra and jowar are abundant in winter, ragi in monsoon. Using principles of therapeutic diet planning, calculate the energy requirement, macronutrient grams, propose a feasible daily menu (quantities in grams) that satisfies carbohydrate, fiber, and GI constraints, and estimate the daily cost based on PDS prices.

(B) Using the prescribed energy target of 1,800 kcal/day, calculate the grams of carbohydrate, protein, and fat required if carbohydrates provide 52 %, protein 18 %, and fat 30 % of total calories.

In early 2025, the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting commissions a retrospective exhibition *“Framing the Nation: Gemini Studios and the Construction of Post‑Independent India”* at the National Museum, New Delhi. The exhibition showcases restored prints of 1950s Gemini Studios newsreels and feature films that were produced under government sponsorship to promote ideals of scientific temper, secularism, and industrial progress. Curators note that the Studios’ extensive use of Pancake makeup was not merely aesthetic; it was deliberately employed to create a uniform, “modern” look for actors portraying scientists, engineers, and citizens in these propaganda pieces. Psychological research attached to the exhibition highlights that audiences exposed to uniformly made‑up faces exhibit heightened **confirmation bias**—they are more likely to accept the film’s ideological messages as factual because the lack of individual facial cues reduces cognitive dissonance and promotes perceived homogeneity of the message‑bearers. The Ajanta caves were excavated in two distinct phases separated by ~300 years. Explain how the differences between the Satavahana-phase caves (Caves 9, 10, 12, 13, 15A) and the Vakataka-phase caves (Caves 1, 2, 16, 17, 19, 26) reflect changes in Buddhist doctrine, artistic practice, and patronage.
Determine the vapor pressure of water above the solution when it contains the maximum allowable mass of glycerol from Part A and 0.15 mol of MgCl₂ (dissolved). Assume ideal solution behavior.

A startup plans to launch a mobile wallet targeting unbanked rural users. The product offers zero‑fee transfers, biometric authentication, and integrated micro‑insurance. Founders must choose a marketing philosophy that balances rapid user acquisition with societal inclusion. Preliminary market research estimates 500,000 potential users in the first year, with an anticipated conversion rate of 8 % if the wallet is promoted as a “financial empowerment tool” (Societal Marketing Concept) versus 4 % if promoted purely on low cost (Marketing Concept). The variable cost per user (server, support, compliance) is Rs. 20, and the fixed cost for platform development and licensing is Rs. 1,50,00,000. The founders expect to price the premium insurance add‑on at Rs. 150 per user per year, anticipating 30 % uptake. The bank’s accountant must prepare a marginal costing statement, compute contribution margin, and determine the price elasticity of demand for the wallet assuming a 10 % reduction in price (zero‑fee to Rs. 2 per transaction) yields a 12 % increase in adoption rate. Additionally, the economist must assess whether the project yields positive externalities measured by a 0.04 increase in the village’s financial inclusion index per 1,000 active users. Using the data, the team needs to (i) select the appropriate marketing philosophy, (ii) compute expected contribution, (iii) derive elasticity, (iv) evaluate the social impact metric, and (v) decide on a pricing strategy for the insurance add‑on using break‑even.

(A) Which marketing philosophy aligns best with the startup’s goal of rapid user acquisition while promoting financial inclusion?

A simplified model of an electric organ in a fish consists of N = 100 identical point charges q = +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (elementary charge) placed uniformly along a straight line of total length L = 2 cm, with spacing d = L/(N−1). The line lies along the x‑axis from x = −L/2 to x = +L/2. A test point P is located on the perpendicular bisector at a distance y = 5 mm from the line. (a) Derive an expression for the net electric field **E** at P due to the chain, exploiting symmetry. (b) Evaluate the magnitude of **E** numerically. (c) If the charges are instead alternating (+q, −q, +q, …) along the chain, determine the net field at P (express in terms of q, d, y, ε₀). (d) Estimate the metabolic energy required to maintain this charge arrangement assuming each charge separation costs 1 eV of work and the organ operates continuously for 1 hour. (e) Using the concept of electric flux, compute the flux through a circular disc of radius r = 3 mm centred at P and oriented perpendicular to the line (i.e., disc’s normal along the line).  
**CONCEPTS_COMBINED:**
**Physics:** c12_phy_cbse_01_004, c12_phy_cbse_01_005, c12_phy_cbse_01_003 (Superposition Principle for Electric Forces), c12_phy_cbse_01_007 (Electric Flux: Definition and Formula)  
**Math:** c11_math_cbse_02_005 (Functions), c11_math_cbse_02_010 (Algebra of Real Functions), c11_math_cbse_01_009 (Union of Sets: Definition and Properties) – to treat the set of charges as a union of subsets for alternating case.  
**Accounting:** c11_acc_cbse_01_006 (Branches of Accounting: Financial, Cost, Management) – for cost‑energy conversion.

(D) Estimate the metabolic energy required to maintain the charge separation in the uniform chain, assuming each elementary charge pair costs 1 eV of work to isolate, and the organ operates continuously for 1 hour. Express your answer in joules.

During a hypothetical zoonotic outbreak, India’s indigenous vaccine candidate shows 78 % efficacy. The government invokes compulsory licensing under Section 92 of the Patents Act, 1970, to produce 350 million doses domestically, earmarking 60 % for Indian citizens and 40 % for COVAX‑style global allocation. Simultaneously, the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) redirects ₹ 9 000 cr from missile‑development programmes to scale‑up vaccine manufacturing, arguing that vaccine security is a component of national security. The remaining vaccine R&D budget (₹ 2 100 cr) is allocated to adjuvant research. Global South nations criticize the move as “vaccine nationalism,” while domestic civil‑society groups praise the health‑security boost. Using concepts of state security, human security, intellectual property law, and opportunity cost, assess whether the diversion of defence funds to vaccine production satisfies the condition that state security measures must not undermine essential human‑security provisions.

(E) Propose a parliamentary oversight mechanism that requires a quarterly impact‑assessment report comparing the NSI loss from defence‑fund diversion to the HSI gain from vaccine production, and specify the statistical test that should be used to determine whether the HSI gain is statistically significant at α = 0.05 given a sample of 30 districts with mean HSI increase = 0.012 and SD = 0.004.

Combine the concept of function definition/call with a simple calculation. Write a function `calculate_simple_interest` that computes simple interest for a fixed principal of ₹5000, rate 8% per annum, and time 2 years, and prints the interest. Then call it once. Then modify the program to call it three times, each time printing the interest, and observe that the same calculation repeats. (Note: This example uses fixed values; parameters will be covered in the next node.)

A wearable ECG acquisition front‑end injects a 1 kHz sinusoidal current through a pair of dry electrodes to measure the thoracic impedance, which is modeled as a pure resistor R_skin ranging from 500 Ω (sweaty) to 2000 Ω (dry). The excitation voltage amplitude is fixed at V₀ = 5 V peak. Safety standards limit the average power dissipated in the skin to 10 mW to avoid thermal injury. The device is powered by a 3.7 V Li‑ion battery with capacity 200 mAh. Determine the instantaneous current, RMS current, power dissipation for the extreme skin resistances, verify safety compliance, and estimate the continuous operating time of the battery assuming the front‑end draws only this power. Link the power calculation to accounting of energy consumption (book‑keeping vs. accounting) and use set theory to categorize safe vs. unsafe resistance ranges.

(B) Compute the RMS current for R = 500 Ω and R = 2000 Ω.

NexusCommerce Ltd. (e-commerce marketplace) has complex capital structure as at 31-Mar-2026. Authorised: ₹2,000 Cr (200 Cr shares ₹10). Outstanding: 80 Cr equity shares (₹10 FV, fully paid). Securities Premium: ₹5,000 Cr. Convertible Debentures: 10 Cr CCDs of ₹1,000 each, 0% coupon, compulsory conversion into equity at ₹2,000/share (5 shares per CCD) on 30-Sep-2026. ESOP: 10 Cr options granted at ₹500 (vested 40%, unvested 60%). Buyback: Board approved buyback of 5 Cr shares at ₹2,500 (max ₹12,500 Cr) from free reserves; 3 Cr shares bought by 31-Mar-2026. Calls in Advance: 2 Cr shares (pre-IPO investors) paid final call ₹100 in advance. Forfeiture: 1 Cr shares forfeited last year (₹8 paid-up), reissued 50 Lakh at ₹1,500.
