He shows: (a) no daily routine, sleeps till 2 PM; (b) avoids eye contact, answers in one word; (c) cannot remember a 3-item shopping list; (d) expresses desire to work but has no skills. Design the *first month* (4 weeks) schedule assigning ONE core rehabilitation component per week. For each week, specify: (i) Component name, (ii) Two measurable session goals, (iii) Primary behavioural technique used, (iv) How progress is recorded.

A consortium plans a 5 km² solar‑powered desalination plant near Mundra, Gujarat, to supply 150 MLD (million litres per day) to industries and nearby villages. The site receives an average annual rainfall of 300 mm with a coefficient of variation (CV) of 0.4. Runoff coefficient for the rocky terrain is 0.15. Groundwater is saline; the plant will also harvest rainwater from its own rooftops (total roof area 0.5 km²) and from a 2 km² watershed upstream that includes agricultural fields (crop coefficient 0.6). The Gujarat‑Rajasthan water sharing agreement allocates 60 % of the seasonal flow of the Luni River to Gujarat. The plant’s capital cost is ₹1,200 crore, O&M cost 5 % of capital per annum, salvage value after 25 years is 10 % of capital, and depreciation follows straight‑line method. Using the data, evaluate the feasibility of meeting the plant’s water demand through rainwater harvesting and runoff, examine the legal basis for inter‑state water allocation, perform a simple financial appraisal, and propose a watershed‑based conservation plan.

(A) Calculate the effective annual freshwater volume (in million cubic metres, MCM) available from direct rainfall runoff over the 5 km² plant site.

A metal rod of length 0.6 m rotates in a horizontal plane about a vertical axis through one end with an angular speed of 20 rad/s. A uniform magnetic field of 0.8 T is directed vertically upward. Find the potential difference between the two ends of the rod. Which end is at higher potential?

A 2023 UNESCO report on urban youth spaces notes that 57 % of adolescents in Tier‑2 Indian cities frequent shopping arcades as primary leisure sites, associating them with identity formation and peer validation. Simultaneously, the National Sample Survey shows that only 31 % of youth from households earning <₹2.5 lakh/annum can afford regular arcade visits, revealing a stark consumption‑based divide. In *Going Places*, Sophie and Jansie walk along the street, Sophie gazing “far down the street” while dreaming of a boutique that would glitter under an “amber glow”. The arcade becomes a metaphorical threshold between her fantasized consumer‑identity and the working‑class reality of the wharf and the “solitary elm”. Leveraging concepts of consumer culture (history of retail evolution), social‑psychology of identity (self‑concept theory), and geography of retail gentrification, evaluate how the arcade functions as a site of both aspiration and exclusion in the narrative.

(B) Using self‑concept theory, analyse how Sophie’s imagined boutique influences her self‑esteem, and contrast this with Jansie’s self‑assessment as “earmarked for the biscuit factory”.

In 2027, a coalition government at the centre comprises four regional parties, each controlling a distinct fiscal zone (North, South, East, West). The coalition’s steering committee, dominated by the finance ministers of the two largest parties, functions like an informal syndicate that allocates 65% of the central plan budget to their respective states, while the remaining 35% is distributed among the smaller partners based on population. The committee also decides which ministries get extra‑budgetary allocations for flagship schemes, often overriding the parliamentary standing committees.  

Simultaneously, the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG) reports that 12% of the central plan expenditures lack proper utilization certificates, and the public accounts committee flags discrepancies in the timing of fund releases versus actual ground‑level spending. A constitutional expert argues that this mirrors the Congress Syndicate’s control over party funds and candidate selection during the 1960s, where a small elite directed resources to maintain electoral dominance.  

A team of political scientists proposes to study whether the coalition’s fiscal syndicate undermines cooperative federalism, using data from the Syndicate era (Congress controlled ~80% of party funds, parliamentary wing ~20%) and comparing it with the coalition’s current split (65/35). They also examine historical precedents of fiscal centralization in the Mauryan Empire where the king’s treasury dictated provincial revenues, and compare with the decentralized fiscal model of the Gupta period.  

Students must (i) quantify the degree of fiscal centralization, (ii) evaluate its impact on cooperative federalism, (iii) draw analogies with historical fiscal systems, (iv) assess audit shortcomings, and (v) recommend reforms that balance efficiency with equity.

(D) Identify the accounting gap in the coalition’s utilization certificates and propose a control mechanism based on and.

A Public Interest Litigation (PIL) challenges the 30‑day notice period under the Special Marriage Act, 1954, arguing it infringes on privacy (Article 21) and facilitates social opposition to inter‑caste, inter‑religious marriages. Data show that in 2023, 12 000 couples filed notices; 18 % withdrew due to family pressure, of which 70 % were hypergamous unions (woman marrying man of higher caste/income). Historical reference is made to the colonial‑era Act III of 1872, which allowed inter‑caste marriage without notice but was repealed after pressure from orthodox groups. Economic analysis estimates that each withdrawn notice results in an average loss of ₹2.5 lakhs in wedding‑related expenditure. The PIL cites the Bombay High Court’s 2020 ruling upholding the notice period as a “reasonable restriction” and references the Hammurabi Code’s marriage provisions as an early attempt to regulate marital contracts.

(D) Evaluate the judicial reasoning likely to uphold or strike down the notice period using horizontal power sharing (judiciary) and precedent on fundamental rights.

A plant biotechnology facility intends to scale up *Vitis vinifera* cell suspension culture from a 5 L shake‑flask to a 500 L stirred‑tank bioreactor for anthocyanin production. The shake‑flask operates at 120 rpm, giving an average shear rate γ̇ ≈ 10 s⁻¹ and a volumetric oxygen transfer coefficient (k_La) ≈ 15 h⁻¹. In the 500 L reactor, a Rushton turbine (diameter D = 0.5 m) runs at N = 40 rpm. Power number (Np) for Rushton turbine ≈ 5.0. Fluid density ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, viscosity η = 1.0 × 10⁻³ Pa·s. The oxygen solubility C* = 0.008 mol L⁻¹. Desired dissolved oxygen (DO) set‑point is 30 % of C*. The culture follows Monod kinetics for growth: μ = μ_max·S/(K_s+S) with μ_max = 0.04 h⁻¹, K_s = 0.2 g L⁻¹ (glucose), and feed glucose concentration S_f = 200 g L⁻¹. Anthocyanin production is growth‑associated with yield Y_P/X = 0.05 g g⁻¹. The inoculum cell density is X₀ = 0.5 g L⁻¹ (dry weight). Genetic instability becomes significant if the cumulative number of doublings exceeds 30.  
Using the data, answer the sub‑parts.

(C) Using the Monod model, compute the specific growth rate μ when glucose concentration S = 20 g L⁻¹. Then determine the biomass concentration X after 24 h assuming exponential growth (dX/dt = μX) with no substrate limitation (i.e., μ constant).

A research team wishes to quantify telomere length amplification in cancer cells using quantitative PCR (qPCR). They design primers that bind to the repeating TTAGGG motif. The PCR mixture contains Taq polymerase, dNTPs, Mg²⁺, and buffer. Each cycle consists of: denaturation at 95 °C (30 s), annealing at 60 °C (30 s), and extension at 72 °C (45 s). The fluorescence signal from a SYBR‑Green dye doubles with each successful amplification of a duplex.  
Assume:  
- The initial template is a single‑stranded telomeric oligonucleotide of 100 nt, present at 10⁹ copies per reaction.  
- Amplification efficiency is 90 % per cycle (i.e., each cycle yields 1.8‑fold increase in duplex number).  
- The free energy change for forming a phosphodiester bond during polymerization is ΔG° = −20 kJ mol⁻¹ (exergonic).  
- The annealing step follows the two‑state model: fraction annealed = 1 / (1 + exp[(ΔH − TΔS)/RT]), with ΔH = −250 kJ mol⁻¹, ΔS = −0.70 kJ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ for the primer‑template duplex.  
- The extension step rate constant k_ext follows Arrhenius: k = A·exp(−Ea/RT) with A = 1×10¹³ s⁻¹, Ea = 55 kJ mol⁻¹.  

Using the above, answer the following.

(A) After 25 PCR cycles, what is the theoretical number of double‑stranded telomeric amplicons assuming 90 % efficiency per cycle?

In 2025, a consortium of multinational mining corporations secures licences to extract rare‑earth elements (REEs) from the Bundelkhand region, spanning parts of Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh. The project involves open‑pit mining across 850 km², requiring the diversion of the Ken River and the clearing of dense teak forests that serve as critical habitat for the endangered Indian giant squirrel. Environmental impact assessments warn that the mining will lower the water table by 12 % in the surrounding watershed and release radioactive tailings (thorium) posing long‑term health risks. Local tribal communities (Gond and Kol) and a coalition of ex‑servicemen, led by a charismatic former paramilitary commander, declare a “Bundelkhand Protection Movement” (BPM). They invoke the legacy of Tantia Tope’s 1857‑58 guerrilla campaign, arguing that the state’s approval of the mining licences violates the principle of “jus in bello” (proportionality in conflict) and the Doctrine of Lapse‑style alienation of natural resources without consent. The state counters that the project will generate ₹1,30,000 crore in export earnings over 20 years, create 45,000 high‑tech jobs, and that the Union’s entry 54 (Banking) and entry 56 (Mines and Minerals) justify central oversight, citing national strategic mineral security.  
You are asked to assess whether the historical analogy to Tantia Tope’s leadership—marked by decentralized guerrilla warfare, reliance on local knowledge, and financing through looted treasuries and voluntary contributions—holds under modern concepts of resource geography, political legitimacy (social contract theory), and financing of insurgencies.

(B) Using the concept of “social contract” (Locke/Rousseau), evaluate whether the state’s approval of the REE mining licences without free, prior, and informed consent (FPIC) of the Gond and Kol tribes constitutes a breach of the contract, and identify which historical analogue from Tantia Tope’s campaign reflects a similar breach.

In the two-sector circular flow model, a student argues: "If firms pay ₹100 crore as wages, rent, and interest, but only ₹80 crore as profit, then total factor income is ₹180 crore, but households only receive ₹180 crore. Where does the extra ₹20 crore go if profit is only ₹80 crore?" Identify the student's conceptual error and explain the correct relationship between factor payments and factor incomes using the circular flow identity.

A research team plans to scale up production of a viral vaccine using Vero cells (anchorage‑dependent) on Cytodex‑1 microcarriers in a 5 L stirred‑tank bioreactor. Each microcarrier is a 150 µm diameter dextran bead with a surface area of 7.0 × 10⁻⁵ cm² per bead (provided by manufacturer). The target cell density is 2 × 10⁵ cells cm⁻² of carrier surface. The bioreactor will be run at 100 rpm, giving an average shear stress of ~2 Pa (safe for microcarriers). Glucose is the limiting nutrient, consumed according to Michaelis‑Menten kinetics: V = V_max·[S]/(K_m + [S]), with V_max = 1.2 mmol L⁻¹ h⁻¹ and K_m = 3 mM. The feed glucose concentration is 25 mM. Assume the culture volume remains constant and that glucose uptake is the sole growth‑limiting step, with a yield Y_X/S = 0.5 g cell dw g⁻¹ glucose (dry weight). The average dry weight of a Vero cell is 200 pg. Calculate: (i) number of microcarriers needed to achieve the target surface area, (ii) initial glucose consumption rate (mmol L⁻¹ h⁻¹), (iii) time to drop glucose from 25 mM to 5 mM if consumption stays at the initial rate, (iv) expected cell concentration (cells mL⁻¹) after that time, and (v) how doubling the agitation speed (to 200 rpm) would affect shear stress and whether it remains safe.

(E) Shear stress in a stirred tank scales roughly as τ ∝ ρ·N³·D². If agitation speed is doubled from 100 rpm to 200 rpm (same impeller diameter), by what factor does τ increase? Is the new τ likely still safe if the original τ was ~2 Pa?

A biotech startup wants to clone the human pre‑proinsulin gene (0.5 kb) into a plasmid backbone (3.0 kb) to express insulin in *E. coli* BL21. The plasmid must maintain a copy number of ~15–20 per cell to achieve a target intracellular insulin concentration of 50 mg L⁻¹ after 6 h induction. The host culture is grown in a 5 L shaken flask at 37 °C with a doubling time of 20 min. After transformation, plasmid DNA is isolated and analysed by agarose gel electrophoresis (1 % agarose, 100 V, 40 min run) to confirm insert size. The restriction enzyme EcoRI (recognising GAATTC) works optimally at pH 8.0 and 37 °C; its activity halves for every 5 °C deviation. The ligation reaction uses T4 DNA ligase requiring ATP (2 mM) and Mg²⁺ (10 mM).  
Using the data above, answer the following sub‑parts.

(C) EcoRI activity at 30 °C is ______ of its activity at 37 °C, given that activity halves for every 5 °C deviation from optimum.

The National Food Security Act (NFSA) provides 5 kg foodgrains/person/month at subsidized prices. Using Sen's capability framework, diagnose why resource delivery (grains allocated) ≠ capability expansion (nutrition security) for this group. A 0.2 kg hockey puck sliding at 10 m/s east strikes a stationary 0.3 kg puck. After collision, the 0.2 kg puck moves at 2 m/s at 30° north of east. Find the velocity (magnitude and direction) of the 0.3 kg puck. (Assume frictionless ice, no external forces).

A student sets up a loan spreadsheet for ₹2,00,000 at 12% for 3 years. She enters `=PMT(12%, 36, -200000, 0, 0)` and gets ₹6,642.89. Her friend says the rate should be 1% (12%/12). Who is correct? Explain the error and compute the correct monthly instalment.

In a study of 200 farmers, the following correlations are found:
- r(fertiliser use, crop yield) = +0.68
- r(fertiliser use, farmer education) = +0.52
- r(farmer education, crop yield) = +0.61
All significant at p < 0.01.
A policy brief states: "Since fertiliser use correlates 0.68 with yield, subsidising fertiliser will raise yields by 68%."
(a) Explain why the 68% claim is statistically invalid.
(b) Draw the three possible causal diagrams (DAGs) consistent with these three correlations.
(c) If farmer education is a confounder, what happens to the estimated effect of fertiliser on yield in a bivariate regression vs. a multivariate regression controlling for education?
(d) Suggest one instrumental variable for fertiliser use that could address endogeneity, and state the two conditions it must satisfy.

In 2024, the Indian Council of Historical Research (ICHR) launched a project examining how mid-20th century Hindi poets encoded socio-political realities through grammatical choices. Researchers analyzed Nagarjun's 1957 poem 'dfork ds cgkus', focusing on verb morphology in stanzas describing peasant exploitation. They found that 63% of verbs in these stanzas used imperfective aspect markers (-raha/-rahi), contrasting with only 22% in stanzas depicting natural beauty. Concurrently, linguistic anthropologists noted that imperfective aspect in Hindi conveys ongoing, unresolved actions without temporal closure—unlike perfective aspect (-a/-e) which implies completion. Historical records showed Nagarjun, as a parliamentary correspondent during the 1949 Constituent Assembly debates, documented heated exchanges where proponents of Sanskritized Hindi (like RV Pant) argued for linguistic unity via grammatical standardization, while advocates for regional inclusion (like SG Moppe) cited the expressive limitations of standardized forms for capturing lived experience. fMRI data from a 2023 study (n=180 Hindi speakers) revealed that stanzas with higher imperfective verb density triggered 29% greater activation in the anterior cingulate cortex—associated with processing unresolved social conflict—compared to stanzas dominated by perfective verbs. Critics of dialectal inclusivity in official language policy argue that such grammatical complexity hinders administrative efficiency, referencing Article 343's mandate for Hindi in Devanagari as the official language. Proponents counter that Article 29 protects linguistic diversity and that Nagarjun's grammatical choices demonstrate how aspectual nuance preserves socio-linguistic authenticity without compromising poetic universality—a balance reflected in the Eighth Schedule's expansion from 14 to 22 languages since 1950.

(E) Project the impact on the poem's thematic effectiveness if Nagarjun had replaced 50% of imperfective aspect verbs in exploitation stanzas with perfective aspect, using the scenario's neuroscientific and historical data to quantify changes in universality perception and linguistic limitation expression.

A hydrogen fuel cell car requires 5 kg of H₂ for a 500 km range. The H₂ is stored at 700 bar in a carbon-fiber tank (system density 40 g/L). Calculate: (a) tank volume needed, (b) energy stored (HHV), (c) if the fuel cell system efficiency is 60%, what is the usable energy in kWh? (1 kWh = 3.6 MJ)

In 1950‑51 India’s external trade was valued at **Rs. 1,214 crore**. By 2020‑21 it had risen to **Rs. 77,19,796 crore** (Table 8.1, NCERT). India’s government is negotiating a **comprehensive economic partnership** with the ASEAN bloc (similar to the RCEP framework) while simultaneously revisiting the stalled **EU‑India FTA**. Political‑science analysts argue that a vertical power‑sharing model (where sovereign states retain key fiscal competencies but delegate trade policy to a supranational secretariat) could accelerate ASEAN integration, echoing the EU’s own evolution.  

Using the data above, answer the following:

(B) Using the 2021‑22 regional shares, determine which region contributes the highest **net export surplus** (exports − imports) to India’s trade balance.

CryptoEdge Partners (profit-sharing 5:3:2 for X (India), Y (Singapore), Z (UAE)) dissolves on 30-Jun-2025. Deed silent on realisation expenses. A streaming platform plans a bilingual (Hindi‑English) web series adaptation of Premchand’s *Godaan* (1936). The producers wish to highlight secondary themes present in the novel: (i) the exploitative debt‑bondage system affecting farmers, (ii) the clash between agrarian traditionalism and nascent capitalist market forces, (iii) the role of women’s informal credit networks, and (iv) the influence of religious‑caste panchayats in dispute resolution. To ensure authenticity, the creative team consults historians, economists, and legal experts. They have access to: (a) district‑level land‑revenue records from 1930‑1945 showing average landholding of 2.3 acres per farmer and 38% of cultivators under debt; (b) RBI historical data indicating rural credit interest rates of 12‑18% per annum in the 1930s; (c) Supreme Court judgments on bonded labour (Article 23) and panchayat jurisprudence; (d) sociological studies on women’s self‑help groups (SHGs) in contemporary rural India. The task is to (1) map each secondary theme to relevant legal statutes and economic principles, (2) assess the feasibility of portraying these themes accurately within a 10‑episode format, and (3) suggest a viewer‑engagement strategy that links the narrative to current policy debates on farm loan waivers and the MGNREGA wage‑rate revision.

(C) Using the RBI historical rural credit interest rate range (12‑18% p.a.), compute the effective annual cost of a ₹1,000 loan over 3 years with compounding, and discuss how this economic burden reinforces the secondary theme of capitalist market forces impinging on traditional agrarian life.

A multidisciplinary think‑tank evaluates the effectiveness of Post‑Partition refugee rehabilitation through a case study of the Kamla Nehru Camp (est. 1949, East Delhi). They examine a rare manuscript version of “लज्जत ले`fr” recovered from the camp’s community centre, containing an additional stanza (stanza 4):  
*“जले‑से चिरौँती धूप में सुकून की किरण,  
खेत की मिट्टी में बसी है mother’s heartbeat,  
बच्चे की हँसी – थाली की खनक,  
पानी की धारा – जीवन की धड़कन.”*  
The team must:  
1. Identify **all five types of sensory imagery** (visual, auditory, tactile, gustatory, olfactory) and **at least two metaphors** in stanza 4.

3. Relate the sensory and metaphorical content to:  
   a. The **specific rehabilitation policy** that allocated **irrigated plots plus seed kits** to women-headed households.  
   b. The **constitutional guarantee** under Article 21 (right to dignified life) as interpreted by the Supreme Court in *Francis Coralie Mullin v. Administrator, Union Territory of Delhi* (1981).  
   c. The **geospatial characteristics** of the camp’s location – proximity to the Yamuna floodplain, soil texture (alluvial loam), and average annual rainfall (≈ 800 mm).  
4. Finally, assess whether the policy’s design (irrigated plots + seed kits) **optimally addresses** the sensory‑metaphoric needs expressed in the poem, suggesting **one evidence‑based improvement**.

(A) List **each of the five sensory images** present in stanza 4, indicating the Hindi phrase and the sense it appeals to.

In mid‑2028, India conducts an anti‑satellite (ASAT) missile test that destroys a defunct microsatellite at 800 km altitude, creating a debris cloud tracked by the U.S. Space Surveillance Network. Preliminary estimates show 120 trackable fragments (>10 cm) and an estimated 900 lethal‑sized fragments (1‑10 cm). Pakistan’s foreign ministry condemns the test as a destabilizing move, citing the potential threat to its own low‑earth‑orbit (LEO) communication satellites at 550 km altitude. Historians note parallels to the Cold War – U.S. Starfish Prime high‑altitude nuclear test (1962) which generated an artificial radiation belt that damaged several satellites. The government of Uttarakhand plans a digital twin of its micro‑grid serving the pilgrimage town of Kedarnath (altitude ≈ 3500 m, seasonal footfall ≈ 2 lakhs). The twin will simulate power flow, renewable generation, and load shedding to improve resilience against landslides and snowstorms. Architecture includes:
- Smart‑meter PAN: Each household’s Zigbee‑based meter (range ≤ 20 m) communicates with a home hub, which relays data via Bluetooth‑LE to a mobile app used by field engineers for on‑site maintenance.
- Local distribution LAN: Fibre‑to‑the‑home (FTTH) links in the town core connect smart inverters, battery storage, and a micro‑data centre in a star topology, using single‑mode fiber (≤ 2 km radius).
- Regional MAN: A microwave link network (24 GHz) connects the town’s micro‑data centre to the district‑level SCADA centre in Rudraprayag (≈ 45 km), traversing valleys and ridges; the link uses line‑of‑sight microwave towers on peaks.
- National WAN: An MPLS‑based leased line (via BSNL) connects the district SCADA centre to the national load‑dispatch centre in New Delhi (≈ 300 km), carrying real‑time twin simulation outputs for policy‑level grid balancing.
Historical constraints prohibit new ground‑based towers in sacred zones; political science inputs involve the Electricity Act 2003 and national renewable‑energy mandates; geographical inputs consider seismic zone V, snow accumulation, and avalanche corridors affecting tower placement.
Answer the sub‑parts below.

(A) Identify the network type for the Zigbee‑based communication between a household smart meter and its home hub, and state one security measure applicable at this layer.

An ISRO Cartosat-3 satellite (panchromatic camera, 0.25 m Ground Sampling Distance) images a school cricket pitch. The pitch is 20.12 m long (22 yards). How many pixels long will the pitch appear in the raw image? A farmer in the Tarai region (Uttarakhand) finds a buried dark horizon at 60 cm depth with thick organic matter, overlain by 60 cm of layered silt. The surface soil shows weak A-Bw-C. Explain the **polygenetic history** and its implication for **nutrient management**.
Given that India has a coastline of 7,516.6 km and 12 major ports, but the west coast has more ports than the east coast, explain why this asymmetry exists using physical geography. (APPLY level)

In the peri‑urban zone of Vidarbha (Maharashtra), 1,200 smallholder farmers cultivate cotton and soybean on plots averaging 0.8 ha. A recent viral WhatsApp forward claims that Bt‑cotton seeds cause infertility in livestock and cancer in consumers, leading to a 35 % drop in Bt‑cotton adoption over two kharif seasons. The state agriculture department has approved a new herbicide‑tolerant (HT) soybean variety, but extension workers report low farmer trust due to prior misinformation. Local data: literacy rate 78 %, smartphone penetration 62 %, average age of farm‑head 48 years, 22 % belong to Scheduled Tribes with distinct dialect. The district has functional Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) and a community radio station (90.8 MHz) broadcasting in Marathi and Gondi. You are tasked with designing an extension communication strategy using the SMCRE model, selecting appropriate teaching methods, applying principles of cultural relevance and problem‑solving orientation, and incorporating insights from belief‑formation psychology (cognitive dissonance, source credibility) and GM‑crop biology (protein expression, non‑target effects) to rebuild confidence and promote informed choice.

(E) Using belief‑formation psychology (cognitive dissonance and source credibility), explain why the WhatsApp forward was persuasive and design a two‑step intervention to reduce its impact, citing relevant nodes.

SolarGrid EPC Ltd., a Gujarat‑based engineering‑procurement‑construction firm, must train 40 site supervisors in advanced solar‑panel mounting techniques. Three off‑the‑job alternatives are under review:  
- **Vestibule training** – full‑scale mock‑up yard with actual mounting structures and torque tools; cost ₹2,00,000 per supervisor; expected to achieve a 90 % learning‑rate (i.e., each doubling of output reduces time per unit by 10 %).  
- **Lecture & demonstration** – expert talks plus video demos; cost ₹50,000 per supervisor; expected learning‑rate 96 % (4 % time reduction per doubling).  
- **Case‑study & simulation** – computerized simulation of mounting sequences; cost ₹80,000 per supervisor; expected learning‑rate 92 % (8 % time reduction per doubling).  

Current average time to mount one panel = 30 minutes; each supervisor oversees mounting of 200 panels per month. Labor cost per supervisor‑hour = ₹600. The firm faces a capital‑rationing limit of ₹30,00,000 for training expenditures this quarter. The company uses a hurdle rate of 2 % per month for project evaluation and applies variance analysis to compare actual vs. standard labor time after training.

(A) Determine which training method(s) satisfy the capital‑rationing constraint (total cost ≤ ₹30,00,000). Compute total cost for each method and state the feasible set.

In 2024 the United Nations launches a Global Child Mobility Initiative (GCMI) proposing a universal standard: children under 130 cm travel free on all public transport, verified by wearable biometric bands that report height in real time to transit authorities. Delegates from low‑income nations argue that the standard ignores variations in nutrition‑related growth, effectively penalising poorer children. Meanwhile, human‑rights lawyers warn that continuous biometric surveillance threatens privacy and could be repurposed for social‑control purposes. Tao Ying’s story—where she navigates a height‑based fare rule through split‑second judgments of conductor demeanor, flashbacks to her own childhood measurement, and a quiet act of maternal protection—offers a literary case study for examining how such policies intersect with authority, social norms, geographic space, and narrative form. Using the story’s three measurement scenes, its linear‑flashback structure, its setting, character, and theme, and integrating concepts from history (post‑1949 Chinese transport/hukou policies), political science (authority legitimacy), sociology (norms and deviance), and geography (urban transport equity), construct a multidimensional argument that (a) explains how the narrative structure reveals the arbitrariness of measurement‑based authority, (b) shows how the protagonist’s habitus mediates formal rules through informal norms, and (c) proposes a policy safeguard derived from the story’s insight that could be applied to the GCMI to protect vulnerable children.

(B) Explain how Tao Ying’s habitus, shaped by her factory‑canteen work (setting node), leads her to employ informal sociological norms (c12_soc_cbse_01_005) as a coping mechanism when confronted with the formal height‑based rule.

A biotech startup registered under Startup India claims ₹2 lakh profit in Year 1. If eligible for 3-year tax exemption, how much tax do they save assuming a 25% corporate tax rate, and what happens in Year 4?

BioPharma Ltd. issued 2,000 convertible debentures of ₹1,500 each on 01‑04‑2021, carrying a coupon of 6% p.a., convertible into equity shares at a conversion price of ₹30 per share (i.e., each debenture converts into 50 shares). The debentures are redeemable at par on 31‑03‑2026. On 01‑04‑2024 a new SEBI regulation (effective 01‑04‑2025) mandates that any company with a debt‑equity ratio > 0.8 must maintain a Debenture Redemption Reserve (DRR) of 25% of the outstanding debenture value, funded annually from profits. Concurrently, the market interest rate for similar debt has risen to 9% due to inflationary pressures (c10_eco_cbse_01_003), causing the debentures to quote at ₹1,200 (implied yield ~8.2%). The company’s articles allow redemption by purchase from the open market and also permit conversion into equity shares at any time before maturity. The CFO wishes to (a) avoid the DRR requirement by keeping debt‑equity ≤ 0.8, (b) minimise the present value of redemption cash outflows, and (c) maximise EPS. Relevant financials as of 31‑03‑2024: Equity share capital = ₹1,00,00,000 (10,00,000 shares of ₹10 each); Securities Premium = ₹20,00,000; Reserves & Surplus = ₹50,00,000; Outstanding long‑term loans (excluding these debentures) = ₹80,00,000 at 7% interest; EBIT = ₹1,20,00,000; Tax rate = 25%. Using the above, answer the sub‑parts.

(B) Assuming the company wants to avoid DRR by purchasing own debentures from the open market, determine the minimum number of debentures that must be bought back and cancelled at the market price of ₹1,200 each to bring the debt‑equity ratio down to exactly 0.80. Show calculations.

In 2023 the European Union debated a strategic partnership with ASEAN to counterbalance China’s Belt‑and‑Road Initiative (BRI). Policy‑makers referenced the ancient Silk‑Road trade network that linked Mesopotamian markets with East Asian economies (c11_hist_cbse_01_009), noting that long‑distance commerce thrived when intermediaries provided trust, standardised weights, and credit mechanisms. Contemporary accountants highlighted that measuring the economic impact of such blocs requires consolidating financial statements of multinational enterprises using the purchase‑method and tracking goodwill arising from cross‑border acquisitions (c11_acc_cbse_01_006). A hypothetical EU‑ASEAN joint venture plans to acquire a Singapore‑based logistics firm for €500 million. The fair value of identifiable net assets is €350 million. The venture expects annual synergies worth €80 million, growing at 3 % per year, discounted at 7 %.  
Using the data, answer the sub‑parts below.

(E) Assess whether the combined economic benefit of the acquisition (goodwill €150 M + PV of synergies €2,000 M) exceeds a strategic threshold of €2.2 bn, and comment on the implication for the EU‑ASEAN partnership’s goal of counterbalancing China’s BRI.

A avian predator (e.g., *Falco peregrinus*) hunts two insect prey types that differ in energy content and handling time. Prey A: energy E_A = 5 J, encounter rate λ_A = 0.8 s⁻¹, handling time h_A = 0.2 s. Prey B: E_B = 12 J, λ_B = 0.3 s⁻¹, h_B = 0.5 s. The predator can allocate a fraction p of its search time to patches rich in prey A and (1−p) to patches rich in prey B. Travel between patches incurs an average flight cost C_f = 0.05 J per meter, with average inter‑patch distance d = 10 m. The predator’s basal metabolic rate is B₀ = 2 J s⁻¹. Using the prey‑encounter model (Poisson process) and the energy budget equation, answer the following.

(E) If the predator’s population follows logistic growth with carrying capacity K_pred = 500 individuals km⁻² and intrinsic rate r_pred = 0.03 day⁻¹, estimate the time required to reach 90 % of K_pred starting from 10 individuals km⁻², using the net energy gain per individual from Part C as a proxy for r_pred (assume r_pred ∝ G).

India and Bangladesh aim to operationalize a 1,200 km inland waterway stretch on the Brahmaputra (from Dhubri to Sadiya) to move containerized textiles from Dhaka’s export zones to Assam’s manufacturing hubs. The waterway has Class VII navigability (minimum depth 2.8 m, bottom width 80 m) allowing 2,000 TEU barges. Average current speed is 2 km/h downstream, 0.5 km/h upstream. A proposed digital customs platform reduces clearance time from 48 hours to 6 hours at each border checkpoint (two checkpoints). Freight rate for barge transport is $0.80 per TEU‑km. Road alternative (via NH‑27) costs $1.50 per TEU‑km with 30 km/h average speed but incurs 15% transit loss due to theft and damage. The textile consignment value is $12 million per 1,000 TEU batch; inventory holding cost is 18% per annum. Using the data, assess the total logistics cost and time for a round‑trip (Dhaka → Assam → Dhaka) via waterway versus road, incorporating customs delay, and recommend the optimal mode under a carbon‑tax of $25 per tonne CO₂ (barge emits 12 g CO₂/TEU‑km, truck emits 85 g CO₂/TEU‑km).

(B) Calculate the total freight cost (in USD) for a round‑trip of 1,000 TEU via waterway, using the rate $0.80 per TEU‑km.

A typical LPG cylinder contains mostly n-butane (C₄H₁₀). Write the balanced equation for its complete combustion. If 11.6 g of butane is burnt, what volume of CO₂ is produced at STP? (Molar volume at STP = 22.4 L/mol)

Two neighboring rural districts in Madhya Pradesh have identical roads and electricity grids. District A has full 4G telecom and high-speed internet coverage, while District B has only basic voice-call telephone coverage. Over five years, District A experiences 40% higher growth in small retail businesses and digital banking transactions. Analyze why this economic divergence occurred despite both districts having physical roads and power.

In 2025 the microstate of **Veridia**, a digital‑hub island nation of 9 000 residents, passes the **Unified Code Act**, mandating that by the next academic year all tertiary‑level courses be delivered exclusively in **Globish**, a constructed lingua‑franca used in international tech firms. Veridia’s indigenous tongue **Veridi**, spoken by 22 % of the population and used in local governance, literature, and oral tradition, is to be phased out from public institutions. The narrative follows **Professor Arin**, a 58‑year‑old Veridi linguist, delivering what she anticipates will be her final Veridi lecture to a mixed cohort of 18 computer‑science students. Attending are:  
- **SysAdmin Leta**, who maintains the university’s legacy Veridi‑encoded servers and remarks, “If the code dies, the culture crashes.”  
- **Student Jorn**, a first‑year who codes in Veridi for fun but worries about job prospects abroad, saying, “I’ll learn Globish; I’ll keep Veridi for my grandparents.”  
- **Old Councilor Tomas**, a former parliament member who sits quietly, holding a 1999 Veridi‑Globish phrasebook from the last language‑rights referendum.  
- The **Minister of Innovation**, who observes the lecture with a tablet logging attendance and compliance.  

Using textual evidence from the scenario, analyze the supporting characters (SysAdmin Leta, Student Jorn, Old Councilor Tomas) in relation to M. Hamel and the villagers, and connect their responses to (a) the historical spread of colonial lingua‑franca in Asia‑Africa, (b) political‑science theories of digital sovereignty and language governance, and (c) geographical notions of island isolation and cultural diffusion.

(C) Explain how Old Councilor Tomas’s silent attendance and his possession of a 1999 Veridi‑Globish phrasebook echo the historical imposition of colonial lingua‑franca in Africa and Asia, citing one concept from the History node.

In 2025, the Ministry of Education launches an AI‑driven subtitle project that automatically translates live parliamentary debates from Hindi into all 22 scheduled languages, aiming to improve accessibility. Critics argue that the AI, trained predominantly on corpora from North‑Indian Hindi sources, systematically mis‑translates idioms from Dravidian languages, flattening regional nuance. A parliamentary committee hearing is held in a retrofitted television studio resembling the set of "Broken Images": a central chair, a semi‑circular table, a plasma screen displaying the Eliot line in real time as subtitles scroll beneath it, and several muted TV sets showing regional news channels. Witnesses include: (1) a historian citing the 1935 Government of India Act’s language provisions and the post‑independent Three‑Language Formula; (2) a political scientist referencing Article 350A (mother‑tongue instruction at primary stage) and recent Supreme Court rulings on AI bias; (3) a psychologist presenting fMRI data showing that bilingual individuals exhibit heightened activity in the anterior cingulate cortex when encountering mistranslated cultural metaphors, indicating emotional distress; (4) a sociologist noting that English‑language media enjoys 78% of national advertising revenue, while regional language channels combined receive only 12%, affecting perceptions of linguistic worth. The committee chair, a bilingual woman who anchors a national news channel, opens with a monologue lifted from Manjula’s soliloquy, reflecting on how her English‑anchored persona feels like a “heap of broken images” when she witnesses her mother‑tongue being reduced to algorithmic errors. Using this scenario, answer the sub‑parts below.

(B) Analyze the use of the Eliot line on the plasma screen as a metaphor that evolves in real time as subtitles appear, and determine how this dynamic metaphor reflects the historical progression from colonial language policy to contemporary AI bias.

A state education board rolls out “Vidya Mitra”, a low‑bandwidth video‑conferencing app for grades 9‑12 in districts with <40 % internet penetration. The app allows text chat, emoji reactions, and breakout rooms. Teachers report that in certain tribal districts, students frequently use abusive language and target peers with memes that ridicule traditional attire, while in urban centres the same features are used for collaborative problem‑solving. As a consultant tasked with improving netiquette on the platform, you must: (i) link the observed aggression to psychological and geographic factors, (ii) evaluate whether the current chat moderation violates netiquette’s “respect” and “privacy” rules, (iii) design a lightweight AI‑assisted prompt that encourages respectful language without increasing bandwidth, and (iv) estimate the latency‑induced increase in message‑re‑transmission probability and its effect on perceived incivility.

(E) Synthesize the findings from Parts A‑D to propose a two‑tier intervention (psychological + technical) that reduces perceived incivility by at least 30 % without increasing average bandwidth usage per message by more than 5 %. Justify each tier with the relevant concept.

A geographer is analyzing temperature and wind data for a station in northern India (Delhi) across the year. A state government launches “Samriddhi Yojana”, a blockchain‑enabled conditional cash transfer (CCT) scheme targeting **nuclear families** with at least one child aged 0‑5 years. To receive ₹2,000 per month, families must upload monthly proof of (i) child’s school attendance (if ≥3 years) and (ii) a government‑approved health‑check‑up showing hemoglobin ≥11 g/dL and weight‑for‑height Z‑score ≥‑2. Funds are released via smart contracts on the 1st of each month; the state’s finance department follows **accrual basis accounting** and requires that expenditures be recorded when the obligation arises (i.e., at the start of the month). The scheme’s pilot covers 12,500 eligible nuclear families in District X. Baseline survey shows 18 % of children have hemoglobin <11 g/dL (anemia) and 12 % are wasted (WHZ <‑2). After six months, monitoring reports indicate anemia prevalence dropped to 10 % and wasting to 7 %. The state allocated ₹30 crore for the six‑month pilot, assuming full compliance.  
Using the data, answer the following sub‑parts.

(D) Assess whether the scheme’s financial allocation (₹30 crore) demonstrates the qualitative characteristic of “prudence” in accounting. Justify with reference to the scenario.

A group aims to edit the OsSPL14 gene in Oryza sativa using a Ti‑plasmid‑derived vector that carries a Cas9‑sgRNA cassette under a light‑inducible promoter (LIP). The vector also contains a hygromycin resistance gene (hpt) for selection. Agrobacterium tumefaciens strain carrying the vector is co‑cultured with rice callus. To enhance transformation, the callus is subjected to a series of square‑wave electric pulses (electroporation) before co‑culture. The pulse parameters are: pulse width τ = 0.5 ms, number of pulses n = 4, electrode spacing d = 0.3 cm, medium conductivity σ = 0.8 S m⁻¹, and relative permittivity ε_r = 80. The electric field E generated by a voltage V across the electrodes is E = V/d. The induced transmembrane voltage ΔΨ on a spherical protoplast of radius r = 6 µm is approximated by ΔΨ = 1.5·E·r·cosθ; for worst‑case (θ=0) ΔΨ_max = 1.5·E·r. Electroporation occurs when ΔΨ ≥ 1 V.  
The light‑inducible promoter activity follows a Hill equation: Activity = A_max·[I]^n / (K_I^n + [I]^n), where light intensity I is measured in µmol m⁻² s⁻¹, A_max = 1 (normalized), K_I = 50 µmol m⁻² s⁻¹, Hill coefficient n = 2.  
The T‑DNA transfer efficiency η_T (fraction of callus cells receiving at least one T‑DNA copy) is empirically related to the electroporation efficacy η_EP and promoter activity A by η_T = η_EP·A, where η_EP = 1−e^(−β·ΔΨ_max) with β = 0.8 V⁻¹.  
Using the data, answer the following:

(B) Calculate the minimum voltage V (in kV) that must be applied across the electrodes to achieve ΔΨ_max = 1 V (the electroporation threshold) for a protoplast of radius r = 6 µm and electrode spacing d = 0.3 cm.

A spacecraft in Earth orbit has a rectangular solar panel of dimensions **0.8 m × 0.5 m**. The panel is illuminated by sunlight, causing photoelectron emission that leaves the panel surface with a uniform positive charge density **σ = +2.0×10⁻⁶ C/m²**. Simultaneously, the spacecraft is bombarded by solar wind protons (charge +e) that strike the panel and embed, giving an additional uniform negative charge density **σₚ = –1.0×10⁻⁶ C/m²** (due to captured electrons neutralizing some protons). The net surface charge density is therefore **σ_net = σ + σₚ = +1.0×10⁻⁶ C/m²**.  
A micron‑sized dust grain (radius **r_d = 2 µm**, material density **ρ = 2500 kg/m³**) carrying a charge **q_d = –5.0×10⁻¹⁵ C** rests on the panel at a point **P** located **0.2 m** from the left edge and **0.15 m** from the bottom edge (origin at bottom‑left corner).  
Treat the charged panel as a continuous sheet; approximate its electric field near the surface as that of an infinite sheet: **E = σ_net/(2ε₀)** directed away from the surface (positive side).  
Using superposition of contributions from infinitesimal charge elements (or the sheet formula), answer: (A) net electric force on the dust grain, (B) position on the panel where the net force on a grain of opposite charge (+5×10⁻¹⁵ C) would be zero if the panel had a non‑uniform charge distribution consisting of two strips: left half σ_L = +2.0×10⁻⁶ C/m², right half σ_R = –1.0×10⁻⁶ C/m², (C) torque on a dipole (p = 4.0×10⁻²⁹ C·m) aligned along the panel’s width (y‑axis) placed at point P, (D) work done in lifting the grain vertically off the panel against electrostatic attraction, and (E) acceleration of the grain if it detaches and moves under the electrostatic force opposed by Stokes drag in the surrounding ultra‑high vacuum (effective drag coefficient **γ = 1.0×10⁻¹⁵ N·s/m**).  
Use **ε₀ = 8.85×10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²)**, **k = 9.0×10⁹ N·m²/C²**, and assume the grain remains close enough to the sheet that the infinite‑sheet approximation holds.

(D) Determine the work done by the electrostatic field in lifting the dust grain vertically off the panel surface to a height **h = 2 mm** (still within region where infinite‑sheet approximation holds).
Why does a statement scale "1 cm = 500 m" printed on a map become incorrect if the map is photocopied at 80% linear reduction?

The Chhattisgarh Tribal Development Corporation proposes to scale up Tasar (*Antheraea mylitta*) sericulture in the sal (*Shorea robusta*) and asan (*Terminalia tomentosa*) forests of Bastar. Each sal tree yields ~25 kg of leaves/year; each asan tree yields ~18 kg/year. A Tasar larva consumes ~0.6 g of leaf per day over a 30‑day larval stage. The target is to rear 2 million larvae per hectare per cycle. Tasar cocoons weigh ~1.5 g each with a silk ratio of 12 % (silk weight / cocoon weight). Tasar fibre has tenacity 2.8 g den⁻¹ and elongation 45 %. The project must comply with the Forest Rights Act, 2006 (FRA) – specifically Section 3(1)(i) for community forest rights – and the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 (regulating access to forest genetic resources). Anthropological surveys note that Gond and Baiga tribes have historically used Tasar silk for “pachra” (traditional loincloth) and “gatla” (ceremonial shawls).  
Answer the following.

(A) Calculate the total leaf biomass (kg) required per hectare to rear 2 million Tasar larvae for one cycle.

In 2023, a special economic zone (SEZ) in Mundra, Gujarat, attracted ₹18 000 crore investment for solar‑panel manufacturing, creating ~90 000 jobs. Recruitment drives targeted workers from Odisha and Chhattisgarh, offering ₹15 000‑₹18 000/month, 8‑hour shifts, and dormitory accommodation. However, only 40 % secured factory dorms; the rest settled in informal settlements on the SEZ periphery, paying ₹3 500‑₹5 000 for a 10 sq m tent‑like unit. Land acquisition for the SEZ displaced 12 000 agrarian households, who received compensation averaging ₹4 lakhs but lacked skills for factory jobs, pushing many into daily‑wage construction. The Gujarat Industrial Policy 2020 mandates that 20 % of SEZ jobs be reserved for local domiciled candidates, but enforcement is weak. Drawing on concepts of working‑class growth, informal housing, circular migration, land‑acquisition politics (horizontal power sharing), and comparative industrial town history (Manchester‑type mill towns), answer the following.

(E) Compare the socio‑spatial layout of the Mundra solar SEZ (factory core, worker dormitories, peripheral informal settlements) with that of 19th‑century Manchester mill towns (factory, company housing, worker slums). Which theoretical concept best captures the similarity in *informal* housing emergence despite differing periods?

A long‑duration spacecraft uses an aqueous solution of 2‑amino‑2‑methyl‑1‑propanol (AMP) as a CO₂ scrubber. AMP is a tertiary amine (structure: (CH₃)₂C(OH)CH₂NH₂? Actually AMP is 2‑amino‑2‑methyl‑1‑propanol: HO‑CH₂‑C(CH₃)(NH₂)‑CH₃). The scrubber operates at 298 K and 1 atm total pressure. CO₂ reacts with AMP to form a carbamate:  
2 AMP + CO₂ ⇌ AMP‑COO⁻ + AMPH⁺  
The equilibrium constant Kₚ at 298 K is 4.5 × 10³ atm⁻¹. The regeneration step (heating to 353 K) reverses the reaction; the enthalpy change ΔH° for carbamate formation is –45 kJ mol⁻¹ (assumed temperature‑independent). The spacecraft needs to remove 0.5 mol CO₂ per hour.  

Answer the following.

(E) Assertion (A): The IUPAC name of AMP contains the locant “1” for the hydroxyl group.  
Reason (R): In IUPAC nomenclature, the principal functional group is chosen based on the priority order –COOH > –SO₃H > –COOR > –COX > –CONH₂ > –CN > –CHO > –CO > –OH > –NH₂ > –C=C > –C≡C.  
Determine the correctness of A and R.

A 20‑year‑old college student, Maya, lives in a metropolitan city with her aging grandmother who raised her after her parents died in a car accident. Maya receives a prestigious internship offer at a Silicon Valley startup, offering a stipend of ₹60,000/month, remote work flexibility, and a potential pre‑placement offer (PPO) worth ₹12 lakhs per annum. However, her grandmother suffers from early‑stage dementia and requires daily supervision; hiring a professional caregiver would cost ₹25,000/month. Maya’s monthly expenses (food, transport, tuition) are ₹15,000. She feels guilty at the thought of leaving her grandmother alone, recalling her grandmother’s stories of sacrificing her own education to raise Maya’s mother. Maya spends evenings scrolling through photos of her grandmother’s youth, hearing the old radio play songs from the 1970s, and experiences a tightness in her chest whenever she thinks about the internship. She wonders whether her inertia is due to fear of failure, loyalty, or a deeper sense of self‑identity tied to caregiving.

(C) Apply the sociological concept of role conflict (The Growth Of Sociology In India) to Maya’s situation. Identify the two opposing roles and the type of conflict.

The story uses three distinct measuring moments: the bus's painted finger (1.10 m), the temple's "earthworm" line, and Tao Ying's home tape measure (1.09 m). Analyze how each measuring tool constructs a different atmosphere and what each reveals about who holds power over definition.

A series LCR circuit has R = 40 Ω, X_L = 70 Ω, X_C = 30 Ω, and is connected to a 230 V, 50 Hz RMS supply. Calculate: (a) the impedance Z, (b) the RMS current, (c) the power factor, and (d) the average power dissipated.

A satellite’s solar array delivers a three‑phase AC voltage (line‑to‑line 28 V rms, 400 Hz) to a full‑wave rectifier built with six SiC diodes (forward drop 1.5 V, negligible reverse current) arranged in a three‑phase bridge (effectively two diodes conduct per phase). Assume ideal transformer, no filtering, and that the three‑phase waveforms are 120° apart.

(A) Find the required transformer turns ratio (secondary:primary) so that the peak phase voltage after transformation yields the needed DC level.

Anju's house is 3 km east and 4 km north of her school. Her friend Binny's house is 5 km east and 12 km north of the same school. If Anju walks directly to Binny's house (shortest path), how far does she walk? Give answer in metres.

Read the case and answer: "Mr. Sharma hired a packers-movers service to transport household goods from Delhi to Mumbai for ₹80,000. A deep‑space probe requires a steady electrical power of 5 kW for its instruments and communication system. The power is generated by a compact U‑235 fission reactor coupled to thermoelectric converters with an overall efficiency of 5 %. Each fission of U‑235 (induced by a thermal neutron) yields on average 2.5 neutrons and releases energy via mass defect. Approximate masses:  m(U‑235)=235.0439 u, m(n)=1.008665 u, m(Ba‑141)=140.9144 u, m(Kr‑92)=91.9262 u. Use 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c² and 1 MeV = 1.602×10⁻¹³ J. The reactor operates at steady state (k=1).

(A) Calculate the energy released per fission of U‑235 using the given masses and mass‑energy equivalence.

The Ministry of Tribal Affairs launches a ₹120 crore, 18‑month “Digital Linguistic Survey” to document 37 endangered languages spoken by Gond, Baiga, and Kol communities in Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh. Field teams use a custom mobile app to record oral narratives, songs, and ritual chants. To accelerate interpretation, senior scholars consult classical Sanskrit texts (e.g., the Mahabharata, Puranas) to decode mythic symbols embedded in tribal folklore, arguing that these texts reveal a “shared civilizational core.” Activists from the Tribal Rights Forum contend that this approach imposes an external Brahmanical lens, echoing colonial orientalist constructions of tribals as “primitive yet mystic.” Simultaneously, a team of social anthropologists from the University of Hyderabad advocates a participatory methodology: co‑designing the survey with village elders, recording metadata on language use in daily life, and treating the communities as knowledge producers rather than subjects of extraction. The survey’s interim report shows 62 % of recorded narratives contain motifs traceable to Sanskrit epics, while 38 % are classified as “unique oral innovations.” The government cites the data to justify a new “Cultural Heritage Grant” scheme, whereas critics warn that privileging textual authority may undermine federal provisions for tribal autonomy under the Fifth Schedule.

(C) The anthropologists’ proposal to co‑design the survey with village elders reflects the methodological hallmark of which tradition?

Mithai Mitra, a heritage sweet‑shop in Jaipur, exports its signature “kesar pista barfi” to the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries. To prolong shelf‑life during transit, the manufacturer adds potassium metabisulphite (INS 224) at 0.02 % w/w as a preservative, releasing sulphur dioxide (SO₂) that inhibits microbial growth. Recent consignments were rejected at Saudi customs because the measured SO₂ exceeded the GCC limit of 100 mg/kg. The exporter notes that under the British‑era Saltpetre Act of 1804, similar preservatives were regulated for gunpowder, not food. Simultaneously, the WTO’s SPS Agreement permits members to set protective measures, but requires scientific justification and non‑discriminatory application. Consumer surveys in the GCC reveal that 55 % of buyers associate “sulphite‑free” labels with higher health safety, affecting purchase decisions. Sociologically, the rejection threatens the livelihood of ~200 artisans linked to the shop’s supply chain, raising concerns about the preservation of intangible culinary heritage. The firm must reformulate, navigate international trade rules, and address consumer perceptions while preserving cultural authenticity.

(D) If a consignment of barfi is found to contain 150 mg/kg SO₂, determine the legal consequence under the GCC’s food safety law (modeled on the UAE Federal Law No. 1 of 2002) for the exporter, assuming the offense is “import of food contrary to prescribed standards”.

EcoFusion LLP (partners P, Q, R sharing 4:3:3) admits S, a climate-finance specialist. New ratio 4:3:3:2 (total 12). S brings ₹40,00,000 for 2/12 share. Goodwill valued at 3 years’ purchase of super profit. Average profit = ₹15,00,000 (growing at 20% CAGR, modeled as exponential growth ). Capital employed = ₹80,00,000. NRR = 10%. Regulatory requirement (SEBI-like): minimum capital adequacy ratio = 15% of risk-weighted assets (RWA = ₹5,00,00,000). Revaluation surplus = ₹10,00,000. Accumulated reserves = ₹20,00,000. Existing capitals after revaluation/reserves: P ₹1,20,00,000, Q ₹90,00,000, R ₹90,00,000. Partners agree to adjust capitals proportionately by cash, but total capital must meet regulatory minimum. If proportionate total capital < regulatory minimum, partners must bring additional capital in new ratio.

(D) Adjust capitals to proportionate basis. Check regulatory capital adequacy: minimum capital = 15% of RWA (₹5,00,00,000) = ₹75,00,000. If proportionate total capital < ₹75L, additional capital needed in new ratio.

Bharat Conglomerates Ltd (listed, NSE/BSE) announces buyback of 1 crore equity shares (FV ₹2) at ₹450 via tender offer (SEBI route). Pre-buyback: Equity Capital ₹200 Cr (100 Cr shares); Securities Premium ₹500 Cr; General Reserve ₹1,200 Cr; Retained Earnings ₹800 Cr; 9% Debentures ₹1,000 Cr; Term Loan ₹500 Cr. Market price ₹380. Buyback tax (Sec 115QA): 20% on distributed income (buyback price - issue price). Shareholders: Promoters (60%, tax-exempt trust), FIIs (25%, treaty benefits), Retail (15%, 10% LTCG >₹1L). Company uses General Reserve + Securities Premium. Economic concepts: Signaling theory, Tax clientele effect (Per Capita Income (Pci) Of A State), Capital allocation efficiency vs. public facility investment (Public Facilities). CFO must: (a) verify Sec 68/SEBI limits, (b) compute buyback tax, (c) pass entries with CRR, (d) analyze post-buyback leverage & EPS accretion/dilution, (e) evaluate if buyback destroys value vs. capex (NPV ₹2,000 Cr project available).

(B) Compute buyback tax (Sec 115QA) liability. Issue price of shares bought back: ₹50 (weighted avg). Distributed income = (450-50)×1 Cr = ₹400 Cr. Tax @ 20% + surcharge 12% + cess 4%. Show journal entry for tax payment.

A 1000 L stirred‑tank bioreactor runs a fed‑batch culture of *E. coli* BL21(DE3) expressing a proinsulin precursor. Target cell density at induction is 15 g L⁻¹ (wet weight). Oxygen uptake rate per cell mass is qO₂ = 0.02 mmol O₂ g⁻¹ cells h⁻¹. Saturation dissolved oxygen concentration at 37 °C, 1 atm is C* = 8 mg L⁻¹ (≈ 0.25 mmol L⁻¹). The process must keep dissolved oxygen (CL) ≥ 40 % of C* to avoid oxygen limitation. Oxygen transfer follows OTR = kₗₐ·(C* – CL).  
Shear sensitivity of the plasmid imposes a maximum allowable shear rate γ_max = 100 s⁻¹. For a Rushton turbine, shear rate correlates with impeller speed N (rpm) as γ = k_s·N with k_s = 0.02 s⁻¹ rpm⁻¹.  
Metabolic overflow produces acetic acid at a rate r_H = 0.1 mmol H⁺ L⁻¹ h⁻¹. The culture is buffered with a phosphate system (pKₐ₂ = 7.20). Determine (a) the required kₗₐ, (b) the impeller speed to achieve this kₗₐ while staying below γ_max, (c) whether the resulting shear rate is safe, (d) the minimum total phosphate buffer concentration needed to limit pH drift to ≤ 0.05 units over 1 h, and (e) the expected volumetric proinsulin yield assuming a yield coefficient Yₚ/ₓ = 0.5 mg protein g⁻¹ cells and a 48 h production phase.

(B) Using the correlation kₗₐ = 0.001·N² (with N in rpm, kₗₐ in h⁻¹), determine the impeller speed N needed to achieve the kₗₐ from Part A.

A tokamak fusion power plant aims to deliver **500 MW_th** of thermal power from D‑T fusion. Each D‑T reaction: ²H + ³H → ⁴He (4.002603 u) + n (1.008665 u) releases 17.6 MeV. The plant operates continuously. Natural deuterium abundance is 0.015 % in hydrogen; tritium is bred from lithium‑6 via n + ⁶Li → ⁴He + ³H (Q = 4.78 MeV). The lithium‑6 blanket must achieve a tritium breeding ratio (TBR) ≥ 1.10 to sustain fuel supply.

(A) Using the given atomic masses, calculate the Q‑value (energy released) of the D‑T reaction in MeV.

Arjun, a Class 11 student in Delhi, sleeps at 12:30 AM, wakes at 6:00 AM (5.5 hrs), commutes 1 hr each way, school 7:30 AM–2:00 PM, tuition 4:00–6:00 PM. He says "I have no time to study." Using NCERT steps, redesign his day to create a 90-minute daily study block while keeping 7.5 hours sleep. Show all categorisations.
Fill in the blank: First, identify the "whole" amount (12 litres) and the fraction you are working with (______/3).

In 2024 a government‑appointed committee on higher education equity recommends that all IITs offer the first‑year core physics, mathematics and chemistry courses in Hindi and major regional languages alongside English. The report cites that 68 % of current IIT entrants come from English‑medium private schools, while only 12 % of rural‑background students achieve the JEE Advanced cut‑off. Proponents argue that vernacular instruction will democratize access to elite technical talent and reduce urban‑rural disparity. Critics warn that it may recreate a bifurcated elite—an English‑speaking global‑market cadre and a vernacular‑confined domestic cadre—mirroring the colonial “English in taste, in opinions, in morals and in intellect” class envisaged by Macaulay’s Minute (1835). The committee also references the 1857‑1905 period when English‑educated Indians led nationalist movements, suggesting that language policy continues to shape who wields power in post‑colonial India.

(D) Using the power‑sharing model from Belgium (The Belgian Accommodation Model), evaluate whether the IIT vernacular proposal accommodates linguistic diversity without threatening national unity.

At the Harappan site of Ganweriwala, archaeologists uncovered a large granary (Structure G1) with internal dimensions 15 m × 10 m × 3 m. Charred wheat grains recovered from the floor layers indicate an average storage density of 0.75 t m⁻³. Regional settlement analysis suggests that the surrounding irrigated fields covered about 120 ha, with an average wheat yield of 1.2 t ha⁻¹ based on phytolith and pollen data. Labor records inferred from seal impressions indicate that maintaining the irrigation canals required approximately 200 person‑days per season, with a daily wage equivalent to 1 silver piece (derived from ration seals). The state invested 500 silver pieces in constructing the canal network, which has an estimated useful life of 20 years and negligible salvage value. Market price for wheat, as inferred from contemporaneous Mesopotamian trade tablets, is 8 silver pieces per tonne. Using these data, answer the following.

(D) Determine the annual depreciation expense (in silver pieces) for the irrigation canal using straight‑line depreciation, given construction cost 500 silver pieces, useful life 20 years, and salvage value 0.

StellarLink, a space‑tech startup, plans to launch a constellation of low‑earth‑orbit satellites to provide global broadband. The firm’s autonomous investment (satellite launch cost) is estimated at **I = 500 bn** (in billions of currency units). The household saving function in the economy is **S = –200 + 0.25Y**, where **Y** is national income. Each satellite costs 200 bn to build and has a useful life of 10 years with zero salvage value; depreciation is charged straight‑line. At the start of the year, StellarLink’s balance sheet shows: Satellite asset 2000 bn, Cash 500 bn, Total Assets 2500 bn, Liabilities 800 bn. Equity is the balancing figure. Biologists warn that the rare‑earth elements required for satellite motors are limited to 1500 tons globally; each satellite needs 100 tons, thus capping the feasible number of satellites at 15 (maximum possible investment 1500 bn). Students must use the S=I approach, compute the multiplier, assess the impact of a change in investment, record depreciation journal entries, and evaluate how the biological resource constraint could alter the autonomous investment assumption.

(C) Determine the change in equilibrium income if autonomous investment increases by 100 bn.

A pharmaceutical team is formulating an IV drug that is a weak base (conjugate‑acid pKa ≈ 9.5). To maximise membrane permeability the drug must be >90 % unionised at physiological pH 7.4, yet remain sufficiently water‑soluble. Three candidate amines are screened: methylamine (CH₃NH₂), dimethylamine ((CH₃)₂NH) and trimethylamine ((CH₃)₃N). For each amine the team must (i) classify the nitrogen, (ii) estimate its basicity from the given pKa of its conjugate acid, (iii) calculate the fraction protonated at pH 7.4 using the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation, (iv) predict whether it gives a positive carbylamine test (indicating a primary amine), and (v) compute the osmotic pressure of a 0.10 M solution at 310 K, taking into account the degree of protonation (van’t Hoff factor).  
**Data:** pKa(CH₃NH₃⁺)=10.6, pKa((CH₃)₂NH₂⁺)=10.7, pKa((CH₃)₃NH⁺)=9.8. R=0.08314 L·bar·K⁻¹·mol⁻¹.

(A) Classify each amine (methylamine, dimethylamine, trimethylamine) as primary, secondary or tertiary and write its condensed structural formula.

A settlement in Rajasthan has a population of 9,800 (Census 2011), area 20 sq km, and 70% of male main workers in non-agricultural activities. The state government has not issued any municipal notification. Is this settlement urban or rural? If the state government notifies it as a municipality next year, how does its classification change? Explain the statistical and administrative logic.

Design a 3-question interview for a hypothetical contemporary of Vaddhegnasoh (e.g., a village woman in 1930s Braj region) that would reveal how Vaddhegnasoh's poems circulated and functioned in their original community. Each question must target a different dimension: linguistic access, thematic resonance, and social consequence. Explain why each question matters for recovering the *reception history* that the textbook only hints at.

In June 2023 the Vidarbha region of Maharashtra recorded a 42 % deficit in southwest monsoon rainfall, the lowest since 1972. Groundwater levels in 1 200 villages fell below the 10‑metre mark, forcing 15 000 households to rely on tanker water. The state launched the “Jal Jeevan Yojana”, promising potable water within 500 m of every home, but implementation lagged due to fund delays and panchayat‑level corruption. News reports showed cracked fields, emaciated cattle, and queues of women with empty pots at distant taps. A local NGO documented a rise in cases of depression and suicidal ideation among farmers who had taken loans for Bt‑cotton seeds that failed to yield.  
Premchand’s *LoaQnxqIr* (written 1935) depicts a village gripped by a similar famine: rains have failed for two consecutive years, the zamindar continues to demand full rent, the village well is dry, and children scavenge for rotting grain. The narrative interweaves vivid sensory details—blistering heat, the hiss of empty wells, the scent of parched earth—with the protagonists’ growing despair and eventual resignation.

(C) Analyze how the interaction of setting (famine‑stricken village) and atmosphere (despair) reveals the psychological state of the protagonist (e.g., Hori/Mangal) in *LoaQnxqIr*, drawing on concepts of stress and coping from psychology.

The newly independent island nation of Atlantica has a population of 2 million at the start of 2025. Vital statistics show a Crude Birth Rate (CBR) of 25 per 1 000 and a Crude Death Rate (CDR) of 8 per 1 000. The government’s skilled‑migrant incentive scheme yields a net migration rate of 15 per 1 000 (in‑migrants minus out‑migrants). Atlantica’s constitution allocates 40 % of total tax revenue to state governments for migrant‑integration programmes. Current per‑capita tax revenue is US $5 000 and is expected to grow at 2 % per annum due to higher productivity of migrants. Assuming the vital rates and net migration remain constant, answer the following.

(D) Project Atlantica’s population after 5 years assuming the annual growth rate remains constant. Use the exponential model Pₜ = P₀(1+ r)ᵗ.

A grandfather clock's pendulum (length = 0.994 m, bob mass = 2 kg) is driven by an escapement mechanism that gives a small periodic impulse each swing. The clock runs in a room where a subwoofer plays a 2 Hz tone at 80 dB. The sound wave exerts a periodic force on the pendulum bob. Given that the pendulum's damping is very light (Q ≈ 1000), will the subwoofer affect the clock's timekeeping? Justify your answer with calculations.

A *Panax ginseng* suspension culture shows the following PCV data: Day 0: 8 mL, Day 1: 9 mL, Day 2: 12 mL, Day 3: 20 mL, Day 4: 38 mL, Day 5: 52 mL, Day 6: 55 mL, Day 7: 53 mL (100 mL medium). (a) Plot log₁₀(PCV) vs time and identify phases. (b) Calculate µ during exponential phase (use Days 2–4). (c) If ginsenoside (secondary metabolite) accumulation starts at Day 4, what is the optimal harvest day for maximum *total* ginsenoside (µg/flask)? Assume specific production rate (µg/g DW/day) is constant from Day 4 onward and DW/PCV = 0.1 g/mL.

You are a town planner. A new census report shows that a rural block's population density has doubled over the past 5 years due to suburban expansion. Propose a simple three-step infrastructure development plan to address this specific demographic change.

A nutritionist in Chennai designs a diet using two cereals: Millet (₹40/kg, 10g protein, 5g iron per kg) and Rice (₹30/kg, 6g protein, 8g iron per kg). Minimum daily requirements: 60g protein, 40g iron. Find the minimum cost diet. Formulate as LPP and identify the type.

In late 2025, intelligence indicates PLA preparations for a limited coercive operation against Taiwan, including cyber‑infiltration of Taiwanese power‑grid SCADA systems and electronic warfare jamming of Taiwanese radar networks. The US NSC evaluates a calibrated hard‑power cyber response: (i) deploying USCYBERCOM’s “Hunt Forward” teams to pre‑position malware strains targeting PLA missile‑command servers; (ii) activating the National Security Agency’s (NSA) “Quantum‑Ready” decryption suite to break PLA encrypted communications in real time; (iii) leveraging the US Cyber Command’s persistent engagement framework to conduct low‑level, continuous cyber‑pressure on PLA logistics networks; (iv) readying a joint cyber‑electronic‑warfare (CEW) cell to synchronize cyber attacks with EA‑18G Growler electronic‑attack aircraft for combined spectrum dominance; and (v) preparing a cyber‑reserve force of 5,000 trained militia‑style cyber volunteers for rapid surge capacity if escalation occurs.  

Relevant data:  
- USCYBERCOM FY‑2024 budget: **US$ 12 billion**.  
- NSA “Quantum‑Ready” suite development cost: **US$ 1.8 billion** (one‑time).  
- Average Hunt Forward team size: **6** personnel; 12 teams deployed globally.  
- Persistent engagement cyber‑ops daily volume: **≈ 2 TB** of data exfiltrated or altered.  
- EA‑18G Growler fleet size: **160** aircraft.  
- Cyber‑reserve volunteer pool: **5,000** individuals (average 20 hrs/month training).  
- PLA cyber‑defence budget (estimated): **US$ 4 billion**.  
- Historical benchmark: Estonian 2007 cyber‑attack response highlighted NATO’s collective cyber defence (Article 5).  

Students must identify cyber‑hard‑power tools, evaluate their strategic effect, calculate force‑like ratios, and consider constraints.

(A) From the scenario, list **three** concrete hard‑power indicators that demonstrate US cyber dominance and explain why each qualifies as hard power (not soft or structural).

India’s services exports rose from ₹12,00,000 crore in FY 2020‑21 to ₹15,00,000 crore in FY 2022‑23, driven mainly by IT‑software (₹9,00,000 → ₹11,50,000 cr) and business‑process outsourcing (₹2,00,000 → ₹2,50,000 cr). Travel services, hit hard by COVID, recovered partially from ₹30,000 cr to ₹80,000 cr. Simultaneously, cross‑border data flows increased, prompting the government to draft a Data Localisation Bill requiring certain categories of personal and financial data to be stored domestically. The bill has sparked debate at the WTO’s e‑commerce work programme, where members argue that localisation measures may violate the General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS) national‑treatment commitment. Using the data on services exports, the direction of IT exports (USA share fell from 55 % to 48 %, while ASEAN share rose from 12 % to 18 %), and the proposed localisation rule, evaluate the quantitative growth, shifting geography, and potential trade‑policy conflict.

(A) Calculate the compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of India's total services exports from FY 2020‑21 to FY 2022‑23.

A pulsed laser beam (central wavelength λ=1064 nm) propagates through a silica fiber exhibiting Kerr nonlinearity. The nonlinear phase shift φ induced on the pulse is given by φ = (2π/λ)·n₂·I·L_eff, where n₂ is the nonlinear index coefficient, I is the instantaneous intensity, and L_eff is the effective length. In a particular regime, the effective length depends on the intensity via L_eff = L₀·sin⁻¹[α·√(I/I_sat)], with L₀=10 m, α=0.8, and I_sat=1 GW cm⁻² the saturation intensity. The pulse intensity varies temporally as I(t)=I_p·exp(−t²/τ²) with peak intensity I_p=5 GW cm⁻² and pulse width τ=2 ps.  
The group delay experienced by the pulse is Δt_g = dφ/dω, where ω=2πc/λ. Using the chain rule and the derivative of sin⁻¹, derive an expression for Δt_g(t) in terms of I(t), its derivative dI/dt, and the given constants. Then compute the peak group delay (maximum magnitude) occurring at t=0. (Physics: wave optics & group velocity; Chemistry: nonlinear polarizability linked to molecular hyperpolarizability.)

(C) Obtain the group delay Δt_g = dφ/dω. Show that Δt_g = (λ²/(2πc))·dφ/dt.

An analyst is reviewing two companies, Alpha Ltd. and Beta Ltd., for a potential investment. Alpha's Revenue grew from ₹50 Cr to ₹75 Cr over 3 years (CAGR 14.5%), while Beta's grew from ₹200 Cr to ₹250 Cr (CAGR 7.7%). Alpha's Employee Expense as % of Revenue went from 12% to 15%; Beta's went from 18% to 16%. 
(a) Which analysis (Horizontal/Vertical) supports the statement "Alpha is growing faster"? 
(b) Which analysis supports "Beta is becoming more efficient in labour cost management"? 
(c) If you could only use ONE analysis to decide which company is a better investment, which would you choose and why?

In 2026, the Ministry of Finance proposes a Digital Services Tax (DST) of 6 % on gross revenue earned by Indian creators of AI‑generated video, music, and text content hosted on global platforms. The tax is justified as compensation for the use of Indian data (user behaviour, language corpora) that trains the AI models. Proponents argue it mirrors historical state claims on surplus, akin to Bernier’s observation that Mughal appropriation of artisans’ profits removed incentives for quality refinement. Opponents contend that, unlike Mughal camp towns where the state was the sole patron, today’s creators earn from a global audience, and the DST risks driving talent abroad or reducing investment in high‑quality AI‑tool development, thereby creating a digital “camp town” dependent on state handouts rather than market‑driven innovation. A parliamentary committee requests an analysis using Bernier’s framework, principles of intellectual property rights (Political Science), and the spatial distribution of digital infrastructure (Geography) to assess whether the DST will stifle or stimulate the AI‑content sector.

(A) According to Bernier’s critique of property rights (c12_hist_cbse_05_010), what specific form of state appropriation did he identify as undermining incentives for producers?

In January 2025, Tata Steel Ltd. acquired a controlling stake (70%) in RuhrStahl AG, a German specialty steel producer, for EUR 4.2 bn. The deal was financed through:  
- EUR 2.0 bn raised via syndicated euro‑denominated term loan at 3.2% p.a. (interest exempt under India‑Germany DTAA).  
- EUR 1.0 bn from internal accruals (₹88,000 cr at ₹88/EUR).  
- EUR 0.6 bn via issue of redeemable preference shares (RPS) to Tata Sons, carrying a cumulative dividend of 5.5% p.a. (payable in EUR).  
- EUR 0.6 bn via fresh equity infusion through a qualified institutional placement (QIP) at a premium of 40% to book value.  
Post‑acquisition, Tata Steel’s consolidated FY 2024‑25 (pro‑forma) figures are:  
- PAT (after tax) = ₹10,500 cr (including RuhrStahl’s contribution).  
- CFO = ₹13,200 cr.  
- Debt‑equity ratio = 0.55 (post‑loan).  
- Effective tax rate = 18% (RuhrStahl profits taxed in India at 20% after treaty relief).  
- The euro loan agreement contains a covenant limiting dividend payout to 20% of PAT until the loan is 40% repaid (scheduled FY 2026‑27).  
- Shareholder profile: 45% domestic institutional investors (prefer stable, growing dividends), 35% foreign institutional investors (FIIs) (favor total return), 20% retail (mixed).  
- Tata Steel’s historical dividend payout ratio has been 18%–22%.  
- Inflation projected at 5% p.a.; the company expects real EBITDA growth of 6% p.a. from RuhrStahl’s high‑margin product mix.  
Using the 11 factors affecting dividend decision, determine an appropriate dividend payout ratio for FY 2024‑25 and justify it, expressing the dividend as rupees per share (face value ₹10).

(A) Compute the maximum dividend allowed by the euro‑loan covenant for FY 2024‑25 in rupees.

A sick PSU in the fertilizer sector (non-strategic) has accumulated losses of ₹3,000 crore and negative net worth. The administrative ministry proposes a revival package of ₹1,500 crore. As a BIFR member, apply the post-1991 policy criteria to decide: revive, close, or disinvest? Justify.
Explain why "proportion" is a critical principle when arranging furniture in a small room (e.g., 3 m × 3 m).

FinStart Ltd. launches a blockchain‑based platform to tokenize commercial real estate worth ₹2000 crore. Each security token represents ₹10,000 of property value (treated as a debenture). The platform also offers futures contracts on the token price (contract size = 100 tokens). To ensure compliance, FinStart applies for SEBI sandbox approval for a pilot of 100 tokens. Tokens are held in a depository (dematerialised). Accounting: tokens are classified as financial assets at fair value through profit and loss (FVTPL). The platform raises working capital by issuing 91‑day Treasury Bills of ₹200 crore at a discount rate of 4% p.a. The RBI has recently cut the repo rate by 25 bps, influencing money‑market yields. Assume each token transaction (buy + sell) generates ₹500 of additional economic activity (multiplier effect).

(B) Compute the proceeds (in ₹) FinStart receives from issuing 91‑day Treasury Bills of face value ₹200 crore at a discount rate of 4% p.a.

A researcher is studying the influence of Hollywood on Indian cinema in the 1950s using Asokamitran’s excerpt from *My Years with Boss*. The passage describes Gemini Studios (established 1940), its make‑up department housed in a building believed to have been Robert Clive’s stables, the brand “Pancake” make‑up bought in truck‑loads, and the narrator’s duty of filing newspaper clippings. The researcher must answer literal questions about the text, infer the meaning of idiomatic expressions (e.g., “blew over”, “struck dumb”), connect the studio’s functioning to post‑Independence cultural policies, and evaluate implications for freedom of expression and state censorship (Political Science node ). The task requires distinguishing literal from inferential questions, locating textual evidence, and constructing PEEL‑style responses that incorporate historical and political‑science insights.

(A) In which year was Gemini Studios set up according to the excerpt?

In 2022 the eastern districts of Rajasthan recorded a 38 % deficit in southwest monsoon rainfall compared to the 50‑year average, causing a sharp decline in bajra and moong yields. Field surveys of 200 households revealed that 62 % of Dalit families reported a shift from traditional agricultural wage labour to MGNREGA‑based unskilled work, while 48 % of upper‑caste families continued to cultivate cash crops using bore‑well irrigation. A Hindi essay in the Antra chapter describes the “धूल में भीगती हथेली, जो कभी जोत की खुशबू को पहचानती थी” (palette drenched in dust that once recognised the scent of the plough) to convey the quiet dignity of rural labour despite changing livelihoods. Using this scenario, answer the following sub‑parts.
